# 2 Peter

## 1:1 Introduction
[Johann Gerhard, Commentarius super Posteriorem D. Petri Epistolam (Jena, 1660). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
PROLEGOMENA.

The principal efficient cause of this Epistle is the Holy Spirit, who, as He was poured out upon the other Apostles, so also upon Peter on the day of Pentecost Acts 2. v. 3., impelled him, so that he would not only preach the Gospel with living voice, but would also embrace the sum of Evangelical doctrine in writings, to which this Epistle also pertains. Therefore, what Peter says in this very Epistle chap. 1. v. 21. concerning holy men of GOD, that they ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερομένους spoke, (which itself is also clearly to be understood concerning their sacred & Canonical writings from 2. Tim. 3. v. 16., where sacred Scripture is called θεόπνευστος), the same we both can and ought to pronounce concerning the Apostle Peter. The Apostles, by reason of their office, were God's Ambassadors 2. Cor. 5. v. 20.. In whatever manner, therefore, whether by preaching or by writing, they set forth the will of God, they are to be judged to have done it in the name, by the command, & by the authority of the One sending. Iren. lib. 3, adv. haeres. cap. 1. p. 169. We have known the disposition of our salvation through no others than those through whom the Gospel came to us, which indeed they then proclaimed; but afterwards by the will of GOD in the scriptures they handed down to us, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith.

JOHANN GERHARD'S ENARRATION ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PETER.

The ministerial cause, or secondary author is Peter, Apostle of CHRIST, as is evident. 1. from ἐπιγραφῇ or inscription. Πέτρου τοῦ Ἀποστόλου ἐπιστολὴ καθολικὴ δευτέρα. 2. from the inspection of the Epistle itself. For in it the Author thereof in express words calls himself Simeon Peter, a servant and Apostle of JESUS Christchap. 1. v. 2. (he not only places the name Peter imposed upon him by Christ, as he had done in the former Epistle, but also adds the ancient name Simeon, so that he may exclude every occasion of doubting) he testifies that he had been an Eyewitness of the transfiguration of Christ on the mount of the same chapter v. 16. (now indeed Peter, together with James and John, out of the whole number of the Apostles was present at it. Therefore this Epistle is either James's, or John's, or Peter's, unless we wish to say that an intolerable error is contained in it. However, it is certain that neither James, who had long since died when this Epistle was written; nor John, to whom no one ever attributed it, is the author of this Epistle. It remains, therefore, that it is Peter's) he makes mention furthermore of his former Epistlechap. 3. v. 1. he enumerates himself among the Apostles of the same chapter v. 2. he calls Paul his brother ἀγαπητὸν of the same chapter v. 15. (Compare Gal. 2. v. 9.) Some add also this argument, that Peter in chapter 1 of this Epistle v. 14. says, that the putting off of his tabernacle had been manifested to him by Christ, by which words he thinks regard is had to John 21. v. 27. but we shall show below that it is to be understood concerning a certain peculiar manifestation, which is not contained in the scriptures. 3. from the testimony of the primitive Church. By the name of Peter this Epistle is placed in the Canon by the Council of Laodicea can. 59. by the third Council of Carthage can. 47. by Athanasius in the Synopsis, by Epiphanius in heresy 76. by Jerome to Paulinus, and Augustine in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 8 Gregory in homily 18 on Ezekiel; Damascene in book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 18; Amphilochius in his Iambics to Seleucus; Nazianzen in his poem on the Scriptures; Rufinus of Aquileia in his exposition of the Creeds; Innocent I in his 3rd Epistle to Exuperius; Isidore in book 6 of the Etymologies, chapters 1 and 2, testify in express words that it is the Epistle of Peter. Bede, in the preface to his commentary on this Epistle, wonders by what reason it could have been doubted concerning the author of this Epistle, since it expresses his name, and he testifies that he was on the mount with the Lord. Clement and Didymus, both of Alexandria, wrote commentaries on this Epistle, fragments of which still exist today in the Scholia of Oecumenius.

(To these witnesses Sixtus of Siena in book 7 of the Bibliotheca Sancta, heresy 9, adds Anacletus in Epistle 3; Jodocus Coccius in volume 1 of the Thesaurus, book 6, article 24, Cornelius in Epistle 2; Baronius in the year 68, number 4, Hippolytus on the Antichrist, and the Roman Council under Damasus; Salmero in Disputation 1 on this Epistle; the Council of Trent; Bellarmine in book 1 of the Word of God, chapter 8, Hyginus in Epistle 1, and the Council of Florence. But the authority of all of them is doubtful and suspect.)

Against these arguments: 1. The diversity of style from the former Epistle is urged. Jerome in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men, under Peter: The second Epistle of Peter is denied by many to be his on account of the dissonance of style. Erasmus in his annotations to this Epistle: The difference of style, both in the thoughts and in the words, is too clear to be concealed. Response 1. Jerome concedes the diversity of style, but denies that it can be inferred from it that this Epistle is not Peter's. He thinks, however, that that diversity of style took its origin from the diversity of interpreters whom Peter used in writing both Epistles, for thus he writes in Epistle 150 to Hedibia, question 11: Blessed Paul had Titus as an interpreter, just as also Blessed

Peter [instructed] Mark, whose Gospel was composed with Peter narrating and him writing. Finally, the two Epistles which are attributed to Peter differ from one another in style and character, and in the structure of their words. From this we understand that, according to the necessity of the matters, he used different interpreters. Clement of Alexandria, in the 7th book of the Stromata, mentions that not only Mark performed this office of interpreter for Peter, but also a certain Glaucias, whom Basilides falsely boasted was his master. (Baronius, in the year 45, no. 32 and following, treats at length of the office of these interpreters, whose labor the Apostles used, which we shall examine a little later.) 2. Even if a certain diversity of style were to occur here, it could not yet be inferred from it that this Epistle was not written by Peter, since the same diversity of style occurs in the Pauline Epistles. Indeed, a diversity of subject matter is accustomed to bring with it a certain diversity of style, and furthermore, different objects of persons and other circumstances vary the style. 3. It is rightly objected to Erasmus that, in order to prove that the commentary of Arnobius on the Psalms is rightly attributed to him, although he uses a different style in his books against the Gentiles, he warns that the holy writers used a double style, one humble and familiar, the other more polished and more exact. 4. But the hypothesis of the argument is most rightly denied, for a mutual comparison refutes the opinion concerning the diversity of style. The authors of the Magdeburg Centuries, Century 1, book 2, chapter 4, column 54, [say]: The style and composition do not differ much from the former Epistle of Peter. In both, certainly, there occurs an artificial brevity joined with the highest majesty. 2. Gregory, in homily 18 on Ezekiel, makes mention of certain ones who indeed conceded that this Epistle is Peter's, but denied that it is the Epistle of Peter the Apostle, attributing it to some other Cephas or Peter, to whom Paul writes that he resisted him to his face Gal. 2. v. 11. But the opinion of those is [refuted] by all those arguments which just now have been brought forward, is refuted, and in its own place it is demonstrated that that Cephas, of whom mention is made Gal. 2. v. 9., was Peter the Apostle, whence Gregory in the said place rightly writes. If they had wished to weigh the words of the same Epistle, they could have weighed them far otherwise. For in it is written: A voice was borne to him from the magnificent glory: This is my beloved son, and it is added: And this voice we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount. Let them therefore read the Gospel and they immediately recognize that when that voice came from heaven, Peter the Apostle stood with the Lord. He therefore wrote this Epistle, who heard this voice on the mount concerning the Lord. 3. The canonical authority of this Epistle. Concerning it, it seems to have been doubted by some in the primitive Church. Eusebius, book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 3, in the beginning: One Epistle of Peter, which is called the former, is received without controversy. This the ancient Presbyters also formerly used in their writings without any hesitation. But that which is called the latter, οὐκ ἐνδιάθηκον εἶναι, we have received not to be legitimate or Testamentary. And yet because it seems useful to many, it has been used with other scriptures. And afterwards: Concerning those things which are attributed to Peter, from which I have known only one genuine Epistle of his to be held in confession among the ancient Presbyters, let this much have been said. In the same book, chapter 22, after he had enumerated the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament, namely the writings of the four Evangelists, the Acts of the Apostles, the fourteen Epistles of Paul, the former of John, the former of Peter, and the Apocalypse, he adds: And these writings indeed are held as indubitable. But those which are contradicted, although they are known to many, are these: the Epistle which is attributed to James, and the Epistle of Jude, and the latter of Peter, and the second with the third of John. Book 6, chapter 24, from Origen's commentary on Matthew, he brings forward these things: Peter left behind him one Epistle, concerning which it is certainly established. But suppose he left also a second, for concerning that it is disputed. Didymus The preceptor of Alexander Jerome concludes his little commentary on this Epistle thus. It is not therefore to be ignored, that the present Epistle is falsified, which although it is published, (that is, publicly read through the Churches) it is not however in the canon. To these testimonies is added, that in the Syriac version it is omitted.

The Papists oppose to these arguments the authority of the Church i. e. of the Council of Trent, (for its voice is the voice of the Catholic Church writes Bellarm. lib. 5. de grat & lib. arbitr. cap. 13.) Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epist. It is not permitted now any longer to doubt concerning this Epistle, since by the sentence of the Church (in the Council of Florence and Trent) it is declared as Peter's own. But this response is insufficient, thus therefore we proceed.

1. We have already shown before, that the Apostle Peter is the author of this Epistle.

2. The Spirit in it is Apostolic.

3. Nothing is held in it, which is opposed to the remaining Canonical books even in the slightest.

4. No cause sufficiently grave can be brought forward, why we ought to doubt concerning the authority of this Epistle.

5. It is referred among the Canonical writings by the principal Doctors of the primitive Church. Origen and Jerome in very many places bring forward testimonies from this Epistle as if from sacred and Canonical Scripture. Whence also B. Luther in the Preface to the Epistle to the Hebrews reckons it among the Canonical books. (Truly Sixtus Senensis lib. 7. Bibl. haeres. 9. attributes to Luther, that he called this Second Epistle of Peter into doubt, but Bellarmine absolves him from this ἐγκλήματι lib. 1. de verb. DEI cap. 18. §. where he says, Luther places this Epistle among the Canonical Scriptures. The same is acknowledged by Lorinus in the comm. of this Epistle cap. 1. v. 10.)

Moved therefore by these reasons, we establish this Epistle as Apostolic and Canonical, and 1, we respond to the testimonies of the Ancients just now brought forward.

1. That there was doubt not so much concerning the Canonical authority of this Epistle, as concerning the secondary author.

2. That it was never rejected among the Apocryphal writings; nor was it doubted by all, but only by some.

3. That by far more received it as Canonical. Meanwhile, on account of this doubt of some of the Ancients concerning it, we refer it among the Canonical books of the second order, which some call ἀντιλεγομένους ὑπὸ τινῶν, and distinguish the same from ἀντιλεγομένοις ὑπὸ πάντων.

2. That this Epistle is not contained in the Syriac version, to that we respond.

1. That proves only this, that this Epistle was not formerly received by all.

2. Ephrem and Damascenus the Syrians bring forward testimonies from this Epistle in their writings, as from a genuine part of Holy Scripture. See Damasc. lib. 4. orthod. fid. cap. 18.

3. Edward Pococke the Englishman published the Syriac version of this Epistle, together with the second and third of John, as also the Epistle of Jude, taken from a manuscript copy of the Bodleian Library of Oxford, at Leiden in the year 630; in the preface of which he mentions, that these Epistles were found in the aforementioned Library, together with the Acts of the Apostles and the other Catholic Epistles, arranged in the order in which they are accustomed to be held in Greek Codices. In the same place, however, he adds, that a certain Dionysius, who illustrated with Syriac Commentaries the Second of Peter, the second and third of John, and the Epistle of Jude, together with the other Canonical Epistles and the Acts of the Apostles and also the Apocalypse, in in the preface to the later Epistle of Peter he warns that it was not translated into the Syriac language with the books which were rendered in ancient days, and therefore it is not found except in the translation of Thomas the Bishop, who was surnamed Heracleensis according to the name of his city, Heraclea. But who this Thomas was, or what his version is like, is not known.

3. To the complaint of Didymus concerning the corruption of this Epistle, I respond. Didymus gathers this wrongly from those things which are held at the end of the Epistle concerning the renovation of the world, where he thinks Platonic revolutions are taught, from which Peter's doctrine differs by the whole, as it is usually said, heaven. Whence, not without reason, some suspect that those words were inserted into the book of Didymus by another, since he neither shows in what way this Epistle was falsified; nor is it likely that so great a man would have wished to publish Commentaries on an Apocryphal Epistle.

4. Objection. Peter Aureolus in Comp. Script. maintains that this later Epistle of Peter was written to the Romans, moved by the argument that in chapter 3 of the same, verse 5, Peter seems to speak of Paul's Epistle to the Romans. But that hypothesis is false, as will be demonstrated in the exposition of that place. This Epistle is inscribed to the same people as the former, to the Jews, namely, those converted to Christ, dispersed through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, 1. Petr. 1. v. 1. as is gathered from cap. 3. v. 1. This, behold beloved, I write to you as a second Epistle. Peter was constituted the Apostle of those people in particular by Apostolic agreement Gal. 2. v. 9. The same can be gathered from cap. 1. v. 19. We have a more firm Prophetic word. For the Prophetic word was made to the Jews, not to the Gentiles. To them were entrusted the oracles of God Rom. 3. v. 2. they had Moses and the Prophets, Luc. 16. v. 29. theirs were αἱ διαθήκαι Rom. 9. v. 4. They also attended to the Prophetic Scriptures, as to a lamp, daily searching them, whether those things which were preached by the Apostles were conformable to them.Act. 17. v. 12. To this can be referred that which Peter in cap. 3. huius Epistolae v. 15. makes mention of an Epistle written to the Hebrews, and testifies that this Epistle also is written by him to the same. Therefore this later Epistle of Peter was written to the Israelites converted from Judaism to Christ. Although indeed it was written principally to converted Jews, yet less principally it was also written to those converted from the Gentiles, as we made manifest in the narration of the prior Epistle.

5. Time of writing. The Apostle wrote this Epistle a little before his death, as is gathered from cap. 1. v. 14. Therefore he utters a swan song in it, and it breathes entirely the ardor of the Spirit, the love of Christ, the zeal of piety, Martyrdom, and heavenly things. According to the computation of Baronius, it was written in the Year of Christ 63, when the prior had been written in the Year of Christ 45, and thus twenty-three years before this later one.

6. Place of writing. Although Peter in this Epistle does not express in explicit words from what place it was sent, as he had said in the prior that it was sent from Babylon, yet it can be verisimilarly established that, as it was written to the same people to whom the prior was, so also it was sent from the same place, namely from Babylon. Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epist. tom. 16. p. 112, when he has persuaded himself that by Babylon, 1. Petr. 5. v. 13., Rome is to be understood, he attempts to prove that this later Epistle of Peter was also written at Rome. He brings forward, however, two arguments for his opinion. The first he takes from the time of writing, because Peter wrote this Epistle a little before his death. Now indeed a certain tradition of the Church holds that he himself was finished at Rome under Nero. Resp. Let us grant indeed that Peter died at Rome, concerning which matter D. Chemnicius writes thus in Harm. cap. 50. p. 277. That Peter was at Rome, all historians agree: but at what time he came to Rome, the annotations are most disturbed. That seems to agree most simply with the History of the Acts, which Origen in his Tome on Genesis. 3. & Nicephorus note, that Peter came to Rome around the end of his life in the last years of Nero: the rest add, that he was affixed to a cross there with his head lowered and his feet inverted: but from that it cannot yet be firmly gathered that this Epistle was written at Rome, since it is not yet established at what time Peter came to Rome. Salmero takes the latter argument from the fact that mention is made of the Epistles of Paul in this Petrine one cap. 3. v. 15. & 16. Peter, he says, writes about Paul & his Epistles, which, while he was at Rome, he could have read and seen, and therefore he commended them to the faithful with such a testimony, which certainly is not as probable to have happened elsewhere as in the city. For a bundle of the letters of Paul, which he had written to the Galatians and Achaeans, was being carried around, so that Seneca, the tutor of the Emperor, could have read them, even to the Prince Nero himself, as Seneca himself testifies in a certain letter of his to Nero.

I reply. 1. Peter could have read the Epistles of Paul just as well at Babylon as at Rome, since they were known to all the Churches, and thus also to the Pontics, to whom Peter writes. 2. Many of the Papists acknowledge that Peter cap. 3. v. 15. of this Epistle speaks specifically about the Epistle to the Hebrews. But it is far more likely that Peter, dwelling at Babylon among those converted from Judaism, saw and read that Epistle to the Hebrews, than at Rome among those converted from Gentilism. 3. Salmero truly labors under a notable ἀκρισίᾳ when he cites the Epistles of Paul to Seneca, and of Seneca to Paul, as witnesses for his opinion. Let him hear the judgment of Baronius concerning them in the year 66, number 11. The Epistle of Seneca to Paul concerning the Neronian fire seems to me in my opinion to have been forged by someone else rather than written by Seneca, since such open lies are asserted in it. For which reason also those remaining ones, both those written to Paul, and those returned by Paul to him, are rendered equally suspect to us, although we know that they were not recently devised, but written in antiquity, and recognized and approved by Jerome in De script. Eccles. regarding Seneca. n. 12. Augustine also knows them, who mentions the same in Epist. 14, although the same Augustine, lib. 6. de Civ. DEI cap. 11, seems to have attributed no faith at all to the said Epistles. We know indeed that Sixtus Senensis, lib. 2. Bibl. sanctae p. 89, proves the authority of these Epistles from the book of Linus on the passion of Paul. But this is to prove the uncertain by the equally uncertain.

7. The idiom of the Epistles. Baronius, Anno 45. n. 28, discourses thus. Jerome seems to affirm that the first Epistle of Peter was translated from Hebrew by Mark the Evangelist, Epist. 150. to Hedibia q. 11. while, after he treated of the Gospel written by Mark, but received from Peter, he says these things: Finally, also the two Epistles which are attributed to Peter differ from one another in style and character, and in the structure of the words, from which we understand that he used different Interpreters according to the necessity of the matters. n. 37. The Epistles of Peter, translated from Hebrew into another language by different Interpreters, are scattered throughout the Church.

Resp. 1. No one among the Ancients affirms that the Epistles of Peter were written in the Hebrew idiom. 2. Hence Bellarmine, lib. 2. de verbo DEI cap. 7. §. 2, writes thus: It is certain that the New Testament was written in Greek by those Apostles or Evangelists whose names are prefixed to the titles of the individual books or Epistles, with the exception only of the Gospel of Matthew and Mark and the Epistle to the Hebrews. And afterwards §. 4. The entire Greek edition of the N. T. has the Apostles and Evangelists as authors. Nor can the contrary be apodictically gathered from the words of Jerome. For the same Baronius, Ann. 45. n. 37, teaches that the office of the Apostolic Interpreters was something else, For a double, he says, reason did Interpreters serve the Apostles, either when to some nation while they themselves were speaking, for instance the Romans, there were others in the audience who were completely ignorant of the Latin speech which the Apostles were speaking to them, for then the office of an Interpreter seemed to be required; or when the same Apostles had spoken things difficult to grasp, then it was the interpreter's task to explain the same. 4. By Interpreter in the words of Jerome, Estius in the prolegomena of this 2nd Epistle of Peter understands Scribe. 5. Whatever the case may be, even if Marcus had translated either one of these Epistles from the Hebrew into the Greek language, nevertheless Peter saw and approved the Greek text, so that consequently that alone is deservedly judged to be authentic.

8. Argument of the Epistle. The Apostle himself explains that in the same cap. 1. v. 12. Wherefore I will not neglect to remind you of these things (which make for constancy in faith and the pursuit of piety) always, ὑπομιμνήσκειν, though you know and are established in the present truth. v. 13. I think it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσει to stir you up by putting you in remembrance. v. 15. Moreover I will endeavor that you may be able after my decease τούτων μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι to have these things in remembrance. cap. 3. v. 1. This second Epistle, beloved, I now write unto you, ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διακονίαν, in which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance. v. 2. μνησθῆναι That you may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy Prophets, and of the commandment of us, the Apostles of the Lord and Savior. From all of which it is gathered that the argument and Scope of the Epistle is. 1. Ὑπόμνησις, by which he wished to recall to their memory those things which he had preached to them by living voice. 2. Διέγερσις, by which he wished to excite them to constancy in faith and the pursuit of piety. Athanasius in the Synopsis of Scripture under the title concerning the third Catholic Epistle. This Epistle is ὑπόμνησις. For when he had known that his departure would be soon the dissolution of his body, he did this diligently, so that all might be admonished of those things concerning which they had previously been instructed through the doctrine of the Gospel. D. Chemnicius in Exam. Conc. Trident. part. 1. de Epist. Apost. p. 66. accurately weighs the word ὑπομιμνήσκειν cap. 1. v. 12. and the phrase ἐκάστοτε ἔχειν ὑμᾶς μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι v. 15. from which he gathers, that Peter recounts two causes of his writing in very illustrious words. 1. That when they were destitute of the living voice of the Apostles, they might nevertheless always, everywhere, and individually have and preserve the memory of the pure doctrine handed down by the Apostles. 2. That they might be fortified against false teachers.cap. 2. v. 1.whose corruptions he calls fictitious speeches, which, to wit, they will feign to have been handed down and received from the Apostles2. Thess. 2. v. 1.

From this argument of the Epistle and from mutual comparison it can be understood that a great kinship exists between this later Petrine Epistle and the Epistle of Jude, which someone might not undeservedly call a compendium of this Petrine one, since it depicts false teachers with almost the same colors with which Peter describes them. Nay, the Epistle of Jude seems to be interwoven with the same words, sentiments, and even words at times, and indeed Iudas v. 17. expressly appeals to it.

9. Disposition. There are two parts of the Epistle. 1. Νουθεσία, exhortation to constancy and progress in faith and the study of piety. 2. Προφητεία prediction, both concerning false Prophets and seducers; and concerning mockers and scoffers, denying the last coming of Christ; from which prophecy is deduced an admonition, that they ought to beware of the former with the greatest zeal, and from the latter indeed to separate themselves, and to prepare themselves for the last coming of Christ by a holy conversation of life. To both parts 1. is prefixed an Exordium, consisting in the inscription and salutation: 2. Is subjoined an Exodium, consisting both of a brief repetition of the exhortation to the study of persisting and progressing in faith; and Δοξολογίᾳ.

B. Luther, in the preface prefixed to this Epistle in his German version, brings forward this οἰκονομίαν. In the first chapter the Apostle shows the state of the Church, near the times of the Apostles, when the Gospel was still preached purely and sincerely. In the second he shows the state of the Church in the times of the dominating Papacy and with human doctrines reigning. In the third he shows the state of the Church after the Antichrist has been revealed, how, namely, men having lapsed into Epicureanism, and being about to hold both the law and the Gospel in contempt, and to believe nothing at all, which, alas, we see obtaining today.

10. Connection with the prior Epistle. Hugo and Dionysius the Carthusian warn, that just as Peter in the prior Epistle fortified the Church against Tyrants, by discoursing on patience in persecutions: so in this latter one he fortifies the same against heretics, whose character and qualities he graphically depicts. The primitive, says Dionysius, Church was attacked by Tyrants with the material sword, and by diverse persecutions, but by heretics with pestiferous doctrines. Just as therefore in the first Epistle the most excellent vertex of the Apostolic choir exhorted the faithful to patience in adversities, lest they should yield to persecutions: so in this second Epistle he exhorts them, lest they be deceived by the figments of heretics. In both he exhorts them to constancy in the truth of the faith and the holiness of life. John Huss in comm. 2. Petr. 1. In the prior Epistle Peter induced those to whom he writes to remain in the goodness of grace, lest they should succumb through the adversities of tribulations. In this latter one he induces them to persevere in the truth of Christian grace, lest they be perverted through the false doctrine of heretics and pseudo-Apostles.

CHAPTER I.

Summary of the chapter. The preface having been set forth, the Apostle exhorts those to whom he writes to constancy and progress in faith and the pursuit of piety.

Disposition. There are two parts of the chapter. 1. Προοίμιον 2. Νουθεσία.

The preface contains. 1. The inscription. 2. The salutation.

The inscription expresses. 1. The ministerial cause, or the secondary author of this Epistle. 2. The object, namely, those to whom this Epistle is written.

The author of the Epistle is described. 1. By name, and that a double one. 2. By office. The object is described by the state of grace, into which those to whom this Epistle is written were translated. v. 1.

The salutation comprises a wish, by which 1. the Apostle prays for an increase of grace and peace for those to whom he writes. 2. he expresses the means of that increase, which is the knowledge of Christ. v. 2.

Νουθεσία is completed in four members. 1. By a commemoration of the benefits already received before, by which those to whom he writes ought to be animated and excited, so that they may apply themselves with the greatest zeal to that to which he exhorts them v. 3. & 4.

2. By an exhortation to the study of progressing in faith and Christian virtues, from v. 5. up to v. 12.

3. By an exposition of the causes, for which he so solicitously reminds them of this study of progressing, from v. 12. up to 16.

4. By an exhortation to constancy in faith, and in the confession of the doctrine delivered to them, from v. 16. up to the end of the chapter.

Latin:

PROLEGOMENA.

Causa efficiens principalis huius Epistolae est Spiritus Sanctus, qui ut in Apostolos reliquos, ita quoque super Petrum in die Pentecostes effusus Actor. 2. v. 3. ipsum impulit, ut non solùm vivâ voce Evangelium praedicaret, sed etiam summam doctrinae Evangelicae Scriptis complecteretur, ad quae etiam haec Epistola pertinet. Quod ergo de sanctis DEI hominibus in hac ipsa Epistola 2. Petrus dicit cap. 1. v. 21. illos ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερομένουςesse locutos, (quod ipsum de sacris & Canonicis illorum scriptis etiam intelligendum esse patet ex. 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. ubi Scriptura sacra vocatur θεόπνευστος) idem quoque de Apostolo Petro pronunciare & possumus & debemus. Apostoli ratione officii sui fuêre Dei Legati2. Cor. 5. v. 20. Quocunque igitur modo, sive praedicatione, sive scriptione voluntatem Dei exposuerunt, Legantis nomine, mandato & autoritate id fecisse iudicandi sunt. Iren. lib. 3, adv. haeres. cap. 1. p. 169. Non per alios dispositionem salutis nostrae cognovimus, quàm per eos, per quos Evangelium pervenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc praeconiaverunt; postea verò per DEI voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum & columnam fidei nostrae futurum.

IOHANNIS GERHARDI ENARRATIO IN POSTERIOREM EPISTOLAM PETRI.

Causa ministerialis, sive autor secundarius est Petrus CHRISTI Apostolus, ut constat. 1. ex ἐπιγραφῇ sive inscriptione.Πέτρου τοῦ Ἀποστόλου ἐπιστολὴ καθολικὴ δευτέρα. 2. ex ipsius Epistolae inspectione. In ea enim Autor illius disertis verbis sese appellat Simeona Petrum, servum & Apostolum IESU Christicap. 1. v. 2. (non tantùm ponit nomen Petri â Christo sibi impositum, ut in priore Epistolâ fecerat, sed etiam addit antiquum nomen Simeonis, ut omnem dubitandi occasionem excludat) testatur, se fuisse Spectatorem transfigurationis Christi in monte cap. eiusd. v. 16. (iam verò Petrus unà cum Iacobo & Iohanne ex omni Apostolorum numero illi interfuit. Ergo haec Epistola aut est Iacobi, aut Iohannis, aut Petri, nisi velimus dicere, intolerabilem errorem in ea contineri. Constat autem non Iacobum, qui iamdum mortuus fuit, cùm haec Epistola scriberetur; nec Iohannem, cui nullus unquam eam tribuit, esse huius Epistolae autorem. Relinquitur igitur, quod sit Petri) mentionem insuper facit prioris suae Epistolaecap. 3. v. 1. annumerat seipsum Apostolis cap. eiusdem v. 2. Paulum vocat fratrem suumἀγαπητὸν cap. eiusdem. v. 15. (Confer. Gal. 2. v. 9.) Quidam addunt etiam hoc argumentum, quod Petrus cap. 1. huius Epist. v. 14. dicat, depositionem tabernaculi sui sibi â Christo manifestatam esse, quibus verbis respectum haberi putat ad Iohann. 21. v. 27. sed ostendemus inferius, de peculiari quadam manifestatione, quae in scripturis non continetur, illud esse intelligendum. 3. ex primitivae Ecclesiae testificatione. Nomine Petri haec Epistola in Canone ponitur â Concilio Laodiceno can. 59. Carthaginensi 3. can. 47. ab Athanasio in Synopsi, Epiphanio haeresi 76. Hieronymo ad Paulinum, Augustino lib. 2. de doctr. Christ. cap. 8. Gregorio homil. 18. in Ezech. Damasceno lib. 4. orth. fid. cap. 18. Amphilochius in Iambis ad Seleucum, Nazianzenus in carm. de Script. Ruffinus Aquileiensis in expositione Symbolorum. Innocentius 1. ad Exuperium Epistola 3. Isidorus lib. 6. Etymol. cap. 1. 2. eam esse Petri Epistolam disertis verbis testantur. Beda in prooem. comm. in hanc Epistolam â se scripti miratur, quâ ratione dubitari potuerit de Epistolae huius autore, cùm nomen suum exprimat, seque in monte cum Domino fuisse testatur. Clemeus & Didymus uterque Alexandrinus Commentarios in hanc Epistolam scripserunt, quorum fragmenta adhuc hodie extant in Scholiis Oecumenii.

(Hisce testibus Sixtus Senensis lib. 7. Bibl. haeres. 9. addit Anacletum Epist. 3. Iodocus Coccius tom. 1. Thesauri lib. 6. art. 24. Cornelium Epist. 2. Baronius ann. 68. n. 4. Hippolytum de Antichristo, & Concilium Romanum sub Damasc. Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epistolam. Concilium Tridentinum, Bellarminus lib. 1. de V. D. cap. 8. Higinum Epist. 1. & Concil. Florentinum. Sed illorum omnium autoritas est dubia & suspecta.)

Contra haec argumenta 1. Urgetur styli â priore Epistolâ diversitas. Hieronymus in catal. vir. Illustr. in Petro. Secundae Petri Epistola â plerisque eius esse negatur propter styli dissonantiam. Erasmus in annot. ad hanc Epist. Styli discrimen tùm in sensibus, tùm in verbis clarius est, quàm ut possit dissimulari. Resp. 1. Hieronymus styli diversitatem concedit, sed negat ex eâ inferri posse, quod haec Epistola non sit Petri. Existimat verò diversitatem illam styli ex Interpretum diversitate, quibus Petrus in utraque Epistola conscribenda usus fuerit, originem duxisse, sic enim scribit Epist. 150. ad Hedibiam q. 11. B. Paulus habebat Titum Interpretem, sicut & B.

Petrus Marcum, cuius Evange lium Petro narrante & illo scribente compositum est. Denique & duae Epistolae, quae feruntur Petri stylo & charactere inter se discrepant, structuraque verborum. Ex quo intelligimus, pro necessitate rerum eum diversis Interpretibus fuisse usum. Clemens Alexandr. 7. stromat. memorat, hoc Interpretis munere apud Petrum functum non solùm Marcum, sed etiam Glauciam quendam, quem Basilides falsò iactitabat suum Magistrum. (De munere horum Interpretum, quorum operâ Apostoli fuêre usi, prolixè agit Baronius Ann. 45. n. 32. & seqq. quae paulò pòst expendemus) 2. Si vel maximè hîc occurreret styli quaedam diversitas, nondum tamen ex ea inferri posset, hanc Epistolam non esse â Petro scriptam, cùm in Epistolis Paulinis eadem styli diversitas occurrat. Nimirum diversitas materiae, etiam styli quandam diversitatem secum trahere consuevit, quin & diversa personarum obiecta & aliae circumstantiae stylum variant. 3. Erasmo meritò hoc opponitur, quod probaturus commentarium Arnobii in Psalmos meritò ipsi tribui, licet in libris contra gentiles alio utatur stylo, moneat, sanctos Scriptores duplici stylo fuisse usos, altero humili & familiari, altero cultiori & magis exacto. 4. Rectissimè verò argumenti hypothesis negatur, mutua enim collatio opinionem de styli diversitate refellit. Autores Hist. Magdeb. Cent. 1. lib. 2. cap. 4. collat. 54. Stylus & compositio â priori Epistola Petri non admodum discrepat. In utraque certè occurrit artificiosa brevitas cum summa maiestate coniuncta. 2. Gregorius homil. 18. in Ezech. mentionem facit quorundam, qui concedebant quidem, hanc Epistolam esse Petri, sed negabant eam esse Petri Apostoli, tribuentes eam alii cuidam Cephae seu Petro, cui Paulus in faciem se restitisse scribatGal. 2. v. 11. Sed illorum opinio omnibus illis argumentis, quae modò adducta sunt, refellitur, ac suo loco demonstratur, Cepham illum, cuius mentio fit Gal. 2. v. 9. fuisse Petrum Apostolum, unde Gregor. d. l. rectè scribit. Si eiusdem Epistolae verba pensare voluissent, longè aliter pensare poterant. In ea quippe seriptum est. Voce delapsa ad eam huiusmodi â magnifica gloria. Hic est filius meus dilectus, atque subiungitur. Et hanc vocem nos audivimus, cùm essemus cum ipso in monte sancto. Legant itaque Evangelium & protinus cognoscunt, quia cum vox ista de caelo venit, Petrus Apostolis cum Domino stetit. Ipse ergo hanc Epistolam scripsit, qui hanc vocem in monte de Domino audivit. 3. Canonica huius Epistolae autoritas. De ea videtur â quibusdam in primitiva Ecclesia dubitatum. Eusebius lib. 3. Histor. Eccles. cap. 3. in Princ. Petri Epistola una, quae prior dicitur, citra controversiam recepta est. Hâc & veteres olim Presbyteri sine ulla haesitatione in suis scripturis usi sunt. Eam vero, quae posterior dicitur,οὐκ ἐνδιάθηκον εἶναιnon esse legitimam sive Testamentariam accepimus. Et tamen quia multis videtur esse utilis, cum aliis est usurpata scripturis. Et postea. De his, quae Petro tribuuntur, è quibus unam duntaxat germanam illius Epistolam apud priscos Presbyteros in confesso habitam cognovi, hactenus dictum esto. lib. eiusd. cap. 22. postquam Scripturas N. T. Canonicas enumeraverat, videlicet scripta quatuor Evangelistarum, Acta Apostolorum, Epistolas Pauli quatuordecim, priorem Iohannis, priorem Petri & Apocalypsin, subiungit. Et haec quidem scripta pro indubitatis habentur. Quibus verò contradicitur, tametsi multis sint cognita, sunt haec. Epistola, quae Iacobo tribuitur, & Epistola Iudae & posterior Petri & altera cum tertia Iohannis. lib. 6. cap. 24. ex Origen. comment. in Matth. haec adducit. Petrus unam Epistolam, de qua certo constat, post se reliquit. Esto autem reliquerit & alteram, de illa namque controvertitur. Didymus Alexandr. Hieronymi Praeceptor commentariolum suum in hanc Epistolam sic concludit. Non est igitur ignorandum, praesentem Epistolam esse falsatam, quae licet publicetur, (hoc est, publicè per Ecclesias legatur) non tamen in canone est. Ad haec testimonia accedit, quod in Syriaca versione praetermittitur.

Pontificii hisce argumentis opponunt autoritatem Ecclesiae i. e. Concilii Tridentini, ( eius enim vocem esse Ecclesiae Catholicae vocem scribit Bellarm. lib. 5. de grat & lib. arbitr. cap. 13.) Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epist. Non licet iam amplius de hac Epistola dubitare, cùm Ecclesiae sententiâ (in Concilio Florentino & Tridentino) ut Petri propria declaratur. Sed haec responsio est insufficiens, sic ergo progredimur.

1. Iam antè ostendimus, Petrum Apostolum esse huius Epistolae autorem.

2. Spiritus in eâ est Apostolicus.

3. Nihil in eâ habetur, quod reliquis Canonicis libris vel in minimo adversetur.

4. Nulla causa satis gravis afferri potest, cur de autoritate huius Epistolae dubitare debeamus.

5. Inter scripta Canonica â praecipuis primitivae Ecclesiae Doctoribus refertur. Origenes & Hieronymus compluribus in locis ex hac Epistola tanquam ex sacra & Canonica Scripturâ testimonia proferunt. Unde etiam B. Lutherus in Praefat. Epistolae ad Hebr. inter Canonicos libros eam recenset. (Sanè Sixtus Senensis lib. 7. Bibl. haeres. 9. Luthero tribuit, quod Secundam hanc Epistolam Petri in dubium vocarit, sed Bellarminus ab hoc ἐγκλήματι eum absolvit lib. 1. de verb. DEI cap. 18. §. ubi dicit, Lutherum hanc Epistolam ponere inter Scripturas Canonicas. Idem agnoscit Lorinus in comm. huius Epist. cap. 1. v. 10.)

Hisce igitur rationibus moti, Epistolam hanc Apostolicam & Canonicam statuimus & 1, ad testimonia Veterum modò adducta respondemus.

1. Non tàm de Canonica huius Epistolae autoritate, quàm de autore secundario dubitatum fuisse.

2. Non fuisse eam unquam inter Apocrypha scripta reiectam; nec ab omnibus, sed tantùm à quibusdam de ea fuisse dubitatum.

3. Longè plures eam ut Canonicam recepisse. Interim ob hanc quorundam Veterum de ea dubitationem inter Canonicos secundi ordinis libros illam referimus, quos quidam appellant ἀντιλεγομένους ὑπὸ τινῶν, eosdemque distinguunt ab ἀντιλεγομένοις ὑπὸ πάντων.

2. Quòd in Syriaca versione haec Epistola non habetur, ad illud respondemus.

1. Illud duntaxat hoc probat, quod haec Epistola non fuerit olim ab omnibus recepta.

2. Ephrem & Damascenus Syri ex hac Epistola, tanquam ex genuina Scripturae Sacrae parte, testimonia in suis scriptis adducunt. Vid. Damasc. lib. 4. orthod. fid. cap. 18.

3. Eduardus Pococke Anglus Syriacam huius Epistolae versionem unâ cum secunda & tertia Iohannis, ut & Iudae Epistola ex Bibliothecae Bodleianae Oxoniensis MSto exemplari depromtam Lugd. Batav. Anno 630. in publicum edidit; in cuius praefatione memorat, Epistolas hasce in praedicta Bibliotheca inventas fuisse, unà cum Actis Apostolicis & Epistolis caeteris Catholicis eo ordine, quo in Graecis Codicibus solent haberi dispositae. Ibid. tamen addit, Dionysium quendam, qui Commentariis Syris Posteriorem Petri, secundam & tertiam Iohannis, ac Iudae Epistolam unà cum caeteris Epistolis Canonicis & Actis Apostolicis nec non Apocalypsi illustravit, in praefatione ad Post. Epistolam Petri monere, eam non fuisse versam in lingvam Syram cum libris, qui diebus antiquis redditi sunt, ideoque non inveniri nisi in translatione Themae Episcopi, qui cognominatus est Heracleensis secundùm nomen Heracle civitatis suae. Quis verò fuerit Thomas iste, vel qualis eius versio, compertum non haberi.

3. Ad Didymi querelam de corruptione huius Epistolae respon. Didymum hoc malè colligere ex illis, quae in fine Epistolae habentur de mundi renovatione, ubi tradi putat revolutiones Platonicas, â quibus Petri doctrina toto, quod dici solet, caelo distat. Unde quod haud sine ratione quidam suspicantur, verba illa in librum Didymi esse ab alio inserta, cùm nec ostendat, in quofalsata fuerit haec Epistola; nec verisimile sit, tantum virum in Epistolam Apocrypham Commentarios edere voluisse.

4. Obiectum. Petrus Aureolus in Comp. Script. statuit, hanc posteriorem Petri Epistolam ad Romanos esse scriptam, argumento motus eo, quod in cap. 3. eiusdem. v. 5. Petrus de Pauli ad Romanos Epistola loqui videatur. Sed hypothesis illa est falsa, ut in expositione illius loci demonstrabitur. Inscripta est haec Epistola iisdem, quibus prior, Iudaeis, sc. ad Christum conversis, per Pontum, Galatiam, Cappadociam, Asiam & Bithyniam dispersis, 1. Petr. 1. v. 1. ut colligitur ex cap. 3. v. 1.Hanc, ecce carissimi, secundam vobis scribo Epistolam. Illorum Apostolus peculiariter Petrus erat constitutus ex conventione Apostolica Gal. 2. v. 9. Idem colligi potest ex cap. 1. v. 19.Habemus firmiorem Propheticum sermonem. Propheticus enim sermo ad Iudaeos fuit factus, non ad gentiles. Illis concredita erant eloquia DeiRom. 3. v. 2. illi habebant Mosen & Prophetas,Luc. 16. v. 29. illorum erantαἱ διαθήκαιRom. 9. v. 4. Illi etiam attendebant Scripturis Propheticis, tanquam lucernae, quotidie eas scrutantes, an ea, quae ab Apostolis praedicabantur, essent illis conformia.Act. 17. v. 12. Hùc referri potest, quod Petrus in cap. 3. huius Epistolae v. 15. mentionem faciat Epistolae ad Hebraeos scriptae, ac ad eosdem etiam hanc Epistolam à se scribi testetur. Ergo haec posterior Petri Epistola ad Israëlitas ex Iudaismo ad Christum conversos scripta est. Quamvis verò principaliter ad conversos Iudaeos scripta sit, tamen minùs principaliter ad conversos ex gentilibus etiam scripta est, ut in enarratione prioris Epistolae manifestum fecimus.

5. Scriptionis tempus. Scripsit Apostolus hanc Epistolam paulò ante mortem, ut colligitur ex cap. 1. v. 14. Cygneam ergo in ea edit vocem, ac totus spirat ardorem Spiritus, Christi amorem, pietatis Zelum, Martyrium & caelestia. Iuxta Baronii computationem scripta est Anno Christi 63. cùm prior scripta fuerit Anno Christi 45. & sic viginti tribus ante hanc posteriorem annis.

6. Scriptionis locus. Quamvis Petrus in hac Epistola non exprimat disertis verbis, ex quo loco ea sit missa, sicut in priore dixerat, eam esse missam ex Babylone, tamen verisimiliter statui potest, ut ad eosdem scripta est, ad quos prior, ita quoque ex eodem loco esse missam, videlicet ex Babylone. Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epist. tom. 16. p. 112. cùm sibi persuaserit, per Babylonem, 1. Petr. 5. v. 13. intelligendam esse Romam, probare conatur, etiam hanc posteriorem Petri Epistolam Romae scriptam esse. Affert autem sententiae suae duo argumenta. Prius desumit ex Scriptionis tempore, quod Petrus paulò ante suum obitum hanc Epistolam scripserit. Iam verò certa Ecclesiae traditio habet, ipsum Romae sub Nerone fuisse consummatum. Resp. demus sanè Petrum Romae fuisse mortuum, quâ de re sic scribit D. Chemnicius Harm. cap. 50. p. 277. Petrum Romae fuisse, omnes Historici consentiunt: quo verò tempore Roman venerit, perturbatissimae sunt annotationes. Illud cum Historia Actorum simplicissimè convenire videtur, quod Origenes Tomo in Genesin. 3. & Nicephorus annotant, Petrum circa finem vitae suae ultimis annis Neronis venisse Romam: reliqui addunt, quod ibi demisso capite & inversis vestigiis cruci affixus sit: sed ex eo nondum potest firmiter colligi, quòd haec Epistola Romae fuerit scripta, cùm nondum constat, quo tempore Petrus Romam venerit. Posterius argumentum Salmero desumit ex eo, quod Epistolarum Paulî in hac Petrina fit mentio cap. 3. v. 15. & 16.Petrus, inquit, scribit de Paulo & eius Epistolis, quas, dum Romae esset, legisse & vidisse potuit, & propterea tanto testimonio illas fidelibus commendavit, quod certè alibi contigisse non tàm est probabile, atque inurbe. Nam circumferebatur faesciculus literarum Pauli, quas Galatis & Achaeis scripserat, ita ut potuerit Seneca Imperatoris Praeceptor eas legere, etiam ipsi Principi Neroni, ut ipsemet Seneca testatur in quadam sua ad Neronem Epistola.

Resp. 1. Pauli Epistolas Petrus aequè potuit legere Babylone ac Romae, cûm notae fuerint omnibus Ecclesiis, adeoque etiam Ponticis, ad quos Petrus scribit. 2. Multi ex Pontificiis agnoscunt, Petrumcap. 3. v. 15.huius Epistolae in specie loqui de Epistola ad Hebraeos. At longè verisimilius est, Petrum Babylone inter conversos ex Iudaismo versantem Epistolam illam ad Hebraeos vidisse & legisse, quàm Romae inter conversos ex gentilismo. 3. Insigni verò ἀκρισίᾳ laborat Salmero, quando Epistolas Pauli ad Senecam, & Senecae ad Paulum testes sententiae suae citat. Audiat de illis iudicium Baronii Anno 66. num. 11. Senecae Epistola ad Paulum de incendio Neroniano meâ sententiâ ab alio quopiam potiùs ficta videtur, quàm â Seneca scripta, cùm tàm aperta in ea asserantur mendacia. Quamobrem & reliquae illae, tùm ad Paulum conscriptae, tùm à Paulo ad eum redditae, aequè nobis suspectae redduntur, quamvis sciamus, eas non esse recens excogitatas, sed antiquitus scriptas, & ab Hieronymo de script. Eccles. in Seneca cognitas atque probatas. n. 12. Novit eas & Augustinus, qui earundem meminit Epist. 14. licetidem Augustinus. lib. 6. de Civ. DEI cap. 11. nullam prorsus fidem dictis Epistolis tribuisse videatur. Scimus quidem, Sixtum Senensem lib. 2. Bibl. sanctae p. 89. autoritatem harum Epistolarum probare ex libro Lini de passione Pauli. Sed hoc est, incertum per aequè incertum probare.

7. Epistolae idioma. Baronius Anno 45. n. 28. sic disserit. Petri Epistolam priorem â Marco Evangelista ex Hebraeo fuisse translatam, affirmare videtur Hieronymus Epistol. 150. ad Hedibiam q. 11. dum, postquam egit de Evangelio â Marco conscripto, sed â Petro accepto, haec ait: Denique & duae Epistolae quae feruntur Petri, stylo inter se & charactere discrepant, structuraque verborum, ex quo intelligimus, pro necessitate rerum diversis eum usum Interpretibus. n. 37. Petri Epistolae ex Hebraeo â diversis Interpretibus in aliam linguam versae, sparsae sunt in Ecclesiam.

Resp. 1. Petri Epistolas Hebraeo idiomate fuisse scriptas, nullus Veterum affirmat. 2. Inde Bellarmin. lib. 2. de verbo DEI cap. 7. §. 2. sic scribit: Constat, Nov. Test. Graecè scriptum esse ab iis Apostolis vel Evangelistis, quorum nomina in titulis singulorum librorum vel Epistolarum praefiguntur, exceptis duntaxat Evangelio Matthaei & Marci & Epistola ad Hebraeos. Et postea §. 4. Graeca editio N. T. universa Apostolos & Evangelistas autores habet. Nec potest contrarium ex Hieronymi verbis apodicticè colligi. Aliud enim munus Interpretum Apostolicorum fuisse, idem Baronius Ann. 45. n. 37. docet, Duplici, inquit, ex causa Apostolis inserviebant Interpretes, vel cum alicui genti ipsis loquentibus, puta Romanis, in auditorio essent alii, qui Latinum sermonem, quem illis loquerentur Apostoli, penitus ignorarent, tunc enim officum videbatur desiderari Interpretis; vel cùm captu difficilia iidem Apostoli locuti fuissent, tunc erat interpretis, eadem explanare. 4. Per Interpretem in verbis Hieronymi Estius in proleg. huius 2. Epist. Petr. intelligit Scribam, 5. Quic quid sit, si vel maximè alterutram ex his Epistolis Marcus ex Hebraeo in Graecum sermonem transtulerit, tamen Petrus Graecum textum vidit & approbavit, ut proinde ille solus meritò authenticus iudicetur.

8. Argumentum Epistolae. Illud Apostolus ipse in eadem exponit cap. 1. v. 12.Quapropter non negligam vos de istis (quae ad constantiam in fide & studium pietatis faciunt) vos semper commonefacereὑπομιμνήσκειν,quamvis peritos & stabilitos in praesente veritate.v. 13.Iustum autem duco, quamdiu sum in hoc tabernaculo,διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσειexpergefacere vos per commonefactionem.v. 15.Sed & studebo, ut subinde vos possitis post exitum meumτούτων μνήμην ποιεῖσθαιhorum mentionem facerecap. 3. v. 1.Hanc ecce iam alteram vobis scribo Epistolam, dilecti,ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διακονίαν,quibus sinceram mentem vestram per submonitionem expergefacio.v. 2.μνησθῆναιut memores sitis verborum, quae praedicta sunt â sanctis Prophetis, & praecepti illius nostri, qui sumus Apostoli Domini & Salvatoris. Ex quibus omnibus colligitur, quòd argumentum & Scopus Epistolae sit. 1. Ὑπόμνησις, per quam in memoriam voluit eis revocare, quae vivâ voce ipsis praedicaverat. 2. Διέγερσις, per quam ad constantiam in fide & studium pietatis eos excitare voluit. Athanasius in Synopsi Scripturae sub tit. de tertia Epist. Catholica. Haec Epistola estὑπόμνησις.Cum enim cognovisset, citò futuram corporis sui resolutionem, diligenter hoc egit, ut omnes admonerentur eorum, de quibus antea per Evangelii doctrinam erant instructi. D. Chemnicius in Exam. Conc. Trident. part. 1. de Epist. Apost. p. 66. accutatè expendit verbum ὑπομιμνήσκεινcap. 1. v. 12. & phrasin ἐκάστοτε ἔχειν ὑμᾶς μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι v. 15. ex quibus colligit, duas scriptionis suae causas verbis valde illustribus Petrum recensere. 1. Ut cùm vivâ Apostolorum voce destituti fuerint, possent tamen semper, ubique & sigillatim memoriam purae doctrinae ab Apostolis traditae habere & conservare. 2. Ut munirentur contra falsos Dd.cap. 2. v. 1.quorum corruptelas vocat fictitios sermones, quos sc. fingent ab Apostolis traditos & acceptos2. Thess. 2. v. 1.

Ex hoc Epistolae argumento & ex mutua collatione intelligi potest, huic Epistolae Petrinae posteriori magnam intercedere cognationem cum Epistola Iudae, quam non immeritò quispiam dixerit huius Petrinae compendium, cùm iisdem ferè coloribus falsos doctores depingat, quibus Petrus eos describit. Quinimò Epistola Iudae iisdem verbis, sententiis, atque etiam verbis interdum videtur intexta, quin & Iudas v. 17. expressè ad eam provocat.

9. Dispositio. Partes Epistolae duae sunt. 1. Νουθεσία,exhortatio ad constantiam & profectum in fide ac studio pietatis. 2. Προφητείαpraedictio, tum de falsis Prophetis ac seductoribus; tumde empaectis & irrisoribus, ultimum Christi adventum negantibus; ex quo vati cinio deducitur commonefactio, quòd ab illis summo studio cavere, ab his verò sese seiungere, & sanctâ vitae conversatione ad novissimum Christi adventum praeparare debeant. Utrique parti 1. praemittitur Exordium, constans inscriptione & salutatione: 2. Subiungitur Exodium, constans tum brevi repetitione exhortationis ad studium perstandi & proficiendi in fide; tum Δοξολογίᾳ.

B. Luther. in praefat. huic Epistolae in versione eius Germanica praemissa eiusmodi profert οἰκονομίαν.In primo capite ostendit Apostolus statum Ecclesiae, temporihus Apostolorum vicina, quandò Evangelium adhuc purè & sincerè praedicabatur. In secundo ostendit statum Ecclesiae temporibus dominantis Papatus & regnantibus doctrinis humanis. In tertio ostendit statum Ecclesiae post revelatum Antichristum, quomodo sc. homines in Epicuraeismum prolapsi, & legem & Evangelium despicatui sint habituri, ac nihil quidquam credituri, quod proh dolor hodie obtinere videmus.

10. Connexio cum Epistola priore. Hugo & Dionys. Carthusianus monent, quod quemadmodum Petrus in priore Epistola Ecclesiam muniverit contra Tyrannos, disserendo de patientia in persecutionibus: ita in hac posteriore eandem muniat adversus haereticos, quorum ingenium & qualitates graphicè depingit. Primitivam, inquit Dionysius, Ecclesiam impugnabant Tyranni gladio materiali, persecutionibusque diversis, haeretici autem doctrinis pestiferis. Quemadmodum ergo in prima Epistola excellentis simus Apostolici chori vertex hortatus est fideles ad patientiam in adversis, ne persecutionibus cederent: ita in hac Epistola secunda eos hortatur, ne haereticorum decipiantur figmentis. In utraque ad constantiam in fidei veritate & vitae sanctitate eos hortatur. Iohann. Huss. in comm. 2. Petr. 1. In priore Epistola Petrus induxit eos, quibus scribit, ad permanendum in gratiae bonitate, ne succumberent per adversitates tribulationum. In hac posteriore inducit eos ad perseverandum ingratiae Christianae veritate, ne pervertantur per falsam doctrinam haereticorum & pseudoApostolorum.

CAPUT I.

Summa capitis. Praemisso prooemio Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, hortatur ad constantiam & profectum in fide & studio pietatis.

Dispositio. Partes capitis duae sunt. 1. Προοίμιον 2. Νουθεσία.

Prooemium continet. 1. Inscriptionem. 2. Salutaetionem.

Inscriptio exprimit. 1. Causam ministerialem, sive autorem huius Epistolae secundarium. 2. Obiectum, ad quos sc. haec Epistola sit scripta.

Autor Epistolae describitur. 1. â Nomine, eodemque duplici. 2. Ab officio. Obiectum describitur â statu gratiae, in quem illi, ad quos haec Epistola scripta est, fuerunt translati. v. 1.

Salutatio complectitur Votum, quo 1. precatur eis, ad quos scribit Apostolus, gratiae & pacis augmentum. 2. exprimit illius augmenti medium, quod est cognitio Christi. v. 2.

Νουθεσία absolvitur quatuor membris. 1. Commemoratione beneficiorum iam antè acceptorum, quibus illi, ad quos scribit, animari & excitari debeant, ut summo studio in id incumbant, ad quod eos hortatur v. 3. & 4.

2. Exhortatione ad studium proficiendi in fide & virtutibus Christianis, â v. 5. usque, ad v. 12.

3. Expositione causarum, propter quas de hoc proficiendi studio tam solicitè eos commonefaciat, â v. 12. usque ad 16.

4. Exhortatione ad constantiam in fide, & confessione doctrinae ipsis traditae, â v. 16. usque ad capitis finem.

## 1:1
Exposition of the text. Συμεὼν Πέτρος. In the former Epistle he calls himself simply Peter, but here Simeon Peter, from which formerly Some, referring to Gregory, homily 18 on Ezekiel, have wished to gather that there is a different author of this latter Epistle than of the former. The argument could be confirmed from the fact that Christ says to Simon Peter John 1. v. 42. You are Simon the son of Jona, you shall be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter. I respond: the name of Peter was not so imposed upon this Apostle that, having received the name of Simeon at circumcision, he ceased entirely to be called by it thereafter, but after that imposition of a new name he was also called Simon, as is conspicuous from very many places in the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles. Thus Gen. 32. v. 28. it is said to the Patriarch Jacob, your name shall not be called any further Jacob, but Israel. Yet the same man is called Jacob several times by Moses in the following chapters. Therefore, the negation according to the customary Hebraism is placed there for a comparison.

Συμεὼν. Certain Greek codices in this place read Σίμων, in which way it is also read Matt. 16. v. 17. which agrees with the Hebrew appellation שמעון Gen. 34. v. 25. derived from hearing. But some read Συμεὼν with the word inflected to the figure of the Greek language, in which way it is also read Acts 15. v. 14. For the Seventy rendered the Hebrew שמוען as Συμεὼν Gen. 34. v. 25. with the letter ε inserted for the sake of euphony. Some also advise this, that it is written more correctly Σιμεὼν than Συμεὼν, for in the Hebrew there is not a Kybbutz, to which the Greek v corresponds, but a Chirek, to which the Greek i corresponds.

Δοῦλος καὶ Ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. With the same periphrasis Paul designates himself here and there in the openings of his Epistles. Rom. 1. v. 1. Phil. 1. v. 1. Tit. 1. v. 1. He calls himself a servant, not for the sake of humility, as Origen wishes, nor principally with respect to his condition, because he was saved by Christ and liberated from the captivity of Satan, but by reason of the Ministry, because he faithfully serves Christ Jesus in preaching the Gospel and in propagating the same by living voice and by writings. But because the name of servant is general, belonging to all faithful Ministers of the Church, indeed in a certain respect to all true believers, therefore he adds to it the special name of Apostle, because the Apostolate is the supreme degree in the ecclesiastical Ministry of the New Testament 1. Cor. 12. v. 28.

Τοῖς ἰσότιμον ἡμῶν λαχοῦσι πίστιν. The Vulgate rendered it, to those who have obtained an equal faith with us. In the Greek it is properly an equally precious faith. A parallel passage stands Acts 11. v. 17. where the same Peter concerning those converted to Christ from Gentilism he says, τὴν ἴσην δωρεὰν God gave the equal gift to them, just as also to us. Λαχοῦσι they have obtained by lot, they have acquired by lot, namely from the ordination of GOD. Thus Luc. 1. v. 9. it is said concerning Zacharias, ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιάσαι he obtained by lot the office of performing the incense offering, but by the ordination of GOD the Priests performed that office by turns. Act. 1. v. 17. concerning Judas, who was chosen to the Apostleship freely and without any merit of his own, it is said, ἔλαχε τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης. Eph. 1. v. 11. ἐν ὣ ἐκληρώθημεν in whom we have been called by lot. Col. 1. v. 12. he has made us worthy εἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων for the portion of the lot of the saints in light. The theme is λαγχάνειν, which signifies not only to cast lots or to draw lots Ioh. 19. v. 24. but also to receive something by lot or to obtain, as the cited examples show. And because those things which come to someone by lot come to him without the merit or debt of the recipient, thence the gratuitous benefits of GOD are said to come to us by lot, that is, freely without our merit, respect undoubtedly being had to the distribution of the land of Canaan, which fell to the Israelites by lot without any merit of their own. Ios. 13. v. 16. as also to the division of inheritances, which come to heirs without merits, and are accustomed to be distributed by lot. August. conc. 2. in Psal. 30. When God finds no merits of ours, he made us safe by the lot of his own will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy, this is the lot Ioh. Huss. in h. l. Just as the lot does not respect persons: so neither is the divine election a respecter of persons. Prosper, looking more to the sense than the force of the word, lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. translates, they have obtained, and nevertheless from this place he proves, that faith is a gratuitous gift of GOD. The Syrian has the word [אשתויו] from the root [שוא] he agreed Matth. 18. v. 19. 1. Cor. 7. v. 5. so that the sense may be, those who have agreed with us in faith equal in honor, so that thus the unity of faith may be commended. Eph. 4. v. 5. Another interpreter, who obtained Dionysius as a commentator, expresses the passage thus. To those who have arrived at a faith equal in honor with us, which he explains thus, they have been placed with us in the same order in the faith, which is in Christ.

Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Various opinions of interpreters, both ancient and modern, occur here, as to what is to be understood by the righteousness of GOD and of Christ.

1. Bede in his commentary explains it concerning the justice of works. Because, he says, faith without works cannot save, therefore it is rightly added, in the justice of our GOD and our Savior Jesus Christ. The Apostle Peter writes the Epistle to those, and greets those, who have obtained a faith equal to his own, and exercise this through the works of justice. But anyone can see that this exposition is forced. For the Apostle is not dealing with the justice of our works, but with the justice of Christ, nor is he occupied with exhorting to that which he wishes to be done by us, but he proclaims what we have received from GOD.

2. Beza, Piscator, and others understand by justice faith in keeping promises. For GOD had promised that in the New Testament He would also call the Gentiles to the kingdom of the Messiah, in which sense they think the name of justice is taken Rom. 3. v. 28. But the word justice in that Apostolic passage is not taken in the sense that they wish, but rather it signifies the justice of GOD manifested in the passion of Christ, which is to say, that He does not remit sins unless satisfaction intervenes.

Those who maintain that this Epistle was written solely or principally to converted Jews understand by the name of justice likewise faith in keeping promises, but they apply it differently; for they say, the mention of this divine justice is made in this place because GOD had promised that He would effectively call and save some from the Jewish people through the preaching of the Gospel. But Peter does not set forth justice simply and absolutely, but he notably adds, in the justice of our GOD and our Savior Jesus Christ.

3. Some, having followed Prosper, book 2, on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 23, ἐν say that it is placed according to the customary Hebraism for διὰ through justice, so that the sense may be, that faith ἰσότιμον happened to those converted to Christ through justice, that is, the merits of Christ himself, for faith is a gift of GOD in Christ. Cajetan on this passage: It is signified that faith is given through the justice of Christ, or through his merits, not through the works of the law, or any others whatsoever done by the powers of Nature. Salmero, Disputation 1 on this Epistle. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: Christ merited for us all grace. Therefore also faith, Eph. 1. v. 3. This exposition does not conflict with the analogy of faith. But it does not seem entirely conformable to the text.

4. Some maintain that the name of justice is placed here for mercy. Emanuel à Sa on this passage. Estius opposes this exposition with the fact that the name of justice is nowhere in the Scriptures signified by the name of mercy. And yet, in the Scriptures, this is not unusual. Ps. 40. v. 10. justice ἐξηγητικῶς is explained by mercy. I have announced your justice in the great assembly, I have not hidden your mercy and your truth,Ps. 51. v. 16.Deliver me from bloodguiltiness and my tongue shall proclaim your righteousness.Ps. 71. v. 2.In your righteousness deliver me. But deliverance is a work of divine mercy. Psal. 143. v. 1. David prays, Hear me O Lord for your righteousness, and yet he adds v. 2. Do not enter into judgment with your servant. Hence interpreters frequently interchange these words of righteousness and mercy of GOD, especially in the article of justification, for in that article the righteousness of GOD is used concerning the goodness and mercy of GOD, by which He absolves those who believe in Christ from sins, imputes the righteousness of Christ to them, and receives them into favor. Rom. 1. v. 17. The righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith. Thus Gen. 19. v. 19. when Lot said to the Angel in the Hebrew text, You have magnified your mercy, the LXX rendered it δικαιοσύνην righteousness. Conversely Ps. 103. v. 6. when David had said in Hebrew, The Lord performs righteousnesses, the LXX rendered it ἐλεημοσύνας mercies. Let the passages Gen. 20. v. 13.cap. 21. v. 23.c. 32. v. 10. be compared. These most wise men would not have taken this liberty for themselves if they had not understood that the righteousness of GOD denotes His mercy, by which He shows Himself kind and beneficial to believers. Hence Lorinus writes thus on this passage: I accept the taking of righteousness for mercy and I know it can be confirmed by examples.Ps. 30. v. 2.Es. 56. v. 1.Matth. 6. v. 1.2. Cor. 9. v. 10. In vain, therefore, does Estius oppose this exposition, that it is destitute of examples from Scripture, although we do not yet see that it is entirely conformable to this text.

5. Estius thinks that ἐν or in this passage is placed for with, in which sense the prefix ב is sometimes used among the Hebrews. Deut. 6. v. 7. You shall speak בם with them.Ps. 60. v. 12. You will not go out with, i.e., with our armies.Act. 7. v. 38. He was with, i.e., with the Church.2. Pet. 1. v. 5. Supply with, i.e., with faith virtue. The sense therefore would be, faith is given with righteousness, i.e., righteousness accompanying, because we are justified through faith, which righteousness is of God as the author, and of Christ as the one meriting it for us. This exposition, accepted in a sound sense, does not at all conflict with the analogy of faith. But Estius understands the name of both faith and righteousness less correctly. For he says that we are justified by faith, as a quality disposing us to righteousness, and obtaining it for us; by the name of righteousness he understands an infused habit of righteousness.

6. It is most simply established that by the name of righteousness here is understood the obedience and satisfaction of Christ, which is imputed to us for righteousness through faith; or, which is the same thing, the righteousness obtained by the passion and death of Christ, which faith apprehends and applies to itself. For when in the preceding verses the Apostle had said that believers ἰσότιμον πίστιν had obtained, he now shows the object of that faith, in respect of which The faith of all believers is called ἰσότιμος, which is the righteousness of Christ, that is, the righteousness obtained through the obedience and satisfaction of Christ, but imputed to us through faith. Christ is τέλος the end and fulfillment of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, Rom. 10. v. 4. that is, he who believes in Christ has what the law requires, namely, perfect righteousness valid before GOD. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. Christ is made unto us of God righteousness, 2. Cor. 5. v. ult. That we might be made the righteousness of God in him. The Arabic version of this passage confirms this exposition, which reads as follows: To them that have obtained like precious faith with us in the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. Luther expressed the sense thus, In der Gerechtigkeit die Gott giebt / which likewise can be understood concerning the righteousness imputed to us through faith. Rom. 3. v. 22. & 24.

Τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτηρίας ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Erasmus thinks that by the name of GOD is understood God the Father, who is a distinct person from Christ, in which way in the following verse these two persons of the Godhead are distinguished. But it is more correctly said that Christ is called in this place God and our Saviour. 1. Because the word σωτῆρος lacks the article. 2. Because that righteousness, which faith embraces in the act of justification, is not the essential righteousness of GOD, but the righteousness obtained by the active and passive obedience of Christ. 3. Because later in v. 11. of this chapter and in v. 18. cap. 3. the same two names are attributed to Christ. 4. A similar repetition of the inserted pronoun occurs in John 20. v. 28. where, however, it treats of Christ alone. Therefore, it cannot be gathered from that, that the discourse here is about distinct persons.

Latin:

Textus expositio. Συμεὼν Πέτρος. In priore Epistola simpliciter se vocat Petrum, hîc verò Simeonem Petrum, ex quo olim aliqui referente Gregorio homil. 18. in Ezech. colligere voluerunt, alium esse autorem huius Epistolae posterioris, quàm prioris. Argumentum confirmari possit, ex eo, quod Christus Simoni Petro dicit Iohan. 1. v. 42.Tu es Simon filius Iona, tu vocaberis Cephas, quod interpretatur Petrus. Resp. non ita fuit nomen Petri huic Apostolo impositum, ut nomine Simeonis in Circumcisione accepto inposterum vocari penitùs desierit, sed post illam novi nominis impositionem etiam Simon vocatus fuit, ut ex plurimis Evangelistarum & Actorum Apostolicorum locis conspicuum. Sic Gen. 32. v. 28. Iacobo Patriarchae dicitur, non vocabitur nomen tuum ulterius Iacob, sed Israël. Idem tamen in sequentibus capitibus aliquoties â Mose vocatur Iacob. Ergo negatio iuxta usitatum Hebraismum ibi ponitur pro comparatione.

Συμεὼν. Quidam Codd. Graeci h. l. legunt Σίμων, quo modo etiam legitur Matth. 16. v. 17. quod congruit cum Hebraea appellatione שמעוןGen. 34. v. 25. ab audiendo deducta. Quidam verò Συμεὼν voce ad Graeci sermonis figuram inflexa, quo modo etiam legitur Actor. 15. v. 14. LXX. enim Hebraeum שמוען reddiderunt ΣυμεὼνGenes. 34. v. 25. literâ ε euphoniae causâ insertâ. Quidam etiam hoc monent, rectiùs scribiΣιμεὼνquàmΣυμεὼν,in Hebraeo enim non est Kybbutz, cui respondet Graecorum v, sed Chirek, cui respondet Graecorum 1.

Δοῦλος καὶ Ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Eadem periphrasi Paulus in exordiis Epistolarum suarum passim sese denominat. Rom. 1. v. 1.Phil. 1. v. 1.Tit. 1. v. 1.Servum se vocat, non humilitatis causâ, ut vult Origenes, nec principaliter respectu conditionis, quod â Christo servatus, & ex captivitate Satanae liberatus sit, sed ratione Ministerii, quod Christo Iesu in Evangelio praedicando, eodemque vivâvoce & scriptis propagando fideliter serviat. Quia verò nomen Servi generale est, competens omnibus fidelibus Ecclesiae Ministris, imò certo respectu omnibus verè credentibus, ideò subiungit illi speciale nomen Apostoli, quia Apostolatus est supremus in Ministerio N. T. Ecclesiastico gradus 1. Cor. 12. v. 28.

Τοῖς ἰσότιμον ἡμῶν λαχοῦσι πίστιν. Vulgatus redididit, iis qui coaequalem nobiscum sortiti sunt fidem. In Graeco propriè est aequè precio sam fidem. Locus parallelus extat Actor. 11. v. 17. ubi idem Petrus de conversis ad Christum ex gentilismo dicit, τὴν ἴσην δωρεὰνaequale donum dedit illis Deus, sicut & nobis.Λαχοῦσιsortiti sunt, sorte adepti sunt, ex DEI sc. ordinatione. Sic Luc. 1. v. 9. de Zacharia dicitur, ἔλαχε τοῦ θυμιάσαιsortitus est munus suffimentum faciendi, ex DEI autem ordinatione Sacerdotes munere illo per vices fungebantur. Act. 1. v. 17. de Iuda ad Apostolatum gratis & sine ullo merito suo electo dicitur, ἔλαχε τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης.Eph. 1. v. 11.ἐν ὣ ἐκληρώθημενin quo sorte vocati sumus.Col. 1. v. 12.dignos nos fecitεἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίωνin partem sortis sanctorum in lumine. Thema est λαγχάνειν, quod significat non solùm sortiri sive sortes ducereIoh. 19. v. 24. sed etiam sorte aliquid accipere vel obtinere, ut ostendunt allata exempla. Et quia quae sorte alicui obveniunt, sine accipientis merito sive debito ei obtingunt, inde gratuita DEI beneficia sorte h. e. gratis sine nostro merito nobis obtingere dicuntur, respectu procul dubio habito ad distributionem terrae Canaan, quae Israëlitis per sortem absque ullo ipsorum merito obtigit. Ios. 13. v. 16. uti etiam ad divisionem hereditatum, quae sine meritis heredibus obtingunt, & per sortem distribui solent. August. conc. 2. in Psal. 30. Quando Deus nulla merita nostra invenit, sorte voluntatis suae nos salvos fecit, quia voluit, non quia digni fuimus, haec est sors Ioh. Huss. in h. l. Sicut sors non respicit personans: ita nec divina electio acceptatrix est personarum. Prosper sensum magis, quàam vim vocis spectans lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. vertit. adepti sunt, ac nihilo tamen minus ex h. l. probat, fidem esse gratuitum DEI donum. Syrus habet verbum [אשתויו] â rad. [שוא]consensitMatth. 18. v. 19.1. Cor. 7. v. 5. ut sit sensus, qui in fidem aequalem in honore nobiscum consenserunt, ut sic fidei unitas commendetur. Eph. 4. v. 5. Alter interpres, qui Dionysium nactus est commentatorem, locum sic effert. Illis, qui in fidem aequalem in honore nobiscum pervenerunt, quod sic explicat, eodem nobiscum collocati sunt ordine in fide, quae est in Christum.

Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Variae hîc occurrunt tum veterum, tum recentiorum Interpp. sententiae, quid per iustitiam DEI & Christi sit intelligendum.

1. Beda in comm. exponit de iustitia operum. Quia, inquit, fides sine operibus salvare non potest, ideò rectè subditur, in iustitia DEI nostri & Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Illis ergo scribit Epistolam, illos salutat Apostolus Petrus, qui coaequalem sibi sortiti sunt fidem, & hanc per opera iustitiae exercent. Sed quilibet videt, hanc expositionem esse coactam. Neque enim de nostrorum operum, sed de Christi iustitia Apostolus agit, nec versatur in eo, ut exhortetur ad id, quod â nobis fieri velit, sed praedicat, quid â DEO acceperimus.

2. Beza, Piscator & alii per iustitiam intelligunt fidem in servandis promissis. Promiserat enim DEUS, se in N. T. etiam gentiles ad regnum Messiae vocaturum, quo sensu iustitiae nomen accipi putant Rom. 3. v. 28. Sed vox iustitiae in loco illo Apostolico non accipitur, eo, quem volunt, sensu, sed potius significat iustitiam DEI in passione Christi manifestatam, quod sc. non remittat peccata nisi intercedente satisfactione.

Qui ad conversos Iudaeos hanc Epistolam solùm vel principaliter scriptam statuunt, iustitiae nomine itidem fidem in promissis servandis intelligunt, sed aliter applicant, dicunt enim, ideò huius iustitiae divinae mentionem hoc loco fieri, quia DEUS promiserat, se aliquos ex populo Iudaico per praedicationem Evangelii ad Christi regnum efficaciter vocaturum ac salvaturum. Sed Petrus non simpliciter & absolutè ponit iustitiam, verùm notanter addit, in iustitia DEI nostri & Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi.

3. Quidam secuti Prosperum lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. ἐνiuxta usitatum Hebraismum positum dicunt proδιὰper iustitiam, ut sensus sit, fidem illamἰσότιμονconversis ad Christum obtigisse per iustitiam h. e. merita ipsius Christi, fides enim est donum DEI in Christo. Caietanus in h. l. Significatur, fidem dari per iustitiam Christi, sive per merita eius, non per opera legis, aut alia quaecunque Naturae viribus facta. Salmero Disp. 1. in hanc Epist. Cornelius â Lapide in h. l. Christus meruit nobis omnem gratiam. Ergo & fidem,Eph. 1. v. 3. Haec expositio fidei analogiae non repugnat. Sed textui non videtur usquequaque conformis.

4. Quidam iustitiae nomen pro misericordia hîc positum statuunt. Emanuel â Sa in h. l. Huic expositioni Estius opponit illud, quòd iustitiae nomen in Scripturis nuspiam misericordiae nomine significetur. Atqui in Scripturis hoc insolens non est. Ps. 40. v. 10.iustitiaἐξηγητικῶς exponitur per misericordiam. Annunciavi iustitiam tuam in coetu multo, non celavi misericordiam & veritatem tuam,Ps. 51. v. 16.Libera me de sanguinibus & praedicabit lingua mea iustitiam tuam.Ps. 71. v. 2.in iustitia tua libera me. Liberatio verò est opus misericordiae divinae. Psal. 143. v. 1. orat David. Exaudi me Domine propter iustitiam tuam, & tamen additv. 2.Ne intres in iudicium cum servo tuo. Inde interpp. frequenter istae vocabula iustitiae & misericordiae DEI in articulo praesertim iustificationis commutant, in eo namque articulo iustitia DEI usurpatur de bonitate & misericòrdia DEI, quâ credentes in Christum absolvit â peccatis, iustitiam Christi ipsis imputat, in gratiam eos recipit. Rom. 1. v. 17.Iustitia Dei revelatur ex fide in fidem. Sic Gen. 19. v. 19. cum Loth diceret ad Angelum in Hebraeo textu, Magnificâsti misericordiam tuam, LXX. reddiderunt δικαιοσύνηνiustitiam. Vicissim Ps. 103. v. 6. cùm David in Hebraeo dixisset, facit iustitias Domin LXX. reddiderunt ἐλεημοσύναςmisericordias. Conferantur loca Gen. 20. v. 13.cap. 21. v. 23.c. 32. v. 10. Hanc licentiam sapientissimi isti viri sibi non sumsissent, si non intellexissent, iustitiam DEI notare eius misericordiam, quâ credentibus benignum & beneficium sese exhibet, Inde Lorinus ad h. l. sic scribit. Acceptionem iustitiae pro misericordiarecipio & exemplis confirmari posse scio.Ps. 30. v. 2.Es. 56. v. 1.Matth. 6. v. 1.2. Cor. 9. v. 10. Frustra igitur huic expositioni Estius opponit, quod destituatur Scripturae exemplis, quamvis huic textui eam ex asse conformem esse, nondum videamus.

5. Estius existimat, ἐνsive in h. l. poni pro cum, quo sensu aliquando praefixum ב apud Hebraeos usurpatur. Deut. 6. v. 7. Loqueris בםcum eis.Ps. 60. v. 12.Non egrederis in i. e. cum exercitibus nostris.Act. 7. v. 38.fuit in h. e. cum Ecclesia.2. Pet. 1. v. 5.ministrate in h. e. cum fide virtutem. Sensus ergo foret, fidem dari cum iustitia i. e. comitante iustitia, quia per fidem iustificamur, quae iustitia est Dei tanquam autoris, & Christi tanquam nobis eam promerentis. Haec expositio sano sensu accepta cum fidei analogia minimè pugnat. Sed Estius & fidei & iustitiae nomen minùs rectè accipit. Fide enim nos iustificari dicit, tanquam qualitate nos ad iustitiam disponente, eamque nobis impetrante; iustitiae nomine intelligit infusum iustitiae habitum.

6. Simplicissimè statuitur, iustitiae nomine hîc intelligi oboedientiam & satisfactionem Christi, quae per fidem nobis ad iustitiam imputatur; sive, quod idem est, iustitiam Christi passione & morte partam, quam fides apprehendit, sibique applicat. Cùm enim in praecedentibus Apostolus dixisset, credentesἰσότιμον πίστινsortitos fuisse, iam ostendit fidei illius obiectum, cuius respectu omnium credentium fides ἰσότιμος dicitur, quod est iustitia Christi, h. e. iustitia per Christi oboedientiam & satisfactionem parta, per fidem autem nobis imputata. Christus estτέλοςfinis & impletio legis adiustitiam omni credenti,Rom. 10. v. 4. h. e. qui credit in Christum, habet quod lex requirit, videlicet perfectam iustitiam coram DEO valentem. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30.Christus factus nobis â Deo iustitia,2. Cor. 5. v. ult.Ut efficiamur iustitia DEI in illo. Hanc expositionem confirmat Arabica huius loci versio, quae sic habet. Illis, qui aequati nobis sunt in honore fidei, quae utique reputata est nobis in veritate DEI & Servatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Lutherus sensum sic expressit, In der Gerechtigkeit die Gott giebt / quod itidem de iustitia per fidem nobis imputata accipi potest. Rom. 3. v. 22. & 24.

Τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτηρίας ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Erasmus existimat, nomine DEI intelligi Deum Patrem, qui est distincta â Christo persona, quo modo in versu seq. hae duae Deitatis personae distinguuntur, Sed rectiùs dicitur, Christum vocari h. l. Deum & Salvatorem nostrum. 1. Quia vox σωτῆρος caret articulo. 2. Quia iustitia illa, quam fides in actu iustificationis amplectitur, non est iustitia DEI essentialis, sed iustitia activâ & passivâ obaedientiâ Christi parta. 3.
