Quia inferiùs in v. 11. huius cap. & in v. 18. cap. 3. eadem duo nomina Christo tribuuntur. 4. Similis repetitio pronominis inserti occurrit Ioh. 20. v. 28. ubi tamen de solo Christo agitur. Ergo ex illa colligi nequit, de distinctis personis hîc sermonem esse.

## 1:1-2 Questions and observations
Observations. 1. Didymus on the Epistle of James, chap. 1. Just as men desiring mortal glory place before their names in their writings the dignities which they are thought to have: so holy men esteem the title of servants of GOD above the rule of the whole world.

2. Truly pious are the Simons, i.e., obedient to the word of Christ; they are Peters, i.e., founded upon Christ, that true rock of salvation, and rooted in faith; they are servants of Christ, serving Him in holiness and righteousness and, out of humility, esteeming themselves the servants of all.

3. Bede in this place: Not legal circumcision, but only Evangelical faith is what associates the peoples of the nations with the ancient people of GOD.

4. To the temptation concerning the weakness of faith, this consolation is to be opposed, that the faith of all who truly believe is ἰσότιμος, because it embraces the same Christ and perceives the same benefits in Him.

5. Augustine in Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, volume 4, refers this form of salutation to the mystery of the Trinity. He understands the Father under the appellation of GOD: the Son under the name of Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit under the terms of the gifts which are expressed in the salutation, because it is predicated of the Holy Spirit by attribution that He is the gift.

6. The foundation of peace, i.e., of a peaceful and quiet conscience, is the grace of GOD procured for us through Christ, offered in the word of the Gospel, and apprehended through faith.

7. The knowledge of the true GOD and of Christ is undivided. John 17. verse 3.1. John 2. v. 23.

The remaining things, which pertain to the inscription and salutation, have been expounded in the narration of the former Epistle.

Latin:

Observationes. 1. Didymus in Epist. Iac. cap. 1. Sicut mortalem gloriam appetentes homines in suis conscriptionibus dignitates, quas putantur habere, praeponunt: ita sancti viri appellationem servorum DEI supra regnatotius mundi aestimant.

2. Verè pii sunt Simones i. e. verbo Christi obedientes; sunt Petri i. e. super Christum veram illam salutis petram fundati & in fide radicati; sunt servi Christi, in sanctitate & iustitia ipsi servientes & ex humilitate omnium servos sese aestimantes.

3. Beda in h. l. Non circumcisio legalis, sed sola est fides Evangelica, quae gentium populos antiquae plebi DEI consociat.

4. Tantationi de infirmitate fidei opponenda haec consolatio, quòd omnium verè credentium fides sit ἰσότιμος, quia eundem Christum amplectitur & eadem in ipso beneficia percipit.

5. Augustinus in Exposit. Epist. ad Rom. tom. 4. refert hanc salutationis formam ad mysterium Trinitatis. Patrem intelligit, sub appellatione DEI: Filium sub nomine Iesu Christi, Spiritum Sanctum sub vocabulis donorum, quae in salutatione experimuntur, quia de Spiritu sancto per attributionem praedicatur, quòd sit donum.

6. Fundamentum pacis h. e. pacificae & quietae conscientiae est gratia DEI per Christum nobis parta, in verbo Evangelii oblata & per fidem apprehensa.

7. Cognitio veri DEI & Christi est indivisa. Iohann. 17. vers. 3.1. Iohan. 2. v. 23.

Reliqua, quae ad inscriptionem & salutationem pertinent, exposita sunt in prioris Epistolae enarratione.

## 1:2
Exposition of the text. By χάριν in such Apostolic salutations is understood the gratuitous favor of GOD, by which he embraces us in Christ, forgiving our sins, justifying and saving us by grace; by Εἰρήνην that principal benefit of divine grace, which being justified by faith we have peace with God Rom. 5. vers. 1. and τὸ Πληθυντῆναι is used both concerning multiplication in discrete quantity; and concerning increase in continuous quantity, we showed in the narration of the former Epistle cap. 1. v. 2. For πληθυντείῃ be multiplied, the Vulgate seems to have read πλειρωθείῃ: for it rendered it, be fulfilled.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν. Certain Greek Codices, as also the German version, have the added name Christ. The Syriac having omitted the little word τοῦ Θεοῦ, he rendered it simply, in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. Some translate ἐπίγνωσιν in this place as super-knowledge, for the reason that the faithful ought to have a certain superior and higher knowledge, exceeding that which the Gentiles had of God, since the knowledge of the Gentiles is from the light of Nature, but that of Christians from the light of Grace. But the compound ἐπίγνωσις is used according to the common custom of Scripture for the simple, namely for γνώσει. Rom. 3. v. 20.cap. 10. v. 2. Furthermore, some explain the phrase ἐν ἐπιγνώσῃ in the same way as the preceding ἐν διηαιοσύνῃ, together with the acknowledgment of Christ, so that he may wish for both grace and peace and the acknowledgment of Christ to be multiplied in them. But it is more correctly taken for διά ἐπιγνώσεως through the acknowledgment of Christ, so that the sense may be: May grace and peace be multiplied to you through faith, which is the saving acknowledgment of GOD, and of whom He sent, our Savior Jesus Christ. Ioh. 17. v. 3. For faith, through which we acknowledge GOD and His Son our Savior Christ Jesus, is that saving medium through which we are rendered participants of divine grace, and stand and are preserved in grace, from which also peace with GOD and tranquility of conscience is obtained by us. Rom. 5. v. 1. In the same way Luther also rendered it. Durch das Erkäntniß Gottes und Jesu Christi.

Q. in this place: With respect to whom does the Apostle say that those to whom he writes have obtained a faith equal to his own? Resp. 1. Some wish respect to be had to the Apostles, that with them all the faithful have obtained an equally precious faith, although by reason of the Apostolic office they are inferior to them. 2. Estius and others think respect is had to the faithful converted from Judaism to Christ, still living in Judea, that the Jews placed in the dispersion are equal in calling and faith to the first faithful living in Judea. 3. It seems simpler to establish that these things are said of the Gentiles converted to Christ, whom the Apostle says to have received an equally precious faith with the Apostles and the converted Jews, inasmuch as they were assumed into the same faith and hope of salvation with the faithful Jews. For we showed in the exposition of the former Epistle that both of Peter's Epistles were indeed written principally to the Jews, meanwhile, however, because after their conversion to Christ not only proselytes, but also Gentiles communicated with the Jews believing in Christ as brothers, and constituted one Church with them, and thus had bishops in common with them, therefore also secondarily And less principally both Epistles were also written to converted Gentiles, as is evident from 1. Epist. 2. v. 10. and other places of both Epistles. Just as therefore Paul Eph. 2. v. 19. says concerning converted Gentiles, that they are no longer guests and strangers, but citizens of the saints and domestics of GOD, and v. 14. that Christ, who is our peace, hath made both that is to say, Jews and Gentiles, one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition, so Peter in this place says, that those converted from Gentilism have obtained a faith equally precious with those Jews converted to Christ. Compare 1. Epist. 2. v. 5. & seqq. up to v. 11.

Ἐναντιοφαν. 1. Since faith has its degrees, and one is strong, another weak, Matth. 8. v. 10. cap. 15. v. 28. how can the faith of different believers be ἰσότιμος.

Resp. 1. Lyranus ἰσοτιμίαν establishes that of faith in this, that in the N. T. the distinction between Jews and Gentiles has been removed Act. 10. v. 35. Rom. 10. v. 12. 2. Faith is considered either by reason of degrees; or by reason of the object, which it embraces; by reason of the equal virtue to justify and save, and by reason of the reward, which follows. By reason of degrees, one faith is strong, another weak. By reason of the object, namely the righteousness of Christ, which it apprehends, the faith of all believers is ἰσότιμος. Luther declares this with an elegant similitude. A giant embraces a gem enclosed in a golden ring, a little boy also embraces it. Although the giant may embrace it more strongly than the little boy, nevertheless the ring remains equally precious and the gem equally precious, whether the giant or the little boy embraces it. By reason of the equal virtue to justify and save, as also by reason of the reward, likewise the faith of all believers is ἰσότιμος, because for all true believers the reward remains the same, namely the enjoyment of God. To this parity of reward the Apostle seems to look primarily here, because Τιμὴ signifies price and reward.

2. Grace, or that gratuitous favor, by which God embraces believers in Christ, does not receive more and less, but behaves itself in the same way toward all believers, since the Apostle says they ἰσότιμον have received faith. In what sense therefore does the Apostle wish for grace to be increased for them?

Resp. The Apostle prays for them, that from the word of the Gospel, which is the word of grace, Act. 20. v. 32. through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of grace Zach. 12. v. 10. they may feel that grace of GOD more and more in their soul, and be confirmed in it; and that the gifts of grace may be increased in them from time to time.

Ἔλεγχος 1. Paul Rom. 1. v. 1. calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and his called Apostle.2. Cor. v. 1.Col. 1. v. 1.2. Tim. 1. v. 1. a called Apostle of Christ through the will of GodGal. 1. v. 1. an Apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father,Phil. 1. v. 1. a servant of Christ,1. Tim. 1. v. 1. an Apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and the Lord Jesus Christ. James calls himself a servant of GOD and of the Lord Jesus Christchap. 1. v. 1. Peter in this place calls himself a servant and Apostle of Jesus Christ, Jude a servant of Jesus ChristEpist. v. 1. which comparison ἰσοτιμίαν καὶ ὁμοουσίαν between God and Christ, and consequently also clearly proves the true divinity of Christ.

2. The carnal boasting of the Jews is brought low by the faith of the ἰσότιμον Gentiles.

3. Christ is called our God and our Savior; by both names his true divinity is established.

4. The proper and adequate object of justifying faith is the righteousness of Christ, that is, his holy obedience, which he performed for us by acting and suffering. Against the Papists.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Estius on v. 1 notes thus: That Peter should bring in here a mention of his primacy was not at all opportune. Resp. 1. Nay rather, if a Monarchical primacy of the Church had been given to Peter by Christ, he would have made mention of it here entirely, for he was engaged in confirming the brethren Luke 22. v. 32. whence the same Estius in his commentary on the 1st Epistle of Peter says, the cause of the writing was this, that Peter, as the Apostle of the circumcision and Pastor of all the faithful, because of the grave persecutions stirred up against the faithful, especially the Jews in those parts, might exhort them through this Epistle to patience and confirm them in the faith. And from that confirmation of the brethren entrusted to Peter by Christ, the Papists attempt to elicit his primacy. Salm. Disp. 1. on 1. Epistle of Peter. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Rom. Pont. c. 22. praerogat. 8. With these words, When you have turned, confirm your brethren, the Lord most clearly shows that Peter would be the Prince and head of his brethren. 2. Lorinus on the same verse argues against those who, from the fact that Peter says he has received an equally precious faith with the rest of the faithful, rise up against the primacy of Peter, to whom he replies, primacy does not consist in the internal gifts of sanctifying glory, but in jurisdiction. But none of us uses this argument.

Latin:

Textus expositio. Per χάριν in huiusmodi salutationibus Apostolicis intelligi favorem DEI gratuitum, quo nos in Christo complectitur, peccata nobis remittens, ex gratia nos iustificans & salvans; per Εἰρήνην praecipuum illud gratiae divinae beneficium, quod iustificati fide pacem habemus apud DeumRom. 5. vers. 1. ac τὸ Πληθυντῆναι usurpari tum de multiplicatione in quantitate discreta; tum de augmento in quantitate continua, ostendimus in enarratione prioris Epistolae cap. 1. v. 2. Pro πληθυντείῃmultiplicetur, Vulgata legisse videtur πλειρωθείῃ: reddidit enim, impleatur.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν. Quidam Codd. Graeci, ut & Germ. versio habent additum nomen Christi. Syrus omissâ voculâ τοῦ Θεοῦ simpliciter reddidit, in cognitione Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quidam ἐπίγνωσιν h. l. vertunt supercognitionem, eò quod fideles debeant habere superiorem & altiorem quandam cognitionem, excedentem illam quam Ethnici de Deo habuerunt, cùm Ethnicorum cognitio sit ex lumine Naturae, Christianorum verò ex lumine Gratiae. Sed compositum ἐπίγνωσις vulgato Scripturae more ponitur pro simplice, videlicet pro γνώσει.Rom. 3. v. 20.cap. 10. v. 2. Caeterùm phrasin ἐν ἐπιγνώσῃ quidam eodem modo ut praecedentem ἐν διηαιοσύνῃ exponunt, unà cùm agnitione Christi, ut sic & gratiam & pacem & Christi agnitionem in illis multiplicari exoptet. Sed rectiùs accipitur pro διά ἐπιγνώσεως per agnitionem Christi, ut sit sensus. Gratia & pax vobis multiplicetur per fidem, quae est salvifica agnitio DEI, & quem ille misit, Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Ioh. 17. v. 3. Fides enim, per quam DEUM & eius Filium Salvatorem nostrum Christum Iesum agnoscimus, est salutare illud medium, per quod gratiae divinae participes reddimur, & in gratia stamus ac conservamur, ex qua etiam pax cum DEO & tranquillitas conscientiae nobis obtingit. Rom. 5. v. 1. Eodem modo etiam Lutherus reddidit. Durch das Erkäntniß Gottes und Jesu Christi.

Q. h. l. Quorum respectu dicat Apostolus, eos ad quos scribit, aequalem secum fidem fuisse sortitos? Resp. 1. Quidam volunt, respectum haberi ad Apostolos, quod cum illis omnes fideles aequè preciosam sortiti sint fidem, licet ratione Apostolici muneris illis sint inferiores. 2. Estius & alii existimant, respectum haberi ad fideles ex Iudaismo ad Christum conversos, in Iudaea adhuc habitantes, quod Iudaei in dispersione positi primis fidelibus in Iudaea habitantibus vocatione & fide pares sint. 3. Simplicius videtur statuere, quòd haec dicantur de gentilibus ad Christum conversis, quos Apostolus dicit, aequè preciosam fidem cum Apostolis & conversis Iudaeis accepisse, utpote assumtos ad eandem fidem & spem salutis cum Iudaeis fidelibus. Ostendimus enim in enarratione prioris Epistolae, esse quidem utramque Petri Epistolam principaliter scriptam ad Iudaeos, interim tamen, quia post suam ad Christum conversionem non solùm proselyti, sed etiam gentiles cum Iudaeis in Christum credentibus tanquam fratres communicabant, & unam cum illis Ecclesiam constituebant, adeoque communes cum illis Episcopos habebant, ideò etiam secundariò & & minùs principaliter utramque Epistolam etiam ad conversos gentiles esse scriptam, uti patet ex 1. Epist. 2. v. 10. & aliis utriusque Epistolae locis. Quemadmodum ergo Paulus Eph. 2. v. 19. de conversis gentibus dicit, quòd non ampliùs sint hospites & advenae, sed cives sanctorum & domestici DEI, acv. 14.quod Christus, qui est pax nostra, fecerit utraque h. e. Iudaeos & gentiles, unum, ac medium parietem materiae solverit, ita Petrus hoc loco dicit, quod conversi ex gentilismo aequè preciosam cum conversis ad Christum Iudaeis fidem sint sortiti. Confer 1. Epist. 2. v. 5. & seqq. usque ad v. 11.

Ἐναντιοφαν. 1. Cum fides habeat suos gradus, & alia sit fortis, alia infirma,Matth. 8. v. 10.cap. 15. v. 28.quomodo diversorum credentium potestesse fidesἰσότιμος.

Resp. 1. Lyranus ἰσοτιμίανillam fidei in eo statuit, quòd in N. T. discrimen inter Iudaeos & gentiles sit sublatumAct. 10. v. 35.Rom. 10. v. 12. 2. Fides consideratur vel ratione graduum; vel ratione obiecti, quod amplectitur; ratione aequalis ad iustificandum & salvandum virtutis, & ratione praemii, quod consequitur. Ratione graduum, fides alia est fortis, alia infirma. Ratione obiecti, videlicet iustitiae Christi, quam apprehendit, omnium credentium fides est ἰσότιμος. Lutherus hoc declarat eleganti similitudine. Gemmam annulo aureo inclusam amplectitur gigas, amplectitur & puerulus. Licet gigas fortiùs eam amplectatur, quàm puerulus, tamen manet annulus aequè preciosus & gemma aequè preciosa, sive gigas, sive puerulus eum amplectatur. Ratione aequalis ad iustificandum & salvandum virtutis, uti etiam ratione praemii itidem omnium credentium fides est ἰσότιμος, quia omnes verè fideles idem manet praemium, videlicet Dei fruitio. Ad hanc praemii paritatem Apostolus potissimùm hîc respicere videtur, quia Τιμὴ significat precium ac praemium.

2. Gratia, seu gratuitus ille favor, quo Deus credentes in Christum complectitur, non recipit magis & minus, sed hahet se eodem modo erga omnes credentes, quippe quos Apostolus dicit, ἰσότιμονfidem accepisse. Quo igitur sensu Apostolus exoptat gratiam illis augeri?

Resp. Precatur eis Apostolus, ut ex verbo Evangelii, quod est verbum gratiae,Act. 20. v. 32. per efficaciam Spiritus sancti, qui est Spiritus gratiaeZach. 12. v. 10. illam DEI gratiam magis ac magis in animo sentiant, & in ea confirmentur; atque ut dona gratiae subinde in illis augeantur.

Ἔλεγχος 1. Paulus Rom. 1. v. 1. sese vocat servum Iesu Christi & vocatum eius Apostolum.2. Cor. v. 1.Col. 1. v. 1.2. Tim. 1. v. 1.vocatum Apostolum Christi per voluntatem DeiGal. 1. v. 1.Apostolum non ab hominibus neque per hominem, sed per Iesum Christum & Deum Patrem,Phil. 1. v. 1.Servum Christi,1. Tim. 1. v. 1.Apostolum Iesu Christi secundùm imperium Dei Salvatoris nostri & Domini Iesu Christi. Iacobus se vocat DEI & Domini Iesu Christi servumcap. 1. v. 1. Petrus hoc loco se appellat servum & Apostolum Iesu Christi, Iudas servum Iesu ChristiEpist. v. 1. quae collatio ἰσοτιμίαν καὶ ὁμοουσίαν inter Deum & Christum, ac proinde etiam veram Christi divinitatem evidenter comprobat.

2. Iudaeorum carnalis gloriatio per ἰσότιμον gentilium fidem deprimitur.

3. Christus Deus noster & Salvator noster vocatur, utroque nomine vera eius divinitas stabilitur.

4. Fidei iustificantis proprium & adaequatum obiectum est Christi iustitia h. e. sancta ipsius oboedientia, quam agendo & patiendo pro nobis praestitit. Contra Pontificios.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Estius ad v. 1. sic annotat. Ut Petrus sui primatus mentionem huc inferret, haud erat oportunum. Resp. 1. imò verò, si Petro Monarchicus Ecclesiae primatus â Christo fuisset datus, eius h. l. omninò mentionem fecisset, versabatur enim in confirmandis fratribus Luc. 22. v. 32. unde idem Estius in comm. 1. Epist. Petri dicit, causam scriptionis fuisse hanc, ut Petrus velut Apostolus circumcisionis & omnium fidelium Pastor ob graves persecutiones adversus fideles, maximè Iudaeos in illis partibus excitatas, eos per hanc Epistolam ad patientiam exhortaretur & in fide confirmaret. Atque ex illa fratrum confirmatione Petro â Christo demandata primatum eius elicere Pontificii conantur. Salm. Disp. 1. in 1. Epist. Petri. Bellarm. lib. 1. de Rom. Pont. c. 22. praerogat. 8. His verbis, Tu conversus confirma fratres tuos, clarissimè Dom. ostendit, Petrum fore Principem & caput fratrum suorum 2. Lorinus ad eund. v. disputat adversus illos, qui ex eo, quod Petrus cum reliquis fidelib aequè preciosam fidem se accepisse dicit, contra primatum Petri insurgunt, quibus respondet, primatum non consistere in internis gloriae sanctificantis donis, sed in iurisdictione. At nemo nostrùm hoc argumento utitur.

## 1:3-4
Connection. 1. Many of the Interpreters join this little verse with the preceding ones and consequently determine that it pertains to the prologue of the Epistle. The reason for the connection could be given as twofold, so that it may be referred either to what is more remote, or to what is more immediate. To the more immediate, see to the Apostolic salutation, in this way. There is no reason why you should doubt this wish of mine, by which I desire for you the multiplication of grace and peace through the knowledge of Christ, will be effective, because God has already previously granted to you out of grace those things which make for life and godliness. Gagnaeus on this passage: Grace and peace of God be fulfilled in you, through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior, just as by His divine power, whatsoever things look toward life and godliness have been granted to you through the knowledge of Him. Gretser, volume 1, Defens. Bellarm., book 2, on the Word of God, chapter 14, page 751, in order to assert the authority of the Vulgate Version, likewise connects these words with those immediately preceding, in this way: Grace and peace be so multiplied to you, as all things of His divine power have been granted to you. Cornel. à Lapide on this passage: Grace and peace be fulfilled to you, how i.e., in the same manner, or just as through this knowledge of God and Christ all divine gifts, which pertain to life and godliness, have been granted to you, so that τό ὡς may be ἐξηγητικὸν, corresponding to the Hebrew כאשר To the more remote, namely to the description of those to whom he writes, in this way: I said, you have obtained equally precious faith in the justice of Christ. That is from this, that God has granted to you out of grace those things which pertain to life and godliness through the saving knowledge of Himself.

2. But because it is the custom for the Apostles to complete a salutation in a few words, and immediately to approach the argument of the Epistle, as appears from the Epistles of Paul, Jude, and the first Epistle of Peter himself, therefore it is more correctly determined that the πραγματείαν, itself of the Epistle, namely its first part, which contains νουθεσίαν for constancy and progress in faith and the pursuit of godliness, begins from this verse 3, according to which hypothesis the meaning of this verse hangs until the beginning of verse 5, in which finally the same is completed.

3. Therefore, in this first νουθεσίας part, the Apostle commemorates the divine benefits which those to whom he writes had long since received from God out of grace, by which commemoration he desires to excite them, so that they may apply themselves with the greatest zeal to that to which he exhorts them.

Disposition. The Apostle exaggerates these divine benefits 1. from the power of the giver. 2. from the heap of gifts. 3. from the means of the donation, which is the divine calling. 4. from the fruit and effect of the gifts.

Exposition of the text. ὡς πάντα ἡμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης. The particle ὡς

1. Some wish it to be of one admiring or exclaiming, through which the Apostle, full of wonder, bursts forth into the proclamation of divine benefits.

Salmero strives to confirm this meaning of the particle ὡς with many examples, Psal. 119. v. 97.Thren. 1. v. 1. Item Psal. 73. v. 1. & 19.Psal. 84. v. 1.Psal. 119. v. 108. But most are irrelevant, and, which is the head of the matter, such exclamations, formed by the particle ὡς, do not occur elsewhere in the openings of the Apostolic Epistles.

2. Most establish that it is a particle of likeness, corresponding to the little word καθὼς, by which the Apostle begins the first Epistle to Timothy, ἐργασίαν as.1. Tim. 1. v. 3. Following this sense, the Vulgate Interpreter rendered it by as.

According to this hypothesis, in v. 5. the particle οὔτως, ἀπόδοσιν would have to be understood, expressing and completing the sentence in this sense. Just as GOD has conferred extraordinary benefits upon you, namely by most kindly bestowing upon you all things which make for life and godliness: so also you ought to apply yourselves with all care and solicitude to this, that those gifts of GOD may remain and grow in you.

3. It is most simply established that the particle ὡς in this place serves for an inference, and signifies the same as ἐπεὶ after that or since, and that τὸ καὶ corresponds to it at the beginning of v. 5. so that the sense is: After that, or since his divine power has given us all things which (pertain) to life and godliness, therefore you ought to confer all zeal upon this, that you may do what God requires of you. In this meaning the particle ὡς is used, Luc. 1. v. 23. ὡς ἐπλείσθησαν αί ἡμέραι. v. 44. ὡς ἐγένετο ἡ φωνὴ. cap. 2. v. 15. ὡς ἐπῆλθαν οἱ Ἄγγελοι. cap. 4. v. 25. ὡς ἐγένετο λιμὸς. cap. 5. vers. 4. ὡς ἐπαύσατο λαλῶν. In the same sense the Syriac rendered it [איך מן] as indeed i. e. since. Luther nach dem.

Some refer the pronoun αὐτοῦ to Christ, whom the Apostle had called our Lord toward the end of the preceding verse, whom the Apostle proves from that to be true God and our Savior, because his divine power has given us all things which pertain to life and godliness. Some to God the Father, of whom mention is likewise made in the preceding verse. Neither opinion is opposed to the analogy of faith or to the context, since it is a matter of an external work; which is common to the three persons of the Godhead.

Some take the participle δεδωρημένης passively, and translate the text thus: After all things of his divine power (namely εὐεργετήματα καὶ χαρίσματα, benefits and effects) which pertain to life and godliness, have been given to us. By which reasoning, instead of a participle of the second case δεδωρημένης, one would have to read a participle of the fourth case δεδωρημένα,, as Lorinus testifies he read in some codices, and it would have to be explained by the verb δεδώρηται.; for it is known that, according to the custom of the Hebrews, participles are very often placed for verbs. The Vulgate version rendered it in this sense: How his divine power, which pertains to life and godliness, has been given to us. (In some Latin codices, however, the singular has been given is held, just as Bede also makes mention of that double reading in his commentary, but the singular has nothing to which it corresponds.) Luther rendered it in the same way: Nach dem allerlei seiner Göttlichen Krafft uns geschencket ist.. But indeed, because the verb δεδώρηται is more frequently used in an active signification (in which sense it is also explained by the Vulgate Interpreter in the verse immediately following, δι' ὧν τὰ μέγιστα ἡμῖν καὶ τίμια ἐπαγγέλματα δεδώρηται, he has given to us) and is otherwise also customary among the Greeks to use past passives in an active signification Heb. 12. v. 26. νῦν ἐπήγγελται,, therefore it is more correctly taken actively in this place also, so that the sense may be: After his divine power has given to us all things which pertain to life and godliness, that is, Since GOD has given to us heavenly force and power out of his mere goodness, so that by the help of the Holy Spirit we might be able to live piously in this age, and through faith apprehend eternal life. Or, which comes to the same thing, After his divine power has bestowed upon us all things which pertain to life and godliness (namely, we have been enriched in all things 1. Cor. 1. v. 5.). According to this hypothesis, δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ is referred to the order of the efficient cause and the author giving, which is more harmonious than if it is referred to the gifts themselves or the effects of the giver, which is done by the former exposition. The Syrian, however, who likewise takes δεδωρημένης actively, seems to refer divine power among the gifts, for thus he rendered the text: As indeed he has given all those things which are of divine power, for life and the fear of GOD.

Τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν. Robert Stephanus testifies, for ζωὴν in some Codices πρὸς εἰρήνην. is read. By this προσδιορισμὸν the universal particle πάντα is as it were restricted, so that those things which make for, or pertain to, life and godliness are understood to be given to us by divine power: for this is the force of the Greek phrase τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν.

By ζωὴν can be understood both the spiritual life and that which is pleasing to GOD, to be led in this world by the pious, which Paul Eph. 4. v. 18. calls the life of GOD or from GOD; according to which exposition the little word καὶ would be placed ἐξηγητικῶς: and also eternal life itself, promised to those believing in Christ, and demonstrating faith through the pursuit of godliness. The former is the principle and part of godliness, the latter indeed the consequence. Divine power has given to us out of grace those things which contribute to both lives.

Διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ἡμᾶς. Some understand this of the knowledge of GOD the Father, to whom we are led through Christ. Iohan. 14. v. 9. He who sees me, sees the Father. They refer the preceding pronoun αὐτοῦ to Christ. Others indeed accept it of the knowledge of Christ, through whom all things looking toward life and godliness are given to us. They refer the preceding pronoun αὐτοῦ to God the Father. Neither exposition is repugnant to the analogy of faith, or to the text, because in the preceding verses mention was made of both GOD and Christ. Furthermore, by ἐπίγνωσιν of him who called us, is not understood a bare knowledge, since through that alone and bare, those things which look toward life and godliness do not yet befall anyone, but knowledge joined with assent and trust, or a fiducial apprehension of Christ, i.e., justifying and saving faith, which is therefore called ἐπίγνωσις, because knowledge is a part of it, through which the whole συνεκδοχικῶς is expressed. Esai. 53. v. 11. Ioh. 17. v. 3. The sense therefore is that God has given us all things looking toward life and godliness through faith in Christ, just as he had said in the preceding verse, that grace and peace may be multiplied through the knowledge of GOD and CHRIST, to which pertains the saying of Christ just cited Iohann. 17. v. 3. This is eternal life.

By calling in this place is understood that to which, on the part of men, the obedience of faith responds, i.e., Calling is here considered not only by reason of the term from which, namely of GOD calling, offering to all in the word of the Gospel the spiritual benefits obtained by the passion and death of his Son: but also by reason of the term to which, namely of men of the called, who embrace the benefits offered by faith in the word of the Gospel, which Paul 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. describes thus. GOD called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus, before the secular times. The Papists and Calvinists call it an efficacious calling, and they distinguish it from an inefficacious calling. But this distinction must be rightly explained, lest the cause of that, if I may so speak, inefficacy be sought in some absolute decree of reprobation, but in men alone, who refuse to embrace the benefits offered in the Gospel, and to give place to the divine calling.

Διὰ δόξης καί ἀρετῆς. The Vulgate rendered it by his own glory and virtue. Prosper in his Epistle to Demetrias and against the Collator, chapter 29, by the virtue of his own glory. But the word ίδίας is not held in the Greek text. That this reading was found in a few Codices, and those of doubtful faith, ἰδίᾳ δόξῃ καὶ ἀρετῇ, Beza mentions in his annotations. Some think the particle διὰ is placed for πρὸς or εἰς, so that διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀρετῆς is the same as πρὸς δόξαν καὶ ἀρετὴν, since the prefix ב among the Hebrews signifies ἐν, εἰς, πρὸς, διά, περὶ, Rom. 6. v. 4. They think, therefore, that by these words the same thing is signified as in those immediately preceding by ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν. For what he had named there ζωὴν, the Apostle in this place calls δόξαν, and what he had named there εὐσέβειαν, he calls in this place ἀρετὴν. According to this opinion, the end of the calling would be expressed by these words, which consists in this, that in this life we may study good works and virtues, and after this life we may be rendered participants of eternal glory. Eph. 4. v. 1. Walk worthily of the calling.

But here προσδιορισμὸς is more rightly referred to God calling, than to men called, In the exposition, however, some diversity still occurs.

1. Bede in his commentary on this place annotates thus. He called us by his own glory and virtue, because he did not send an Angel for our salvation, he did not send an Archangel, he did not find in us any merit of good, for which we might be saved, but rather seeing us weak and inglorious, he recovered us by his own virtue and glory.

2. Dionysius the Carthusian thinks that αὐτοπροσώπως insinuates the Son of GOD and in the proper glory of his majesty joined with human Nature to have come, that he might redeem us, and call us to himself. Both insist on the Vulgate version, which has by his own glory and virtue.

3. Some understand by glory that majesty of Christ, of which the Apostle treats in v. 17. & following: by power they understand the virtue which Christ demonstrated in miracles, for by both he confirmed the Gospel, by which we have been called.

4. Salmeron in almost the same way understands by glory and virtue the divinity and majesty of Christ, since the calling of the Apostles was not done without a miracle, in which the glory and majesty of Christ shone. Luc. 5. v. 10.

5. The same man brings forward another sense, which he prefers to the former: The perfect, he says, justice of Christ, by which he lived on earth, and his glory, which the Disciples saw before and after the passion, and in the transfiguration and resurrection and his miracles shining, called the Apostles and through them all. But both of Salmeron's expositions are opposed by the fact that Peter here is not speaking of a special calling to the Apostleship, but of a general calling, and one common to all believers to Christianity.

6 Some refer the name of both glory and virtue to the Gospel, inasmuch as it is called the glory and power of God Rom. 1. v. 16. 2. Cor. 3. v. 8. 1. Tim. 1. v. 11.

7. By virtue most understand the power of GOD, so that glory and power through a customary Hebraism and the figure ένδιαδὺς may be the same as glorious power of GOD, ἀρετὴ for in GOD is the same as ἡ θεία δύναμις, says Hesychius.

8. But because δύναμις differs from ἀρετῇ in meaning, and since calling is attributed in the Scriptures not so much to power as to divine grace and mercy, therefore the name ἀρετῆς is more correctly taken in that sense in which Peter in his former Epistle cap. 2. v. 9. uses it, namely for Φιλανθρωπία, καὶ Χρηστότητι τοῦ Θεοῦ, as the Apostle calls it, Tit. 3. v. 4. for the kindness, mercy and clemency of GOD, which he demonstrated in the gratuitous calling. Since we ought to celebrate that with perpetual proclamations of praise, just as also in the place just alleged Peter says that we ought to announce the virtues of him who called us to his marvelous light, therefore it is joined to it in this place δόξα, in the sense that it is glorious virtue, that is, to be perpetually glorified by us. The Syrian has the name [מיתרותא] which he also uses a little later in v. 5., when we are commanded to exhibit virtue in faith, where Dionys.

the commentator notes, that this is a general name for all good actions and works.

V 4. Δι' ὧν τὰ μέγιστα ἡμῖν καὶ τίμια ἐπαγγέλματα δεδώρηται.

Δι' ὧν. 1. Certain Latin Codices have through whom, who without doubt read δι'οὗ, in the Greek, which reading Athanasius hints at in oration 2 against the Arians, and Lorinus and Cornelius à Lapide in their commentary judge it to be genuine. Robertus Stephanus noted that one Codex had δι' ὅν through whom, namely Christ, in whom are all the promises of GOD ναί καί Αμὴν 2. Cor. 1. v. 20. 2. Bede in his commentary on this place reads, through which, (namely θεοῦ ἐπίγνωσιν ) from which he gathers that the more perfectly one knows GOD, the more deeply he perceives the greatness of His promises. Ambrose reads in the same way, or rather Prosper in Epistle 33 to Demetrias. 3. But the reading of one Codex, or even of a few Codices, is not to be preferred to more and more approved Codices. Those indeed have δι' ὧν through which, namely His glory and virtue God has given to us the greatest and precious promises, that is to say, φιλανθρωπία and kindness impelled God, so that He might give the greatest and precious things to us.

Erasmus takes the word δεδώρηται passively, but it is more correctly taken actively, in which way the Vulgate also rendered it, so that it may be referred to GOD calling, of whom mention had been made in the verse immediately preceding.

By τὰ ἐπαγγέλματα μετωνυμικῶς are understood the promised goods, for speaking properly, promises are not given, but the goods which had been promised; thus Hebr. 10. v. 26. to carry back the promises, is to carry back the promised goods. Moreover, those promised goods are spiritual and heavenly gifts, which according to the promise made to the Fathers in the O. T., and so often repeated by the Prophets, the Son of GOD was to bring in His advent and incarnation, which are the redemption of the human race, reconciliation with God, the remission of sins, adoption into the sons of God, the gift of righteousness and eternal life, 2. Cor. 1. v. 20. 1. Iohan. 2. v. 25. not that in the O. T. no one became a partaker of those benefits through faith, the contrary of which even the example of Abraham alone shows, Rom. 4. v. 1. and following, but because the Son of God in assumed flesh through His passion and death in the N. T. finally merited them, but that passion of Christ was profitable before it existed. The Syrian rendered it, through which [שוודעא] he gave you great knowledges and honors. But Pococke in his commentary warns that it must be written [שוודיא] promises, since this error of the Scribe was easy from the extension of a single little line. These things are called ἐπαγγέλματα, that is, promised goods μέγιστα καί τίμια,, with respect had to temporal and bodily benefits, concerning which likewise divine promises exist, but which are in no way to be compared with these spiritual, heavenly, and eternal benefits.

Ἵνα διὰ τούτων γένηθαι θείας κοινωνοί φύσεως. The end of those greatest and precious promises is expressed by these words, which is θείας φύσεως κοινωνία. Διά τούτων ἐπαγγελμάτων through those promises fulfilled and performed in the work itself. Luther refers to the whole preceding speech, rendering it thus, durch dasselbe. In the word γένηθε the Apostle passes from the first person, which he had used in the preceding, to the second person, which does not lack emphasis. For lest anyone should think that the Apostles alone were made participants of this honor and benefit, Peter therefore notably says that the believers, to whom he writes, have arrived at the fellowship of the same honor and benefit. Bede in his commentary on this place: He suddenly changes the person, which he does not do by chance, but providently. Therefore, he says, the Lord gave to us, who by nature are Jews, who were born under the law, who were imbued by his teaching even bodily, and who revealed all the secrets of his divine power; therefore he gave to us, namely his disciples, the greatest and precious promises of his Spirit, so that through these even you, who are from the Gentiles, who could not see him bodily, might be granted to be participants of his divine nature, namely with us teaching you what we heard from him, and consecrating you through his mysteries. But in what that τῆς θείας φύσεως κοινωνία, consists will be explained in the question a little later.

Ἀποφυγόντες τῆς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς. Some translate the participle ἀποφυγόντες, conditionally, if you shall have escaped, just as Luther also rendered it, so ihr fliehet die vergängliche Lust. For those finally are and remain partakers of the divine nature, who flee the corruption which dominates in the world through evil concupiscence, by which reasoning Peter would say the same thing that John 1. Epist. 1. v. 5.God is light and there are no darknesses in him,v. 6.if we say that κοινωνίαν we have with him, and walk in darkness, we lie,v. 7.But if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, κοινωνίαν we have with one another. God is the highest purity, incorruptible cleanliness. If we say that we have κοινωνίαν with him, and we indulge in the corrupt and depraved concupiscences of the flesh with the world, we lie. But if we flee the corruption of concupiscence which is in the world, just as he himself is pure and incorrupt, we have κοινωνίαν with one another.

But it is more correctly said that τό ἀποφυγόντες in this place is to be translated not so much conditionally and hypothetically, as assertively and categorically, in this way: When you have fled, or after you have fled the corruption of concupiscence, in which way the Syrian also rendered it, [כד ערקין] when you have fled the corruption of concupiscences. For the Apostle is not yet engaged in exhorting, but in preaching divine benefits, from which preaching he afterwards finally infers an exhortation. He teaches, therefore, that through that τῆς θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν, this benefit has been obtained by those believing in Christ, that they have fled the concupiscences of the flesh and the world, to which he afterwards chap. 2. v. 19. opposes those who are δοῦλοι τῆς φθορᾶς and v. 20. who are again entangled in the defilements of the world, which they had fled.

By φθορὰν 1. Some understand destruction or ruin, since the Apostle seems to have wished to oppose two things to two things, namely φθορὰν τῇ ζωῇ, καί τῇ δόξῃ, ἐπιθυμίαν truly εὐσεβείᾳ καί ἀρετὴ in v. 3.in which sense they also think that the name φθορᾶς is to be taken chap. 2. of this Epistle v. 19.

2. Some think that by φθορὰν here is understood that baseness by which human nature is dishonored and corrupted through foul and illicit lusts, since this Epistle is opposed to Simon Magus and his followers, who permit, or rather teach, foul and filthy lusts of the flesh.

3. But it is more correctly said that by φθορὰν in general is understood the whole genus of depraved concupiscence, as the added word ἐπιθυμίας. shows. For they should certainly take heed, and must take heed, not only from foul lusts, but from all the works of the flesh, who through faith in Christ have been made ὑιοθεσίας participants, and through the Holy Spirit are born again and renewed, Gal. 5, v. 24. Those who are Christ's, have crucified the flesh with the affections and ἐπιθυμίαις. He proves this general φθορᾶς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ meaning of corruption in concupiscence, that is, of corrupt and depraved concupiscence, by a parallel passage c. 2, v. 19. and 20. For after he had said that those false teachers, of whom he treats, are δούλους τῆς φθορᾶς, ἐξηγητικῶς he adds, that they are entangled μιάσμασι in the pollutions of the world, which they had escaped.

Some take the little word φθορᾶς joined with ἐπιθυμίᾳ passively, so that φθορὰ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ is the same as φθαρτικὴ ἐπιθυμία corruptible and quickly passing concupiscence Luth. die vergängliche Lust. But it is more correctly taken actively, for concupiscence corrupting and destroying man, if the reins are securely loosened for it. That ἐν κόσμῳ is added for this reason, because those depraved concupiscences dominate carnal and worldly men, since they do not resist them at all through the Spirit. Nor is it absurdly thought that at the same time regard is had for the little word καλέσαντος in the preceding verse. For because the pious have been chosen and called out of the world, John 10, v. 19. therefore they no longer follow the depraved concupiscences which dominate in the world, and to which worldly men securely indulge.

It is asked in this place, what the Apostle understands by that τῆς θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν; Resp. 1. Truly believing people are called partakers of the divine Nature, by reason of renewal and new qualities, which the Holy Spirit effects in their hearts, and through them restores in them the divine image lost through the fall. For after the Apostle had said, that you might become partakers of the divine Nature, he adds, escaping the corruption that is in the world through concupiscence. Certainly, the depraved desires of the flesh, the depraved concupiscences, which are to be mortified by the Spirit in the reborn, are opposed to the renewal of the Spirit, so that they may remain partakers of the divine Nature. These Apostolic sayings speak of this interior renewal of the pious. 2. Corinth. 4. vers. 16. Our interior man is renewed from day to day. Ephes. 4. vers. 23. Be renewed in the Spirit of your mind. vers. 24. And put on the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth. Coloss. 3, vers. 9. stripping off the old man with his deeds vers. 10. and putting on the new one, who is renewed in knowledge, according to the image of him who created him. And this is that conformity to GOD and conformity to Christ, of which the pious ancients speak so often, which does not consist in a certain essential conversion of our substance into the Nature of GOD or Christ, but in a change of qualities and the restoration of the divine image. Dionysius on the Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 1. ἡ σωτηρία οὐχ ἑτέρως γενέσθαι δύναται μὴ θεουμένων τῶν σωζομένων, ἡ δὲ θέωσις ἐστὶν ἡ πρὸς θεὸν, ὡς ἐφικτὸν, ἀφομοίωσις τὲ καὶ ἕνωσις. The interpreter of Dionysius rendered it commingling with God, but in the Greek nothing is held regarding commingling. Basil, homily 10 on the Hexaemeron. Τὶς ἔστι Χριστιανισμὸς; θεοῦ ὁμοίωσις κατὰ τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον ἁνθρώπου φύσει Nicephorus, book 1 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22. Just as that end is proposed to every Teacher, that he may render the disciple, as far as it is possible for it to be done, very similar to himself by the communication of discipline: So it is established for Christ, as much as human fragility permits, to conform to himself each one approaching him through the Gospel, and thus to present those so conformed as sons to the Father. As much as each one has of the conformity to Christ, or conformity with Christ, so much he has of true Christianity.

Besides this interior renewal of the truly pious, the Apostle looked 2. to the incarnation of the Son of God, which was promised in the Old Testament through the Prophets, and therefore is deservedly considered μέγιστον καὶ τίμιον ἐπάγγελμα. Through it we have truly been made θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως, because the Son of GOD, who according to the assumed flesh has been made όμοούσιος, for us in the unity of person is true God, to the heavenly Father according to his Deity όμοούσιος, hence we are called flesh of his flesh, and bone of his bones,Ephes. 5, verse 3. joined to him by consanguinity of nature and the closest proximity of flesh, just as the brothers of Joseph say concerning their brother. He is our flesh,Gen. 27, v. 37. Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 1, p. 316. The Son of GOD on account of his immense love became what we are, that he might perfect us, which is what he himself is. Gregory Nazianzen, oration 38, f. 620. πτωχεύει τὴν ἑμὴν σάρκα, ἳνα ἑγὼ πλουτήσω τὴν αὐτοῦ θεότητα. He undergoes the poverty of my flesh, that I may attain the riches of his divinity. Athanasius, oration 5 against the Arians, page 103. GOD was made man, that he might deify us in himself, which he repeats himself in the Church to Adelphius against the Arians, page 333. Ambrose, book 5 of On the Faith, chapter 5. CHRIST offered himself as a partner of our fragility in the flesh, that he might make us in his virtue of the divine Partakers of the Nature. The same person in Epist. 38. teaches, that we are made partakers of the divine Nature through Christ, for in Christ our Nature was made a partaker of the divine, because it is united to the same most closely in the same hypostasis of the Word. Augustine lib. 9. de Civ. Dei cap. 15. The blessed and beatifying GOD, having been made a participant of our humanity, provided a compendium of participating in His divinity. lib. 21. de C. D. cap. 15. The only Son of GOD by Nature, for our sake, was made by mercy the son of man, so that we, by nature sons of man, might become sons of GOD through Him by grace. cap. 16. He was made a participant of our mortality, so that He might make us participants of His divinity. serm. 9. de temp. GOD was made man, so that man might become GOD. Anselm lib. de excell. Virg. Mariae cap. 12. To this end our GOD was made our brother, so that just as He Himself deigned to become a partaker of our humanity: so we might deserve to become partakers of His divinity.

3. To the gratuitous adoption into the sons of God. If those are called the offspring of God,Act. 17. v. 29. that is, partakers of the divine offspring, who were created by God as rational men, endowed with the faculty of understanding and willing, how much more can they be called partakers of the divine Nature, in their own way, who are born of God.1. Ioh. 4. v. 7. and adopted into the sons of GodIoh. 1, v. 9. It is said of the Magistracy Psal. 82, v. 6. I said, You are Gods and all of you are children of the most High. where those are called Gods who are sons of God, and to whom the word of God came.Ioh. 10. v. 35. how much more therefore can they be called Gods, that is, partakers of the divine Nature, who through faith in Christ have been made sons of GOD, and co-heirs of Christ, and thus participate in the Nature of GOD, just as sons participate in the Nature of the father. Just as God, when He produced Adam, whom Luke calls the son of God cap. 3. v. ult. breathed into his face, and gave him human and animal life,Gen. 2. v. 7. so when He receives someone as a son, He makes him a participant of Spiritual life, which is from GOD,Ephes. 4. v. 18. and communicates to him certain divine properties, and a right to the entire inheritance of GOD. Christ has been given to us with all His merit, and with all His benefits, through which, having received imputed righteousness, adoption into sons, and regeneration of the Holy Spirit from eternal life, we are rendered from sons of wrath into sons of grace, and are transformed into the image of GOD. Hence Ambrose lib. 1. de Spiritu Sancto c. 6. explains this Apostolic passage, concerning the spiritual commerce of the grace of adoption, which is brought about in us through the Holy Spirit.

4. To the spiritual union with Christ. To it likewise the Apostolic saying can be applied, Ephes. 5. v. 30. we are members of the body of his, of his flesh, and of his bones. For as Adam says of the spouse brought to him by God Gen. 2. v. 23. This is flesh of my flesh and bone of my bones: so Paul, applying the type to the antitype, expresses by these words the spiritual and most intimate union of Christ and the Church, but to the Church belong all believers, as true and living members of it. The formal aspect of this union does not consist in the fact that Christ, according to the assumed human Nature, is όμοούσιος, to us, since this benefit is common to all men, whereas on the contrary the mystical union is the property of true believers alone: but in the fact that Christ through faith grafts us into himself, makes us sons of GOD, members of his mystical body, and heirs of eternal life, and thus applies to us the fruit of his incarnation and passion, as the sayings testify. Iohann. 14, v. 23. If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our abode with him. 1. Cor. 6, v. 15. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Galat. 2, v. 20. Christ lives in me. Eph. 3, v. 17. Christ dwells in our hearts through faith. Theophylactus on chapter 14 of John. I am in you, as the head in the members; and you in me, as members in the head. Simon de Cassia book 12 on the Gospel, chapter 3. We are in Christ in the unity of faith, love, and grace, like branches in a tree, rays in the Sun, streams in a fountain, members under one head. Luther in comm: on this place Tom. 2. Germ. Ien. f. 395. What is the Nature of GOD? eternal truth, justice, wisdom, eternal life, peace, joy and pleasure, and whatever good can be named. Therefore, he who becomes a participant in the divine Nature obtains all these things, so that he may live forever, so that he may obtain eternal peace, joy and pleasure, so that he may be pure, just and omnipotent against the Devil, sin and death. Just as this cannot be taken away from GOD, so that he would be less than eternal life and eternal truth: so also eternal life cannot be snatched away from those united to Christ through faith. No one can oppress the pious, unless he oppresses God himself.

5. To the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit. 1. Cor: 3, v. 16. Do you not know that you are the temple of GOD, and the Spirit of GOD dwells in you? 1. Cor. 6. v. 19. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you? The Holy Spirit is not separated from his sanctifying gifts, but in that temple, which he adorns with his gifts, he himself also dwells. Since therefore the Holy Spirit is one true God with the Father and the Son, therefore also through that gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit we are rendered partakers of the divine Nature. 1. Cor. 6. v. 17. He who adheres to the Lord is one Spirit with him, is united to GOD through the Holy Spirit, and is ruled by the Holy Spirit, 1. Iohann. 3, v. 24. In this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit which he gave to us, cap. 4, vers. 3. In this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, because he gave to us of his Spirit. Irenaeus lib. 5. cap. 2. pag. 317. The Lord poured out the Spirit of the Father into the union and communion of GOD and men, indeed bringing down GOD to men through the Spirit, but again raising up man to GOD through his incarnation. Basil in his homily on the Holy Spirit says, that the saints are Gods on account of the indwelling Holy Spirit, and from there he proves, that the Holy Spirit is GOD by essence. It is necessary, he says, that the Spirit be divine, and be from GOD, who is the cause of divinity to the Gods. Athanasius in Dial. 1. de S. Trinit. We are rendered partakers of the divine Nature from this, that we partake of the Holy Spirit. But if from the participation of the Holy Spirit we turn out to be endowed with the divine Nature, is not that Spirit much more of the divine Nature, who effects these things in us. Ambrose lib. 1. de Spiritu Sancto cap. 6. Who would dare to say that the Holy Spirit is separate from GOD the Father and Christ, since through him we deserve to be in the image and likeness of GOD, and through him it happens, just as the Apostle Peter said, that we are partakers of the divine Nature, in which certainly there is not the inheritance of carnal succession, but the spiritual commerce of adoption grace.

6. To the communion of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist. Christ exhibits his body and blood to us to be eaten and drunk not only spiritually, but also Sacramentally in the Eucharist, so that he may most tightly join us to himself. 1. Cor. 10, v. 16. The bread, which we break, is it not κοινωνία of the body of Christ, The cup, which we bless, is it not κοινωνία of the Blood of Christ? But because the Son of GOD raised this his body, which he exhibits to us to be eaten by means of bread, and this his blood, which he exhibits to us to be drunk by means of wine in the Eucharist, to the sublimity of his divine person, therefore also this κοινωνίᾳ of the body and blood of Christ through true by faith, θείας φύσεως κοινωνία, we are made. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. mystag. 4. Thus Χριστοφόροι we shall be, when we have received his body and blood into our members, and we shall be made partakers of the divine Nature. Cyril of Alexandria, book 6, on John, chapter 17. Just as if someone were to pour one wax into melted wax, he mixes one with the other throughout: so it is necessary, if anyone receives the flesh and blood of the Lord, to be joined with him, so that Christ may be found in him, and he in Christ. book 10, chapter 13. We do not deny that we are spiritually joined to Christ by right faith and sincere charity, but that there is no manner of conjunction for us with him according to the flesh, that we certainly deny, and we say that it is alien to the divine scriptures. ibid. By the communication of the body and blood of Christ, he himself is in us and we in him. Gelasius in the book against Eutyches and Nestorius. therefore he says that the Eucharistic bread and wine pass into the divine substance, because through them we are made partakers of the divine Nature, the body and blood of Christ having been communicated to us.

7. To the closest conjunction with GOD in eternal life. That obscure and imperfect knowledge of GOD, which in this life comes to us through the word and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, brings it about that we are said to have κοινωνίαν with him 1 John 1, v. 6. How much more, therefore, will the intuitive vision of GOD, which embraces the clearest and most perfect knowledge of GOD, place us in κοινωνίαν a far richer and closer conjunction with GOD. Whence that manifestation, which follows in eternal life, Christ explains through μονὴν or the dwelling of the heavenly Father, and thus of the whole Most Holy Trinity in the elect John 14, v. 23. to which also pertains the Apostolic saying 1 John 3, v. 2. When he shall appear in his glory, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Nazianzen, oration 4, On Theology. We shall no longer be, as in this life, οὐδὲν ὅλως θεοῦ ἣ ὁλίγοι ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς φέροντες having nothing at all of GOD or little in us, ἀλλ'ὅλοι θεοειδεῖς, ὅλου θεοῦ χωρητικοὶ καὶ μόνου totally like and conformed to GOD, and capable of the whole of GOD. The same, oration 42, says, that man attains divinity, so that he may see the brightness of GOD. as Nicetas. Deification is the end of every action and contemplation. where by Deification he understands the vision of God. The same in the funeral oration for his Father ὅπου γενόμενοι θεός αὐτός (ἵνα τολμήσεις ἔπω) χόντες ὅλην τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος τὴν ἔλλαμψιν. John Huss on 1 John 3. Then we shall be By participation of God, not by a fellowship of equality, but of participation through grace in this, through glory in the future age.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. If the divine power has given us all things which pertain to life and godliness, therefore we can work nothing from ourselves and our own powers in matters pertaining to our salvation 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. Thence Prosper in Epist. ad Demetr. & contra Collatorem cap. 29. from the word δεδωρημένης gathers, that all things which are of godliness, even the very seeds of the virtues, are gratuitous gifts of God. Does he not, he says, who has stirred up in us the seeds of the virtues, which we have naturally implanted, by his own assistance? but, he says, who now has given us all things which pertain to life and godliness, by which saying what beginning of virtue has he placed in Nature, which has not been bestowed by him, who has given all things. This must be opposed to the merit of congruity of the Papists.

2. The Apostle in verse 3 defines faith by ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ. This is to be noted against Bellarmine, who in lib. 1. de Iustif. cap. 7. argues, that faith is better defined by ignorance than by knowledge. But ἐπίγνωσις is not ignorance, but cognition and knowledge. Estius in h. l. by the acknowledgment of the Son, that is, by faith, by which we believe in him. Lorinus ad v. 14. of this chapter, I am not ignorant that the name of knowledge is sometimes used for faith itself.

3. The corruption of the world is not outside us, but in us, because depraved concupiscence is in us. Rom. 7. v. 18.Iac. 1. v. 14. Therefore by withdrawal into a Monastery we do not escape that concupiscence which is in the world.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Beza in annot. ad v. 4. By θείαν φύσιν he denies that the very οὐσίαν, of God is understood, but says that by it certain qualities are to be understood, which the power of God effects in us. He thinks furthermore, that those who say that believers have been made partakers of the divine Nature itself, patronize the errors of Servetus, who imagined a certain transfusion of the divine essence into the pious. Piscator in Schol. h. l. likewise by θείαν φύσιν understands divine qualities of the soul, referring to the Nature of God, namely heavenly wisdom and holiness. Resp. 1. Even we ourselves not only repudiate and condemn the transfusion of Servetus, by which he makes the substance of GOD mutable and a part of all things, but also the dreams of Weigel and the Methists, by which they introduce a certain essential conversion of our souls, and even of our bodies, into the divine Nature we judge, saying from Cyprian, sermon on the Lord's Supper, Our conjunction with him neither mixes persons, nor unites substances (by some essential conversion or transfusion) but associates affections and confederates wills. The Apostle says Ephes. 3. v. 17. that Christ dwells in our hearts through faith. And yet neither the inhabitant is changed into the dwelling, nor the dwelling into the inhabitant. The personal union of two Natures in Christ introduces no essential change, how much less will a spiritual union bring about a transmutation of the united things? 2. We concede this also, that we are called partakers of the divine Nature, by reason of renewal and new qualities, which the Holy Spirit effects in our hearts. 3. But that besides that renewal, and the restoration of the divine image, nothing else is understood in this Apostolic passage by κοινωνίας θείαν φύσεως, this we indeed deny. For the contrary is evident from what has been said.

2. Socinus in the Posnanian animadversions, Defense, p. 136, writes thus. We are κοινωνοὶ of the divine Nature, or certainly will be such at some time, namely then, when we shall be gifted with blessed immortality in the resurrection of the just, on account of which we shall also be sons of GOD. Luc. 20. vers. 36. Resp. That κοινωνία is obtained by believers not only in eternal life, but also in this life, as both this passage of ours teaches, and the Apostolic saying 1. Cor. 1. vers. 9. God is faithful, by whom you were called εἰς κοινωνίαν into his Son. 1. Iohann. 1. v. 3. so that κοινωνία our fellowship may be with GOD and with his Son Jesus Christ v. 27. If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, κοινωνία we have mutual fellowship (The same is to be judged concerning that which Ambrose, Epist. 38, accepts this fellowship of the divine Nature concerning the gift of rational Nature, and which Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian, asserts that through virginity we become partakers of the divine Nature. And yet that κοινωνία is θαίας φύσεως both of the few and of all truly faithful.)

3. Some in the time of Gerson imagined that they were so united to GOD through contemplation, that in reality their Nature is submerged in the deep abyss of divinity, suppose humanity is annihilated and passes entirely into divinity, to which opinion the Methistic error concerning our essential union with Christ is a twin. And yet κοινωνία, is one thing, μεταποιΐα. is another.

4. Andreas Osiander from this κοινωνίᾳ of the divine Nature infers he willed, that we be justified by the essential righteousness of GOD dwelling in us. Resp. That we are made partakers of the divine Nature, Peter says; but that we are justified before GOD by the participation and indwelling of the divine Nature of essential righteousness, this is not the doctrine of Peter, but the gloss of Osiander.

5. Certain Papists attempt to establish the invocation of saints from this passage, concluding in this way. Those who are partakers of the divine Nature, they are also deservedly considered partakers of divine worship, namely, of religious invocation. But the departed saints are partakers of the divine Nature. Therefore. Resp. 1. The Papists themselves do not wish it to be seen that they attribute purely divine worship to the departed saints, but worship greater than human and civil, yet inferior to divine, or intermediate, as Bellarmine speaks; or external worship, as Costerus speaks. 2. Peter testifies concerning the saints living on earth, that they have been made partakers of the divine Nature through Christ. But if, therefore, the worship of religious invocation could be inferred from that θειας φύσεως κοινωνιά, it would follow that the saints still living on earth could be religiously invoked. 3. The pious are called partakers of the divine Nature, not because they are Gods by participation, as Bellarmine speaks in De beat. sanct. cap. 9, but through regeneration, renewal, adoption as sons, the restoration of the divine image, the gracious indwelling of God, etc., as we showed above.

6. Bellarmine, lib. 2. de iustif. cap. 5, establishes, that we become partakers of the divine Nature through charity, inasmuch as through it we are rendered sons of GOD, and those who are sons of GOD, they are partakers of the divine Nature. He thinks he can prove that from two sayings of Scripture 1. John 3. v. 1. See what manner of charity GOD has given to us, that we should be called and be the sons of GOD! cap. 4. v. 7. Charity is of GOD, and everyone who loves is born of GOD and knows GOD. v. 8. He who does not love does not know GOD, because GOD is charity. Resp. 1. We concede that charity pertains to that θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν, of which the Apostle treats. For it pertains to renewal and the restoration of the divine image, in which we said above that θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν consists. 2. We also concede this, that adoption as sons or υἱοθεσία pertains to that θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν,, as we likewise warned above.

3. We deny, however, that we are made children of GOD through charity, because charity is not υἱοθεσίας a cause, but rather a sign and an effect. 1 John 3:14 We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. Scripture attributes this to faith, that it is υἱοθεσίας a medium. John 1:12 As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of GOD, even to them that believe on his name. Gal. 3:26 Ye are all the children of GOD by faith in Christ Jesus. 4. In the passage 1 John 3:1 it is not a matter of the charity by which we love God, but of the charity by which God loves us. 1 John 4:7 Charity is not established as the cause of regeneration from GOD and υἱοθεσίας, but its sign and effect.

7. Lorinus the Jesuit comments on this passage thus: It is proved from this passage that our righteousness is a permanent and internal gift, just as the name of Nature signifies not merely an external denomination or non-imputation: hence it is that justification is called regeneration, Tit. 3:5 and a new creature Gal. 6:15 James 1:18 Resp. That which Bellarmine, in book 2 of Justification, chapter 5, answers to Osiander, who attempts to prove from this passage that we are justified by that righteousness by which Christ is essentially righteous not as man, but as GOD, we can also oppose to Lorinus. The Apostle Peter says that we become partakers of the divine Nature, but that we are justified before GOD through that participation of the divine Nature, is not the opinion of Peter, but the gloss of Lorinus; just as Bellarmine writes, The Apostle does not say that we are made partakers of the divine [nature] through the indwelling of essential righteousness, for this is the gloss of Osiander, not the opinion of Peter. It is manifest from the text that the Apostle is not speaking here of justifying grace or the mode of justification, but of a gift, through grace, and a consequence of justification.

8. Salmero gathers from v. 4 that we will not be partakers of the divine Nature without our will and cooperation. Resp. The Apostle is speaking of the reborn, who through the Spirit given to them divinely both can and ought to mortify the lusts of the flesh.

Observat. I. Through the knowledge of Christ, that is, through true faith in Christ, all things which pertain to life and godliness are given to us.

2. Calling is a work of the glorious grace of God. 2 Tim. 1:9 God He demonstrates his glory most greatly by showing mercy and calling, his power by sparing.

3. As Paul Eph. 1. v. 19. & 20. celebrates the power of GOD in the bestowing of faith: so Peter attributes the bestowing of spiritual benefits to divine power.

4. Faith is a gratuitous gift of GOD, not proceeding from the merits or powers of men.

5. Leo, sermon on the nativity: Acknowledge, O Christian, your dignity; and having been made a partner of the divine Nature, do not return to your former baseness by a degenerate way of life. Remember of what head and body you are a member. Recall that you have been rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the light and kingdom of GOD; through the Sacrament of Baptism you have been made a temple of the Holy Spirit; do not drive away such a dweller by your depraved actions and subject yourself again to the servitude of the Devil, because your price is the blood of CHRIST.

6. Bede in commentary on this place: He says well, that the concupiscence of the world has corruption, and therefore it is to be fled, because there is also an incorruptible concupiscence, of which it is sung: My soul has longed and faints for the courts of the Lord.

7. Depraved concupiscence is the source both of the corruption of the dead, and of eternal destruction and ruin.

8. Ambrose, book 10, Epistle 84: If GOD has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness by his divine power, nothing is more to be fled than the appetite of this concupiscence, which denies the virtue of the divine work by the love of its own dignity. And when other desires only diminish those goods to which they are opposed, this one, while it draws all things to itself, at the same time corrupts them all. Ambrose speaks, however, specifically about pride.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Multi ex Interpp. hunc versiculum coniungunt cum praecedentibus eundemque proinde ad prooemium Epistolae pertinere statuunt. Ratio connexionis dari posset duplex, ut referatur vel ad remotius, vel ad propinquius. Ad propinquius, vid. ad salutat. Apostolicam, hoc modo. Non est, quod dubitetis, votum hocce meum, quo vobis multiplicationem gratiae & pacis per cognitionem Christi adprecor, fore efficax, quia iam antè Deus ex gratia vobis donavit, quae ad vitam & pietatem faciant. Gagnaeus in h. l. Gratia & pax DEI impleatur in vobis, per cognitionem Domini & Salvatoris nostri, quemadmodum divinâ virtute suâ, quaecunque ad vitam & pietatem spectant, vobis donata sunt per cognitionem eius. Gretserus tom. 1. Defens. Bellarm. lib. 2. de V. D. cap. 14. p. 751. ut autoritatem Vulgatae Versionis asserat, itidem haec verba cum proximè praecedentibus connectit, hoc modo. Gratia & pax vobis ita multiplicetur, quomodo omnia divinae virtutis suae vobis donata sunt. Cornel. â Lapide in h. l. Gratia & pax vobis adimpleatur, quomodo i. e. perinde, vel sicut per hanc DEI & Christi cognitionem omnia divina dona, quae ad vitam & pictatem pertinent, vobis donata sunt, utτό ὡς sit ἐξηγητικὸν,respondens HebraeoכאשרAd remotius, videlicet ad descriptionem eorum, adquos scribit, hoc modo. Dixi, vos aequè preciosam fidem sortitos in iustitia Christi. Illud ex eo est, quod DEUS ex gratia vobis donavit, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent per salutarem sui cognitionem.

2. Sed quia Apostolis in more positum est, salutationem paucis verbis absolvere, ac statim ad Epistolae argumentum accedere, ut ex Pauli, Iudae & ipsius Petri priore Epistolis apparet, ideò rectiùs statuitur, ab hoc v. 3. ipsam Epistolae πραγματείαν, videlicet priorem eius partem, quae νουθεσίαν ad constantiam & profectum in fide, ac studio pietatis continet, incipere, iuxta quam hypothesin versiculi huius sententia pendet usque ad initium versiculi 5. in quo demum eadem completur.

3. Ergo in hac priore νουθεσίας parte commemorat Apostolus beneficia divina, quae iamdum illi, ad quos scribit, ex gratia â Deo acceperant, quâ commemoratione eos excitare cupit, ut summo studio in id, ad quod eos hortatur, incumbant.

Dispositio. Divina isthaec beneficia exaggerat Apostolus 1. â donantis potentia. 2. â donorum cumulo. 3. â donationis medio, quod est divina vocatio. 4. â donorum fructu & effectu.

Textus expositio. ὡς πάντα ἡμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης. Particulam ὡς

1. Quidam volunt esse admirantis vel exclamantis, per quam Apostolus admirabundus in praedicationem divinorum beneficiorum prorumpat.

Hanc particulae ὡς significationem Salmero multis exemplis confirmare satagit, Psal. 119. v. 97.Thren. 1. v. 1. Item Psal. 73. v. 1. & 19.Psal. 84. v. 1.Psal. 119. v. 108. Sed pleraque sunt aliena, &, quod caput rei est, eiusmodi exclamationes, per particulam ὡς formatae, in exordiis Epistolarum Apostolicarum alibi non occurrunt.

2. Plerique statuunt, esse particulam similitudinis, respondentem voculaeκαθὼς,per quam prioris ad Timotheum Epistolae,ἐργασίανApostolus exorditur.1. Tim. 1. v. 3. Hunc sensum secutus vulgatus Interpres, reddidit per quomodo.

Iuxta hanc hypothesin in v. 5. Subintelligenda foret particula οὔτως, ἀπόδοσιν exprimens, & sententiam complens hoc sensu. Sicut DEUS in vos eximia contulit beneficia, omnia sc. ea benignissimè vobis largiendo, quae ad vitam & pietatem faciunt: ita & vos omni curâ ac solicitudine in id incumbere debetis, ut dona illa DEI in vobis permaneant atque crescant.

3. Simplicissimè statuitur, particulam ὡς h. l. servire illationi, ac significare idem, quod ἐπεὶpostquam vel siquidem, eique respondere τὸ καὶ in principio v. 5. ut sit sensus. Postquam, vel siquidem divina eius virtus omnia, quae ad vitam & pietatem (pertinent) nobis donavit, ideò omne studium in id conferre debetis, ut faciatis, quae Deus â vobis requirit. In hac significatione particula ὡς usurpatur, Luc. 1. v. 23.ὡς ἐπλείσθησαν αί ἡμέραι.v. 44.ὡς ἐγένετο ἡ φωνὴ.cap. 2. v. 15.ὡς ἐπῆλθαν οἱ Ἄγγελοι.cap. 4. v. 25.ὡς ἐγένετο λιμὸς.cap. 5. vers. 4.ὡς ἐπαύσατο λαλῶν. Eodem sensu reddidit Syrus [איך מן] sicut quidem i. e. siquidem. Lutherus nach dem.

Pronomen αὐτοῦ quidam referunt ad Christum, quem Apostolus sub finem vers. praeced. vocaverat Dominum nostrum, quem Apostolus ex eo probet esse verum Deum & Servatorem nostrum, quia divina ipsius virtus omnia, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent, nobis donavit. Quidam ad Deum patrem, cuius itidem fit mentio in v. praeced. Neutra sententia vel fidei analogiae vel contextui adversatur, cum agatur de opere ad extra; quod est tribus Deitatis personis commune.

Participium δεδωρημένης quidam passivè accipiunt, ac textum sic vertunt. Postquam omnia divinae virtutis eius ( scil.εὐεργετήματα καὶ χαρίσματα,beneficia & effecta) quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent, nobis donata sunt. Quâ ratione pro participio casus secundi δεδωρημένης legendum foret participium casus quarti δεδωρημένα, ut in nonnullis Codd. se legisse testatur Lorinus, ac explicandum per verbum δεδώρηται. notum enim est, more Hebraeorum participia saepissimè proverbis poni. Hoc sensu reddidit vulgata versio. Quomodo nobis divinae virtutis suae, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent, nobis donata sunt. (In quibusdam tamen Codd. Latinis habetur singulare, donata est, sicut & Beda in comment. duplicis illius lectionis mentionem facit, sed singulare nihil habet, cui respondeat) Eodem modo reddidit Lutherus. Nach dem allerlei seiner Göttlichen Krafft uns geschencket ist. Verumenimverò, quia verbum δεδώρηται frequentius in activa significatione usurpatur (quo sensu etiam in vers. proximè sequente â Vulgato Interprete exponitur, δι' ὧν τὰ μέγιστα ἡμῖν καὶ τίμια ἐπαγγέλματα δεδώρηται,nobis donavit) ac alioqui etiam apud Graecos usitatum, praeteritis passivis uti in significatione activa Hebr. 12. v. 26.νῦν ἐπήγγελται, ideò rectiùs etiam hoc loco activè accipitur, ut sit sensus. Postquam divina eius virtus omnia, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent, nobis donavit, id est, Quando quidem DEUS nobis caelestem vim & virtutem ex mera sua bonitate nobis donavit, ut Spiritus Sancti ope piè in hoc seculo vivere, & per fidem vitam aeternam apprehendere possimus. Vel, quod eodem redit, Postquam divinâ eius virtute omnia, quae ad vitam & pietatem pertinent, nobis largiente (sc. in omnibus ditati sumus1. Cor. 1. v. 5.) Iuxta hanc hypothesin δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ refertur ad ordinem causae efficientis ac autoris donantis, quod concinnius est, quàm si referatur ad dona ipsa sive donantis effecta, quod fit per priorem expositionem. Syrus tamen, qui δεδωρημένης itidem activè accipit, videtur divinam virtutem inter dona referre, sic enim textum reddidit. Sicut quidem omnia illa, quae sunt potentiae divinae, ad vitam & timorem DEI dedit.

Τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν. Rob. Stephanus testatur, pro ζωὴν in quibusdam Codd. legi πρὸς εἰρήνην. Per hunc προσδιορισμὸν particula Universalis πάντα quasi restringitur, ut ea divinâ virtute nobis donata intelligantur, quae ad vitam & pietatem faciunt, sive pertinent: haec enim vis est Graecae phraseos τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν.

Per ζωὴν potest intelligi, tum vita Spiritualis ac DEO grata, in hoc mundo â piis ducenda, quam Paulus Eph. 4. v. 18. vocat vitam DEI vel ex DEO; iuxta quam expositionem vocula καὶ poneretur ἐξηγητικῶς: tum ipsa vita aeterna, credentibus in Christum, & fidem per studium pietatis demonstrantibus promissa. Illa pietatis est principium & pars, haec verò consequens. Quae ad utramque vitam conferunt, divina virtus ex gratia nobis donavit.

Διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ἡμᾶς. Quidam hoc intelligunt de agnitione DEI Patris, ad quamper Christum ducimur.Iohan. 14. v. 9.Qui videt me, videt Patrem. Illi praecedens pronomenαὐτοῦreferunt ad Christum. Quidam verò accipiunt de agnitione Christi, per quam omnia ad vitam & pietatem spectantia nobis donantur. Illi praecedens pronomenαὐτοῦ referunt ad Deum Patrem. Neutra expositio vel fidei analogiae, vel textui repugnat, quia in praecedentibus & DEI & Christi facta fuit mentio. Caeterùm per ἐπίγνωσιν illius, qui vocavit nos, non intelligitur nuda notitia, quippe per quam solam & nudam nondum ea, quae ad vitam & pietatem spectant, alicui obtingunt, sed notitia cum assensu & fiducia, seu fiduciali apprehensione Christi coniuncta h. e. fides iustificans & salvifica, quae ideò vocatur ἐπίγνωσις, quia notitia est eius pars, per quam totum συνεκδοχικῶς exprimitur. Esai. 53. v. 11.Ioh. 17. v. 3. Sensus igitur est, quòd Deus omnia ad vitam & pietatem spectantia, per fidem in Christum nobis dederit, sicut in versu praeced. dixerat, quod gratia & pax multiplicetur per agnitionem DEI & CHRISTI, quò pertinet dictum Christi modò citatum Iohann. 17. v. 3.Haec est vita aeterna.

Per vocationem h. l. intelligitur ea, cui ex parte hominum respondet fidei oboedientia, h. e. Vocatio hîc non tantùm consideratur ratione termini â quo, videlicet DEI vocantis, in verbo Evangelii spiritualia beneficia, passione & morte Filii sui parta, omnibus offerentis: sed etiam ratione termini ad quem, videlicet hominum vocatorum, fide oblata in verbo Evangelii beneficia amplectentium, quam Paulus 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. sic describit. DEUS vocavit nos vocatione sanctâ, non secundùm opera nostra, sed secundùm propositum suum & gratiam, quae data est nobis in Christo Iesu, ante tempora secularia. Pontificii & Calviniani eam appellant vocationem efficacem, eamque distinguunt â vocatione inefficaci.
