Socinus in explicat. Locor. Script. p. 115. talem affert gradationis huius connexionem. Ex assensu praedicationi Evangelii adhibito proficisci debet, ut homo Christianus postea se viriliter gerat, & vires sumat. Hinc veram & solidam cognitionem ac scientiam rerum divinarum petit, unde nascitur, ut sese contineat ab omni carnis cupiditate, & in hoc sibi vim faciat, toleret ac perseveret, quae continet verbumὑπομονὴ.Nunc non tantùm continens est, quae est virtus erga seipsum. Vel & ita potest explicari, aliis non nocet, sedpius etiam evadit, hoc est, Spretis carnis voluptatibus, & abiectâ rerum mundanarum curâ, totus ad DEUM & religionem sese convertit. Ita affectus amat fratres & caritatem exercet, neque vitam suam pro fratre ponere recusat.

Sed quilibet videt, coactum hoc esse, si quis demonstrare conetur, in hac gradatione priorem virtutem semper esse causam posterioris, quale & illud est, quod per fidem Socinus intelligit nudum assensum, cùm tamen Apostolus voce πίστεως in eadem significatione hîc utatur, in qua usurpatur v. 1. videlicet pro fide iustificante, quae notitiam, assensum & fiduciam complectitur, quodque per virtutem intelligunt fortitudinem & vires, cùm tamen in Graeco non sit δύναμις, sed ἀρετὴ, quâ voce in eadem significatione Apostolus hîc utitur, in qua usurpatur v. 3. quamvis virtutes DEO insint per modum essentiae, piis autem per modum accidentium. Simpliciùs ergo statuitur, voculam ἐν h. l. idem significare quod cum, ut non tam origo unius virtutis ex altera, quàm congeries quaedam pulcherrimarum ac praecipuarum virtutum describatur, sicque de ratione ordinis non sit magnopere laborandum. Flacius in comm. h. l. In hac gradatione non tàm rerum naturalium consecutio, quàm harum omnium virtutum necessaria cum fide coniunctio spectanda est. In illa significatione praefixum ב usurpatur Gen. 32. v. 1.In baculo transivi Iordanem1. Sam. 1. v. 24.cum iuvencis tribus.Psal. 2. v. 11.Servite Domino cum timore.Psal. 60. v. 12.cum exercitibus nostris.Ose. 4. v. 3.cum bestia agri & volucri (ita reddiderunt LXX) cap. 5. v. 6.cum pecore suoMatth. 25. v. 16.Abiit, qui acceperat quinque talenta, & operatus est in eis.Actor. 7. v. 38.Hic est, qui fuit in Ecclesia i. e. cum Ecclesia in solitudine. Eodem modo particulam ἐν etiam Syrus h. l. reddidit. Adiicite fidei vestrae, vel supra fidem vestram, utitur enim praepositione [על] Interim non negamus, esse quandam in hisce septem virtutum gradibus connexionem, quae utiliter investigatur, etiamsi prior non semper sit causa posterioris. Hoc enim certum est, fidem in hoc catalogo ideò primo loco poni, quia est omnium virtutum Christianarum basis ac fundamentum, absque qua DEO placere impossibileHebr. 11. v. 6. & ex qua quicquid non est, peccatum est.Rom. 14. v. 23.

Q. 3. Quid per γνῶσιν h. l. intelligatur? Quidam per γνῶσιν in-telligunt uberiorem divinorum mysteriorum cognitionem, per quam in fide crescamus, in qua significatione haec vox accipitur in cap. 3. seqq. v. 18.Cresciteἐν γνώσειDomini nostri & Salvatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Ita accipit Cyrillus in h. loc. 2. Oecumenius in comm. dicit per γνῶσινsignificari, quòd mysteria fidei non modò debeamus credere, sed aliquatenus etiam intelligentiâ assequi. 3. Luth. in vers. Germ. videtur accipere de Christiana prudentia ac moderatione, per quam fratres possimus Christo lucrifacere. Sic enim reddidit. In der Tugend Bescheidenheit.

4. Sed in comment. nobiscum intelligit prudentiam virtutum omnium moderatricem. Dion. Carth. in h. l. Per scientiam intelligitur discretio, quae est directrix & auriga virtutum, docens observare moderamen, congruum locum, tempus aptum, ut omnia ordinatè agantur, & regiâ viâ tendamus, ut sit rationabile obsequium nostrum.

Q. 4. Quare Apostolus scientiae coniungi velitἐγκράτειαν? Resp. 1. Beda in comm. hancce reddit causam. In scientia abstinentiam, ut cùm bona facere didicerint, mox â malis abstineant, ne in vacuum caelestium scientia cedat, si se ab illecebris terrestribus quis continere neglexerit. 2. Quidam putant, Apostolum ideò mentionem facere continentiae, quia gentiles simplicem scortationem soluti cum soluta non iudicabant esse peccatum. 3. Simplicissimè respondetur, Apostolum ideò cum prudentia coniungere temperantiam, quia prudentia non potest habere locum sine temperantia. Anima prudens in sicco dicitur habitare ac σωφροσύνη dicitur q. σώζουσα τὴν φρόνησιν.

Q. 5. Quare patientiae pietatem Apostolus velit coniungi? 1. August. lib. 10. de Civ. Dei cap. 1. dicit, εὐσέβειανpietatem, licet propriè congruat Deo, tamen saepe in misericordiae operibus frequentari, quia haec mirè placent Deo. Inde per pietatem quidam hoc loco intelligunt benignitatem, beneficentiam, misericordiam. Beda in comm. h. l. Ut erga eos, quos patienter tolerat, etiam pius existat, iuxta illud Apostoli. Caritas patiens est, benigna est. Lorinus in h. l. Fortassis perεὐσέβειανex vulgari notione voluit Petrus benignitatem ac misericordiae opera intelligere. Non enim satis est Christiano, illatas ferre iniurias ac tormenta, nisi pium quoque adversus haec inferentes, ac benignum & beneficum gerat animum. Sed de hisce virtutibus ad secundam Decalogi tabulam pertinentibus in seqq. agit Apostolus 2. Quidam hanc reddunt connexionis rationem, quòd afflictiones hominem reddant humilem, eumque cogant ut per preces ad Deum confugiat, eiusque auxilium imploret. 3. Lutherus in h. l. ideò pietatem cum patientia coniungi docet, quia in omnibus, quae agimus velpatimur, unicè Dei honorem & servitium, non nostrum honorem vel commodum quaerere debeamus. 4. Simplicissimè respondetur, in patientia propterea pietatem subministrandam requiri, ut in Deum sperantes, eumque religiosè colentes, liberationem ex omnibus adversis in filiali fiducia expectemus.

Q. 6. Quareἀγάπην φιλαδελπίᾳconiungi Apostolus requirat? Resp. 1. Quidam volunt, amori fratrum ideò coniungendam praecipicaritatem, ut significetur, fratres debere diligi non carnali aut seculari amore, sed spirituali, vid. propter Deum super omnia diligendum, quem amorem Scriptura passimἀγάπηνvocat. 2. Cum hac expositione congruit, quod quidam statuunt, per ἀγάπην intelligi dilectionem, quâ in Deum ferimur, ut quòd fratres diligamus, id ob amorem Dei fiat. Beda in comm. h. l. Caritatem appellat specialiter eam, quâ conditorem diligimus, quae proficientibus virtutum gradibus meritò amori fraternitatis adiungitur, quia nec DEUS sine proximo, nec proximus sine DEO, perfectè valet amari. 3. Quidam per φιλαδελφίαν intelligunt animi affectum: per ἀγάπηνofficia, quae ex illo affectu perficiscuntur. Is enim verè diligit, qui reipsâiuvat, quos diligit.Luc. 10. v. 37. 4. Sed rectiùs statuitur, per ἀγάπην intelligi amorem generalem, quo omnes homines complectimur, quem cur Apostolus φιλαδελφίᾳ coniungi velit, eius rei causam exposuimus superiùs.

Ἔλεγχος. Quia praeceptum hoc Apostolicum, quo ἐν τῇ γνώσει τὴν ἐκράτειαν subministrari iubet, generale est, non solùm ad caelibes, sed etiam ad coniugatos pertinens, exeo colligitur, Bellarmin. perquàm ἀπαιδεύτως lib. de Clericis cap. 19. sic concludere. PaulusTit. 1. v. 8.â Ministris Ecclesiae requiritἐγκρατείαν.Ergo â coniugio abstinere debent. Atqui non solùm praesens locus Apostolicus, sed etiam alia Scripturae dicta, Sirac. 26. v. 20.Gal. 5. v. 23. testantur, ἐγκράτειαν etiam in coniugatis locum habere posse.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Ex participio παρεισενέγκαντες colligunt Pontificii vires liberi arbitrit in Spiritualibus. Lorin. in h. l. Participium Graecum significans eos, qui intulerunt vel intrò tulerunt praeter aliquid aliud, qui contulerunt ad illud, seu cum alio studium & operam, denotat concursum atque cooperationem liberi arbitrii nostri. Estius in h. l. Hic locus facit pro cooperatione liberi arbitrii cum gratia DEI, quae tamen ipsa cooperatio tota est attribuenda DEI auxilio, operantis in nobis & velle & perficere.Phil. 2. v. 13. Cornelius â Lapide in h. l. Haec vox significat, gratiam per se solam non sufficere ad salutem, sed requiri cooperationem liberi arbitrii, ut subinferatur etiam adnitendo nostrae voluntatis efficacia. Resp. 1. παρεισφέρειν semel tantùm in N. T. legitur. Notum a. est composita saepè pro simplicibus usurpari, ut in voce composita non semper quaeri possit emphasis. 2. Petrus hîc loquitur de renatis, illos esse gratiae DEI συνέργους, libenter concedimus. August. lib. 2. de peccat. merit. cap. 5. postquam ex precibus probaverat, auxilium gratiae esse necessarium, subiungit. Nec ideo tamen de hac re solis votis agendum est, ut non subinferatur adnitendo etiam nostrae efficacia voluntatis. Adiutor enim noster Deus dicitur, nec adiuvari potest, nisi qui etiam aliquid sponte conatur, quia non sicut in lapidibus insensatis, aut sicut in eis, in quorum Natura rationem voluntatemque non condidit, salutem nostram Deus operatur in nobis. Quaestio autem inter nos & Pontificios non est de renatis & conversis, sed de naturalibus liberi arbitrii viribus tùm ante conversionem, tùm in ipsa conversione. 3. Si tota liberi arbitrii cooperatio tribuenda est auxilio Dei, operantis in nobis velle & perficere, ut h. l. scribit Estius; ac si τὸ παρὰ significat, voluntatem suis viribus non posse quidquam operari in hisce actibus, sed omnes vires ad eos operandos accipere â gratia, ut h. l. scribit Cornelius â Lapide, & â similitudine ferri igniti illud declarat, utique liberum arbitrium etiam post conversionem non agit naturalibus suis, sed novis â Spiritu Sancto donatis viribus. 4. Nequaquam igitur Apostolus hoc vult, quòd de nostro ad Dei gratiam & fidem aliquid erogare debeamus, sed quòd non sufficiat de fide gloriari, verùm etiam virtutibus & bonis operibus, velut fructibus eam demonstrandam esse.

2. Estius ad eundem v. 5. annotat, Petrum ideò requirere, ut fidei coniungamus virtutum opera, ne fides sit inanis, informis & mortua. Cornelius â Lapide ibid. Fides enervis & infirma est, nisi virtute suffulciatur. Resp. bona opera non sunt forma fidei, sed necessarium eius consequens & effectum. Gal. 5. v. 6. Dicitur â Iacobo cap. 2. v. ult.fides sine operibus mortua, quia bona opera de fidei vita testantur, sicut respiratio de vita corporis. Pari ratione bona opera non addunt animam vel vires fidei, sed fides potius bonis operibus omnem dignitatem ac robur addit. Rom. 14. v. ult.Hebr. 11. v. 6.

3. Lorinus ad eundem vers. sic annotat: Bonorum operum necessitatem ad salutem praeter fidem, ex hoc loco colligit Esaias Abbas, ut & Sixtus Papa tertius. Resp. vera fides licet sine operibus iustificet, tamen non est sine operibus. Licet bona opera sint simul cum fide, & quidem necessariò sint cum fide coniuncta, modò fides sit vera & viva, tamen non simul cum fide iustificant, sed vis iustificandi in ordine causae instrumentalis soli fidei competit.

4. Idem Lorinus ibid. sic commentatur. Utilis ac etiam Ecclesiae necessaria est Theologia, non singulis, quemadmodum nec â singulis fides aequè explicita exigitur. Unde perperam hac ex scientia colligunt haeretici, merum commentum esse de fide implicita, Resp. 1. per γνῶσιν fatetur Lorinus â Cyrillo & Oecumenio in textu Apostolico intelligi mysteriorum Christi cognitionem, arcanorum Dei mysteriorum scientiam, ab Aria scientiam sacrarum Scripturarum. 2. fatetur & hoc, de fidei cognitione verbum sciendi aliquando usurpari. 3. Cùm ergò fidei Apostolus coniungi iubeat γνῶσιν, & verò hoc praeceptum Apostoli sit generale, ad omnes omninò Christianos pertinens, consequens est, omnium omninò Christianorum fidem γνῶσιν debere coniuncta habere, ac perinde non tàm per ignorantiam, quàm per notitiam esse definiendam. 4. Quamvis v. cognitionis illius sint certi gradus, nec ab omnibus Christianis Theologia h. e. accurata illa mysteriorum divinorum cognitio, quae in Ecclesiae Doctoribus esse debet, requiratur, pii tamen non debent esse implicitâ fide, quae nihil aliud est, quàm in cognosendis divinis mysteriis negligentia, contenti, sed quotidie maiores in cognitione Dei & Salvatoris Iesu Chr. progressus facere debent.

5. Salmero ad v. 7. sic annotat. Adverte, principium salutis nostrae esse fidem, perfectionem v. caritatem, quae vinculum perfectionis vocatur â Paulo.Col. 3. 14. Eodem modo Estius. Corona virtutum ideò concluditur in caritate, quod illa sit omnium virtutum forma, perfectio & complemen, tum. Resp. 1. Caritas non est fidei iustificantis forma, sed ἐνέργεια effectiva, sive effectus, perpetuo & indissolubili foedere cum ea coniunctus. Gal. 5. v. 6.Iac. 2. v. 18. 2. Propria & specifica iustificantis fidei forma, est fiducialis apprehensio Mediatoris Christi, & beneficiorum eius, quae in verbo Evangelii nobis offeruntur. 3. in exercitiis Christianae pietatis, quae spectantur in iustificatis, caritatem fide maiorem esse concedimus 1. Cor. 13. v. 13. non quòd fidem informet, vel actum iustificationis ingrediatur, vel magis iustificet quàm fides, sed tùm propter obiecti latitudinem, fidei enim res est cum solo Deo & Mediatore Christo, caritas autem ad Deum & proximum refertur: tùm propter perpetuam durationem, quia in vita aeterna fidei succedet visio, spei fruitio, caritas autem durabit & plenè perficietur. 4. Caritas dicitur πλήρωμα legis Rom. 13. v. 10. quia omnia praecepta divina ad caritatem referuntur, ut loquitur August. in Enchir. c. 121. non tamen qualiscunque, sed perfecta & numeris omnibus absoluta dilectio totius legis impletio censenda. 5. Caritas Col. 3. v. 14. vocatur συνδεσμὸς τῆς τελειότητος, non quòd caritas nos reddat perfectos ad consistendum coram Dei iudicio, sed quia singuli fideles, tanquam unius corporis mystici membra per caritatem ita perficiuntur, ut nulli quidquam desit, sed singulis necessaria suppetant ex mutuo cum caeteris membris consortio.

Observ. 1. Scala virtutum inchoatur â fide, & terminatur in caritate, quia totus Christianismus absolvitur fide & caritate. Ignatius Epist. 7. τὸ ὅλον πίστις ἡ εἰς τὸν θεὸν καὶ ἀγάπη πρὸς τὸ ὁμόφυλλον. 2. Inter virtutes est connexio arctissima, quae mysticè significatur Cant. 7. v. 1.per monilia, manu artificis fabricata. Quemadmodum enim in aureo monili, quod periti artificis manu fabrefactum, quilibet annulus cum reliquis eo modo est connexus ut singuli invicem atque cum reliquis iuncti sint universi: sic in virtutum studio, quod absque speciali summi artificis auxilio constare & exerceri nequit, unaquaeque virtus alteri virtuti arctissimè est connexa, singulaeque cum omnibus prout hoc loco ab Apostolo velut in preciosi monilis forma nobis ob oculos ponuntur.

3. Beda in comm. ad hanc scalam virtutum accommodat, quod de aedificio in monte constructo in visione Prophetica diciturEzech. 40. v. 34.Et in octo gradibus ascensus eius.

4. Fides in hoc virtutum catalogo ideò primo loco ponitur, quia est omnium virtutum Christianorum basis ac fundamentum absque quâ DEO placere impossibile,Hebr. 11. v. 6.ac quicquid non est ex fide, peccatum est.Rom. 14. v. 23. Origenes lib. 1. in Ioh. tom. 2. fol. 3. Sicut nihil est delectabile hominibus sine luce: sic nihil est delectabile & acceptum DEO absque fidei lumine. Gregorius Nazianzenus orat. 13. p. 347. Absque fide nulla actio fructuosa esse potest. August. lib. 19. de Civ. DEI cap. 25. Nulla virtus vera apud DEUM sine fide. Epist. 143. Fides est mater & radix bonorum operum. Alcuinus lib. 1. de Trin. cap. 1. Fides est bonorum omnium fundamentum. Lombardus lib. 3. sentent. dist. 40. & 41. ex Ambrosio; Fides est genitrix bonae voluntatis & iustae actionis; ex Gregorio, est vestibulum, per quod pervenitur adbona opera.

5. Bernhard. serm. 49. in Cant. Scientia practica sive Spiritualis prudentia est omnium virtutum auriga.

6. Umbram aliquam pulcherrimae illius συζυγίας inter continentiam & patientiam viderunt etiam Ethnicorum Philosophi, quorum hoc fuit praeceptum, ἀνέχου καὶ ἀπέχουsustine & abstine. Epictetus apud Gellium lib. 17. N. A. c. 19.

7. Gregor. part. 3. Curae Pastoral. admon. 20. Nisi mentes abstinentium plerunque abstinentia â sinu tranquillitatis excuteret, nequaquam Petrus, dum diceret: Ministrate in fide vestra virtutem, in virtute scientiam, in scientia autem abstinentiam, protinus vigilanter adiungeret, dicens. In abstinentia autem patientiam, deesse quippe abstinentibus patientiam praevidit, quae eis ut adesset, admonuit.

8. Beda in hoc loco. Abstinentiam necesse est semper ut patientia comitetur, ut quicunque â voluptatibus mundi sese continere didicit, eius quoquo adversa quaeque firmè sustineat, â dextris vide licet & â sinistris, per arma iustitiae munitus. quod repetit Glossa interlinearis.

9. Dorotheus doctr. 6. Studeat unusquisque pro virili parte cohaerere proximo suo. Quò enim magis proximo in amore & benevolentia cohaeserit, eò amplius & DEO cohaerebit. Bernh. in meditat. cap. 5. col. 1195. Si DEUM diligimus, etiam imaginem eius diligamus. Idem in lib. de dilig. DEO. Ut perfecta fiat iustitia tua in dilectione proximi, Deum in eam habere necesse est, alioquin proximum purè diligere non potest, qui Deum non diligit. Oportet ergo Deum diligi priùs, ut in Deo diligatur & proximus.

10. Beda in h. l. In pietate amorem fraternitatis ministrare iubet, ut non alterius rei intuitu pietatis opera suis quisque adversariis impendat, nisi fraternae tantùm dilectionis; hoc videlicet totae intentione procurans, ut quos docendo solùm vel redarguendo nequit, ad effectum pietatis orando velbenefaciendo convertat.

11. Tertullianus ad Scapulam, cap. 1. Amicos diligere, omnium est; inimicos autem, solorum Christianorum.

12. Irenaeus lib. 4. advers. haeres. cap. 27. Aptum te omnibus atque utilem praesta proximo, non illorum malitiam intuens, sed tuam bonitatem perficiens.

13. Basilius serm. de Instit. Monach. Sicut DEUS promiscuè omnibus lucem imperitutr: sic imitatores DEI, caritatis ipsorum radium, aequaliter communicare omnibus debent.

## 1:5-11 Questions and observations
Observations. 1. To γνῶσιν in a true Christian there ought to be added πρᾶξις.

2. Those destitute of good works are like unfruitful trees. It was a sin to appear empty before the LORD.Exod. 23. vers. 15.Deut. 16. v. 16.

3. Good works are not the self-chosen worship of hypocrites, but those which are divinely prescribed in the word.

4. He who is destitute of true faith, charity, and the remaining virtues enumerated by the Apostle in this place, is blind and like a blind man gropes at noon, because he has not yet been freed from connate spiritual blindness, nor has the light of faith been kindled in his heart by the light of the word. 1. Iohann. 2. vers. 9. He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now. v. 10. He who loves his brother remains in the light and there is no scandal in him. verse 11. But he who hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. Gloss. ordinar. on this passage. The eye designates knowledge, the hand operation. He is blind and groping with his hand who, not having the knowledge of right operation, performs whatever seems right to himself, and being ignorant of the light of truth, as if extending a hand to a work which he does not see, he directs his steps into a path which he does not foresee, and therefore the wretch falls into the ruin of perdition, which he could not foresee.

5. Those who are spiritually blind, and have nowhere to set their foot, stumble with easy effort, always stagger, and finally relapse into their former darkness.

6. He who neglects the pursuit of good works shows by the very fact that he has forgotten the benefit received, namely the remission of sins, since he does not show himself grateful for it, as was fitting.

7. It is useful in many ways never to lay aside the memory of former sins, even though they have been forgiven. Gregory, book 22 of the Morals, chapter 2. It is one thing to see sin through judgment, which the penitent does by condemning himself, another through appetite.

8. Our calling and election is made firm, not by curious and idle speculations, by which we strive to break into the inner chambers of divine judgments, but by the sense of divine grace, by the testing of whether we are in the faith, and by the pursuit of good works. Staupitz to Luther. Let your disputation about predestination begin from the wounds of Christ.

9. But our calling and election is made firm not only for us, but also for others through the pursuit of good works. Phil. 1. vers. 6. Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ. Meanwhile, the certainty in us is from the judgment of faith, the certainty in others is from the judgment of charity.

10. He who exerts himself diligently and zealously in good works fortifies himself against more serious falls: just as a soldier who exercises himself daily in arms is less exposed to the snares of enemies.

11. A fall happens in two ways, in the doctrine of faith and in life. A strengthened knowledge of Christ, exerting itself diligently in the pursuit of good works, prevents both falls and fortifies us against them.

12. To the pious πλουσίως an entrance into the eternal kingdom of Christ is richly supplied, because God, who called and chose us to his eternal kingdom, is πλούσιος in mercy Eph. 2. vers. 4. is πλούσιος unto all who call upon him, Rom. 10. vers. 12. Christ by his poverty made us πλούσιους 2. Cor. 8. v. 9. and thus most abundantly merited for us the heavenly inheritance, and poured out his Holy Spirit πλούσιους richly upon us, Tit. 3. v. 6.

13. Those who exert themselves strenuously in the pursuit of piety overcome the terror of death, and are transferred with joy into the heavenly kingdom.

14. All the kingdoms of the world are transitory, nay, momentary: only the kingdom of Christ is eternal, in which heavenly and eternal goods are distributed to the citizens of that kingdom.

15. That kingdom of Christ is described thus, that of it there shall be no endLuc. 1. v. 33. that for believers it is prepared from the foundation of the world,Matth. 15. v. 34. that in it a most ample inheritance is prepared for believers,Eph. 5. v. 5. that it is a heavenly kingdom2. Tim. 4. v. 18.

16. Christ, because He is our Lord, that is, true GOD in the unity of person, therefore He could become our Savior: conversely, because Christ is our Savior, therefore He is also our Lord, not only according to His divine, but also according to His human Nature, because He acquired us for Himself as His own property with His own blood.

Latin:

Observationes. 1. Ad γνῶσιν in vero Christiano debet accedere πρᾶξις.

2. Destituti bonis operibus sunt velut infrugiferae arbores. Nefas erat, vacuum apparere coram DOMINO.Exod. 23. vers. 15.Deut. 16. v. 16.

3. Bona opera non sunt cultus electitii hypocritarum, sed quae divinitus in verbo praescripta.

4. Qui destitutus est vera fide, caritate & reliquis virtutibus, ab Apostolo hoc loco enumeratis, coecus est & instar coeci in meridie palpat, quia nondum liberatus est â connata coecitate spirituali, necdum in corde eius per lucem verbi accensa est lux fidei. 1. Iohann. 2. vers. 9.Qui dicit, se in luce esse, & fratrem suum odit, in tenebris est usque huc.v. 10.Qui diligit fratrem suum, in lumine manet & scandalum in eo non est. vers. 11. Qui autem odit fratrem suum, in tenebris est & in tenebris ambulat, & nescit, quò eat, quia tenebrae obcoecaverunt oculos suos. Gloss. ordinar. in h. l. Oculus scientiam, manus operationem designat. Coecus est & manu tentans, qui scientiam rectae operationis non habens, quicquid sibi rectum videtur, operatur, & lumen veritatis ignorans, quasi manum ad opus, quod non videt, extendens, gressus in iter, quod non praevidet, extollit, ideoque miser in ruinam perditionis, quam praescire nequibat, incidit.

5. Qui spiritualiter coeci sunt, nec habent ubi pedem figant, facili negotio impingunt, semper titubant, & tandem in pristinas tenebras relabuntur.

6. Qui studium bonorum operum negligit, reipsâ ostendit, se accepti beneficii, videl. remissionis peccatorum esse oblitum, cùm pro eo sese gratum, uti decebat, minimè praestet.

7. Multis modis utile est, nun quam deponere memoriam pristinorum peccatorum, quamvis remissorum. Gregorius lib. 22. moral. cap. 2. Aliud est videre peccatum per iudicium, quod paenitens facit damnando seipsum, aliud per appetitum.

8. Vocatio & electio nostra fit firma, non curiosis & otiosis speculationibus, quibus in adyta divinorum iudiciorum irrumpere satagimus, sed gratiae divinae sensu, probatione, an simus in fide & studio bonorum operum. Straupitus ad Lutherum. Disputatio tua de praedestinatione incipiat â vulneribus Christi.

9. Non nobis autem solùm, sed etiam aliis per bonorum operum studium firma fit vocatio & electio nostra. Phil. 1. vers. 6.Confidens hoc ipsum quia qui coepit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet usque in diem Iesu Christi. Interim certitudo in nobis est ex iudicio fidei, certitudo in aliis ex iudicio caritatis.

10. Qui in bonis operibus gnaviter & sedulò sese exercet, contra graviores lapsus sese praemunit: sicut miles, qui in armis quotidie sese exercet, minùs expositus est hostium insidiis.

11. Lapsus dupliciter contingit, in doctrina fidei & vita. Utrumque lapsum impedit & contra eum nos praemunit firmata Christi cognitio, in bonorum operum studio gnaviter sese exercens.

12. Piis πλουσίως opulenter suppeditatur introitus in aeternum Christi regnum, quia Deus, qui vocavit & elegit nos ad regnum suum aeternum, estπλούσιοςin misericordiaEph. 2. vers. 4. est πλούσιοςin omnes, qui invocant ipsum,Rom. 10. vers, 12.Christus suâ inopiâ fecit nosπλούσιους2. Cor. 8. v. 9. adeoque abundantissimè caelestem hereditatem nobis promeruit, & Spiritum suum sanctumπλούσιουςopulenter in nos effudit,Tit. 3. v. 6.

13. Qui in studio pietatis strenuè sese exercent, mortis terrorem vincunt, & cum gaudio in regnum caeleste transferuntur.

14. Omnia mundi regna sunt transitoria, imò momentanea: solum Christi regnum est aeternum, in quo caelestia & aeterna bona civibus illius regni distribuuntur.

15. Regnum illud Christi sic describitur, quòd eius non sit futurus finisLuc. 1. v. 33. quòd credentibus illud sit paratum â constituitione mundi,Matth. 15. v. 34.quòd in eo credentibus hereditas amplissima sit parata,Eph. 5. v. 5.quòd sit regnum caeleste2. Tim. 4. v. 18.

16. Christus, quia noster Dominus h. e. in personae unitate verus DEUS, ideò potuit fieri noster Salvator: vicissim quia Christus est noster Salvator, ideò etiam est noster Dominus, non solùm secundum divinam, sed etiam secundum humanam Naturam, quia in peculium suo sanguine nos sibi acquisivit.

## 1:8
Connection. To the ladder-like enumeration of virtues, to the progress of which he exhorts, the Apostle subjects the arguments of the exhortation, the first of which is taken from the end of the calling to the kingdom of Christ, which is fruitfulness in good things, and progress in the stadium and study of virtues.

Exposition of the text. ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα. Certain Latin codices read: Unless these things are present with you and abound. Others, however: for when these things are present with you and abound. But the former version is more consistent with the text: for the Apostle is engaged in exhorting, and teaches how useful and salutary it will be for them if they strive to abound and become rich in the enumerated virtues, which virtues the context shows are denoted by ταῦτα in this place. The participles ὑπάρχοντα (for which certain codices read παρόντα) καὶ πλεονάζοντα) can be rendered in the best way such that one of them is expressed by an adverb, as if the Apostle had said ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν πλουσίως ὑπ/αρχοντα. Unless these things are abundantly present with you, in which way Luther also rendered it. Denn wo solches reichlich bei euch ist. The Vulgate rendered the participle by abound, but it would have translated it more correctly by exuberate. The Syriac has the verb [יתר] it abounded, when it is used concerning quantity; it excelled, when it is used concerning quality. Oecumenius elegantly annotates on this place: If these are profitable, παρουσία, much more. περιουσία. Moreover, that abundance of virtues can be understood not only of internal, and as is usually said, intensive increase, but also external, so that they may exert themselves outwardly and go forth into work. οὐκ ἀργοὺς, οὐδὲ ἀκάρπους καθίστησεν. The Vulgate rendered the word ἀργοὺς as empty, but it is more correctly translated as idle, vacant from work, just as the Syriac also rendered it by [בטילא] idle, slothful, vacant from work and labor. For ἀκάρπους certain manuscript codices, as also the Aldine and Basle editions, and Oecumenius, published at Verona in the year 1532, read ἀπράκτους, which Erasmus rendered laboring in vain, others useless, doing no work. But the Apostle had already said this before in the word ἀργοὺς. The truer reading therefore has ἀκάρπους unfruitful, in which there is an elegant metaphor, derived from the fruits of trees, with which good works are also compared elsewhere in the Scriptures. Matth. 3. vers. 10.cap. 7. vers. 17. 18. & 19. Ordinary Gloss on this place: They will not constitute you empty of virtues in this age, or without fruit in the future. Or not empty in yourselves, like a vessel empty of every good liquid, nor without fruit in others, whom by your example you shall turn. The Vulgate rendered the word καθίστησεν in the future tense, they shall constitute you. But the Greek word is of the present tense, which nevertheless seems to be placed here for the future. For the sense is, if these things are abundantly present to you, they will not suffer you to be idle or unfruitful. At the same time, however, it signifies that they themselves will be very full and abundant in the fruits of good works, for by denying he affirms more than if he were simply to affirm.

Εἰς τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπίγνωσιν. Some establish that the preposition εἰς in this place denotes a comparison, so that the sense may be: If your life is compared to the knowledge of CHRIST, with which you are endowed. But because it can hardly be proven by any suitable example that εἰς denotes a comparison, therefore it is more correctly said that εἰς is placed for ἐν, so that the sense may be: If those enumerated virtues are not only present to you, but also abound, that is, are abundantly present, you will not be idle and unfruitful in the knowledge of CHRIST, but industrious and fruitful, for from the negation the contrary affirmation is understood.

Latin:

Connexio. Enumerationi virtutum scalari, ad quarum profectum hortatur, subiicit Apostolus exhortationis argumenta, quorum primum sumitur â fine vocationis ad regnum Christi, qui est fructificatio in bonis, ac in stadio & studio virtutum profectus.

Textus expositio. ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα. Quidam Codd. Latini legunt. Haec nisi vobiscum adsint & superent. Alii vero, haec enim vobis cùm adsint & superent. Sed prior versio textui magis congruit: versatur enim Apostolus in exhortando, ac docet, quàm utile & salutare ipsis sit futurum, si enumeratis virtutibus abundare ac divites fieri studeant, quas virtutes per ταῦτα h. l. denotari, contextus ostendit. Participia ὑπάρχοντα (pro quo Codd. quidam legunt παρόντα) καὶ πλεονάζοντα optimâ ratione sic reddi possunt, ut alterum eorum exprimatur per adverbium, ac si dixisset Apostolus ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν πλουσίως ὑπ/αρχοντα.Haec nisi abundanter vobis aderunt, quo modo etiam Lutherus reddidit. Denn wo solches reichlich bei euch ist. Vulgata participium reddidit per superent, sed rectiùs vertisset per exuberent. Syrus habet verbum [יתר]abundavit, cum de quantitate; excelluit, cum de qualitate usurpatur. Oecumenius eleganter ad hunc locum annotat. Si horum prodestπαρουσία,multò magisπεριουσία.Abundantia autem illa virtutum intelligi potest non de solo interno, ac ut dici solet, intensivo incremento, sed etiam externo, ut sese foràs exerant & in opus exeant.οὐκ ἀργοὺς, οὐδὲ ἀκάρπους καθίστησεν. Vocem ἀργοὺς vulgata reddidit vacuos, sed rectiùs vertitur otiosos, ab opere vacantes, sicut & Syrus reddidit per [בטילא]otiosos, desidiosos, ab opere & labore vacantes. Pro ἀκάρπους quidam Codd. Manuscripti, uti etiam editio Aldina ac Basilëensis, & Oecumenius, Veronae Anno 1532. editus, legunt ἀπράκτους, quod Erasmus reddidit in irritum laborantes, alii inutiles, nihil operis agentes. Sed hoc iam antè dixerat Apostolus in voce ἀργοὺς. Verior igitur lectio habet ἀκάρπουςinfructuosos, in quo est elegans metaphora, â fructibus arborum deducta, cum quibus bona opera etiam alibi in Scripturis comparantur. Matth. 3. vers. 10.cap. 7. vers. 17. 18. & 19. Gloss. ordinar, ad hunc locum. Non constituent vos vacuos virtutibus in hoc seculo, vel sine fructu in futuro. Vel non vacuos in vobis ipsis, sicut vas omni bono liquore vacuum, nec sine fructu in aliis, quos exemplo vestro convertitis. Verbum καθίστησεν Vulg. reddidit in futuro, constituent vos. Sed verbum Graecum est temporis praesentis, quod tamen pro futuro hîc videtur poni. Sensus enim est, si haec vobis abundanter adsint, non patientur vos esse otiosos vel infructuosos. Simul tamen significat, ipsos in fructibus bonorum operum valde plenos & abundantes fore, plus enim negando affirmat, quam si simpliciter affirmaret.

Εἰς τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπίγνωσιν. Quidam statuunt, praepositionem εἰς hoc loco notare collationem, ut sit sensus. Si vita vestra comparetur ad cognitionem CHRISTI, quâ praediti estis. Sed quia vix poterit idoneo aliquo exemplo probari, quod εἰς collationem notet, ideò rectiùs dicitur, εἰς poni pro ἐν, ut sit sensus. Si enumeratae istae virtutes vobis non solùm adsint, sed etiam exuberent, hoc est, abundanter adsint, non eritis in cognitione CHRISTI otiosi & infructuosi, sed operosi & frugiferi, ex negatione enim intelligitur contraria affirmatio.

## 1:9
Connection. This is the second argument of the exhortation, sought from the consequent absurdity. Unless you strive for the progress of virtues, you will demonstrate by the very fact that you are spiritually blind and forgetful of the former benefits received from GOD. For he who is truly illuminated by the saving knowledge of GOD and worthily weighs the benefits received, he strives to serve GOD piously and to show himself grateful to such a benefactor.

Exposition of the text. ᾧ γὰρ μὴ πάρεστι ταῦτα. This member ἀντιθετικῶς corresponds to that which had been said in the preceding verse, ταῦτα ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα. But the Apostle softens the exhortation by a change of person. In the preceding part of the antithesis he had said ταῦτα ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα, in the second person; here, however, he speaks absolutely and indeterminately in the third person, ᾧ μὴ πάρεστι ταῦτα, signifying that he hopes well out of charity concerning all to whom he writes, that the enumerated virtues are present in them, and indeed abundantly. The Syriac in this place has the same word [שכיחן] which he had used in the preceding verse. He, in whom these are not found.

Τυφλὸς ἔστι μυωπάζων. For μυωπάζων the Aldine edition reads μουπάζων, which the Syriac rendered, not seeing: The Vulgate Interpreter, groping with the hand. Erasmus, groping the way with the hand.

Λήθην, λαβὼν τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ τῶν πάλαι αὑτοῦ ἁμαρτιῶν. To receive oblivion is the same as to forget, just as the Syriac also rendered it simply. [טעא] he has forgotten, he has been ignorant, he has neglected the purgation of former sins. Concerning the adverb πάλαι the participle πεποιημένων of sins formerly committed is to be understood. The sense therefore is that he who neglects the pursuit of the enumerated virtues shows by the very deed that he has forgotten that he has been purged from his old sins.

Latin:

Connexio. Alterum hoc est exhortationis argumentum, â consequente absurdo petitum. Nisi profectui virtutum studebitis, reipsâ demonstrabitis, vos esse spiritualiter caecos & pristinorum beneficiorum â DEO acceptorum oblitos. Qui enim falutari DEI cognitione verè illuminatus est & beneficia accepta dignè expendit, is DEO piè servire & tanto benefactori se gratum praestare studet.

Textus expositio. ᾧ γὰρ μὴ πάρεστι ταῦτα. Hoc membrum ἀντιθετικῶς respondet illi, quod in praecedente versiculo dictum erat, ταῦτα ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα. Emollit autem Apostolus exhortationem mutatione personae. In praecedente antitheseos parte dixerat ταῦτα ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα, in secunda personâ; hîc verò absolutè & indeterminatè in tertia persona dicit, ᾧ μὴ πάρεστι ταῦτα, significans, se de omnibus, ad quos scribit, ex caritate benè sperare, quòd virtutes enumeratae ipsis adsint, & quidem abundanter. Syrus h. l. habet idem verbum [שכיחן] quo usus fuerat in vers. praeced. Ille, in quo non inveniuntur haec.

Τυφλὸς ἔστι μυωπάζων. Pro μυωπάζων Aldina editio legit μουπάζων, quod Syrus reddidit, non videns: Vulgatus Interpres. manu tentans. Erasmus, manu viam tentans.

Λήθην, λαβὼν τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ τῶν πάλαι αὑτοῦ ἁμαρτιῶν. Oblivionem accipere idem est quod oblivisci, sicuti etiam Syrus simpliciter reddidit. [טעא]oblitus est, ignoravit, neglexit priorum delictorum purgationem. Circa adverbium πάλαι subaudiendum participium πεποιημένων peccatorum olim commissorum. Sensus igitur est, quòd is, qui studium enumeratarum virtutum negligit, reipsâ ostendat, se oblitum esse, quòd â veteribus suis peccatis sit purgatus.

## 1:10
Connection. This is the third argument of the exhortation, taken from the useful or consequent benefit. Through progress in the pursuit of virtues, you will be able to make your calling and election firm, and to be guarded from more serious falls.

Exposition of the text. Διὸ μᾶλλον σπουδάσατε. Vulgate. Wherefore brethren, labor the more, therefore study much more, or give effort. τὸ μᾶλλον is not of one increasing, but of one correcting, rather labor, give effort. The word [יצף] is proper to the Chaldeans and Syrians, he was solicitous, he took care with the highest zeal, Matth. 10. v. 19. Luc. 10. v. 35.

Βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι. Βεβαίαν Estius determines that it is more correctly translated firm, than sure. 1. because that Greek word properly signifies, Rom. 4. v. 16. βεβαία ἐπαγγελία is a firm promise 2. Cor. 1. v. 7. ἡ ἐλπὶς βεβαία firm hope. Hebr. 2. v. 2. 2. Petr. 1.

v. 19. λόγος βέβαιος firm word. Compare Heb. 3. v. 6. & 14.c. 6. v. 19.c. 9. v. 17. 2. because the Vulgate Interpreter elsewhere rendered that as firm, as is evident from the cited passages. 3. because a fall is opposed to firmness, in the part immediately following. We willingly concede that βεβαίαν is rightly translated as firm, but we deny that that firmness is to be opposed to certainty, which Estius asserts to that end, so that he may weaken the argument which we draw from this Apostolic passage for the certainty of election, concerning which matter we shall see later. κλῆσις in this place is understood as that which is joined with acceptance on the part of man, and justification through faith, as appears from the added word ἐκλογῆς. It is therefore accepted in that sense in which Rom. 8. vers. 30. Whom God predestined, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified, and whom he justified, them he also glorified. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. God called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the secular times.

Ἐκλογὴ is understood concerning election to glory, which was made from eternity, in this sense. Give diligent effort, so that you may make your calling, by which you were called in time to the kingdom of grace, and your election, by which you were elected from eternity to the kingdom of glory, certain and firm. The Vulgate version here inserts, by good works, concerning which προσδιοριοσμῷ what is to be determined, we shall see later. ταυξα γαρ ποιουντες. By ταῦτα are understood the virtues enumerated in v. 5. 6. & 7., which are likewise denoted by the pronoun ταυξα in vers. 8.. The pronoun ταῦτα can also be referred to the sentence immediately preceding. For doing these things, i.e., if you make your calling and election firm. οὐ μὴ πταίσητε πότε. The Vulgate rendered, you shall not sin at any time. Ambrose, book 3 de fide chapter 6, and Idacius against Varimadus cite, you shall not err at any time. But the Greek πταίειν properly signifies to slip, to stumble, to offend. Rom. 11. v. 11. μὴ ἔπταισαν, ἵνα πέσωσι, where the Vulgate also rendered. Have they so stumbled, that they should fall? Iac. 2. v. 10. Whoever shall have kept the whole law, πταίσει δὲ where the Vulgate likewise rendered, but shall offend in one, he is made guilty of all. chapter of the same v. 2. In many things πταίομεν πάντες. the Vulgate likewise rendered, we all offend. And immediately. Εἴτις ἐν λόγῳ πταίει. Vulgate If any man offend not in word. Deservedly therefore Erasmus also criticizes the Vulgate Interpreter on this account, That he did not always express one and the same Greek word with one and the same Latin word. The Syrian has the word [שרל] which is general, he erred, he sinned, he offended, he slipped. But in the word πταίειν there is a metaphor drawn from those who, while walking or running, strike their foot, whence Eustathius explains it by προσκόπτω and derives it from πτῶ whence πίπτω. Suidas explains it by προσκρούω, adding this proverb μὴ πολλάκις πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν λίθον πταίειν, do not strike against the same stone too often. This metaphor fits this passage beautifully. For the Christian life is compared to a stadium, in which one must proceed in a continuous and unoffending course, until we arrive at the proposed goal of eternal life. 1. Cor. 9. v. 24. Do you not know that those who run in a stadium, all indeed run: but one receives the prize. So run, that you may comprehend. Phil. 1. vers. 10. that you may be ἀπρόσκοποι without offense unto the day of Christ. cap. 3. vers. 14. Forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching myself forth to those that are before κατὰ σκόπον διώκω to the prize of the eternal calling: Jude, penultimate verse τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ φυλάξαι ἡμᾶς ἀπταίστους. The sense, therefore, of the Apostolic saying is this. If you will give diligent effort to the virtues enumerated thus far, in the study and course of your calling you will not strike, you will not fall into sins that devastate the conscience, nor will you fall from grace, but you will happily continue your course, and will arrive at eternal happiness, or which is the same thing, you will not fall from that to which you have been called, namely from the heavenly inheritance, which will be a certain argument of election. Gloss. ordin. You will not sin at any time i. e. you will attain to eternal life, where you will no longer sin. But this is forced. Therefore it is added, or you will avoid criminal sins from which he remains immune, with GOD helping, who has surrendered himself to the above-mentioned virtues.

Latin:

Connexio. Tertium hoc est exhortationis argumentum, ab utili sive consequente commodo petitum. Per profectum in studio virtutum, vocationem & electionem vestram firmam facere, & à gravioribus lapsibus custodiri poteritis.

Textus expositio. Διὸ μᾶλλον σπουδάσατε. Vulgat. Quapropter fratres magis satagite, propterea multò magis studete, seu operam date. τὸ μᾶλλον non est augentis, sed corrigentis, potius satagite, operam date. Verbum [יצף] est Chaldaeis & Syris proprium, solicitus fuit, summo studio curavit,Matth. 10. v. 19.Luc. 10. v. 35.

Βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι. Βεβαίαν Estius statuit, rectiùs verti firmam, quàm certam. 1. quia Graecum verbum illud propriè significat,Rom. 4. v. 16.βεβαία ἐπαγγελίαest firma promissio2. Cor. 1. v. 7.ἡ ἐλπὶς βεβαίαfirma spes.Hebr. 2. v. 2. 2. Petr. 1.

v. 19.λόγος βέβαιοςfirmus sermo. Confer Heb. 3. v. 6. & 14.c. 6. v. 19.c. 9. v. 17. 2. quia vulgatus Interpres alibi illud reddidit per firmum, ut patet ex allatis locis. 3. quia firmitati opponitur lapsus, in parte proximè sequente. Nos libenter concedimus, βεβαίαν rectè verti per firmam, sed negamus, firmitatem illam opponendam esse certitudini, quod Estius eo fine asserit, ut argumentum, quod pro certitudine electionis ex hoc loco Apostolico ducimus, enervet, quâ de re postea videbimus. κλῆσις hoc loco intelligitur ea, quae cum acceptione ex parte hominis, & iustificatione per fidem est coniuncta, ut apparet ex addita voce ἐκλογῆς. Accipitur ergo eo sensu, quo Rom. 8. vers. 30.Quos Deus praedestinavit, hos & vocavit: & quos vocavit, hos & iustificavit, quos a, iustificavit, illos etiam glorificavit.2. Tim. 1. v. 9.Deus vocavit nos vocatione sancta, non secundùm opera nostra, sed secundùm propositum suum & gratiam, quae data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia.

Ἐκλογὴ intelligitur de electione ad gloriam, quae facta est ab aeterno, hoc sensu. Operam date sedulam, ut vocationem vestram, quâ in tempore ad regnum gratiç vocati estis, & electionem, quâ ab aeterno ad regnum gloriae electi estis, certam ac firmam faciatis. Vulgata versio hîc inserit, per bona opera, de quo προσδιοριοσμῷ quid statuendum sit, postea videbimus. ταυξα γαρ ποιουντες. Per ταῦτα intelliguntur virtutes in v. 5. 6. & 7. enumeratae, quae itidem per pronomen ταυξα in vers. 8. denotantur. Potest etiam pronomen ταῦτα referri ad sententiam proximè praecedentem. Haec enim facientes, h. e. si vocationem & electionem vestram firmam facietis. οὐ μὴ πταίσητε πότε. Vulg. reddidit, non peccabitis aliquando. Ambros. lib. 3. de fide cap. 6. & Idacius contra Varimadum citant, non errabitis aliquando. Sed Graecum πταίειν propriè significat labi, impingere, offendere.Rom. 11. v. 11.μὴ ἔπταισαν, ἵνα πέσωσι, ubi Vulg. etiam reddidit. Nunquid sic offenderunt, ut caderent?Iac. 2. v. 10.Quicunque totam legem fervaverit,πταίσει δὲ ubi Vulg. itidem reddidit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. cap. eiusd. v. 2.In multisπταίομεν πάντες. Vulg. itidem reddidit, offendimus omnes. Et statim. Εἴτις ἐν λόγῳ πταίει. Vulg. Si quis in verbo non offendit. Merito igitur Erasmus vulgatum Interpretem etiam hoc nomine perstringit, quod unum idemque verbum Graecum non uno eodemque verbo Latino semper expresserit. Syrus habet verbum [שרל] quod est generale, erravit, peccavit, offendit, lapsus est. Caeterùm in verbo πταίειν est metaphora ducta ab illis, qui inter ambulandum vel currendum pedem impingunt, unde Eustathius exponit per προσκόπτω & derivat â πτῶ unde πίπτω. Suidas exponit per προσκρούω, subiungens hoc proverbium μὴ πολλάκις πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν λίθον πταίειν,ne saepius ad eundem lapidem impingas. Haec metaphora pulchrè huic loco congruit. Vita enim Christiana comparatur stadio, in quo continuo & in offenso cursu progrediendum, donec ad propositum vitae aeternae scopum perveniamus. 1. Cor. 9. v. 24.Nescitis, quod qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currunt: sed unus accipit brabeum. Sic currite, ut comprehendatis.Phil. 1. vers. 10.ut sitisἀπρόσκοποιsine offensa in diem Christi.cap. 3. vers. 14.Quae retrò sunt obliviscens, ad ea verò, qua sunt priora, extendens meipsumκατὰ σκόπον διώκωad brabeum aeternae vocationis: Iudae versu penult. τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ φυλάξαι ἡμᾶς ἀπταίστους. Sensus igitur dicti Apostolici hic est. Si virtutibus hactenus enumeratis sedulam dabitis operam, in studio & cursu vocationis vestrae non impingetis, non ruetis in peccata vastantia conscientiam, neque ex gratiâ excidetis, sed cursum vestrum feliciter continuabitis, & ad aeternam felicitatem pervenietis, vel quod idem est, non excidetis ab eo, ad quod vocati estis, videlicet ab hereditate caelesti, quod erit certum electionis argumentum. Gloss. ordin. Non peccabitis aliquando i. e. ad vitam aeternam attingetis, ubi ampliùs non peccabitis. Sed hoc coactum. Ideò subiicitur, vel criminalia vitabitis â quibus immunis iuvante DEO permanet, qui supra dictis virtutibus sese mancipaverit.

## 1:11
Connection. The Apostle continues in explaining the utility, following the progress in the enumerated virtues, and having explained in the preceding verse

To the twofold utility he adds a third, which is the end of our faith, eternal life. 1. Pet. 1. v. 5. & 9.

Exposition of the text. οὕτω γὰρ namely, If you make your calling and election sure, and diligently beware of more serious falls, but if you are overtaken by a fall, you may quickly rise again. Gal. 6. v. 1.

Πλουσίως ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται ὑμῖν ἡ εἴσοδος εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον βασιλείαν τοῦ κυρίου ὑμῶν, καὶ σωτῆρος Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ. The Vulgate rendered the little word πλουσίως as abundantly, but it signifies properly opulently, Col. 3. v. 16. 1. Tim. 6. v. 17. Tit. 3. v. 6. The Syriac rendered it [עתיראית] opulently, abundantly, from the root [עתר] multiplied, from the Hebrew עשר he was enriched, he was made wealthy. Ambrose, book 3 of On the Faith, chapter 6, reads more abundantly, so that it may be signified that God rewards our works more abundantly and more than they deserve in themselves.

The Vulgate rendered the word ἐπιχορηγέσεται as shall be ministered, using the simple for the compound, shall be sub-ministered. The Syriac has the word [מתיהבא] there shall be given to you an entrance into the eternal kingdom, that is, you shall have a free and open entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. For εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον βασιλείαν certain codices read ἐπουράνιον βασιλείαν.. Ambrose in the said place and Idacius against Varimadus read, into the eternal empire. The same Ambrose reads, of God and our Lord Savior Jesus Christ, and from this he argues against the Arians, that the kingdom of the Father and the Son is not divided but equal, and the same for both, and therefore they are consubstantial, since it cannot be that the right of the kingdom of the Father, whom the Arians say is greater than the Son, is lesser, nor that the kingdom of the Son, if he is lesser according to his divinity, is equal.

Furthermore, in the word ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται the Apostle looks back to verse 5, in which he had said, ἐπιχορηγήσατε in faith virtue; and to verse 8, in which he had said, ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα. Therefore he wishes to say this. If you have ministered virtue in faith, and the rest previously enumerated, and thus have been rich in good works, God out of grace will opulently supply to you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of Christ, and thus you will be rich in heavenly rewards, which will be conferred upon you by grace from our Lord and Savior Christ. If you demonstrate faith by good works, an increase of faith will be supplied to you, and perseverance in faith, so that you may run in the way of the divine commandments, as if in a race toward the proposed goal, but also your heart will be filled with joy, and with fortitude, and with an ardent desire for true glory, so that you may be able to make your election firm.

Q. 1. Why are good works compared to the fruits of trees? Resp. 1. On account of testimony. Just as the goodness of the fruits testifies to the goodness of the tree: so good works testify to the interior renewal of the heart. 2. On account of good pleasure. Just as good fruits affect the taste of man with their sweetness: so good works are pleasing to GOD. 3. On account of danger. Just as a fruitless tree is cut down and cast into the fire: so those destitute of good works are the material of infernal fire.

Q. 2. Whether μυωπάζων is more correctly translated as shortsighted, or, groping with the hand? Resp. 1. μυωπάζων is derived from the noun μύωψ, since μυωπάζων is nothing other than μύωξ εἰμὶ.. However, who are called μύωπες, can be known from the passage of Aristotle in Problem. sect. 31, where he asks, διὰ τὶ οἱ μύωπες συνάγοντες τὰ βλέφαρα ὁρῶσιν; why μυωπες do they see with contracted eyelids? and afterwards he adds: οἱ ἐκ γενετῆς τὰ μὲν ἐγγυς βλέποντος, τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἀποστάσεως οὐχ ὁρῶντες, sc. μύωπες they are called; because from their first birth they indeed see things that are near, but they do not see things that are remote. Afterwards he adds, ἐναντία δὲ πάσχουσιν οἱ γηρῶντος τοῖς μυωπάζουσιν, τὰ γὰρ ἐγγὺς μὴ ὁρῶντος τὰ πόῤῥωθεν βλέπουσι. But a defect contrary to this happens to old men, since old men, not seeing things brought near, see things removed far away. Because of this passage of Aristotle, Rob. Stephanus in the Thesaurus of the Greek language, and in the Concordances of the N. T., judges that μυωπάζων is most conveniently translated, seeing nothing from afar, by which reasoning the sense of the Apostolic statement would be: He to whom these virtues are not present is shortsighted, and he is blind in such a way that he directs the sharpness of his eyes to worldly things, as being near, but he is unable to direct it to heavenly things, as being placed far away. 2. To this meaning of the participle μυωπάζων it could be referred, that according to the etymology, or the composition itself μυωπάζων it is said as if μύων ὦπα or ὦπας, who blinks with his eyes. For those who are unable to see things placed far away close their eyes a little bit in part, and blink, so that the sharpness of them [may be directed] thither they can intend. This meaning is also favored by what Budaeus reports, that Dionysius the Areopagite uses this word for being dim-sighted, and by what Gellius says in book 4, N. A., chapter 2, μύωπα is called lusciosus by the Latins. 3. But since the noun τυφλὸς, has preceded, which absolutely and simply signifies a blind man, therefore by μυωπάζων in this place, one cannot understand him who is dim-sighted or is dim-sighted, or sees with blinking eyes, or is unable to see things placed at a distance; for such a person cannot be called blind, since he still sees, although he may labor under some defect of the eyes or of sight. More correctly, therefore, μυωπάζων is rendered as groping with the hand, which is characteristic of the blind, who seek their way by groping not only with their hands, but also with their feet. 4. Hence Erasmus derives this name from μυῶν from mice, which see nothing outside their caverns, but are accustomed to follow a wall, or a board, or whatever else may be in their way, until they have found a hole. Robertus Stephanus thinks that Erasmus was openly deceived in this etymology, although Stephanus himself acknowledges that μυωπίαν is used regarding the little cavern of mice, being so called from μῦς & ὀπὴ, with ο changed into ω, in which meaning the word μυωπία is used by Aristotle in his book on animals, 6. μυωπίας ὕες ἀνορύττουσι, and by Aelian, who writes thus about mice, καὶ μελλούσης τῆς οἰκίας ἀπολισθαίνειν, ἀπολείπουσι τὰς μυωπίας αὐτῶν. The Greek Scholia μυωπάζων explain it by τυφλώττειν to be blinded, to grope out the way in the manner of the blind, and they establish that the metaphor is drawn from subterranean mice, which they call moles, because they are perpetually blind. 5. The sense, therefore, of the Apostolic saying is this. To whom the enumerated virtues are not present, he is blind; he gropes with his hand like a blind man, not knowing where he may direct his journey. Without doubt, the Apostle looks to the Mosaic passage, Deut. 28. vers. 28, The Lord shall strike you with madness and blindness and astonishment of heart v. 29. and you shall grope in the midday, as the blind man gropes in the darkness. Estius opposes this comparison, because in that place there are different expressions in the Greek by which that groping is signified. But even if a parallelism of words does not have a place here, nevertheless there is a parallelism of things, such as can also be established in other sayings of Scripture compared with this Apostolic passage. Job 5. vers. 14. By day they shall meet with darkness and as in the night, so shall they grope in the midday. cap. 12. v. 25. They shall grope as in the dark and not in the light, and he shall make them stagger like drunken men. Esai. 59. v. 10. We have groped for the wall like the blind And as if without eyes we have groped, we have stumbled at midday. 6. Some, in order to maintain that he, to whom the enumerated virtues are lacking, is said in a different respect to be blind and dim-sighted, or blinking with his eyes, bring forward the Pauline passage 1 Cor. 8 v. 2 as if it were parallel to this of ours, so that the sense may be: Although he thinks that he sees and knows something, yet in reality he sees and knows nothing, in which sense Christ almost says to the Pharisees, John 9 v. 41 Because you say, we see, your sin remains. But it is manifest that τὸ μυωπάζειν is not attributed to κατὰ δόξαν, but to κατ' ἀληθείαν those of whom the Apostle speaks. 7. Some think that the participle μυωπάζων is placed under the noun τυφλὸς by a kind of correction, as if the Apostle were saying: He is blind, or if not entirely blind, dim-sighted, he is blind like a dim-sighted person, as one who does not rightly look at and estimate the benefit of the purgation from sins. But by this reasoning the disjunctive particle ἢ τυφλὸς ἔστι ἢ μυωπάζων. should have been inserted. Now, however, the Apostle says by apposition τυφλὸς ἔστι μυωπάζων. Therefore μυωπάζων does not signify something less than τυφλὸς.

Q. 3. Of what purgation of sins does the Apostle speak? 1. Some wish the Apostle to look specifically to that purgation of sins which is done in Baptism, and that those sins are called old which were committed before Baptism. Oecumenius in this place: When he has known, while he was purged by holy Baptism, that he had been washed and freed from a multitude of sins, and that from that washing he had received holiness, when he ought to act soberly and give effort that he might preserve for himself the sanctification without which no one will see God, he himself committed this to oblivion. Gloss. ordin.: He sins mortally, he seems to have forgotten the covenant which he entered into with GOD in Baptism. 2. But it is more rightly said that the Apostle speaks in general of the remission of sins, whether it was obtained in Baptism or after Baptism in true repentance through faith. For to this end God out of grace, both in Baptism and also after Baptism in true repentance through faith, remits sins to us, that in the future we may abstain from sins, and serve GOD in true holiness and righteousness, Luke 1 v. 74 just as Christ says to the man healed by Him, John 5 verse 14 Behold, you have been made whole, in the future do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you. As many, therefore, as allow themselves to be entangled again in former sins are deservedly said to have forgotten that former purgation, since they do not observe, nor fulfill the end, on account of which that former of sins purgation happened to them by grace, which is damnable ignorance ἀχαριστία,, the exaggeration of which the Apostle adds in cap. 2. v. 20. & following.

Q. 4. Whether the Apostle speaks of the certainty of calling & election with respect to ourselves or others? Resp. 1. Bede, as also the Greek Scholia, say that calling and election are to be made firm with respect to others, so that the sense is: Make your election and calling certain to other men, so that they, clearly perceiving the integrity of your life, and the probity of your morals, and the excellence of your good works, may recognize and be compelled to confess that your calling and election, i.e., the discipline of the faith and of the Christian religion, to which you have been called and elected by GOD, and which you cultivate and profess, is true and holy and has proceeded from GOD. In the same way Hugo, Dionysius the Carthusian, the Ordinary Gloss, and others explain it. 2. But the consequences show that the Apostle is dealing with the certainty of calling & election with respect to ourselves: for it follows, For doing these things you will not sin at any time, for thus an entrance into the kingdom of heaven will be abundantly ministered to you. 3. The passage therefore parallel to this of ours is 2. Corinth. 13. vers. 5. Prove yourselves, whether you are in the faith, or do you not know yourselves, that Christ is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobates?

Q. 5. Whether the Apostle speaks of election to grace, or indeed to glory? Resp. 1. Some think that by ἐκλογὴν in this place is understood election to grace, which is the same as κλήσει.. Ambrosius Catharinus denies that the discourse in this place is about the predestined, because neither did Peter know the predestined to whom he was writing, nor if he did know, would it have mattered to reveal that to them. He maintains, therefore, that Peter is speaking of that election through which some are snatched from the great crowd of men and directed to the knowledge of the faith and of Christ. Lorinus says that this explanation does not displease him. 2. But if the Apostle were speaking of this election to grace, the noun ἐκλογῆς, & ἐξηγητικῶς should have been placed before, and the noun κλήσεως, should have been added in that sense. Strive to make firm the election, i.e., your calling. But because the noun κλήσεως, is placed before, which denotes calling in time, therefore the noun ἐκλογῆς is more correctly taken concerning the election which was made from eternally to glory, in this sense. Give diligent effort, that you may make your calling, by which you were called in time to the kingdom of grace; and your election, by which you were elected from eternity to the kingdom of glory, certain and firm.

Εναντιοφανειαι 1. He to whom these things are not present, is blind, v. 9. But John 9. v. 14. Christ says to the Pharisees. If you were blind, you would not have sin.

Resp. 1. Lorinus reconciles it thus, that Peter perhaps spoke better, that he is blinded, than that he is blind. But this is to correct the text. 2. Christ calls those blind, who acknowledge their own native and acquired blindness, and seek to be illuminated by Him, as being the light of the world, as the opposition shows.

2. For doing these things, you shall not stumble at any time. v. 10. But James 3. v. 2. πολλὰ πταίουσιν ἅπαντες. Resp. 1. James speaks of the lapses of infirmity, from which one immediately rises again through repentance. Prov. 24. v. 16. The just man falls seven times in a day and rises again. (Although this saying directly and properly seems to treat of liberation from calamities. Compare Tarnov. in Exercit. p. 49. of the prior edition.) Peter, however, speaks of lapses of such a kind, from which a man does not rise again through repentance. 2. Indeed τὸ πταίειν is common both to greater and graver; as well as to lesser and lighter lapses; and it signifies, not only to offend and stumble, but also to slip and fall down, and so to fall, that one does not rise again. Among Aristides πταίσαντες τῶν μαχῶν i.e. ἐν μάχαις are called those who have succumbed in battle. Therefore, according to the reason of the subject matter, it is to be understood concerning graver or lighter lapses. Bede in this place speaks of greater sins, which whoever has committed, does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of GOD and of Christ, and from which everyone, who has surrendered himself to the aforementioned virtues, remains immune by the Lord. 3. From which it also appears, what must be answered to Salmeron, who gathers from this place, that a man can be without sin.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Now for the third time in v. 8. the Apostle makes mention of τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπιγνώσεως, through which he understands faith in Christ. v. 2. he prays, that grace and peace to them, to whom he writes, may be multiplied in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. v. 3. Through the knowledge of Him, who called us, all things, which make for life and godliness, have been given to us, he asserts. In this v. 8. he teaches, that that knowledge of Christ ought to render us fruitful in good works. At the end of the Epistle chap. 3. v. 18.

he admonishes them, that they may grow in grace and in the knowledge of Christ. Since therefore the Apostle so often defines faith by γνῶσιν καί ἐπίγνωσιν,, it is manifest from this how absurd Bellarmine is, when in book 1 of Justification, chapter 7, near the end, he maintains that faith is better defined by ignorance than by knowledge.

2. From v. 9. it can be gathered against the Anabaptists and Calvinists, that those who have obtained the cleansing of their sins can be involved in them again, and consequently can fall away again from the faith, through which they were made partakers of that cleansing, and from the grace of God, which is joined with the remission of sins by an inseparable bond. Nor can it be objected that their faith was not true, because the cleansing of sins happens to no one except through true and living faith. Tossanus explains it only concerning the offering of this benefit in the word of the Gospel, and the signification of the same in Baptism. But it is manifest that the Apostle is speaking not only of the offering, but also of the bestowal of this benefit, and thus of the remission of sins once received through faith, but lost again through sins against conscience.

3. From v. 10. it is gathered that the truly pious and those believing in Christ can be certain of their election, not indeed with an absolute certainty, that is, depending on an absolute decree of God, but with an ordered one, that is, depending on the purpose of God, manifested to us through Christ in the Gospel. For thus we conclude from this place. Those who can and ought to make their election firm, they can be certain of their election. Those truly believing in Christ can and ought to make their election firm. Therefore, those truly believing in Christ can be certain of their election. Hence Thomas in his commentary on this place rightly comments thus: That through good works, namely exterior ones, you may make it certain, that is, you may show your calling to faith from time, and election through predestination from eternity, so that, namely, you may be certain that you are called and chosen by God.

The Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 12, maintains the contrary, and the Papists adhering to its decision, Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 1. Disp. 1. q. 23. punct. 6. assert. 4. Bellarmine lib. 3. de iustif. cap. 12. Becanus tract. 1. Theol. Schol. cap. 14. q. 6. §. 6. Cornelius â Lapide on chapter 16 of Leviticus. Bened. Iustin. in comm. Phil. 2. v. 12. Lorinus and Estius on this place. Pererius disp. 8. on chapter 8 of Romans. Their exceptions, therefore, must be examined.

Bellarm. on the word of God, book 1, chapter 9, last section, objects, that this testimony cannot be brought forward for our opinion concerning the certainty of election. 1. since we wish certainty to be prior to works, not posterior. 2. since the certainty which is born from works cannot be of faith, but is conjectural. 3. since the Apostle is not speaking so much of certainty on the part of the subject, as on the part of the object. For he advises this, that by good works we make our calling and election certain, that is, ratified and firm. For since GOD has chosen us, that we might be holy, Eph. 1. they confirm their election and render it certain, who strive to become holy and blameless, and who, with God helping, progress more and more in love.

I reply. 1. By the name of good works, either only external good works are understood, or interior renewal. Priority is one thing of order, another of time. Certainty is one thing of grace and present faith, or justification: another of glory and persevering faith or election. Both depend either on the interior testimony of the Holy Spirit, or on the exterior testimony of good works. Certainty is prior to good works, if one asks about external good works, about priority of time, and about the certainty which depends on the exterior testimony of good works. Certainty is posterior to good works, if one asks about renewal, which is joined with regeneration in an individual bond, about priority of order, and about the certainty which depends on the interior testimony of the Spirit. 2. Conjectural certainty is ἀντικείμενον ἐν προσκειμένῳ. 3. The Apostle deals entirely with certainty on the part of the object, for he requires that believers make their election certain, certainly not before God, but in their own minds, so that they may firmly establish that they are in the number of the elect.

2. Estius, Pererius, Lorinus, Iustinianus in the same place object, βεβαίαν that it is more correctly translated as firm than certain, so that the sense is, that a Christian man is strengthened and established by a constant zeal for good works, lest he fall from his calling and election, that is, from that to which he has been called and elected, in which sense Apoc. 3. v. 11. it is said. Hold what you have, lest another take your crown. He proves this from the fact, that βεβαίαν properly signifies firm, and because a fall is opposed to firmness in the part immediately following, whereas doubt or uncertainty ought to be opposed to certainty.

I reply. We do not acknowledge the opposition between firm and certain, 1. because firmness includes certainty. That which is firm to someone, that is also certain to the same. Firmness is the stabilization of a thing; certainty is the stabilization of a concept, of a thing corresponding in the mind. 2. The Vulgate version in this place βεβαίαν rendered certain; from its authority the Papists do not dare to depart by the Council of Trent. 3. The Syrian rendered it by [שריר] which signifies, firm, solid, certain, stable. 4. Wherever in the Scriptures the word βεβαία, is used, there it not only signifies firmness, but also connotes certainty. Thus Rom. 4. v. 16. a firm promise is also a certain promise. 2. Cor. 1. v. 7. a firm hope is also a certain hope. Estius saw this, therefore he thus παραφράζει. Diligently give effort, that you may make your calling, by which you were called through the grace of GOD, and election, by which you were from eternity elected and predestined to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, certain and firm.

And afterwards: Moreover, the calling and election of each one is rendered certain and firm through good works. And with some things interjected, after he had said, the mind of the Apostle is more properly explained, if βεβαίαν is translated, firm, he adds. Nevertheless, whether you understand certainty or firmness here, it is sufficiently clear from the sense which I have given, that the words of Peter do not at all help those who demand from everyone a special faith of his own election, by which he most certainly determines that he is elected, which is not faith, but a rash presumption; and the doctrine by which men are taught that they are bound to that special faith, is so far from being a doctrine of faith, that on the contrary it is a lost and soul-destroying heresy, condemned by the Fathers of the Council of Trent.

3. Estius therefore objects otherwise; the calling and election of each one is made certain through good works, because the pursuit of good works is a sign of election certain in its own way that is in the genus of well-probable signs: for thus certainty is frequently accustomed to be used, Pererius in the same place n. 37. concedes. by the assiduous exercise of a man in good works his justification can be made certain to him, not however by the certainty of divine faith, to which in no way can falsehood be subject, but by a certain human and moral certainty.

Resp. 1. We have already said before, that we do not establish an absolute certainty of election, but an ordered one. 2. That certainty does not only depend on good works, from which, as from certain signs, we are confirmed that we are truly faithful and elected by God. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 18. & 19. but also on other foundations to be enumerated a little later, among which stands out the interior testimony of the Holy Spirit. Rom. 8. v. 16. The Spirit Himself bears witness to our spirit, that we are children of God. 3. This testimony of the Spirit is not merely probable and uncertain, but infallible and most certain. 4. Therefore this certainty is not merely conjectural, as Bellarmine speaks, nor in the class of well-probable signs, as Estius speaks, but certainty properly so called, such as is that of firm and infallible things. 5. Estius shows by no example that certainty properly so called has a place in the class of well-probable signs, for τεκμήρια certain signs and εἰκότα probable and likely signs are distinct. Estius himself in his commentary on Rom. 8. v. 38. concedes that a truly believing and pious man can and ought to number himself among the assembly of the elect, and that with so much the greater confidence, the more and greater signs of election he perceives in himself.

4. Lorinus objects thus. Good works generate confidence joined with great probability and likelihood, as all expositors here note, but they leave behind and even demand pious fear and diligent care for protecting salvation. Response: that pious or filial fear, and diligent care for protecting salvation, is not denied by us, nor is it excluded by the certainty of faith.

5. There is also this exception of Lorinus, that calling and election are made βεβαίαν certain and known to others through good works, not so much to us. Response: we have seen above what is to be determined concerning this exposition. And if our calling and election can be made certain to others, much more so to ourselves.

Since therefore it has been proven from this Apostolic passage that the pious can and ought to be certain of their election, it must now further be explained by what reasoning they can be certain of their election. 1. Beyond controversy, the issue here is not concerning the certainty of election before GOD, but concerning the certainty in the hearts of the pious, because before GOD election was certain when believers did not yet exist in act, and before Him election is always firm and immovable, on account of the immutability of His will. Esai. 46. vers. 10.Rom. 11. v. 29.2. Timoth. 2. v. 19. even from eternity before believers do any good thing. Rom. 9. v. 11. 2. Election by the ordination of God is of those who, by faith, embrace the benefits obtained by the passion and death of Christ and offered to them in the word of the Gospel, and who persevere in faith until the very end of life. Therefore, such as is the certainty of faith and perseverance, such also is the certainty of election. 3. That truly pious believers in Christ can be certain of their faith is manifest from the passage Apostolic 2. Cor. 13. v. 5. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobates? Certainly, therefore, a truly pious person can know for certain that he is a participant of the true faith and consequently also of the benefits of Christ. 4. Moreover, one can be certain of his faith both a priori, namely by reason of the causes, which are the grace of GOD in the order of the Principal cause; the word and the sacraments in the order of instrumental causes. When those causes are placed in act and not hindered, i.e., when we hear the word, use the sacraments, and do not place an obstacle to the Holy Spirit, the effect follows, viz., faith itself; and a posteriori, namely from the effects and consequences of faith, which are interior renewal, (which is known from the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit Gal. 5. v. 17., since that has a place only in the reborn and truly believing) the displeasure and detestation of sins, the interior testimony of the Holy Spirit, the studious observance of the divine law, embracing the love of GOD and neighbor, patience in the cross, and other exercises of good works. From the exercise of these good works we understand that we are led by the Spirit of GOD, because good works are the fruit of the Spirit, Gal. 5. v. 22. For those who are led by the Spirit of GOD, they are the sons of GOD. Rom. 8. v. 14. certainly through faith Iohan. 1. v. 9. Beda in h. l. Those who persistently add good works also to the Sacraments of faith, which they have received, they will make their calling and election certain to those who behold. 5. Many sayings of scripture speak of this means of knowledge. Rom. 8. v. 14. Those who are led by the Spirit of GOD, these are the sons of GOD. v. 16. The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit, that we are the sons of GOD. Gal. 5. v. 24. Those who are Christ's, crucify the flesh with its concupiscences and affections. 1. Iohann. 2. v. 3. In this we know that we have known him, if we observe his commandments. v. 5. Whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of GOD is perfected. In this we know that we are in him. cap. 3. v. 14. We know that we have been translated from death to life, because we love the brothers. v. 24. In this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit, which he has given to us. cap. 5. vers. 10. Whoever believes in the Son of GOD, has the testimony of GOD in himself. 6. And not only of faith, but also of the perseverance of faith, those who truly believe in Christ can be certain, not indeed absolutely, but in their own way. The foundations of that certainty are of two kinds; some on the part of GOD, some on our part. On the part of OF GOD, first the good will of GOD and His infallible promise. Because God has promised that He not only wills to begin the good in us, but also to complete it, Phil. 2. v. 12. from this we can be certain that He will preserve us in faith. Secondly, the virtue of God and His own power, 2. Tim. 1. vers. 12. I know whom I have believed and I am certain that He is powerful to keep my deposit until that day, 3. The faithfulness of God. 1. Cor. 1. v. 9. God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son v. 8. who also will confirm you unto the end without blame. cap. 10. v. 3. God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able. On our part, first the serious invocation of GOD. Because God has promised that He will hear our prayers, and will give us those things which are necessary for salvation, therefore asking for perseverance from God, we can be certain of it. 1. Ioh. 5. v. 14. If we have asked anything according to His will, He hears us. Secondly, the continued use of the means. By which means God first kindles faith in us, by the same means, namely the hearing of the word and the use of the Sacraments, He will increase and preserve the same in us, therefore from the use of those means we can be certain of perseverance. Thirdly, the serious purpose of not resisting the Holy Spirit, nor consenting to mortal sins. The reborn can by the grace of the Holy Spirit avoid mortal sins, therefore by a firm purpose of avoiding them they can be certain of perseverance. August. de bono perseverantiae cap. 22. You ought to hope for the very perseverance of obeying from the Father of lights and to ask for it in daily prayers, and by doing this to trust that you are not alienated from the predestination of His people, because He Himself grants even this, that you may do so. From all these things it can easily be gathered what kind of certainty of election we establish, and from what foundations we deduce that certainty, and therefore what is to be established concerning the fact that some derive it from the study of good works alone.

4. From vers. 10. it can again be proven that the reborn and justified can fall from the grace of GOD and salvation through sins against conscience. For if the reborn do not fall only when they diligently continue to study good works, it follows that those ceasing from the study of good works fall and perish. This is to be opposed to the error of the Anabaptists and Calvinists, which was already long ago condemned in Jovinian at Rome, as Jerome reports in lib. 2. contra Iovianian. as also in a certain African Council.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. From verse 8. the Papists gather, that true faith can exist without good works, but does not profit.
