Is, qui non rapinam arbitratus est, esse se aequalem DEO,Phil. 2. v. 6.& mox â Baptismo, quem accepit, vidit caelos apertos,Matth. 3. v. 16. latronem admisit in Paradisum h. e. in beatificam DEI visionem, quae ubicunque percipiatur, Paradisus est: sed cùm in iustorum limbo sive in sinu Abrahae iustis ac latroni ipsi eo die Christus exhibiturus erat, ut rectè Maldonatus docet in Matt. 27. v. 3. non satis benè â Thoma Malvenda confutatus lib. de Paradiso cap. 91.

Resp. 1. Limbus Patrum non solùm est ἄγραφος, sed etiam ἀντίγραφος, ut suo loco fuit demonstratum. 2. Nec potest limbus ille fictitius ex hoc loco statuminari. Quae enim consequentia; Piis in N. T. opulentè ministratur introitus in regnum Dei. Ergo pii in V. T. ab introitu in regnum Dei fuêre exclusi? Num & hoc modo velimus concludere. Piis in Nov. T. datur Spiritus Sanctus. Ergo pii in V. T. non acceperunt Spiritum Sanctum. Piis in N. Test. dantur praemia non solùm futurae, sed etiam huius vitae. 1. Timoth. 4. v. 8. Ergo Pii V. T. non acceperunt praemia huius vitae? 3. Lorinus dicit, ante Christi adventum nulli patuisse introitum in regnum DEI. Sed alii Pontificii dicunt, ante Christi in caelos ascensionem nemini patuisse aditum in regnum caeleste. 4. Quomodo verò latroni in limbo Patrum beatifica Dei visio fuit praestita, cùm Patres in limbo dicantur â beatifica Dei visione exclusi, adeoque poenae damni subiecti. 5. Est omninò Sanguis Christi clavis Paradisi, ut loquitur Hieronymus in Epistol. ad Heliodorum, quod Lorinus pro limbi assertione urget, sed agnus occisus fuit ab origine mundi,Apoc. 13. v. 8. & passio Christi profuit, antequam fuit.

18. Guilielmus Estius ex eod. vers. colligit merita bonorum operum. Postquam enim dixerat, ad hunc locum quadrare illud Pauli.2. Cor. 9. v. 6.Qui seminat in benedictionibus, de benedictionibus etiam metet, subiungit. Significant huiusmodi sententiae proportionem meritorum & praemiorum apud Deum. Observanda haec sunt contra Sectarios nostri temporis, qui merita bonorum operum negant. Item contra veterem haereticum lovinianum, qui virtutum ac praemiorum disparitatem tollebat. Lorinus eodem modo. Hic fructus maximus bonorum operum, introeundi potestas in possessionem sempiternae felicitatis per abundantem & copiosam gratiam, quae suppeditatur â Deo exercentibus se in dictis operibus, quanquam ipsimet sibi per eadem promerentur.

Resp. 1. bona opera non esse merita vitae aeternae propriè sic dicta, suo loco multis confirmavimus. Quid clarius dicto Apostolico Rom. 6. v. 23.Stipendia peccati morsτὶ δὲ χάρισμαgratuitum autem Dei donum vita aeterna in Christo Iesu Domino nostro? 2. Nullam esse proportionem nostrorum meritorum apud Deum, evidenter colligitur, ex Rom. 8. v. 18.Existimo igitur, quod non sint condignae passiones huius temporis ad futuram gloriam, quae revelabitur in nobis.2. Cor. 4. v. 17.Τὸ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν, καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατεργάζεται. At si inter passiones nostras & praemia vitae aeternae nulla est proportio, multò minus inter bona opera nostra, & praemia vitae aeternae erit proportio, quia pati mala plus est quam agere bona. Inde ipsimet Scholastici dicunt, Deum bona praemiari supra condignum, mala punire infra condignum. 3. Nec ex hoc loco Apostolico contrarium evinci potest. Neque enim bona opera & praemia vitae aeternae conferuntur ut causa meritoria & effectus, sed ut antecedens & consequens. Qui divites sunt in bonis operibus, divites erunt in praemiis caelestibus, non ex operum suorum merito, sed ex gratuito DEI promittentis dono. 4. Inde merces bonis piorum operibus promissa vocatur, ἀνταπόδοσις τῆς κληρονομίας.Col. 3. v. 24. quia est talis merces, qualis est ampla hereditas, quae adoptato in filium obtingit, quae datur post oboedientiam, non autem propter oboedientiam. 5. Lorinus ad h. l. sic annotat. Abundantiae gratiae respondet maior copia beatitudinis, redundat quoque propter exemplum in alios, quò quisque melior est. Abundantia item in dicto introitu potest designare firmam possessionem beatitudinis. Denique videtur Simonis errori occurri, non sufficere Christum & ab Angelis ipsius impediri posse ingressum in caelum. Sed & abundantia innuit accessum novae gratiae acceptâ bene utentium. Habenti dabitur. Has expositiones si amplectamur, nihil patrocinii meritis operum ex hoc loco accedet. 6. Ioviniani errorem de paritate peccatorum nobis affricare conatur Campianus rat. 8. Hoc quoque, inquit, tritum est in hac fece Protestantium, peccata esse paria: hac trutina non leviùs in Deum deliquerit ille caupo, qui gallum gallinaceum, quàm qui hominem occiderit. Sed ab eo nos absolvit hoc loco Estius, Ioviniani errorem â nostra sententiâ disseparans; absolvit etiam Bellarminus lib. 3. de Iustificat. cap. 16. in princ. Lutherani, inquit, non dicunt, quod sciam, virtutes esse pares aut paria peccata, neque negant, hominem crescere posse spe, dilectione aliisque virtutibus.

## 1:12
Connection. 1. The Apostle explains in these words the argument of the Epistle, that he wishes those who were already instructed in the faith before, and confirmed in the truth, nevertheless ὑπομιμνήσκειν, and as is held in the next verse following ἐν ὑπομνήσει διεγείρειν to remind and by reminding to stir up, so that they may constantly persevere in the faith, and demonstrate the same through the pursuit of good works.

2. He also explains the causes of this his reminding and exhortation, the first of which he deduces by way of inference from the preceding. For this reason, that is, because my reminding is useful to you in so many ways, therefore I did not wish to deny or withhold it from you, even though I know that you are knowledgeable of the heavenly truth and well confirmed in it.

Exposition of the text. Διό οὐκ ἀμελήσω ἡμᾶς ἀεὶ ὑπομιμνήσκειν περὶ τούτων. The little word διό therefore, for this reason, has respect to the preceding, since it is an illative particle. Because an entrance into the kingdom of Christ will be abundantly supplied to you, if you supply virtues in faith, and all these things are abundantly present to you, therefore I will not neglect to always remind you of these things. He explains therefore the cause of the writing as final, which is the promotion of the salvation of those to whom he writes. The Syriac rendered it emphatically. [ועל הדא] And for this very reason. οὐκ ἀμελήσω. The Vulgate rendered it, I will begin, concerning which version what must be determined, we shall see in the questions. Ἀμελεῖν In the Greek it is to neglect, not to have care of some thing, Matt. 22. ver. 5. Heb. 2. v. 3. ἀμελεῖν σωτρίας, chap. 8. v. 9. Therefore οὐκ ἀμελεῖν is not to neglect something, but to have careful and diligent care of some thing. 1. Tim. 4. v. 16. μὴ ἀμέλει τοῦ ἐν σοι χαρίσματος. The rule must therefore be repeated in this place, that negative words are sometimes put for their contrary affirmative ones not without emphasis, because sometimes less is said, and more is understood. Certain ones express this rule thus. The negation of the contrary sentiment is sometimes more vehement than the simple affirmation of the other. Flacius part. 2. Clavis col. 357. Adverbs of denying often express with emphasis the contrary affirmed of that which they express. Exod. 20. v. 7. GOD will not hold him innocent, who shall have taken his name in vain, i. e. he will most severely punish. Lev. 10. v. 1. which was not commanded to them, i. e. which was most severely forbidden to them. 1. Sam. 12. v. 21. Do not turn aside to vain things, which will not profit you i. e. to idols, which will most greatly harm. Psal. 18. v. 37. My footsteps have not been weakened, i. e. they are most strongly strengthened. Psal. 25. v. 3. Those who wait for you, will not be confounded, i. e. they will be gloriously and certainly delivered. John 14. ver. 18. I will not leave you orphans i. e. I will most certainly be present with you in whatever calamities and I will deliver you. Rom. 4. v. 19. He was not weakened in faith, i. e. he was most strongly confirmed in faith. Thus in this place, I will not neglect to remind you i. e. I will assiduously and solicitously remind you.

For ἀμελήσω the Syriac has [לא ממאן אנא] which word as often as it occurs elsewhere in the books of the N. T., is used as an impersonal, but here it is constructed as a personal, in the present, namely Aphel, and is rendered by Pococke, I do not cease from weariness, namely, or boredom, or I do not grow weary. For it signifies, according to Amira the Syrian, to be weary, or to grow weary with a certain boredom and disgust. Etzelius translates, I do not delay at all, or it does not weary me, to warn you. For ἀεί the Syriac has [אמינאית] which Etzelius rendered faithfully, but rather in this place it must be translated assiduously, diligently, perseveringly, perpetually, because the root [אמן] includes all these things, and corresponds in this place to the Greek ἀεί. Ὑπομνάομοι (for which ὑπομιμνήσκω is used) signifies the same as ἀναμιμνήσκω I cause to remember, I remind, I admonish; it is placed here with the accusative of the person, with the addition of the preposition περὶ, expressing the subject matter of the reminder or the thing. Thence ὑπὸμνημα, which signifies a writing, by which some thing is recalled to memory. Budaeus in his commentaries p. 178 says it is a commentary and a brief writing for the aiding of memory. Chemn. in Exam. Part 1. page 66. ὑπομνήματα are called Commentaries or books, which are compiled for the aid of memory with brief annotations from reading or hearing. John 14. v. 26. concerning the Holy Spirit Christ says, he himself ὑπομνήσει ὑμᾶς πάυτα, from which it can be gathered, that Peter in this ὑπομνήσει was a salutary instrument of the Holy Spirit. 2. Tim. 2. vers. 14. Paul says to Timothy, ταῦτα ὑπόμνησκε and to Tit. 3. vers. 1. ὑπόμνησκε αὐτούς ἀρχαῖς ὑποτάσσεσθαι, from which it is understood, that ὑπόμνησιν pertains not only to the Apostles, but to any faithful Teachers of the Church. The compound ἐπαναμιμνὴσκειν the Vulgate version Rom. 15. vers. 15. rendered, to bring to memory. John 14. vers. 26. the word ὑπομιμνήσκειν it rendered by to suggest; 2. Timoth. 2. vers. 14. Epist. Jude vers. 5. by to remind, Tit. 3. vers. 2. by to admonish; ὑπομιμήσιν it rendered by remembrance 2. Timoth. 1. vers. 5. and by admonition 2. Peter 3. vers. 1.

Καίπερ εἰδότας καὶ ἐστριγμένους ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ. the Vulgate rendered; and indeed knowing. It is more correctly rendered, although knowing, Luth. wiewohl ihrs wisset. The Syrian when you are also well knowing. i.e. although you know well. The sense is. Although you are sufficiently instructed in the truth of the faith and confirmed in it, nevertheless I will not neglect to remind you of these things through this Epistle. Thus therefore by these words he meets the tacit objection of those to whom he writes. We are already informed in the truth and confirmed in it, why therefore do you write to us about it? The Apostle answers that this is required both by the condition of those to whom he writes, and by his own Apostolic office. The condition of those to whom he writes required that, because even those who know must be reminded, since they dwell on the earth of oblivion: and they are confirmed to be stirred up to the study of good works, since they are still subject to the snares of the flesh, of Satan, and of the world. He treats of his Apostolic office in the verse immediately following.

We weighed the emphasis of the word σηρίττειν,, from which is ἐστηριγμένους founded, established, confirmed, in the exposition of the former Epistle, chap. 5. vers. 10. By ἀλήθειαν παρούσιαν he understands the doctrine of the Gospel, which is the word of immovable truth, concerning which he was already treating and writing to them, and in which they were well instructed. The Syrian rendered it, founded upon that truth. Places parallel to this of ours are Rom. 15. vers. 14. I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, so that ye may be able to admonish one another. vers. 15. Nevertheless, brethren, I have written the more boldly unto you in some sort, ὡς ἐπαναμιμνήσκων ὑμᾶς, through the grace that is given to me of GOD. 1. Iohan. 2. vers. 21. I have not written unto you because ye know not the truth, but because ye know it. Jude vers. 5. ὑπομνήσαι δὲ ὑμᾶς βούλομαι εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ τοῦτο. But also in this latter Petrine Epistle a parallel place occurs, chap. 3. vers. 1. This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you, ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν. vers. 2. μνησθέναι. etc.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Exponit Apostolus in his verbis argumentum Epistolae, quòd velit eos, qui in fide iam antè erant instructi, inque veritate confirmati, nihilo tamen minùs ὑπομιμνήσκειν, & ut habetur in v. prox. seq. ἐν ὑπομνήσει διεγείρειν commonere & per commonitionem excitare, ut in fide constanter perseverent, & per studium bonorum operum eandem demonstrent.

2. Explicat etiam causas huius suae commonefactionis & exhortationis, quarum primam per modum illationis deducit ex praecedentibus. Propter quod h. e. quia commonefactio mea tot modis vobis utilis est, ideò eam nolui vobis denegare vel substrahere, etiamsi noverim, vos esse caelestis veritatis gnaros & in ea probè confirmatos.

Textus expositio. Διό οὐκ ἀμελήσω ἡμᾶς ἀεὶ ὑπομιμνήσκειν περὶ τούτων. Vocula διό propterea, propter hoc, respectum habet ad praecedentia, cùm sit particula illativa. Quia vobis opulenter introitus in regnum Christi subministrabitur, si in fide virtutes subministretis, & haec omnia vobis opulenter adsint, ideò non negligam vos de his semper commonere. Explicat igitur causam scriptionis finalem, quae est promotio salutis eorum, ad quos scribit. Syrus emphaticè reddidit. [ועל הדא]Et propter hoc ipsum.οὐκ ἀμελήσω. Vulgata reddidit, incipiam, quâ de versione quid statuendum sit, in quaestionibus videbimus. Ἀμελεῖν Graecis est negligere, non habere alicuius rei curam,Matth. 22. vers. 5.Hebr. 2. v. 3.ἀμελεῖν σωτρίας,cap. 8. v. 9. Ergò οὐκ ἀμελεῖν est non negligere aliquid, sed sedulam & diligentem alicuius rei curam habere. 1. Tim. 4. v. 16.μὴ ἀμέλει τοῦ ἐν σοι χαρίσματος. Repetenda ergo hoc loco regula, quòd verba negantia ponantur quandoque pro contrariis affirmantibus non sine emphasi, quia quandoque minus dicitur, & plus intelligitur. Quidam hanc regulam sic efferunt. Negatio contrariae sententiae aliquando vehementior est, quàm simplex alterius affirmatio. Flacius part. 2. Clavis col. 357. Adverbia negandi saepe eius quod exprimunt contrarium affirmatum cum emphasi exprimunt.Exod. 20. v. 7.Non habebit DEUS innocentem illum, qui assumserit nomen eius in vanum, h. e. gravissimè puniet. Lev. 10. v. 1.quod eis praeceptum non erat, h. e. quod erat eis gravissimè prohibitum. 1. Sam. 12. v. 21.Nolite declinaread vana, quae non proderunt vobis i. e. ad idola, quae maximè oberunt. Psal. 18. v. 37.Non sunt infirmata vestigia mea, i. e. validissimè sunt firmata. Psal. 25. v. 3.Qui expectant te, non confundentur, i. e. gloriosè & certò liberabuntur. Iohan. 14. vers. 18.Non relinquam vos orphanos h. e. certissimè vobis adero in quibus cunque calamitatibus & vos liberabo. Rom. 4. v. 19.Non infirmatus est fide, h. e. fortissimè in fide fuit confirmatus. Sic hoc loco, non negligam vos commonefacere h. e. assiduè & solicitè vos commonefaciam.

Pro ἀμελήσω Syrus habet [לא ממאן אנא] quod verbum quoties alibi in N. T. libris occurrit, usurpatur ut impersonale, hîc verò construitur ut personale, in praesenti sc. Aphel, ac redditur à Pococke, non cesso ego praepigredine sc. aut taedio, seu non pigresco. Significat enim, teste Amira Syro, taedere, seu cum taedio ac fastidio quodam pigrescere. Etzelius vertit, non moror ego quidquam, vel non taedet me, ut vos moneam. pro ἀεί Syrus habet [אמינאית] quod Etzelius reddidit fideliter, sed potiùs hoc loco vertendum assiduè, sedulò, perseveranter, perpetuò, quia radix [אמן] haec omnia includit, ac respondet hoc loco Graecorum ἀεί. Ὑπομνάομοι (pro quo usurpatur ὑπομιμνήσκω) significat idem quod ἀναμιμνήσκωreminisci facio, commonefacio, admoneo; ponitur hic cum accusativo personae, additâ praepositione περὶ, materiam commonefactionis sive rem exprimente. Inde ὑπὸμνημα, quod significat scriptum, quo res aliqua in memoriam revocatur. Budaeus in comm. p. 178. dicit esse commentarium & breve ad iuvandaem memoriam scriptum. Chemn. in Exam. P. 1. pag. 66. ὑπομνήματαvocantur Commentarii sive libri, qui in subsidium memoriae brevibus annotationibus ex lectione seu auditione conficiuntur.Ioh. 14. v. 26. de Spiritu sancto dicit Christus, ipseὑπομνήσει ὑμᾶς πάυτα, ex quo colligi potest, Petrum in hac ὑπομνήσει fuisse salutare Spiritus sancti organum. 2. Tim. 2. vers. 14. dicit Paulus ad Timotheum, ταῦτα ὑπόμνησκε & ad Tit. 3. vers. 1.ὑπόμνησκε αὐτούς ἀρχαῖς ὑποτάσσεσθαι, ex quo intelligitur, ὑπόμνησιν illam non solum ad Apostolos, sed ad quosvis fideles Ecclesiae Doctores pertinere. Compositum ἐπαναμιμνὴσκειν Vulgata versio Rom. 15. vers. 15. reddidit, in memoriam reducere.Iohan. 14. vers. 26. verbum ὑπομιμνήσκειν reddidit per suggerere;2. Timoth. 2. vers. 14. Epist. Iudae vers. 5. per commonere,Tit. 3. vers. 2. per admonere;ὑπομιμήσιν reddidit per recordationem2. Timoth. 1. vers. 5. & per commonitionem2. Petr. 3. vers. 1.

Καίπερ εἰδότας καὶ ἐστριγμένους ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ. Vulgata reddidit; & quidem scientes. Rectius redditur, etsi scientes, Luth. wiewohl ihrs wisset. Syrus cùm bene etiam scientes sitis. h. e. quamvis benè sciatis. Sensus est. Quamvis sufficienter in veritate fidei sitis instructi inque ea confirmati, tamen non negligam vos de hisce per Epistolam hanc commonefacere. Sic ergo verbis hisce occurrit tacitae obiectioni eorum ad quos scribit. Iam antè in veritate sumus informati & de ea confirmati, cur ergo de ea ad nos scribis? respondet Apostolus hoc requirere tum eorum, ad quos scribit, conditionem, tum suum officium Apostolicum. Conditio eorum ad quos scribit, illud requirebat, quia etiam scientes commonefaciendi sunt, cùm versentur in terra oblivionis: & confirmati sunt ad studium bonorum operum excitandi, cùm carnis, Satanae & mundi insidiis adhuc sint obnoxii. De officio suo Apostolico agit in versu proximè sequente.

Emphasin verbi σηρίττειν, ex quo est ἐστηριγμένουςfundatos, stabilitos, confirmatos, expendimus in enarratione prioris Epistolae cap. 5. vers. 10. Per ἀλήθειαν παρούσιαν intelligit doctrinam Evangelii, quae est verbum immotae veritatis, de qua iam tractabat & ad illos scribebat, & in qua ipsi probè instituti erant. Syrus reddidit, fundatos super veritatem istam. Loca huic nostro parallela sunt Rom. 15. vers. 14.Persuasus sum, fratres mei, etiam ego ipse de vobis, quoniam & ipsi pleni estis benignitate, repleti omni scientiâ, ita ut possitis vos invicem admonere. vers. 15. Audacius autem scripsi vobis fratres, ex parte,ὡς ἐπαναμιμνήσκων ὑμᾶς,per gratiam, quae mihi data est à DEO.1. Iohan. 2. vers. 21.Non scripsi vobis quasi ignorantibus veritatem, sed quasi scientibus eam. Iudae vers. 5. ὑπομνήσαι δὲ ὑμᾶς βούλομαι εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ τοῦτο. Sed & in hac Epistola Petrina posteriore occurrit locus parallelus cap. 3. vers. 1.Hanc ecce, carissimi, secundam vobis scribo Epistolam,ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν. vers. 2. μνησθέναι. &c.

## 1:12-15 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place 1. Did the Latin Interpreter rightly οὐκ ἀμελήσω in verse 12 render, I will begin? Lorinus comments on that verse thus. The Apostle signifies that he diligently meets the imminent enemy Simon and with errors disseminated by him, so that he may always admonish anew, just as if he were beginning for the first time. That is, either not to omit, or to neglect, or not to defer, or to prolong, which the Interpreter expressed most learnedly by 'I will begin'. To Estius it seems very probable that the Latin Interpreter read μελλήσω, for which he translated 'I will begin', since the Greek word μέλλειν most commonly signifies that it will be, which elsewhere the Vulgate Interpreter has rendered 'I will begin'. John 4 v. 4. Acts 23 v. 27. James 2 v. 12. so that the sense is, for which reason I will henceforth always remind you. But I reply 1. All Greek codices consistently read οὐκ ἀμελήσω,, except for one, which Robert Stephanus mentions, which reads οὐ μελλήσω.. 2. But this reading does nothing at all for the Vulgate version, which, with the negation omitted which all Greek codices have added, rendered it I will begin. 3. The future μελλήσω nowhere occurs in the sacred scriptures. 4. Nor is it correctly translated by I will begin, as the examples brought forward by Estius show. 5. But especially in this place it is absurdly rendered by the verb to begin. For what is I will always begin to remind you? Was the Apostle always going to begin a reminder, never to finish it? Lorinus's exposition, I will begin i.e. I will not omit, is highly catachrestic. 6. Then Lorinus himself adds: 'I will begin' or 'I will not neglect' can be understood as placed for 'I have begun', 'I have not neglected', namely in the former Epistle. But Peter is not dealing with what he has already done, but what he is going to do henceforth. 7. Weighing all these things, Estius finally gives in, writing thus: Because the future μελλήσω is hardly in use among the Greeks, although it may be read somewhere in Plato, certainly it is nowhere in the sacred scriptures: therefore I judge that reading to be truer which all, or almost all, Greek codices have. For all have the negation; almost all ἀμελήσω,, which word fits this place very well. So that, he says, you may receive ample rewards from God, I will not neglect to exhort you to practice good works, i.e. I will assiduously and solicitously remind and exhort you. 8. But what will become of the decree of the Council of Trent, which says that it should be permitted to no one under any pretext to appeal from the Vulgate version to the Greek codices?

Q. 2. Why does the Apostle call his body a tabernacle? Reply. Bede on this passage: We are accustomed to use a tabernacle on a journey or in war, and therefore the faithful rightly testify that as long as they are in the body and are traveling away from the Lord, they are in tabernacles, in which they carry out the journey of this life, and against let them wage a contest against the adversaries of the truth. Bernard, sermon 26 on the Song of Songs, Tabernacle is a pastoral and military term. Therefore the Apostle looks, 1. To the tabernacles of the Patriarchs. The Patriarchs used tents and tabernacles while they were seeking the land of promise, having meanwhile an uncertain and not long-lasting dwelling: thus we posit an uncertain and likewise not long-lasting dwelling in this body, we who are pilgrims from the Lord, but desire to be present with him, 2. Cor. 5. v. 6. for we do not have here a lasting city. Hebr. 13. v. 14. 2. To the tabernacle of the covenant, in which God was indeed graciously present, but yet the tabernacle itself was carried through the desert from place to place: thus the pious are the dwellings of the Holy Spirit, and of the whole Most Holy Trinity, Iohan. 14. v. 23. 1. Cor. 3. v. 16. cap. 6. v. 16. Eph. 3. v. 17. but as long as they wander in the desert of this world, they do not have a stable and fixed seat. 3. To military and pastoral tabernacles, and indeed, firstly by reason of the short stay. Tabernacles are temporary habitations, in which soldiers dwell only in time of war, which is common to them with pastoral tabernacles. Esai. 38. v. 12. Thus short is the stay of the soul in this body. Secondly by reason of the vile and weak structure. Tabernacles are for the most part built from vile material: thus our body formed from earth is extremely fragile and weak, whence in this life we are said to inhabit houses of clay. Iob. 4. v. 19. The body is clothed with skin, as a tabernacle with hides against the injuries of the sky. Iob. 10. v. 11. It is stretched with nerves as with ropes, for the mast and other wooden instruments there are bones, the feet perform the office of nails. Thirdly by reason of labor and troublesome occupation. We live in a tabernacle in the time of warfare. Thus the whole life on these lands is nothing other than warfare. Iobi 7. v. 1. Living in a tabernacle one feels many defects, inconveniences, and straits: thus in this body we suffer very many miseries. Living in a tabernacle one sighs for home: thus the faithful in this life sighs for heaven. Fourthly by reason of the perishable condition and mature migration. We dwell in a tabernacle as pilgrims, not as tenants: thus in this life we are pilgrims from the Lord. 2. Cor. 5. v. 6. But we are citizens and members of the household of GOD. Eph. 2. v. 20. This tabernacle is torn away in death, the nails of the feet totter in old age, the skin is wrinkled, the nerves are loosened, but afterwards this destroyed tabernacle will be raised up, when we shall be introduced into the eternal tabernacle of heaven, Luke 16. v. 9. then a firm and stable building will succeed this vile and temporary tabernacle, when our body shall have been endowed with immortality; then we shall obtain a house ἀχειραποιητὸν 2. Cor. 5. v. 1. 1. whose τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς builder is GOD himself. Heb. 11. v. 10. & 16.

Q. 3. When was it manifested to Peter by Christ that it would shortly come to pass that he would lay aside the tabernacle of his body? Resp. 1. The interlinear Gloss, the marginal concordances, and Hugo Cardinalis refer us to the prophecy of Christ John 21. v. 18. When you were old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish. But Christ there predicts to Peter a violent death or Martyrdom, and as some wish, a kind of death, namely crucifixion, but not the time of a death immediately impending. For although he adds, when you were old, nevertheless old age sometimes extends for many years, so that from old age a near death cannot immediately be inferred. 2. Simeon Metaphrastes in Surius, 29. June, reports, to Peter, when he was acting in Britain, it was said by an Angel, Peter, the time of your resolution is at hand and it behooves you to go to Rome, where when you have sustained death by the cross, you will receive the reward of justice. But that Metaphrastes, who is believed to have lived in the ninth century after the birth of Christ, is acknowledged to be a writer of suspected and slight credibility by Baronius Ann. 31. n. 30. Ann. 859. n. 53. Bellarmine de scriptor. Eccles. under the word Metaphrastes, Croquetius in Catech. 215. Hence Estius to this passage annotates thus. What Metaphrastes reports about Peter being informed by an Angel of his death is of suspected credibility, as are some other things about Peter by the same author. Certainly Bede, knowledgeable of British affairs if anyone is, mentions nothing of the sort, neither in his commentary nor in his Ecclesiastical History. Lorinus to this passage: Metaphrastes has some things about Peter that are little certain, indeed even false, for example, that having returned to Rome he found Linus already dead, and substituted Clement for him, when it is sufficiently established that he lived after Peter and is believed to have described his acts and death. 3. Egesippus lib. 3. de excidio Hierosolym. cap. 2. Ambrose Epist. 32. Tom. 3. p. 125. Gregory in Ps. 4. paenit. The Acts of Processus and Martinian in Surius 2. July record such a thing about Peter. Peter, having defeated Simon, when he was sowing the precepts of GOD among the people and teaching chastity, stirred up the minds of the gentiles, and as they were seeking him, Christian souls begged that he might yield for a little while. And although he was desirous of passion, nevertheless he was swayed by the contemplation of the praying people.

For he was asked to reserve himself for the instruction and strengthening of the people. Why say more? By night he began to go out by the wall, and seeing CHRIST meet him at the gate and enter the city, he said, Lord, where are you going? CHRIST answered, I am coming to Rome to be crucified again. Peter understood that the divine response pertained to his own cross. For CHRIST could not be crucified again, who had put off the flesh by the passion of the death he had undergone, etc. Peter therefore understood that CHRIST was to be crucified again in his servant. And so he returned of his own accord, gave an answer to the Christians who were asking, and having been immediately seized, he glorified the Lord Jesus through his own cross. Salmero approves this apparition of Christ made to Peter with his own vote in Disp. 1 on this Epistle of Peter, Vol. 16, page 112, and Disp. 2, page 119. Lorinus likewise, for thus he comments on this place: There exists even today a famous monument on the Appian Way, in the place where Christ appeared to Peter, who, yielding to the prayers of the faithful, was fleeing Nero's persecution, and said that he was coming to Rome to be crucified again, which Peter, interpreting as concerning himself, turned his journey back into the city, and a little later suffered the cross for Christ. But neither can this Apostolic passage be accepted concerning this manifestation, because immediately after it he was taken away to martyrdom. 4. Leo the Great insinuates that the span of his age had been revealed to Peter before he came to Rome, for thus he writes in Sermon 1 on the birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul: Nor did you bring the trophy of the cross of Christ into the Roman citadels as one doubtful of the progress of the work, or ignorant of the span of your age, where both the honor of power and the glory of the passion preceded you by divine preordinations. But neither sacred nor ecclesiastical history makes mention of this revelation. 5. It is therefore safest to confess that the time of his death, which was immediately imminent, had indeed been revealed to Peter (whence also Dionysius in the Syriac commentary on this place adds, as the Lord indicated to me [בחסוא] in a vision, that is, in a revelation,) but as to what kind that vision was, or at what time and place this revelation was made to Peter, nothing certain can be affirmed about it. A similar revelation seems to have been made to Paul. 2. Tim. 4. v. 6.

Ἐναντιοφανεὶαι. 1. Peter says in this place that it will soon come to pass that he will lay aside the tabernacle of his body in death. verse 14. But CHRIST attributes this to himself alone, that he has the power of laying down his soul, and that he lays it down of himself. Ioh. 10. v. 18.

Resp. 1. In the Greek text it is said simply, that the putting off of the tabernacle is soon to follow, which can be taken both passively and actively. 2. Even if it were taken most actively, yet Peter is not said to put off the tabernacle of his body in the same sense in which Christ is said to lay down His soul, that is, His life. Christ was not bound by the necessity of dying, because ἀναμάρτητος and because in the unity of His person He is true GOD, therefore He says that He lays down His soul of Himself, that is, not only to die voluntarily, but also to die when and where He wills, which is of divine power: but Peter, on account of sin, was subject to the necessity of dying, meanwhile, however, he patiently submitted himself to the divine will in enduring death, which was an act of piety. Luther's version removes the doubt. Ich weiß / daß ich meine Hütte bald ablegen muß.

2. Peter says here that it will be brief, that he may put off the tabernacle of his body in death, which is an indication that he himself died voluntarily. But Christ John 21. v. 18. says: When you were old, another will gird you, and lead you where you do not wish.

Resp. 1. Eusebius, book 3 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 1, records that Peter undertook the cross for Christ with such readiness of mind that he wished to be crucified with his head lowered to the ground and his feet inverted, saying that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same way as Christ, namely, with his head upright. 2. Therefore, what Christ says about Peter's death, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish, the Scholastics respond to that by distinguishing between natural will and deliberate will. Peter died voluntarily for Christ, as far as the deliberate will is concerned, even if the will, like ours, protested. Augustine, tractate 123 on John, expresses it thus: that Peter came to death unwilling, but afterwards, having left behind the affection of infirmity, by which no one wishes to die. 3. And indeed there is no doubt that Peter overcame the affection of the flesh, which shudders at death, by the strength of the Spirit; meanwhile, however, since in the very torture of the cross, Peter's flesh remained flesh, that is, surrounded by infirmities, therefore the matter can be best explained in Peter by the distinction between Spirit and flesh. When Peter was beaten with scourges before the Jerusalem Council, he went out from the presence of the Council rejoicing; Acts 5. v. 41. with the same affection he also undertook the cross. But this ready will to die did not proceed from the flesh, but from the Spirit: but Christ speaks of the refractory flesh of Peter, in which sin still dwells, Rom. 7. v. 18. which still resists the Spirit. Gal. 5. v. 17.

and concerning the law of the members, which wars against the law of the mindRom. 7. v. 23. Confer. Harmon. on the resurrection, chap. 11. p. 393.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. John Huss against 13. comments thus: I wonder that Peter, being the immediate and certain Vicar of Jesus Christ, did not grant Indulgences, through which he could have enticed subjects to a meritorious life and freed them more quickly from the punishments of Purgatory! But he warned them that, by perfecting virtuous works in faith, they should be certain of their calling and election, because then an entrance into the eternal kingdom would be ministered to them: but if they should fail in virtuous works, then they would remain like blind men groping, empty and void of grace. The solution to the wonder is Peter's just information,

2. The authors of the Magdeburg Centuries rightly ask, Why does Peter in this place v. 14. not make mention of his successor Clement, if Clement was his successor in the Papal See? Francis Turrianus answers in book 2 for the Epistles of the Pontiffs, chap. 15: although Peter writes that the laying aside of his tabernacle is swift, and revealed to him, he does not assert how swift, and precisely at what time, nor that this was revealed to him as well. This response of Turrianus is not approved by Lorinus, who judges that a better solution can be given, namely: that it was not necessary to write about these things. And yet it was entirely necessary to commend the future successor, as the head and Monarch of the Church, the infallible Judge of all controversies, and the authentic Interpreter of Scripture, to the Church by letter and to reconcile authority to his successor.

Ἐδίκησις, 1. Bellarmine, book 4 on the Word of God, chap. 12, § But that from v. 12, gathers: the chief end of Scripture is not that it should be the rule of faith, but that by various documents, examples, and exhortations, now by holding, now by instructing, now by threatening, now by consoling, it might help us in this pilgrimage. In the same place, in the response to argument 2, he writes: the proper and chief end of Scripture was not that it should be the rule of faith, but that it should be a certain useful reminder for preserving and fostering the doctrine received from preaching.

Resp. 1. That Scripture was written for that end, and indeed chiefly so that it might be the rule of faith, is taught by all those sayings in which we are recalled to the word of GOD, first indeed preached by a living voice, afterwards by the will of GOD reduced into Scriptures, as to the unique Rule of faith and divine worship. Deut. 4. v. 2.cap. 5. v. 32.cap. 12. v. 32.Esai. 8. v. 19.Luc. 16. v. 29. and those things which teach that Christ and the Apostles in all controversies of faith, to have appealed solely to the Scriptures, Matt. 19. v. 4.ch. 22. v. 31. & 43.Mark 9. v. 12.Luke 10. vers. 26.ch. 24. v. 26.Acts 3. v. 20.ch. 7. v. 2.ch. 13. v. 33.ch. 18. v. 26.ch. 26. v. 22.ch. 28. v. 23.Rom. 4. v. 3.1. Cor. 15. v. 3.Gal. 3. v. 64. 2. This is so evident that Bellarmine himself in the same book & chapter, § I say secondly &c, asserts that Scripture, although it was not made primarily to be the rule of faith, is nevertheless a rule of faith, not total, but partial. But if Scripture is a rule of faith, it was certainly also written to that end, that it might be a rule of faith; otherwise, contrary to the intention of God, by whose impulse Scripture as θεὸπνευστος was written, it would be attributed to it that it is a rule of faith. 3. The very appellation of Canon attributed by the Holy Spirit to the written word of GOD Ps. 19. vers. 5. ( Rom. 10. v. 18.) Isa. 28. v. 10.Gal. 6. v. 16.Phil. 3. v. 16. shows that the end of Scripture, published by the holy men of God, is not that it should be a mere reminder, but that it should be a certain & perpetual rule of faith, worship, and morals in the Church. 4. We concede, therefore, that the end & use of Scripture consists in reminding, but it cannot be inferred from that, that it consists only in reminding; and that its principal & primary end is not to teach what is necessary for salvation and to propose a rule of faith. For the accessory & secondary does not take away the principal. 5. The Holy Spirit was suggesting all things to the Apostles, John 14. vers. 26. where likewise the word ὑπομιμνήσκειν, is placed; yet it was the same, their teacher leading them into all truth. John 16. v. 13. 6. Indeed, Scripture obtains a twofold end by reason of different objects. It perfectly informs and instructs those ignorant of the mysteries of faith; but it reminds those to whom the mysteries of faith are already known from the preaching of the word.

2. From the word tabernacle it might seem that the error of the Platonists is supported, who established that the human body is merely extrinsic, as it were a custody and sepulcher of the soul, which σῶμα is said παρὰ τὸ σώζειν to preserve and guard; or as if it were σῆμα i.e. a sepulcher. But the body is just as much an essential part of man as the rational soul itself, but also Christ redeemed not only the soul, but also the body, and will render it, together with the soul, a participant in heavenly glory and happiness.

3. Lorinus in his commentary on v. 14 mentions that Pope Alexander 2 raised the question to Peter Damian, why the Bishop of the Apostolic See never lived longer, but within a short space of time closed his final day, so that after the Apostle Peter, who presided for about five years of lustra, that is, for almost 25 years, no Roman Pontiff afterwards has equaled this span of the Prelacy, according to Peter Damian, lib. 1. Epist. 17. Damian replied, that the order of heavenly judgment had arranged this, so that it might strike fear of death into the human race, and might evidently show how much the glory of temporal life is to be despised, in the very Principate of glory, as it were, suffering an eclipse like the Sun. Lorinus adds other reasons. The very weight and care of all the Churches by itself can shorten the course of life for those who indeed estimate and take it upon themselves: and on the other hand, the kind God does not allow those so burdened to be oppressed, but unburdens them more quickly. Finally, for this reason it may happen that men less desire a dignity which they are almost certain will not last long. What if in this matter also God wished regard to be had for the dignity of Peter, on account of which no one after him wished to bear the name of Peter in the Pontificate.

But 1. that Peter acted as Pontiff in Rome for 25 years is false. 2. That the Roman Pontiffs are successors of Peter in the Papal See is equally true. 3. In later centuries the Pontiffs were more concerned about temporal dominion than about the salvation of the Church. 4. The principal reason is omitted, that most Pontiffs are removed from the midst by poison, so that the way to that dignity may be open to others, whence it is tossed about in a proverb. Poison is the death of Pontiffs. 5. Panormitanus judges, that impious Pontiffs are therefore removed from the midst by premature death, lest they scandalize and disturb the Church with their crimes.

4. Salmero Disp. 1. on this Epistle, Tom. 6. p. 112, from the fact that Peter was crowned with martyrdom in Rome, concludes, that this Epistle was written in Rome, concerning which matter what is to be determined was set forth in the prolegomena. He concludes moreover from this another thing, which is of greater moment. Peter, he says, offered the merits of his blood and cross for the Romans, and promised the patronage of his most efficacious intercession forever. Just as also Paul, the Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles, glorified the Lord in the same city, so that he might enrich the city, which he had illustrated with doctrine and signs, also with the merits of his own blood, and as their advocate might perpetually plead their cause before God.

Resp. 1. Salmero attributes to Peter such a thing as belongs to Christ alone. For He alone offered the merits of His blood and cross for the Romans and all men, and promised the patronage of most efficacious intercession to believers forever. 2. Nay rather, Salmero attributes more to Peter than to Christ. From the fact that Peter died at Rome, he gathers that Peter promised that the patronage of his most effective intercession would be for the Romans in perpetuity, which he explains elsewhere thus: that those who hold the Roman see of Peter cannot err in doctrine, but enjoy the perpetual assistance of the Holy Spirit. And yet, not even of Christ, who died at Jerusalem, can it be said that the Bishop of the Jerusalem see obtained infallibility from that fact. 3. Concerning the two Prophets and witnesses who are to fight against the Antichrist Apoc. 11. v. 8. it is said, their bodies shall lie in the street of the great city, which is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. But shall we say that those Prophets also offered the merits of their blood and death for the inhabitants of that city?

5. Johannes Gagnaeus on v. 15 annotates thus: I do not think that one ever finds ἔχειν for 'to be able' joined to another infinitive. Perhaps Peter, when he had prefixed ἔχειν, because of a long hyperbaton, no longer mindful of the aforementioned word, added again ποιεῖσθαι, for either one can suffice. I will make an effort that after my departure you may have a memory of these things or may bring it about. Similar things occur in Salmeron, Disp. 2 on this Epistle.

Resp. 1. Lorinus in his commentary on this place rightly writes that he in no way wishes to say that about Peter's forgetfulness. 2. Because this futile conjecture of Gagnaeus is an injury to the Holy Spirit himself, the principal author of Scripture, and differs little from blasphemy. For if Peter wrote this Epistle at the dictation of the Holy Spirit, certainly if, unmindful of the aforementioned word ἔχειν, he added again ποιεῖσθαι,, then the Holy Spirit himself is accused of negligence. 3. The cause which moved Gagnaeus to conclude thus is nothing. For if the word ἔχω used in other moods can be joined with another infinitive, why could it not also, when placed in the infinitive, be joined with another verb of the infinitive mood? But the former can be confirmed by many examples. Iohan. 8. v. 6. ἵνα ἔχωσι κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ. Actor. 4. v. 14. οὐδὲν εἶχον ἀντειπεῖν. Eph. 4. v. 28. ἵνα ἔχῃμεταδιδόναι. 2. Iohann. vers. 13. πολλὰ ἔχων ὑμῖν γρὰφειν. Demosth. pro Corona. οὐκ ἔχειν ἀπολύσασθαι τὰ κατηγοροῦμενα δόξω. I shall seem not to be able to refute the objections.

6. Salmero Disp. 21 on 1. Cor. 13. and Disp. 2 on 2. Peter. Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 3. Disp. 6. q. 2. punct. 9. Franciscus Turrianus lib. 2. pro Epist, Pontif. cap. 13. Nodinus in cap. 8. Exod. Iodocus Coccius, Vol. 1. book 5. of the Treasury art. 4. p. 471. Laurentius Fauntaeus on the invocation of saints th. 79. Iosephus Acosta sermon 2. on the feast of John the Apostle. Suarez. Vol. 2. on Thomas q. 37. Disp. 23. sect. 2. Bellarm. book 1. on the beatitude of the saints chap. 18. Costerus in Enchir. chap. 14. Cottonus book 1. Instit. chap. 15. Ludovicus Richeomus on the saints chap. 10. Petrus de bollo on the authentic proof of the Christian sacrifice. Fevardentius, Catharinus, Lorinus, Cornelius â Lapide in their commentaries on this place from verse 15 attempt to prove, that the saints after death take care of the living, and therefore are to be religiously invoked,

Resp. 1. It is evident from the genuine exposition of the text brought forward above, that the Apostle does not promise, that he wishes to be mindful of them in his prayers, to whom he writes, but that by leaving behind the monuments of his Epistles he wishes to take pains that the faithful, even after his death, may retain the memory of those things which they had heard from him while he was still among the living. 2. This exposition is confirmed not only by the Ordinary Gloss, Thomas Aquinas, Lyranus, Hugo the Cardinal, Dionysius the Carthusian, but also among the more recent Papists by Caietanus, Erasmus, Guillaudus, Emanuel Saa. Estius in his commentary on this place, and from there Lorinus himself on this place annotates thus. The more common opinion of the expositors is that Peter signifies that he, because he must shortly depart from this life, wishes to take care that he may leave behind this monument of his Epistles and of the things so salutary in them, lest they ever fall out of their memory. 3. Guillaudus beautifully on this place: Just as the best teachers are accustomed to hand down to their disciples, of whose study they are most desirous, lest the pious and holy things which they learned from them fall out of their minds, so that they may be able to profit not only them but also all posterity by teaching, letters and monuments of virtues written by them, as mirrors for composing their minds: so also our Apostle wished to destine for those Asians, or rather for the whole Christian Church, and as it were to bequeath by testament this Epistle, by which they may not only perceive his divine, pure, sincere, and integral mind, but also, even when he is dead, have that which may admonish them of the doctrine once handed down by him. 4. This exposition is manifestly elicited from the scope and context. v. 12. The Apostle says, I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though ye know them, and be established in the present truth. v. 13. He subjoins, Yea, I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by putting you in remembrance. v. 15. He adds, Moreover I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance, you may make a memorial. Here anyone sees that the scope and sense of the Apostle is that he wishes to explain what he intends to do while still existing among the living, so that the faithful might be able to retain a perpetual memory of those things which they had learned from him even after his death, and not what he wishes to do after his death. 5. Cornelius à Lapide is compelled to admit that this sense is very plain, easy, and obvious; yet he does not rest in it, but brings forth a plainly new exposition, ἔχειν, he says, signifies to impel, to drive, to direct, to incite, as if to say: I will drive, I will direct, and I will impel you, so that you may remember these things. For Peter is the charioteer of the Church, driving and stirring the faithful to good, even when he enjoys GOD in the heavens. Although this meaning of the word ἔχειν is indeed plainly unusual and infrequent, yet if this is accepted regarding the usage of Petrine Scripture, we can concede the thing itself. 6. Salmero objects to this exposition of ours, that according to it Peter would have said the same thing three times. But Peter first says in general that it pertains to his office to remind them, then he explains in particular both what he wishes to do while still established in the tabernacle of the body, and what memorial of this reminding of his he intends to leave to them even after his death. 7. Bellarmine in d. 1. §. The fourth passage &c. brings forth such a paraphrase of this passage. I will however take pains that you may frequently have, namely, commended, or in mind after my decease, that you may make a memorial of these things. But whom will Bellarmine persuade of this enallage of persons? Peter speaks of the memory of the holy faithful to whom he writes, but Bellarmine explains this as the recollection of Peter. He also commits the fallacy of composition and division, by dividing those things which are joined in the Apostolic text. For the following μνήμην ποιεισθ. depend upon the word ἔχειν I will take pains that you may have that of which you may be mindful after my decease: and the word ἔχειν is not referred to Peter, but to those to whom he was writing, namely, not that Peter may have them, but that they may have a memory of them. Who has ever spoken thus: I will take pains that I may have you i.e., that I may have care of you. 8. Franciscus Turrianus in the same place admits indeed that τὸ ἐχειν should be translated as, that you may be able, not ἵνα ἔχω ὑμᾶς, but ἵνα ὑμεῖς ἔχητε. But he refers that, after my decease, to the word σπουδάσω, which is a manifest perversion of the text. How does σπουδάζειν; also befit the saints after death? 9. Salmero, Bellarmine, Coccius, Lorinus, in the said places appeal to the Greek Scholia in Oecumenius, of the walls, in which it is said, that some of the ancients not ineptly gathered from this, that the saints after death have care for those living. But they conceal that Oecumenius prefers our exposition to that one. The entire passage reads thus. Some understand it by hyperbaton in this way. I will also take pains, even after my departure, for you to have these things always or daily and continuously in memory, wishing to show from this, that even after death the saints remember those things which they performed here for the living. Others, however, treating that saying simply, understand it thus. I will take pains that you also always have, after my departure, that mention of these things be made, that is, do not wonder, nor consider it burdensome, that constant mention of these things is made to you. For I do not do this condemning your ignorance, but persevering through continuous teaching about these things, I exhibit to you an immovable support of these things, so that, confirmed by these, you may have even after my death a living and indelible doctrine of these things. 10. Before Oecumenius, whose age falls in the tenth century, no one divined that this was the sense of that passage. Indeed, Chrysostom's Oration on the Princes of the Apostles is produced, in which he implores the patronage of Peter and Paul, and demands, that they fulfill their promises in this matter, bringing forward this reason, that Peter said. I will strive after my arrival to make mention of you. But what is to be determined concerning this oration attributed to Chrysostom, we shall soon see. 11. Weighing all these things, Bellarmine in the said place confesses, that the argument drawn from this passage for the religious invocation of the saints is not evident, but only probable. For let us grant that it can be proven from this passage that the deceased saints bear a memory of those things which they did in these lands, and that they pray in general for the living in these lands, can it immediately be inferred from that, that the deceased saints are to be religiously invoked? 12. Nay, Estius in express words repudiates that argument, which other Papists draw from this passage for establishing the invocation of the saints. Certain, he says, Catholic writers think that the intercession of the saints for the living can be proven from these words of Peter, making this sense. I will take pains, that after my death I may be mindful of you, namely, about to pray to God for you, that you may have a memory of these things which I write. Thus Chrysostom accepted it in his sermon on Peter and Paul, if indeed it is entirely his, for toward the end it varies wonderfully. Nor does he cite the words of Peter as they are read in him, but in this way. I will strive after my departure to make mention of you. Oecumenius he also mentions this interpretation, but prefers the other as simpler. Certainly it was not fitting that he should say, I will give effort, I will take care, σπουδάσω, since the saints do that without care and anxiety. Now what does it avail to wish to establish a most certain doctrine with an uncertain argument, when other most certain ones are by no means lacking? Therefore, the solicitude of Peter is to be observed and praised here, by which he strives that, even when he is dead, right doctrine may remain among the faithful and be transmitted to posterity. 13. Estius deservedly accuses that sermon concerning Peter and Paul, which exists in Vol. 5 of the works of Chrysostom, of being suspect. Casaubon in Exercit. adver. Baronium p. 169 writes thus concerning it: Out of shame this encomiastic homily on the Princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, was not inserted into the works of Chrysostom, for its author abuses and falsifies his Scriptures. Peter and Paul pray for us without ceasing, for you promised. You, Paul, when you said, Come with me and we shall not lack good things, You, Peter, I will give effort that after my death you may make mention of these things.

7. Thomas Bozius, de signis Ecclesiae lib. 18. cap. 3, strives with wonderful artifice to prove the primacy of the Roman Pontiff from this passage. How, he says, did Peter give effort that after his death all the Churches might always be reminded? For he promises that he himself will do it specifically. And who ever did this in the name of Peter? For this is necessary, otherwise Peter would be said to have given effort to these things no more than anyone else. Therefore two things are necessary, both that someone did this, and that he did it according to the prescription of Peter himself. But only the Roman Pontiff accomplished this. Therefore, by the mandate of Peter, he himself has the right over all Churches of reminding and seeing to it that they are mindful of the commandments of Peter and of GOD. And that must be noted, I will begin to remind always. Therefore, already about to die, he says that he is beginning. But he began through letters and other ways of this kind: Therefore he continued through the same, so that the progress might correspond to the beginning.

Resp. 1. None of the ancient or recent Interpreters in their commentaries on this place dreamed anything of the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. 2. But what is this συνέχεια. Peter reminds all the Churches after his death. Therefore he executes this through the Roman Pontiffs? Nay rather, through these very Epistles, written for the perpetual use of the whole Church, he performs that, just as many of the Papist Interpreters themselves accommodate this little verse to μνημόσυνον of the Epistles. Let us hear only Estius; after he had proposed such a paraphrase of this place: But also

I will take care and pains, that after my departure you may at all times be able to renew for yourselves the memory of these things, of which I now write; he adds, he did that, however, by leaving them a monument of his Epistles, by the frequent rereading of which it would come to pass that they would never forget his precepts and admonitions. 3. Let us grant, indeed, that Peter admonishes all Churches through the Roman Bishops: does it follow from that, that he performs this through the Roman Pontiffs alone? Nay, rather, he performs that through all the faithful Doctors of the Church. For all are successors of the Apostles, and thus also of Peter, says Jerome in his Epistle to Evagrius. 4. Let us grant, by hypothesis, that that admonition is made through the Roman Bishops alone, yet it would not thereby be confirmed that there is a primacy of Monarchical power, but only of order and dignity. 5. Not even Peter himself arrogated to himself a Monarchical primacy, but he calls himself συμπρεσβύτεραν 1. Epist. 5. vers. 1. and forbids κατακυριεύειν τῶν κλήρων. v. 3. how much less, therefore, will a Monarchical primacy belong to those through whom Peter carries out the duties of admonishing, by this name? 6. The Roman Pontiffs have not at all times admonished the universal Churches concerning heavenly truth, since at times they have been heretics, or supporters of heretics, at times slothful in their office, at times entirely inept for the duty of teaching. But if, therefore, Peter had promised that he would always admonish the Churches through the Roman Pontiffs, the event would not have corresponded to the prediction, nor would there have been a fulfillment of the promise. 7. As many Papists as attempt to prove the invocation of deceased saints from this passage, they are compelled to establish that Peter performs what he promises in this passage by himself, not through other vicars and intermediate persons. 8. Nor is there any reason why Bozius should urge the word I will begin in v. 12. for it is a fault of the Vulgate version, since in the Greek it is οὐκ ἀμελήσω, concerning which matter a judgment can be made from the exposition of that verse handed down above.

Observations. 1. It is not sufficient to hand down the mysteries of faith and the doctrine of morals to hearers once, but there is need of perpetual admonition and exhortation, hence Rom. 12. v. 7. and 8. διδάσκων καὶ παρακαλῶν are joined together. Bede in this place: Why does he wish to admonish them always concerning good works, whom he says have knowledge, and are confirmed in the presence of the truth? unless perhaps for this reason, that the knowledge which they know, let them exercise themselves in works and keep with a fixed mind the truth, by whose presence they have been confirmed, lest at any time they fall away from the simplicity and chastity of the faith through the teachers of error. Compare. Isa. 58. v. 1.c. 62. v. 6.1. Tim. 4. v. 13.2. Tim. 4. v. 2.

2. No one ought to seem so skilled and confirmed in the truth of the faith to himself, that he thinks he no longer needs admonition. 1. Cor. 13. v. 8. It is frequently necessary to be reminded of what this world compels one to forget, says the Angelic Thomas in this place, quoting Bernard.

3. Our soul in this life dwells in the body as in a tabernacle: in eternal life it will dwell in a glorified body as in a temple. The tabernacle of the covenant was built in the desert, by which desert the present age is prefigured, in which, as pilgrims and those tending elsewhere, we only tarry for a time in this mortal body. But the temple was built in Jerusalem, which is a type of eternal life, in which, as in a fatherland, we shall have a fixed seat, nor will the dissolution of soul and body, that is, the departure of the soul from the dwelling of the body, ever be to be feared again. 2. Cor. 5. v. 1. We know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of GOD, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Hence Paul Philip. 1. verse 23. says, that he is held by a desire εἰς τὸ ἀναλύσαι to depart, namely from the transitory tabernacle of the body to the heavenly dwelling.

4. Although believers are children of light, Luke 16. v. 8. and children of the day, 1. Thess. 5. verse 5. and do not sleep as others, verse 6. who are lulled to sleep by the lethargy of sins, yet sometimes even they doze Matt. 25. verse 5. and the danger threatens them that they might be overcome by sleep: it is therefore required of the faithful teachers of the Church that they rouse them and exhort them to perpetual vigilance. 2. Timoth. 1. verse 6. ἀναμιμνήσκω σε ἀναζωπορεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ. Luther in this place Wir sind alle mit dem alten faulen Sack beladen/ mit unsern Fleisch und Blut / das wil immerdar den Holtzweg / zeugt uns immer zu sich herrunder / daß die Seele leichtlich entschläfft. Darümb muß man immer treiben und anhalten / wie ein Haußvater das Haußgefinde treibet / daß es nicht faul werde / ob sie gleich wol wissen was sie thun sollen.

5. Bede on this passage and from him the Ordinary Gloss: Most beautifully Blessed Peter calls his death the putting off of the tabernacle, because indeed it is thus for the perfect servants of GOD to cast off the bonds of the flesh, just as for travelers when finished to go on a journey to one's own home for the habitation of a tabernacle, just as those placed in an expedition, with the enemy put to flight or laid low, return to their fatherland. For they know only one home, only one citizenship, only one fatherland for themselves in the heavens.

6. That tabernacle of ours is sometimes quickly removed, like the shepherd's little hut. Esai. 38. v. 12. Let us therefore prepare ourselves maturely. The closer the goal, the swifter should be the course.

7. Simeon the elder calls his death ἀπὸλυσιν a dissolution Luc. 2. vers. 29. as if he were held in this life by a certain necessity of chains, not by will, says Ambrose on the good of death, chapter 2. Paul calls it ἀνάλυσιν 2. Timoth. 4. vers. 6. a resolution, a regression.

8. The liberation of the Israelites from Egyptian servitude is called ἡ ἔξοδος, as ἐπιγραφὴ of the second Mosaic book shows, & Hebr. 11. vers. 12. Peter looks to that when he calls his death ἔξοδον. Such ἔξοδος is the death of all the truly pious, because our soul, as long as it dwells in the body, is pressed by miserable captivity and servitude, Rom. 7. v. 14. 23. 24. but when it departs from the body, then it is freed from those chains. Psal. 142. v. 8.

9. The faithful Doctors of the Church ought to apply themselves with all zeal to this, that the integrity of heavenly doctrine be propagated to posterity. Actor. 20. vers. 28. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, v. 29. I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter, 1. Tim. 6. v. 20. O Timothy, guard the deposit. 2. Tim. 1. v. 14. Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit. 2. Tim. 2. v. 2. The things which you have heard from me through many witnesses, these entrust to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others also. Lyranus in this place: A good Shepherd desires and seeks the salvation of his flock, not only for his own time, but also for the future.

10. Among other causes, on account of which God willed that His word, previously preached by living voice, be reduced to Scriptures, is also the weakness of human memory. Peter in this place says that he will give effort so that after his departure they might be able to have the memory of those things, of which he writes, always, he accomplished this by leaving them the monuments of his Epistles. Compare Eusebius book 2, History, chapter 34, book 3, chapter 24, book 6, chapter 13.

11. We ought not only to read the book of Scripture once, but to re-read and meditate upon it, for to that end the Prophets and Apostles deposited their writings with the Church.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco 1. Rectene Interpres Latinusοὐκ ἀμελήσω in vers. 12. reddiderit, Incipiam? Lorinus ad illum vers. sic commentatur. Significat Apostolus, diligenter se occurrere imminenti hosti Simoni & disseminatis ab illo erroribus, ita ut de integro semper admoneat, per inde ac si tum primùm inciperet. Id est, vel non omittere, seu negligere, vel non differre seu protrahere, quae Interpres per incipiam expressit doctissimè. Estio admodùm verisimile videtur, Interpretem Latinum legisseμελλήσω,pro quo verterit incipiam, cùm verbum Graecumμέλλεινusitatissimè significet futurum esse, quod alibi Vulgatus Interpres reddiderit. Incipiam.Ioh. 4. v. 4.Actor. 23. v. 27.Iac. 2. v. 12.ut sit sensus, propter quod deinceps semper vos commonebo. Sed resp. 1. Graeci Codd. omnes constanter legunt, οὐκ ἀμελήσω, excepto uno, cuius meminit Rob. Stephanus, qui legit, οὐ μελλήσω. 2. Sed haec lectio nihil quidquam facit pro versione vulgata, quae omissâ negatione, quam omnes Graeci Codd. additam habent, reddidit incipiam. 3. futurum μελλήσω nuspiam in sacris literis occurrit. 4. nec rectè vertitur per incipiam, ut ostendunt exempla ab Estio adducta. 5. Cumprimis verò hoc loco absurdè redditur per incipiendi verbum. Quid enim est semper incipiam vos commonere? num semper erat commonitionem incepturus Apostolus, nequaquam finiturus? Lorini expositio, incipiam i. e. non omittam, est valde catachrestica. 6. Inde Lorinus ipse addit. Potest incipiam vel non negligam, positum intelligi pro incepi, non neglexi, sc. in priore Epistola. Atqui Petrus non agit de eo, quid iam fecerit, sed quid porrò facturus sit. 7. Haec omnia expendens Estius victas tandem dat manus, sic scribens. Quia futurumμελλήσωvix est in usu apud Graecos, licet alicubi apud Platonem legatur, certè nusquam in sacris literis: idcircò veriorem arbitror eam lectionem, quam habent omnes, aut penè omnes Graeci Codices. Nam omnes habent negationem; penè omnesἀμελήσω,quod verbum optimè convenit huic loco. Ut, inquit, ampla praemia recipiatis à Deo, non negligam vos ad exercenda bona opera adhortari i. e. assiduè atque solicitè vos commonefaciam & adhortabor. 8. Sed quid fiet decreto Concilii Tridentini, quod nemini licere debeat quovis praetextu à vulgata versione ad Codices Graecos provocare?

Q. 2. Quare Apostolus corpus suum vocet tabernaculum? Resp. Beda in h. l. Tabernaculo solemus in itinere vel in bello uti, & ideò se rectè fideles, quamdiu sunt in corpore & peregrinantur à Domino, in tabernaculis esse testantur, in quibus iter huius vitae peragant, & contra adversarios veritatis certamen agant. Bernhardus serm. 26. in Cant. Tabernaculum est vocabulum pastorale & militare. Respicit ergo Apostolus 1. Ad tabernacula Patriarcharum. Patriarchae tentoriis & tabernaculis utebantur, dum terram promissionis sectabantur, incertam interim mansionem nec diuturnam habentes: sic incertam eandemque non diuturnam ponimus mansionem in hoc corpore, qui peregrinamur â Domino, sed cupimus illi praesentes esse,2. Cor. 5. v. 6.neque enim habemus hîc civitatem manentem.Hebr. 13. v. 14. 2. Ad tabernaculum foederis, in quo Deus gratiosè quidem praesens erat, sed tamen ipsum tabernaculum per desertum ê loco in locum portabatur: sic pii sunt habitacula Spiritus Sancti, ac totius Sacratissimae Trinitatis, Iohan. 14. v. 23.1. Cor. 3. v. 16.cap. 6. v. 16.Eph. 3. v. 17. sed quamdiu in deserto huius mundi vagantur, non habent stabilem ac fixam sedem. 3. Ad tabernacula militaria & pastoralia, & quidem, Primò ratione brevis morae. Tabernacula sunt habitationes temporariae, in quibus belli duntaxat tempore milites habitant, quae de loco in locum transferuntur, quod cum Pastoralibus tabernaculis ipsis est commune. Esai. 38. v. 12. Sic brevis est animae in hoc corpore mora. Secundò ratione vilis & imbecillis structurae. Tabernacula ex vili plerunque materia extruuntur: sic corpus nostrum ex terra formatum perquam fragile est & imbecillum, unde in hac vita dicimur inhabitare domus luteas.Iob. 4. v. 19. Cute vestitum est corpus, ut tabernaculum pellibus adversus iniurias caeli. Iob. 10. v. 11. nervis ut funiculis intenditur, pro malo & aliis ligneis instrumentis ossa sunt, pedes clavorum funguntur officio. Tertiò ratione laboris & occupationis molestae. In tabernaculo degimus tempore militiae. Sic tota in his terris vita nihil aliud est, quàm militia.Iobi 7. v. 1. In tabernaculo degens multos sentit defectus, in commoda & angustias: sic in hoc corpore plurimas patimur aerumnas. In tabernaculo degens suspirat ad domum: sic fidelis in hac vita suspirat ad caelum. Quartò ratione conditionis caducae & migrationis maturae. In tabernaculo habitamus ut peregrini, non ut inquilini: sic in hac vita â Domino peregrinamur.2. Cor. 5. v. 6.DEI autem cives sumus ac domestici.Eph. 2. v. 20. Avellitur hoc tabernaculum in morte, pedum in senio nutant clavi, cutis corrugatur, laxantur nervi, sed postea destructum hoc tabernaculum erigetur, quando in aeterna caeli tabernaculi introducemur, Luc. 16. v. 9. tunc vili & temporario huic tabernaculo succedet aedificium firmum ac stabile, quando corpus nostrum immortalitate fuerit donatum; tunc obtinebimus domum ἀχειραποιητὸν2. Cor. 5. v. 1. 1. cuius τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς immediatus est ipse DEUS. Hebr. 11. v. 10. & 16.

Q. 3. Quando Petro fuerit â Christo manifestatum, quòd brevi futurum sit, ut corporis sui tabernaculum deponat? Resp. 1. Glossa interlin. Concordantiae marginales, ac Hugo Cardinalis remittunt nos ad vaticinium Christi Iohan. 21. v. 18.Cum senueris, alius te cinget & ducet, quò non vis. Sed Christus ibi mortem violentam sive Martyrium, & ut quidam volunt, genus mortis, videlicet crucifixionem Petro praedicit, non autem tempus mortis proximè instantis. Quamvis enim addat, cùm senueris, tamen senectus ad multos usque annos quan doque extenditur, ut ex senectute non statim mors propinqua inferri possit. 2. Simeon Metaphrastes apud Surium. 29. Iunii refert, Petro, cùm in Britannia ageret, ab Angelo fuisse dictum, Petre, instat tempus tuae resolutionis & oportet te ire Romam, ubi cùm mortem per crucem sustinueris, recipies mercedem iustitiae. Atqui Metaphrasten illum, qui nono post Christum natum seculo vixisse creditur, esse suspectae & sublestae fidei scriptorem agnoscunt Baronius Ann. 31. n. 30. Ann. 859. n. 53. Bellarminus de scriptor. Eccles. in verbo Metaphrastes, Croquetius in Catech. 215. Inde Estius ad h. l. sic annotat. Quod refert Metaphrastes de Petro per Angelum de sua morte edocto suspectae fidei est, ut & alia nonnulla de Petro eiusdem autoris. Certè Beda rerum Britannicarum gnarus, si quis alius, nihil tale meminit, nec in commentario nec in Historia Ecclesiastica. Lorinus ad h. l. Metaphrastes nonnulla habet de Petro parùm certa, imò & falsa, verbi gratia, quòd Romam reversus Linum repererit iam mortuum, & pro eo Clementem substituerit, cùm satis constet, vixisse post Petrum & credatur eius acta & mortem descripsisse. 3. Egesippus lib. 3. de excidio Hierosolym. cap. 2. Ambrosius Epist. 32. Tom. 3. p. 125. Gregorius in Ps. 4. paenit. Acta Processi & Martiani apud Surium 2. Iulii tale quid de Petro memorant. Petrus victo Simone cùm pracepta DEI populo seminaret, castimoniam doceret, excitavit animos gentilium, quibus eum quaerentibus Christianae animae deprecatae sunt, ut paulisper cederet. Et quamvis esset cupidus passionis, tamen contemplatione populi precantis inflexus est.

Rogabatur enim ut ad instituendum & confirmandum populum se reservaret. Quid multa? nocte muro egredi caepit & videns sibi in porta CHRISTUM occurrere, urhemque ingredi, ait, Domine, quo vadis? respondit CHRISTUS. Venio Romam iterum crucisigi. Intellexit Petrus, ad suam crucem divinum pertinere responsum. CHRISTUS enim non poterat iterum crucifigi, qui carnem passione susceptae mortis exuerat. &c. Intellexit ergo Petrus, quòd iterum CHRISTUS crucifigendus esset in servulo. Itaque sponte remeavit, interrogantibus Christianis responsum reddidit, statimque correptus per crucem suam honorificavit Dominum Iesum. Salmero hanc apparitionem Christi Petro factam suo suffragio approbat Disp. 1. in hanc Epistolam Petri Tom. 16. pag. 112. & Disp. 2. pag. 119. Lorinus itidem, sic enim ad h. l. commentatur. Extat hodieque celebre monumentum viâ Appiâ, in loco ubi Petro, qui fidelium cedens precibus, Neronis fugiebat persecutionem, Christus apparuit, seque Romam venire dixit iterum crucifigi, quod de seipso Petrus interpretans in urbem reflexit iter, ac paulò pòst pro Christo crucem passus est. Sed nec de hac manifestatione locus hic Apostolicus accipi potest, quia statim post eam ad Martyrium fuit abreptus. 4. Leo magnus insinuat, Petro revelatum fuisse aetatis suae spacium, prius quam Romam veniret, sic enim scribit serm. 1. in natali Apostol. Petri & Pauli. Nec ut dubius de provectu operis, aut de spacio tuae ignarus aetatis trophaeum crucis Christi Romanis arcibus inferebas, quò te divinis praeordinationibus anteibant & honor potestatis & gloria passionis. Sed nec huius revelationis vel sacra vel Ecclesiastica meminit Historia. 5. Tutissimum igitur est, fateri, revelatum quidem fuisse Petro tempus mortis proximè imminentis (unde etiam Dionysius in Syriaco huius loci commentario addit, sicut indicavit mihi Dominus[בחסוא]in visione h. e. revelatione,) sed qualis fuerit illa visio, vel quo tempore & loco haec revelatio Petro fuerit facta, de eo nihil certi affirmari posse. Similis revelatio videtur Paulo facta. 2. Tim. 4. v. 6.

Ἐναντιοφανεὶαι. 1. Petrus hoc loco dicit, brevi futurum, ut corporis sui tabernaculum in morte deponat. vers. 14. At CHRISTUS hoc sibi soli tribuat, quod potestatem habeat ponendi animam suam, quodque eam ponat â semetipso.Ioh. 10. v. 18.

Resp. 1. in Graeco textu simpliciter dicitur, quod brevi secutura sit depositio tabernaculi, id quod tùm passivè, tùm activè potest accipi. 2. Si vel maximè activè accipiatur, non tamen eo sensu Petrus dicitur deponere tabernaculum sui corporis, quo Christus animam h. e. vitam suam ponere dicitur. Christus non erat obstricutus moriendi necessitati, quia ἀναμάρτητος & quia in personae unitate versus DEUS, ideò dicit, se animam suam ponere â semetipso, h. e. non solùm voluntariè mori, sed etiam quando & ubi vult, mori, quod est divinae potestatis: sed Petrus propter Peccatum moriendi necessitati erat obnoxius, interim tamen voluntati divinae in morte sustinenda patienter sese subiecit, quod fuit pietatis. Lutheri versio dubium tollit. Ich weiß / daß ich meine Hütte bald ablegen muß.

2. Petrus h. l. dicit, breve futurum, ut tabernaculum corporis sui in morte deponat, quod est indicium, ipsum voluntariè fuisse mortuum. Sed ChristusIoh. 21. v. 18.dicit. Cùm senueris, alius te cinget, & ducet, quò non vis.

Resp. 1. Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 1. memorat, Petrum tantâ animi promtitudine crucem propter Christum suscepisse, ut voluerit capite in terram demisso & inversis vestigiis crucifigi, indignum se dicens, qui eo modo crucifigatur, quo Christus erecto sc. capite. 2. Quod ergo de Petri morte Christus dicit, alius cinget te & ducet, quò non vis, ad illud respondent Scholastici distinguendo inter voluntatem naturalem & deliberatam. Petrus voluntariè pro Christo mortuus est, quantum ad voluntatem deliberatam attinet, etsi voluntas, ut nostra, reclamaret. August. tract. 123. in Iohann. illud sic effert, Petrum nolentem ad mortem venisse, sed postea affectum infirmitatu, quo nemo vult mori, reliquisse. 3. Et sanè dubium nullum, quin Petrus affectum carnis mortem horrescentis Spiritus robore superaverit, interim tamen cùm in ipso crucis supplicio, caro Petri manserit caro h. e. infirmitatibus circumdata, ideò distinctione Spiritus & carnis in Petro res optimè explicari potest. Petrus cùm coram Concilio Hierosolymitano flagris caederetur, gaudens â conspectu Concilii exivit;Actor. 5. v. 41. eodem affectu etiam crucem suscepit. Sed haec promta moriendi voluntas profecta non est â carne, sed ex Spiritu: Christus verò loquitur de refractaria Petri carne, in qua adhuc habitat peccatum,Rom. 7. v. 18. quae Spiritui adhuc repugnat.Gal. 5. v. 17.

ac de lege membrorum, quae repugnat legi mentisRom. 7. v. 23. Confer. Harmon. de resurrect. cap. 11. p. 393.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Iohannes Huss adv. 13. sic commentatur. Miror, quòd Petrus existens immediatus & certus Vicarius Iesu Christi non dedit Indulgentias, per quas potuisset subditos ad vitam meritoriam allicere & de poenis Purgatorii citius liberare! Sed monuit eos, ut in fide perficientes opera virtuosa, de vocatione & electione sua forent certi, quia tunc introitus in regnum aeternum ipsis ministraretur: quod si ab operibus virtuosis deficerent, tunc velut coeci palpitantes manerent â gratia vacui & inanes? Solutio admirationis est Petri iusta informatio,

2. Autores Centuriae Magdeburgenses meritò quaerunt, Quare Petrus hoc loco v. 14. non faciat mentionem de successore suo Clemente, si Clemens fuit illius in Sede Papali successor? Respondet Franciscus Turrianus lib. 2. pro Epist. Pontif. cap. 15. quamvis Petrus velocem scribat, futuram depositionem tabernaculi sui sibi revelatam, non tamen quàm velox, & praecisè quo tempore, nec id sibi quoque revelatum asserit. Haec Turriani responsio Lorino non probatur, qui meliorem solutionem dari posse censet, videl. nihil necesse fuisse de his scribere. Atqui omnino necessarium erat, futurum successorem, utpote Ecclesiae caput & Monarcham, omnium controversiarum infallibilem Iudicem, & authenticum Scripturae Interpretem, per literas Ecclesiae commendare ac successori suo autoritatem conciliare.

Ἐδίκησις, 1. Bellarminus lib. 4. de Verbo Dei cap. 12. §. Quod autem ex v. 12. colligit, finem Scripturae praecipuum non esse, ut sit regula fidei, sed ut variis documentis, exemplis, adhortationibus nunc tenendo, nunc instruendo, nunc minando, nunc consolando adiuvet nos in hac peregrinatione. Ibidem in resp. ad arg. 2. scribit, Scripturae finem proprium & praecipuum non fuisse, ut esset regula fidei, sed ut esset commonitorium quoddam utile ad conservandam & fovendam doctrinam ex praedicatione acceptam.

Resp. 1. Scripturam esse fine eo, & quidem praecipuè exaratam, ut esset regula fidei, docent omnia illa dicta, in quibus ad verbum DEI primùm quidem vivâ voce praedicatum, postea per DEI voluntatem in Scripturas redactum, tanquam ad unicam fidei & cultus divini Regulam revocamur. Deut. 4. v. 2.cap. 5. v. 32.cap. 12. v. 32.Esai. 8. v. 19.Luc. 16. v. 29. quaeque docent, Christum & Apostolos in omnibus fidei controversiis unicè ad Scripturas provocasse, Matth. 19. v. 4.cap. 22. v. 31. & 43.Marc. 9. v. 12.Luc. 10. vers. 26.cap. 24. v. 26.Act. 3. v. 20.cap. 7. v. 2.cap. 13. v. 33.cap. 18. v. 26.cap. 26. v. 22.cap. 28. v. 23.Rom. 4. v. 3.1. Cor. 15. v. 3.Gal. 3. v. 64. 2. Id tam evidens est, ut Bellarm ipse lib. & cap. iisd. §. Dico secundò &c, asserat, Scripturam, etsi non sit facta praecipuè, ut sit regula fidei, esse tamenregulam fidei non totalem, sed partialem. Atqui si Scriptura est regula fidei, utique etiam fine eo exarata est, ut sit regula fidei, aliàs praeter intentionem Dei, cuius impulsu Scriptura utpote θεὸπνευστος est exarata, ei tribueretur, quòd sit fidei regula. 3. Ipsa appellatio Canonis â Spiritu Sancto verbo DEI scripto attributa Psal. 19. vers. 5. ( Rom. 10. v. 18.) Esai. 28. v. 10.Gal. 6. v. 16.Phil. 3. v. 16. ostendit, finem Scripturae â sanctis Dei hominibus editae esse, non ut sit nudum commonitorium, sed ut sit certa & perpetua fidei, cultus, ac morum regula in Ecclesia. 4. Concedimus igitur, finem & usum Scripturae in commonitione consistere, sed ex eo inferri nequit, quòd tantùm in commonitione consistat; ac quòd finis eius principalis & primarius non sit, necessaria ad salutem docere & fidei regulam proponere. Accessorium enim & secundarium non tollit principale. 5. Spiritus Sanctus Apostolis suggerebat omnia,Iohann. 14. vers. 26. ubi itidem ponitur verbum ὑπομιμνήσκειν, idem tamen erat ipsorum doctor ducens illos in omnem veritatem. Iohann. 16. v. 13. 6. Nimirum duplicem finem ratione diversorum obiectorum Scriptura obtinet. Ignaros mysteriorum fidei perfectè informat & instruit; eos verò, quibus iam dum fidei mysteria ex verbi praedicatione cognita commonefacit.

2.
