Therefore, let all the Scriptures be taken from our midst, which were kindled for us in the night of this age like lamps, lest we remain in darkness. The same, sermon 237 de temp. In the day we walk in comparison to the infidels; but in comparison to that day, when the dead shall rise, we are still night. Bede in comm. h. l. In the night of this age, full of dark temptations, where it is difficult to find anyone who does not stumble, what would we be if we did not have the lamp of the Prophetic word? But will the lamp always be necessary? Certainly not. Until, he says, the day dawns. For in the morning I will stand and contemplate. It pertains to the nocturnal lamp that we are children of GOD, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. And indeed, in comparison to the impious, we are day, as Paul says: You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. But if we are compared to that life in which we are to be, we are still night and we need a lamp. But who is this Morning Star, of whom the Apostle speaks, and the Morning Star arises in your hearts? If you say the Lord, it is too little. The Morning Star itself is our clear intellect. For it itself arises in our hearts: it itself will be illuminated, it itself will be manifested. There will be love, such as we now desire, and because it is not, we sigh; and such as it will be, we shall see each in each, just as we now see our faces one another: which words of Bede the Ordinary Gloss brings forward in h. l., insisting on the footsteps of Augustine and Bede, Cajetan comments thus on h. l. Peter likens the entire state of this life to a dark place, needing the light of a lamp, which is Holy Scripture: the future life is likened to a clear day, in which the Morning Star, i. e., Christ, arises not corporally, but spiritually in the hearts of men. 4. But by the dawning day and the rising Phosphor is more correctly understood a more abundant, more perfect, clearer, and more explicit knowledge of Christ and divine mysteries. For just as Paul Rom. 13. v. 12. calls the time of the O. T. night, because it was clearly a time of shadows, having respect to the revelation of the Gospel and the light of the knowledge of Christ in the N. T., so Peter in this place teaches that the Prophetic writings exhibited a certain thin and restricted light in the time of the O. T., such as is accustomed to be that of a lamp lit in the time of night, meanwhile, however, this light of the lamp shining in a dark place was to be used entirely, until through the word of the Gospel and the operation of the Holy Spirit a more abundant, clearer, and more perfect light of divine knowledge in the N. T. had followed; nay, with the most clear radiance of the N. T. already risen, those converted from the Jews rightly do so, because they attend to the Prophetic Scriptures as to lamps, until the day of the N. T. may shine even upon them, and the day-star, i. e. the more abundant message of Christ, may arise in their hearts, and with the darkness dispelled, a clearer light may shine upon them. Thus, therefore, the Apostle compares the Prophetic discourse to a lamp shining in the time of night; but he compares the Apostolic discourse, or the preaching of the Gospel in the N. T., to the day-star and to the day bringing full light, and for this reason he attributes greater clarity of doctrine to the New Testament. 5. We approve this exposition, first from the fact that ἡμέρα, is said without the article, although when the day of judgment is signified by the name ἡμέρας in the Scriptures, either ἐκεινη ἡμέρα, or the article δεικτικὸς ἡ ἡμέρα. is always added. Secondly, because the final coming of Christ to judgment does not seem to be compared quite fittingly with the rising of the day-star. Indeed, Christ Apoc. 22. v. 16. calls himself the bright and morning star i. e. Phosphorus or the day-star (and as it is rendered emphatically in the Syriac Paraphrase, that bright star, that morning one, in distinction from the Angels, who are likewise called morning stars, Iob. 38. v. 7.) but this is done with respect to the benefits which we obtain from him in this life, because, namely, he announces that the day and light of divine grace are present, and he kindles the light of divine knowledge in the minds of men. On the last day, however, he is more rightly compared to the Sun shining at midday, because coming in his glory he will far surpass the meridian splendor of the Sun, and he will bring with him not a certain dimmer light, such as that of the day-star shining in the morning twilight, but the clearest and most perfect light, such as that of the Sun shining in its strength, i. e. at midday. Cyril, lib. 1. de Trin. near the beginning, teaches that Christ is the radiance, the day, and the day-star, who irradiates the minds of the faithful through the Spirit, and illuminates them more clearly than all the Prophets, just as the day-star glows more clearly than the other stars. Theodoret in Expos. Psal. 1. interprets the law of Moses as a lamp, and Christ as the light, since the former illuminated scarcely one nation, the latter the whole world. Thirdly. Although indeed the Syriac version rendered the name Phosphorus by Sun, yet it is certain that only the Greek text is authentic; indeed, another Syrian Interpreter, insisting more closely on the Greek text, rendered [כוכב נוגהא] as to a bright and shining star, i. e. attending to the day-star or Phosphorus. Fourthly Principally here the Apostle deals with converted Jews, who indeed had been led to the faith of Christ, meanwhile however they searched the Prophetic writings daily, whether the preaching of the Apostles concerning Christ in every part agreed with them, Act. 17. v. 11. whose zeal Peter commends, and asserts that they could and ought to be led to the clearer light of the Gospel through the lamp of Prophetic Scripture. Fifthly, meanwhile we do not deny that what the Apostle asserts in this place concerning Prophetic Scripture in particular, can also be accommodated to Apostolic Scripture, and thus to the whole of Scripture, since the whole of Scripture is θεόπνευστος and has proceeded from God, who is light itself, nay rather the New Testament is like the Sun, from which the Old Testament like the Moon or the Morning Star borrows its light. We grant this also, that the whole time of the present life compared to the light of eternal life is a certain dark night, but that eternal life will be clearer than the midday light. For just as the time of the O.T. was night with respect to the New; so the time of the N.T. can be called night, if it is compared with the future age, which will be in glory, where we shall no longer need the lamp of Scripture, since there will be no night there, no shadow, no cloud, no darkness, but immense and eternal brightness and perpetual day.Apoc. 21. v. 23. Thence also we ourselves have followed this latter interpretation, which understands by the day the state of the future life, and by the Morning Star the fullest knowledge of Christ in eternal life, in Exeges. tom. 1. Loc. 1. de Script. §. 375. For neither exposition is repugnant to the analogy of faith.

Q. 5. Why does the Apostle inculcate this admonition, that Scripture is not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, so seriously to those to whom he writes? Bede answers in the annotations to v. 16 of this chapter that heretics (as also Jews not yet converted) having received the mysteries of the word of GOD, have studied from then on not to attend to the divine Scriptures, but rather to transfer them to their own erroneous sense by interpreting them badly.

Q. 6. What does that φορὰ of the Holy Spirit, which Peter attributes to the holy men of GOD in the last verse, comprise? Resp. It comprises 1. ἔλλαμψιν the interior illumination of the mind, by which an excellent knowledge of divine things and heavenly mysteries is kindled in them through the Holy Spirit. Ioh. 16. v. 13. The Holy Spirit will lead you into all truth. 2. the gift of infallibility, that the Prophets in the O.T. and the Apostles in the N.T. could not err in doctrine, whence we are said to be built upon the foundation of the Prophets and ApostlesEphes. 2. vers. 20.

13. The Gift of Prophecy, in that they were able to predict future things, in which respect the Prophets of the O. T. were called Seers, because they were able to see not only absent things and those hidden from the eyes, but also future things. Concerning the Apostles, Christ says John 16. v. 13. the Holy Spirit will announce to you the things that are to come. 4. A peculiar motion and instinct of the Holy Spirit, by which they were impelled to preaching and writing. Acts 17. v. 16. when Paul was at Athens, his spirit was stirred within him. To this interior motion there was sometimes added an external command. Rev. 1. v. 10. I heard behind me a great voice as of a trumpet. v. 11. saying, write what you have seen. Gregory, book 2, Dialogues, chapter 3, The mind of the Prophet is driven by the power of the heavenly Divinity. 5. Δύναμιν ἑρμηνευτικὴν, by which they were able to propose divine mysteries in clear, proper, and perspicuous words, both by living voice in sermons and also in writings to their hearers. Luke 21. v. 15. I will give στόμα καὶ σοφίαν.

Ἐναντιοφαν. Peter compares the Prophetic writings to a lamp shining in a dark place. But Acts 8. v. 35. Philip explains the Prophecy of Isaiah to the Eunuch of Queen Candace. In the same place v. 31. The Eunuch, being asked whether he understands what he has read in Isaiah, replies. How can I, unless someone shows me.

Resp. 1. That prophecy of Isaiah concerning the passion of Christ, which the Eunuch was reading, is sufficiently perspicuous, but the mind of the Eunuch was fascinated by a preconceived opinion about an earthly kingdom of Christ, whence by accident that Prophetic prophecy was obscure to him. 2. None of us says that the Scriptures, especially the Prophetic ones, are so perspicuous in all places that the means of interpretation are to be removed, or that there is no use for Ecclesiastical Ministry in interpreting the Scriptures. 3. Nor does it follow. Some Prophetic oracle was obscure to the proselyte Eunuch. Therefore, the whole Prophetic Scripture is commonly obscure to everyone.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Peter, whom the Papists wish to have been the Monarch of the Church, no one doubts, commits the judgment of his doctrine to his hearers, so that they may judge concerning it from the writings of the Prophets. Therefore, the Pope, who boasts that he is the successor of Peter, should not take it ill if we wish to pass judgment on his doctrine from the Prophetic and Apostolic writings. The example of Paul is conformable, Acts 17. v. 11. 1. Cor. 10. v. 15.

2. Peter calls the word of the Prophets more firm by his preaching and testimony. Therefore, the testimony of the Scriptures is far firmer than the testimony of the Church, nay rather, the testimony of the Church relies solely upon the testimony of Scripture. The connection is proven, because if the Prophetic Scripture was firmer than the testimony of Peter, then speaking with a living voice, it will be much firmer than the testimony of other Doctors of the Church, whom they understand by the name of the Church, since they do not rise to the pinnacle of Apostolic dignity. Gretser objects in tom. 1. Defens. Bell. pag. 1908. that Peter calls the Prophetic discourse firmer, either by putting the comparative for the positive, or by calling it firmer not absolutely, but with respect to the hearers, who, on account of the opinion of antiquity and holiness, more willingly had faith in the ancient Prophets than in the Apostles living at that time.

Resp. 1. Gretser says that that substitution of the comparative for the positive is not infrequent in the sacred letters, but we oppose to him the words of Estius in his commentary on this place, opposed to Erasmus who asserted the same thing. Erasmus ought to have shown (Gretser) by examples that which he says, especially those sought from Holy Scripture, which would certainly be difficult for him. 2. The latter exposition of Gretser supports us. For we conclude from the greater to the less in this way. If Peter the Apostle, who was endowed with the gift of infallibility, did not hesitate to call the Prophetic discourse firmer than his own testimony, how much more must the Prophetic and Apostolic discourse be established as firmer than the testimony of the Church, concerning which it is not yet certain that it is absolutely and simply infallible? 3. Therefore, even if it were most true what Gretser asserts, that the testimony of the Church is not merely human, or human divinely inspired, but divine by participation and in itself entirely infallible, nevertheless our argument would remain unmoved, that those who doubt concerning this infallibility of the Church can and ought to judge concerning the testimony of the Church from the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, concerning whose infallibility they are certain.

3. Peter commends the study of the Scriptures. This must be opposed to the Gnosimachi, of whom Damascenus makes mention in his book on heresies, that they taught that labor concerning the knowledge of the Scriptures is vain, and that God requires only good actions; to Muntzer and the Anabaptists, who sent men away to peculiar divine revelations, from whose order was Hermann Riswich, who called Scripture foolish, the Bible fictitious, the Gospel delirious; to Swencfeld, who asserted that the study of the Scriptures is vain and empty, because Scripture is a creature, nor does it befit one to be too addicted to Scripture.

4. Peter says that those to whom he writes do well and rightly consult their own salvation, because they attend to the prophetic word. But among those to whom he writes, there were also laymen, as they are called. Therefore, laymen also are to be exhorted to the reading and study of the Scriptures. Matt. 5. v. 15. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house. But Holy Scripture, as Peter teaches, is a lamp. Therefore, in the Church, which is the house of God, 1. Tim. 3. v. 15. it must be placed upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all. The use of a lamp ought to be common to all who are in the house. Therefore, the use of Scripture also ought to be granted to all who are in the Church. Peter praises the faithful to whom he writes on this account, that they attend to the prophetic Scripture. Those who today boast themselves to be successors of Peter in the Apostolic see disapprove of the reading of Scripture among the faithful. Yet the force of truth extorted this from Benedictus Justinianus, that in his explanation of Rom. 15. v. 4. he acknowledged that CHRIST John 5. vers. 39. and Peter by these words provoke their hearers to turn over the Scriptures.

1. Stapleton objects in his Antidote, Peter's words command to attend to the Scriptures. But this is done, not only when the Scriptures are read, but much more and more safely, when they are explained by the voice of the preaching Church. Resp. 1. We invert the argument. Peter commands to attend to the Scriptures. But that is done, not only when the prophetic Scriptures are explained by the voice of the preaching Church, but also when they are read by the faithful. Therefore, the Apostle also commends the reading of the Scriptures. 2. The following words, knowing this first, that no prophecy is of private interpretation, show that the Apostle is speaking about the reading of prophetic Scripture. The Ordinary Gloss from Bede on the passage: Just as the prophets wrote not their own words, but GOD'S: so the reader ought not to use his own interpretation, lest he deviate from the faith, but should labor to attend to how He who wrote wished His words to be understood. 3. The explanation of the Church is not λόγος προφητικὸς, but λόγου προφητικοῦ ἐπίλυσις.. But Peter commands to attend to the prophetic word. Therefore, he urges the reading of the prophetic text itself. 4. When the public Ministry is corrupt, it is safer that the Scriptures be read than that one attends to the exposition of Doctors.

2. Estius objects, it is not denied by the Papists that those faithful are to be exhorted to the study and reading of the Scriptures, for whom it is expedient, that the Scriptures Let Pastors and Prelates judge, otherwise it is established by the most certain experience, that there are very many for whom it is not expedient for various reasons. Resp. 1. Estius commits the fallacy of the accident. It is to be attributed not to the reading of the Scriptures itself, but to the vice and abuse of the reading, that for some that reading is not expedient, but because of the abuse the true use is not to be abolished. 2. We therefore urge Estius in this way. Those who wrote for the use of all, their writings are also to be read by all. The Prophets and Apostles, as they preached to all, so also wrote for the use of all. Therefore their writings are to be read by all. Those who are bound by divine command to read the Scriptures, they both can and ought to read the Scriptures without the prior concession of a Bishop. But all men whatsoever are invited and bound to read the Scriptures. Deut. 6. v. 8. & following cap. 31. v. 11. & following Esai. 34. v. 16.Ioh. 5. v. 39.Col. 3. v. 16.cap. 4. v. 16.1. Thess. 5. v. 27. Therefore all men whatsoever can and ought to read the Scriptures without the prior concession of a Bishop. That which can wholesomely instruct the Laity, supply them with life-giving consolation, correct the vices of morals in them, arm them against Satan, and make them wise unto eternal life, from that no one of the Laity is to be barred, but rather invited to it. The reading of Holy Scripture can provide all these things to the Laity. Iohan. 5. v. 39.cap. 20. v. 31.Rom. 15. v. 4.Eph 6. v. 17.2. Tim. 3. v. 15. & following. Therefore from the reading of Scripture no one of the Laity is to be barred, but rather invited to it. 3. Finally, we urge the confession of Bellarmine lib. 1. de verbo DEI cap. 2. in the beginning. Moses, the Prophets, Christ, John and the Apostles certainly exhorted others to read the Scriptures. He could have said, they exhorted all, for the sayings of Scripture brought forward by Bellarmine prove that.

5. Peter calls the writings of the O. T. the Prophetic word. From it we form such an argument. Every Canonical book of the O. T. is a Prophetic word i. e. written by a Prophet from the impulse and inspiration of the Holy Spirit. But those books of the O. T. about which there is controversy between us and the Papists, that they might belong to the canon, do not contain the Prophetic word i. e. they are not written by Prophets from the impulse and inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Therefore they are not Canonical books. The major is proved not only from this Apostolic place, but also from other sayings of Scripture. Luc. 16. v. 29.cap. 24. v. 27. & 44.Act. 3. v. 23.

Rom. 16. v. 26.Eph. 2. v. 20.Hebr. 1. v. 1. The minor premise is established from the consideration of time. For all those disputed books were written after the times of Malachi, who was the last Prophet of the O. T., as witnessed by Jerome in book 13 on Isaiah chapter 49, Augustine in book 17 of the City of God chapter 24, etc.

6. Peter compares Prophetic Scripture to a lamp shining in a dark place, from which we form such an argument. Whatever is compared to a lamp shining in a dark place, that is clear and perspicuous. Prophetic Scripture is compared to a lamp shining in a dark place. Therefore, Prophetic Scripture is clear and perspicuous. Moreover, what Peter asserts concerning Prophetic Scripture, the same must also be accepted much more concerning the Apostolic Scripture of the N. T. For those things which were proposed more obscurely in the O. T., those were manifested more clearly in the N. T. after a clearer light had arrived. And just as the Scripture of the O. T. is compared to a lamp Psalm. 119. v. 105.Prov. 6. v. 23. so also the Apostolic Scripture of the N. T. can likewise be compared to a light, because Matth. 5. v. 14. the Apostles are called the light of the world by reason of their doctrine, first indeed preached by living voice, but afterwards by the will of GOD reduced into Scriptures, and Paul explicitly says 2. Cor. 4. v. 3. If our Gospel is hidden, it is hidden in those who are perishing, in whom the god of this world has blinded the eyes of the unbelievers, so that the illumination of the glory of Christ might not shine upon them. That which is obscure and hidden only by accident, that is perspicuous in itself. The Gospel first preached by the Apostles by living voice, but afterwards by the will of God reduced into Scriptures, is obscure and hidden only by accident. Therefore, it is perspicuous in itself.

Bellarmino objects 1. in book 3 of the Word of God chapter 2, in response to the 4th argument, that the voices of the Prophets are called a lamp, not because they are easily understood, but because when understood they illuminate and show the way to Christ, who is the true Sun of justice. In the same way Lorinus in his commentary on this passage, Heretics have nothing from this to prove that the Scriptures are clear and easy in themselves, but only that if they are understood, they illuminate and show the way to Christ, who is the true Sun of justice. I respond 1. by this reasoning Scripture would not be perspicuous in itself, but only by accident, and it would not be compared to a lamp, and indeed a shining one in a place , in itself, but because of something else, namely because of the light of interpretation to be brought to it by the Church. But that which is perspicuous only by accident and because of something else cannot be called a lamp, and indeed one shining in a place dark. 2. Whatever is lucid in such a way that it illuminates and illustrates other things, that thing has light inherent in it, nor does it need to be illuminated by an alien light, or to receive and borrow light from another. But Scripture is said to be lucid in such a way that it illuminates other things, for Peter commands to attend to the prophetic word that is, to the writings of the Prophets as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns. Psal. 19. v. 9. The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes.

2. Iacob. Gretserus tom. 1. Defens. pag. 1146. repeats Bellarmine's exception, that Scripture then at last shows its light and clarity to men, if a legitimate interpretation is added, just as Metaphysics also shows its clarity to listeners, if an Interpreter is added. Afterwards he adds. Those gross innovators seem to reason about Scripture in all things, just as about the Sun or a lamp lit in some room, for he who has eyes, and does not deliberately turn his face away, can immediately behold both that, and this: thus they seem to think about Scripture, as if whoever looks at and reads it, is immediately illuminated by its rays, which is far otherwise, since it is a sealed book, and therefore to be unsealed through interpretation; a covered Sun, and therefore to be unfolded through explanation, so that it may be able to emit its brightness; a covered lamp, whose cover must be removed through explanation, so that it may be able to dispel the darkness. Resp. 1. We do not exclude interpretation. But the question is, whether it is to be brought in from the outside, or truly to be drawn out from Scripture itself. Gretserus wants the former, who asserts that the interpretation of Scripture is to be sought from the Church, we assert the latter, and we prove it from this very Apostolic passage, in which Scripture is compared to a lamp, which certainly has light inherent in it, nor does it need an alien and extrinsic light. 2. If no other perspicuity of Scripture is given, than that which is of Metaphysics, having been previously expounded by an Interpreter, then Scripture is not clear in itself, but by accident, nor can it be compared to a shining lamp, but to a lamp still to be lit. 3. If Scripture is called a lamp, because when it has been understood, it illuminates the mind, shall we say of tradition, that it has this peculiar thing over the Scriptures, that it illuminates even when not understood? But if therefore this is also required for tradition, that it be understood, if it is to illuminate the mind, certainly this very thing detracts nothing from the light of Scripture, that its understanding is required, so that it may be able to perform the office of illumination.

4. If there is no other clarity of Scripture than that, when it has been understood, it illuminates, it would follow that there is no greater light of Scripture than that of the most obscure Delphic oracles. For when those have been understood, they likewise illuminate, and yet they are not called lucid, but obscure. Therefore, that which, when understood, that is, explained from elsewhere, illuminates, cannot be called lucid. 5. There is, therefore, an ambiguity in the phrase, Scripture understood illuminates. For this is said either in the sense that the understanding of the words of Scripture is required; or that an explanation must first be brought to it from elsewhere. We concede the former, but this does not remove the perspicuity of Scripture; the latter removes the perspicuity of Scripture, but assumes what is false. 6. We cannot, nor ought we, think otherwise of Scripture than of a lamp shining in a room, the light of which all can behold who are not blind, nor turn their face away on purpose. For thus Peter taught us, when he called Scripture a lamp shining in a dark place. 7. For although certain places in the Scriptures are given as more obscure, those nevertheless either derive light from other clear and perspicuous sayings, or can be ignored without danger to salvation. August. lib. 2. de doctr. Christi cap. 6. Almost nothing is extracted from those obscurities which is not found stated most clearly elsewhere. lib. eiusd. cap. 9. In those things which are openly placed in the Scriptures, all things are found which contain faith and the morals of living. 8. Scripture is not a sealed book except to despisers Esai. 29. v. 11. upon whose eyes a veil is placed, 2. Cor. 3. v. 13. & seqq. whose eyes the god of this world has blinded, cap. 4. v. 3. in itself truly and by itself it is an open book Apoc. 5. v. 5. a shining lamp, as it is called in this place, a Sun shining most splendidly. Clemens Alexandrin. in protrept. p. 29. The word is hidden from none, it is a light common to all, it shines upon all. There is no Cimmerian darkness in the words, no shadows. The Word is the Sun of the soul, which if it has risen in the depth of the mind, its eye also is illuminated.

3. Cornelius â Lapide objects in various ways.

Firstly, that a lamp signifies a nocturnal light, and therefore an obscure one. Resp. Peter speaks specifically of the Prophetic writings, which, when a comparison is made to the light of the N. T., had a more obscure light, but in the N. T. the clearer light of the Morning Star and of the day has arrived.

Secondly, that Peter properly calls the Prophetic [word] a lamp, but it is agreed that this is obscure. Resp. Prophecies derive light from their fulfillment, which is described in the N. Nor can it be said of all the prophecies of the Old Testament that they are obscure; certainly in most of them very clear predictions about the Messiah exist.

Thirdly, that this lamp is said to shine in a dark place. Therefore, by the place it is reflected and dulled, and it itself becomes dark, so that it illuminates nothing except what is near, and that moderately and somewhat obscurely. Response: The darkness of the place into which a lamp is brought does not diminish the light of the lamp, but rather is scattered and dispelled by it.

Fourthly, that Scripture is a lamp, but placed upon the candlestick of the public and infallible authority of the Church, not under the bushel of a private man, as Ambrose writes in book 7 on Luke, chapter 52. The same is urged by Lorinus in his commentary on this passage. Response: The seventh book of the commentaries of Ambrose on Luke reaches only as far as chapter 16. The words of Ambrose on chapter 11 of Luke are as follows: Because in the preceding he preferred the Church to the Synagogue, he exhorts us that we should rather transfer our faith to the Church, etc. The Word of God is light, faith is a lamp, etc. Let no one place faith under the law. For the law is within measure, grace is beyond measure. The law overshadows, grace clarifies. And therefore let no one include his faith within the measure of the law, but let him confer it to the Church, etc. There is nothing here about the infallible authority of the Church, nothing about the bushel of the private Spirit. Meanwhile, we willingly concede that the light of the Word is to be placed on the candlestick of the Church, and that the Scriptures are not to be expounded by private judgment, but that its genuine sense is to be drawn from Scripture itself.

Fifthly, just as oil must frequently be supplied to a lamp so that it may shine: so a learned and pious explanation must be inserted into the Holy Scriptures by Doctors, so that it may breathe the light of doctrine and the warmth of devotion into the hearers. Response: This explanation of the Doctors ought not to be brought into Scripture, since it is in no way in need of an alien and adventitious light, but it ought to be drawn from Scripture itself. Therefore, Cornelius ignorantly attributes to Bishops and the Pope the same authority and infallibility of interpreting as to the Apostles.

7. Peter says that those to whom he writes do well, because they attend to the prophetic word, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns. Therefore, he sends them back to the prophetic Scripture as the unique rule of faith and divine worship. For without doubt, as a mutual comparison shows, the Apostle points his finger to the prophetic passage Isa. 8, v. 20. To the law and to the testimony, if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. On which words Jerome comments thus. If you wish to know what is doubtful, rather entrust yourselves to the law and to the testimonies of the Scriptures. But if your congregation does not wish to seek the word of the Lord, it will not have the light of truth, but will be turned about in the darkness of errors. Therefore, just as in that Prophetic passage the hearers are sent back to the law and to the testimony, that is, to the word, which is the testimony of the divine will, Psalm 19. v. 8. Psalm 78. v. 5. Isaiah 5. v. 16. as to the unique rule of faith and divine worship: so Peter does the same in this place, and asserts that those who diligently attend to the Prophetic word set forth in the sacred Scriptures, as to a lamp showing the way in the gloom of this life, obtain from it the light of saving θεογνωσίας unto eternal life. Genebrardus on Psalm 119, upon the words: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. The word of GOD is light, a lamp, a luminary, because it directs toward God in things to be done, believed, hoped for, and loved, and provides guidance, lest we stumble anywhere and slip in the darkness of this life, and lest we wander from that way which leads to the blessed life; for it is the rule of faith and life, showing the way in the darkness of the world to eternal life. Guillaudus on this passage: As a lamp placed in a dark place opens the way for those passing by, lest they strike against something: so Scripture, read with an attentive and faithful mind, opens the way of truth to readers, lest they strike against anything anywhere that might lead them away from the truth, and turns them away from the thorny byways of heretics. Gretser objects in Vol. 1 of his defense of Bellarmine, page 1794: that the Prophetic word extends more broadly than the Prophetic Scripture. I reply: At the time when Peter wrote these things, there was no other Prophetic word than the written one. No prophets were any longer extant preaching with a living voice, as in the time of the Old Testament, but their prophecies were read in the Canon of Scripture. Augustine, sermon 237 de temp.: We walk by the lamp of Scripture, just as the Apostle Peter says, we have a more firm Prophetic word. In the same way, namely concerning Prophetic Scripture, Cajetan, Salmero, Gagnaeius, Lorinus, Estius, etc., accept this Apostolic passage.

8. If the Prophets wrote while impelled and moved by the Holy Spirit, they certainly did not err, nor could they have erred, even in the slightest. Therefore, it is false that Albert Pighius, Cardinal, Erasmus, Socinus, etc., attribute a lapse of memory to them. Cornelius à Lapide writes correctly on this passage: Although the Prophets and the other writers of Holy Scripture knew some of the things which they write naturally, for instance, because they had seen or heard them, as when they write the histories of their own time, nevertheless in those very things they were incited by the Holy Spirit to write them, and that in that manner and way which the Holy Spirit wished, who therefore assisted them, so that they would not err even in a point: for as St. Augustine says in Epistle 8. to Jerome. Faith will totter, if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers. Anselm on 2 Tim. 3. Those Scriptures hold the citadel of authority, which have been brought forth by the Spirit of GOD, which are also called Canonical.

9. When Peter says, that holy men of GOD spoke, being impelled and inspired by the Holy Spirit, he also includes their writing at the same time, since that also is θεόπνευστος 2. Timoth. 3. vers. 16. It is therefore false, what the Papists say, that Scripture is a mute judge, and cannot say who is the true sense &c. I note here an excellent confession of Lorinus, commenting on this passage thus. Holy men of GOD are said here to have spoken being inspired by the Holy Spirit, by the word of speaking comprehending also the writing &c. hence the holy books are called the oracles of GOD, Rom. 3. v, 2. &c. hence it is, that Christ citing David says, Matth. 22. vers. 44. that he spoke in the Spirit, and that Isaiah prophesied well, Matth. 15. vers. 7. Paul however Rom. 9. vers. 17. reports that Scripture said to Pharaoh, what it is established that GOD said Exod. 9. vers. 16. He also writes that GOD spoke to the Fathers in the Prophets, who afterwards in the Son Hebr. 1. vers. 1. Likewise through Isaiah, Acts last. vers. 25. and again through the mouth of David, the Apostles assert Act. 4. v. 25. and he himself, who previously was speaking (in the Prophets) says of himself, because I myself who was speaking, behold I am present, Esai. 52. v. 6. namely the Son of GOD, then made man. All these things Lorinus.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Lorinus on v. 19. comments thus. From these things it can be gathered, that the Scriptures had not been corrupted then (in the times of the Apostles) by the Jews, indeed for the space of two thousand years. Philo in the book on the departure from Egypt, whom Eusebius cites book 8. on preparation chap. 2. is a witness, that nothing in them has been changed, and the same Eusebius says, that the Jews would have preferred to die a thousand times, rather than to invert even a tittle, and worshipped the Bible as if it were God. That they may have done so afterwards out of hatred for Christians, can hardly be denied, with so many Fathers affirming it.

Resp. 1. The testimonies, which are brought forward by Christ and the Apostles from the Old Testament into the New, are still read today in the sources in the same way in which they were brought forward by them. Therefore the Hebrew sources have not been corrupted by the malice of the Jews.

2. The Jews neither wished, nor were they able to corrupt the sources. He confirms the former, both by their own religion toward the sacred books, which Lorinus himself acknowledges, which in the progress of time has not been changed in them, and by the integrity of the principal testimonies concerning Christ. For if the Jews had wished to corrupt the divine Scriptures in hatred of the Christians, they would have either removed or changed the principal prophecies concerning Christ: but they are so far from having done this, that stronger arguments can be brought forth against them from the Hebrew text than from the Latin version. He confirms the latter, both by their dispersion throughout the whole world, and by the diligent caution of the Christians, and by the multitude of Biblical copies, and by the variety of versions. 3. To the sayings of the Fathers, namely Justin, Origen, Chrysostom, Eusebius, Jerome, Bellarmine responds in book 2 of the word of GOD, chapter 2. That Justin and Eusebius nowhere wrote that the Hebrew text was corrupted by the Hebrews, but the Greek text of the LXX Interpreters; that Origen likewise speaks of the corruption of the Septuagint version; that Chrysostom speaks of the Jewish Interpreters, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion; that Jerome in the cited places is in doubt, but in the commentaries on Isaiah, which he wrote later, openly laughs at those who think that the Hebrew Codices have been falsified. 4. In the same chapter Bellarmine attacks that insipid opinion of Lorinus, Gordon Huntlaeus, and certain other Papists with these arguments. First, that the Hebrews neither before, nor after the coming of Christ corrupted the Scriptures. Second, that it is not credible that the Jews wished to snatch the truth from their Codices, so that they might detract from the authority of ours, and even if they had wished this most of all, they could not have done so in such many and so far and widely dispersed Codices. Third, that the incredible religion of the Jews toward the sacred books does not permit one to believe this. Fourth, if the Jews had wished to falsify the Sacred Scriptures in hatred of the Christians, without a doubt they would have removed the principal prophecies, but they did not do this in the least, since the Hebrew Codices sometimes vex the Jews more than the Greek or Latin ones. Fifth, it is not likely that GOD would have allowed the words of so many illustrious Prophets to be generally falsified; especially since for this end He dispersed the Jews throughout the whole world and wished them to carry around the books of the law and the Prophets, so that as enemies they might provide testimony to the Christian faith.

2. The same Lorinus annotates on the same verse thus. By the rising of Lucifer is indicated the more imperfect knowledge of this life, which however great it may be, can take increases, etc. The Church itself makes progress, which from time to time through councils and Pontiffs declares and proposes things to be believed that were obscure, the Holy Spirit, just as Christ had promisedJohn 16. v. 12.not being able to carry and grasp all things at once, teaching and suggesting all things which He leads to be necessary for the circumstances. Resp. 1. The Church today is not governed by new revelations, nor are new articles of faith handed down to it by the Holy Spirit, but it is content with its own limits, namely the Holy Scriptures. Our faith, says Thomas part. 1. q. 1. art. 8. relies on the revelation made to the Prophets and Apostles, who wrote the Canonical books, but not on revelations which were made to other Doctors. The same in the Supplement part. 3. q. 6. art. 6. Because the Church is founded on faith and on the Sacraments, therefore it does not pertain to the Ministers of the Church to publish new articles of faith, or to remove those published, or to institute new Sacraments, or to remove those instituted, but this belongs to the power and excellence which is owed to Christ alone, who is the foundation of the Church. 2. Neither to Councils nor to Pontiffs does αὐτοκρατορικὴ power and simple infallibility in the interpretation of Scripture belong, but they are bound to expound the sacred Scriptures from the Scriptures. 3. The Holy Spirit does not suggest other or new things, but the same things which Christ taught, and which were noted down through the Apostles in the Scriptures from the mouth of Christ.

3. Estius on v. 20 notes, the name of Prophecy in the sacred letters does not signify Prophetic Scripture or a Prophetic oracle, which is written or brought forth, but the Prophetic prediction itself, or even the sacred exposition of Prophetic Scripture and of the divine word altogether. Resp. the places from Apoc. 1. v. 3.chap. 22. v. 7.10.18. and 19. brought forward above testify to the contrary.

4. Calvin ἐπίλυσιν in the same verse translates impulse or inspiration, as if it were written πᾶσα προφητεία ἰδίας ἐπηλύσεως οὐκ ἔστι. In the same way Hemmingius in his commentary on this place ἐπίλυσις here does not signify interpretation, but impetus and impulse. Although this opinion pleases Beza vehemently, he nevertheless warns. 1. Nowhere in the Greek Codices ἐπήλυσιν is η found. 2. The name ἐπιλήσεως is Poetic. And yet for these reasons the Calvinists ought rather to have repudiated that novelty. 3. Add that by this reasoning Peter would say the same thing in verse 20, which he says in the verse 21, following. 4. Ἐπίλυσιν written with an iota signifies among the Greeks impetus or impulse Hemmingius he does not confirm it with any suitable example, nor do I think it can be confirmed.

5. Bede in his commentary on verse 21 refutes the insipid opinion of those who maintain that the Holy Spirit so acted upon and impelled the holy men of GOD that they did not understand what they were saying, nor did they have it in their power not to speak. Ridiculously, he says, someone has interpreted these words of blessed Peter, saying that just as a pipe receives the breath of a human mouth in order to resound, yet does not itself understand the sound which it provides, because it is of an insensible nature: so the Prophets, inspired by the Spirit of GOD, would bring forth with their mouths those things which the same Spirit willed, yet they would not hold in their own minds the things which they were saying, according to that saying of Maro, 'It gives forth a sound without a mind,' which it is clearly evident is of a most impudent error. For how would they give such sound counsels for living to those who were listening, if they themselves, being in their right minds, did not know what they were saying? For what reason are the Prophets called seers? By what logic is it written, 'the word which Isaiah saw,' or any other Prophet, unless it is because in the secret place of heavenly visions, they knew with a most lucid intuition of the mind the mysteries which they would bring forth openly to their hearers in whatever words they might?

6. Estius on the same verse annotates thus. The opinion of Peter lashes heretics and all those who, with contempt or neglect of the sense of the Church, to which Christ promised His Spirit, bring their own private senses or those of their masters to interpret the Scriptures. And afterwards. Peter sets out to prove that prophecies are not to be interpreted by private sense and judgment, but that which he leaves to be understood is that in their interpretation one must always look to the sense of the Church, which has the Spirit of GOD. For certainly they are to be interpreted by the same Spirit by which they were written and brought to us, that is, by the divine Spirit, which Christ promised to His Church. Similar things occur among other Papists. Salmero on this passage: Among the proud, the contumacious, and the arrogant, such as are the heretics rising up against the Catholic Church, who lack the Spirit of GOD, the true interpretation of the Scriptures is not, nor can it in any way be. Lorinus on this passage. Catholics establish certain judges and interpreters of Scripture, namely a Council of Bishops approved by the Pontiff, or the Pontiff himself, whose it is to open such things by the key of knowledge which he bears. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. From this passage is refuted the error of our Gnostics and Illuminati, who say that Scripture is to be interpreted by everyone by their own private spirit, etc. Scripture It is not a private, but a public dogma, handed down by GOD to the whole Church; therefore it is not to be explained by the private spirit of any individual, but by the common and public spirit of the Church and of the Holy Spirit assisting her. It is for the Church to judge concerning the true sense and interpretation of Scripture, as the Council of Trent says, session 4. By the Church, understand the Presidents of the Church, namely the Bishops and especially the supreme Pontiff.

Resp. 1. We concede, and from this very Apostolic passage we likewise teach, that the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures (of which, in this part, the reason is the same, as Estius rightly advises) must be interpreted by the same Spirit by which they were written, that is, by the divine Spirit, and therefore that prophecy does not admit of a private interpretation, sought from the judgment of human reason, but that every legitimate and solid interpretation of Scripture ought to be established according to the sense of the Holy Spirit, since He is the principal author of Scripture, and consequently also its highest and authentic Interpreter. 2. As Scriptures composed by natural light need the light of Nature in order to be understood: so Prophetic Scriptures, being composed by supernatural light and sent to us, must be interpreted and understood by divine light. Bernard in the Epistle to the brothers of the mount of GOD. By the Spirit that the Scriptures were made, by that Spirit they desire to be read, and by Him also they are to be understood. 3. It is fair that, from where the law proceeded, the interpretation should also proceed, according to the Canon Law, l. c. Inter alia §. ut igitur de sent. excomm. where the Gloss says: To whom the constitution of the law pertains, to him also pertains the interpretation. And Just as it is granted to the Emperor alone to establish laws, and therefore it is fitting that it be worthy of the imperial power alone to interpret laws, according to the Civil Law, L. Si imperialis C. de legibus: so it is much more the right of Him alone to interpret Scripture authentically, by whom it was first handed down. 4. Hence Bellarmine, book 3, de verbo DEI chapter 3, §. Convenit &c. writes thus: It is agreed between us and the Adversaries that the Scriptures ought to be understood by the same Spirit by which they were made, that is, by the Holy Spirit; which the Apostle Peter teaches in his 2nd Epistle, chapter 1. Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the Scripture is of any private interpretation &c. where Blessed Peter proves that the Scriptures ought not to be expounded from one's own ingenuity, but according to the dictation of the Holy Spirit, because they were not written by human ingenuity, but by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. 4. But the whole question is, where that sense and that interpretation of the Holy Spirit is to be sought?

We say that that is the sense of the Holy Spirit, which is gathered from the words of Scripture taken in their native and proper signification, and which agrees with the scope of each passage. Likewise with the antecedents and consequents, and which does not fight with the analogy of faith, that is, the perpetual and constant opinion of Scripture, delivered in clear and perspicuous passages concerning individual articles of faith, and therefore we say that Scripture is to be interpreted by Scripture: which thing Bellarmine in that very book and chapter in a way acknowledges, when in §. But although etc. he writes thus. That sense, which is gathered immediately from the words of Scripture, it is certain, is the sense of the Holy Spirit. But if therefore we can gather the sense immediately from the words of Scripture, as we can, certainly we can also gather the sense of the Holy Spirit from them.

6. The Papists, however, send us back to the Church, and assert that the infallible interpretation of Holy Scripture must be sought solely from it. But what they wish to be understood by the name of the Church is not clear to everyone at the very first glance. For if they wish to understand the Fathers of the Church, we oppose to them the fact that they themselves depart from the common exposition of the Fathers in many things, as can be demonstrated to many even from the single Maldonado. If they send us off to Councils, not all texts of Scripture are expounded in them. If they send us off to Bishops addicted to the Roman See, they do not possess the gift of infallibility, and very many of them are destitute of the requirements necessary for the interpretation of Scripture, nay more, with the Papists themselves admitting it, Bishops are not to be heard, except insofar as they agree with the Roman Pontiff, the Bishop of Bishops. 7. Finally, therefore, after long detours, they send us back to the Roman Pontiff, and contend that the gift of interpretation is so bound to the Roman Papal see that he who presides in it is to be considered to have all divine and human laws in the cabinet of his breast, and not to be able to err in the interpretation of Scripture. But that authentic Interpreter has not yet published an exposition of all and individual passages of Scripture that come into controversy, nor is access to him always open to everyone, so that his opinion may be asked concerning any passage of Scripture. 8. Add that it has not yet been confirmed by suitable arguments that the Roman Pontiffs are infallible judges of controversies and authentic Interpreters of Scripture; which many of them are destitute of the gift of interpretation; because we are nowhere in the Scriptures sent away to this chest of the Papal breast for this; because the interpretations of the Pontiffs are very often absurd, erroneous, foreign, etc. 9. ἰδία ἐπίλυσις in this place of the Apostle does not signify the private and proper industry of each Christian, and the sincere study in eliciting the sense of Scripture from Scripture itself, but a private sense, which anyone fashions for himself at will and imposes it upon Scripture. We admit the former, but we reject the latter. 10. Bellarmine therefore burdens us with calumny when he attributes to us in the said place, that we remit men to the private spirit of each one in the exposition of Scripture. If some private person judges concerning a certain controversy of religion from clear and perspicuous places of Scripture, this does not proceed from a private spirit, but is the public judgment of the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures. Conversely, if a person even constituted in the public Ministry of the Church brings forth something beyond and outside of Scripture, this is, having proceeded from a private Spirit, even if he be the Pope himself, or some highest Bishop. Whence Gerson, Panormitanus, Picus Mirandula, rightly say, the opinion of one private person is to be preferred to the definition of the Pope, if the opinion of the former relies on better reasons than the decision of the latter. 11. The matter therefore returns to this, Every legitimate and solid interpretation of Scripture ought to proceed from the Holy Spirit, from whom Scripture first came forth. Therefore either from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, or from Scripture itself. But the former, as being extraordinary, has long since ceased in the Church, and the Church has long since bidden farewell to prophecies with the Paraclete of Montanus τῶν ἐνθουσιασθῶν. There remains therefore the latter, which is the ordinary way of interpretation.

7. Lorinus on the same verse comments thus. That which the Apostle says without exception, every prophecy of Scripture is not made by private interpretation, snatches from heretics the escape of saying. Although this or that place of Scripture may be obscure and difficult in itself, it can be understood and expounded with easy effort by the collation of other places, and Scripture can be perceived certainly and infallibly from Scripture in controversial questions. The certain, infallible intelligence of any place, and to which all are bound to assent, demands in the Church a common authority, through which the Holy Spirit may speak commonly, and teach all. Resp. 1. When the sense of Scripture is from Scripture itself, namely from the series of antecedents and consequents, From the scope, from the original text, and from the collation of parallel passages, it is elicited that this is not ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, but the exposition of the Holy Spirit Himself. 2. Lorinus attributes that common authority in the Church to the Roman Pontiff; Until, he says, the approval of the supreme Pastor is added, any interpretation whatsoever does not create faith. But he is destitute of the promise concerning infallibility and the means of legitimate interpretation. 3. To the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scriptures and through the Scriptures, and informing us through the clearer passages of Scripture, and exercising us through the more obscure ones, that common authority of infallible exposition, which all are bound to acknowledge, belongs uniquely and entirely. 4. The Holy Spirit does not speak to us through the Pontiff, except insofar as the Pontiff brings forth those things which are conformable to the Holy Scriptures, because Scripture is the voice of the Holy Spirit, from which whatever departs or disagrees cannot be held as the doctrine and speech of the Holy Spirit. 5. It is not yet agreed among the Papists whether that common authority of infallible exposition resides with the Pontiff or with an ecumenical Council. For those who establish that a Council is above the Pope seek that authority not in the Pontiff, but in the Council.

Observations. 1. To Scripture is attributed βεβαιότης firmness, not only in itself, but also ἐνεργητικῶς effectively, because it can make us firm in the true knowledge of GOD and in faith Luc. 1. v. 3. It seemed good to me also, having followed all things from the beginning diligently in order, to write to thee v. 4. that thou mightest know the certainty of those words, wherein thou hast been instructed, ἀσφάλειαν Phil. 3. vers. 1. To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not wearisome, but for you ἀσφαλὲς, it makes you firm and safe.

2. To Scripture is also attributed λαμπρότης clarity and perspicuity, not only in itself, but also ἐνεργητικῶς effectively, because it is compared to a lamp shining in a dark place. Psal. 19. v. 9. The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. 2. Cor. 3. v. 6. As in the article of creation God produced light through His word: so in the article of sanctification He kindles spiritual light in our hearts through His word.

3. August. tract. 23. in Iohann. All Prophecy is one great lamp to CHRIST. We use Scripture as the ministry of a lamp, until Christ the true Sun of righteousness shines upon our hearts.

4. The Prophetic writings are a lamp; the preaching of the Gospel and the Apostolic writings are the dawn and the Morning Star; the beatific vision of GOD in eternal life is the noon.

5. Lactantius book 5 of the Institutes, chapter 3, advises, not only for this reason is Christ believed by us to be God, because He performed miracles, but also because we have seen that all things have been fulfilled in Him which were announced to us by the prophecy of the Prophets. Thence the Apostles so often appeal to the testimonies of the Prophets concerning Christ. Acts 3. verse 18.21.chapter 10. verse 43. To this end is applied by some the passage Apoc. 19. v. 10. The testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of prophecy.

6. Humbertus of Le Mans, Bishop of Silva Candida, in his book on unleavened bread. With the O. T. deleted, the new will vanish and will be thought a fable entirely, nor will it be able to be retained without its character, since neither will a wall stand without a foundation, which the Lord Himself placed under His deeds and words and inspired in His Apostles, His preachers, so that He might secure the course of His narrative with the anchor of the N. Testament.

7. The knowledge of Christ in this life has its own increments. For just as the morning star and the day itself succeed the lamp shining in a dark place: so the pious daily progress in the true and saving knowledge of Christ, if they diligently attend to the Prophetic and Apostolic writings.

8. The Prophet & (of whom there is an equal reason in this part) the Evangelists & Apostles wrote by divine impulse, Their tongue was the pen of a scribe writing quickly, Ps. 45. v. 2. i. e. of the Holy Spirit speaking and writing through them. Cypr. sermon on Almsgiving The H. Spirit was the Scribe, the Prophets were His pens, to whom the H. Spirit dictated the things to be written. Therefore also Zechariah Luke 1. v. 70. attributes one mouth to them, because they spoke and wrote impelled by one Spirit.

9. Origen homily 2 on Exodus The sacred volumes breathe with the fullness of the Spirit, and there is nothing, whether in prophecy or in the law, or in the Gospel, or in the Apostle, which does not descend from the fullness of the divine majesty. Chrysost. homily 21 on Genesis beseeches, that we do not simply accept those things which are contained in sacred Scripture, since they have many riches of meanings, since they were dictated by the Holy Spirit, and there is not a syllable or article in the sacred letters in whose depth there is not a huge treasure.

10. Bede in this place Just as the Prophets wrote not their own, but God's words: so also their reader cannot use his own private interpretation, lest he deviate from the sense of truth, but he ought in every way to attend to how He Himself, who wrote, wished His words to be understood. Certainly Scripture ought not to be expounded by human ingenuity and judgment any more than it was first proposed.

11. Because holy men of GOD (Prophets & Apostles) inspired by the Holy Spirit, and impelled by Him spoke (and wrote), therefore holy Scripture is θεόπνευστος 2. Tim. 3. v. 15. and the infallible word of GOD. Hence if GOD were still speaking to us today immediately from heaven, He would not speak in other words than those which are noted through the Prophets & Apostles in the O. and N. T. Chrysost. homil. 3. on the incomprehensible Nature of GOD. When I say Isaiah, I understand the sentence of the Holy Spirit. For the Prophet writes and speaks nothing except those things which are divinely inspired.

12. Because the holy men of GOD were the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit in writing out the Biblical Codices, therefore also for this reason it is rightly called holy Scripture. Rom. 1. v. 2. 2. Tim. 3. v. 15. There is added the Nature of the principal cause, which is God, that Holy of Holies, Esai. 6. v. 3. Dan. 9. v. 24. the matter, because it contains sacred & divine mysteries, holy precepts of life Psal. 105. v. 42. finally the end & effect, because the Holy Spirit has sanctified man through the reading & meditation of it, Iohan. 17. v. 17.

CHAPTER II.

Summary of the chapter. He predicts that false Teachers will come, and graphically depicts their character & morals.

General arrangement. There are two parts of the chapter. 1. Προφητεία. 2. Προσωπογραφία.

Προφητεία or prediction concerning the false teachers who are to come includes ὑπόμνησιν admonition concerning avoiding them. Προσωπογραφία or graphic description of those false teachers includes the doctrine concerning recognizing them, just as Christ also, Matth. 7. v. 15. joins these two members.

The admonition concerning avoiding false teachers is not proposed in explicit words, but only in implicit ones, when the Apostle says, that they will introduce sects of perdition, denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction v. 1. For those who are such, they are to be avoided by all with the greatest zeal.

He adds the cause of the admonition v. 2. because, namely, very many will be followers of them.

The description of those false teachers expresses. 1. Their avarice, to which part of the description is joined a repeated prediction of destruction. v. 3. and by ἐπεμβολὴν that prediction is confirmed by three examples. First, of the evil Angels v. 4. Second, of the antediluvian men v. 5. Third, of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites, v. 6. 7. 8. & 9.

2. Their lusts, pride and audacity. v. 10. & 11.

3. Their blasphemy, to which part of the description for the third time a prediction of destruction is subjoined. v. 12.

4. Their injustice, luxury and frauds, v. 13. to which part of the description is joined a repeated commemoration of three vices, lustfulness, craftiness and avarice v. 14. which is illustrated by the example of Balaam v. 15. & 16.

5. Their vain-speaking and fallacious promises, by which they ensnare others and lead them with themselves into destruction v. 17. & 19. to which part of the description is joined an exaggeration of the sin of those who allow themselves to be persuaded by the fallacious promises of these pseudo-teachers, so that they are again entangled in the pollutions of the world, which they had escaped. v. 20. 21. & 22.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quo sensu Propheticus sermo dicatur firmior Apostolico de Christi transfiguratione testimonio? Resp. 1. Erasmus, Gagnaeius & aliistatuunt, comparativum hoc loco usurpari pro positivo. Possumus, inquit Gagnaeius, firmiorem non comparativè, sed positivè sumere, quomodò saepè & Graecè & Latinè sumitur, Syrus eodem modo. [ואית לן דשרירא דנביותא אף מלתא]Et est nobis firmum (certum, verax) etiam verbum Prophetiae. Luth. Wir haben ein festes Prophetischs Wort. Sed positivum poni pro comparativo, comparativum pro superlativo, item positivum pro superlativo exemplis demonstrari potest; quod autem comparativus pro positivo ponatur, eius vel nulla vel rara dantur exempla. Act. 7. v. 21.καινότερον ponitur pro καινὸν. 2. Quidam censent, comparativum positum esse pro superlativo. Habemus firmiorem sermonem, i. e. firmissimum sermonem. Huius enallages exempla in Scripturis N. T. passim occurrunt. Matth. 11. v. 11.ὁ μικρότεροςminimus in regno caelorum.cap. 22. v. 13.σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερονsunt tenebrae extimae,cap. 23. v. 11.ὁ μείζων ὑμῶνqui maximus inter vos.Marc. 4. vers. 21. 32.Sinapi estμικρότερονminimum inter omnia semina & fitμεῖζονmaximúm inter omnia.Iohann. 10. v. 29.Pater estμείζωνmaximus inter omnes.cap. 13. v. 27.fac citiùs i. e. citissimè.Act. 25. v. 10.κάλλιστοςoptimè nosti.1. Cor. 13. v. 13.μείζωνmaxima caritas.cap. 15. vers. 19.ἐλεεινότεροι πάντων ἀνθρώπων,omnium hominum miserrimi Sirach. 1. v. 4. sapientiaπροτέρα πάντων i. e. πρώτη. 2. Sed cum absque urgente necessitate â litera non sit discendendum, ideò rectiùs statuitur, propriam comparativi significationem esse retinendam, stante hac hypothesi iam porrò

Q. 2. Cuius respectu sermo Propheticus statuatur firmior? Resp. 1. Quidam Codd. Graecipro τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον legunt τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον, ut sit sensus, Habemus firmiorem sc. visionem & vocem Patris caelestis in Christi transfiguratione auditam Propheticis sermonibus. Sed genuina lectio habet τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον, quae contrarium planè sensum parit. 2. Quidam ergo putant respectum haberi ad vers. 16. in quo mentio factaσεσοφισμένων μύθων,quibus longè certior & firmior sit sermo Propheticus, utpote omnibus Iudaeorum & gentilium fabulis ac omnibus humanis traditionibus & doctrinis longissimo intervallo anteferendus, Sed perquam dura est comparatio sermonis Prophetici h. e. divini cum fabulis Iudaicis & Ethnicis h. e. cum doctrina Daemoniorum 3. Quidam censent, respectum haberi admiraculosam Christi transfigurationem, ac Mosis & Eliae in ea apparitionem, quarum utrâque firmior dicatur sermo Propheticus, cum miracula non tàm solidum fidei fundamentum praebeant, quàm ipsum DEI verbum, quò referri posset dictum Apostolicum Gal. 1. v. 8.Licet nos, aut Angelus de caelo evangelizet vobis, praeterquam quod evangelizavimus vobis, anathema sit, ubi Evangelium ab Apostolis praedicatum Angelorum praedicationi antefertur, in quem locum Chrysostomus sic commentatur pag. 973. edit. Comm. Apostolus Angelis praeponit Scripturas, idque valde congruenter: siquidem Angeli, quamlibet magni, tamen servi sunt ac ministri. Coeterum omnes Scripturae, non â servis, sed ab universorum Domino DEO venerunt ad nos. Proclus in serm. de fide ad Armenos p. 15. hunc locum Apostoli adducens addit, λειτουργεῖν γὰρ Ἄγγελος ἐτάχθη, οὐ δογματίζειν,in ministrandi ordine locatus est Angelus, non dogmata praescribendi. Sed si vel maximè certo respectu praedicatio Apostolorum praedicationi Angelorum praeserripossit, tamen nulla videtur dari posse ratio, cur in se ac per se Propheticus sermo, vel voci Patris caelestis, vel miraculosae Christi transfigurationi ratione firmitatis praeferatur. Ac si vel maximè velimus dicere, Propheticum sermonem ideò vocari firmiorem miraculosâ Christi transfiguratione, & Mosis ac Eliae apparitione, propterea quòd miracula non tàm solidum fidei praebeant fundamentum, quàm ipsum Dei verbum: nondum tamen difficultas tollitur, quia ex textu manifestum, non solùm respectu miraculosae Christi transfigurationis, sed etiam respectu vocis paternae, in illa transfiguratione ê caelo allatae, firmiorem dici Propheticum sermonem. 4. Affinis huic expositioni ea est, quam affert Cornelius â Lapide in h. l. quod fides & lumen fidei, ostendens, oracula Prophetarum esse divina & á DEO profecta, firmius & certius sit omni scientiâ, demonstratione & visione sensitivâ, ac quovis testimonio oculari & aurito, & sic sermo Propheticus non tantùm aliis, sed etiam ipsi Petro firmior erat visione & auditione suâ. Atqui ab illa auditione Petri non potest excludi illius obiectum, vox scilicet Patris caelestis. Manet ergo adhuc difficultas, quomodo sermo Propheticus, voce Patris caelestis â Petro auditâ possit dici firmior? Regerit Cornelius; licet vox Patris obiectivè & in se fuerit certissima & verissima, aequè ac oracula Prophetarum, tamen subiectivè, quatenus scil, in auribus Petri sensibiliter recipiebatur & resonabat, non erat tàm certa & firma quàm visiones Prophetarum: auditus enim, omnisque sensus falli potest, visio verò Prophetica falli nequit, quia fit per lumen supernaturale ac divinum. Atqui negari nequit, unà cum illius vocis auditu lumen fidei supernaturale & divinum menti Petri illuxisse, ut fide divinâ, certâ & indubitatâ crederet, hanc vocem esse veram & â DEO profectam. 5. Quidam ergo respondent, verba Apostoli non esse accipienda in sensu distributivo, ac si voce Patris caelestis simpliciter dicatur firmior sermo Propheticus; sed in sensu complexo, ut dicatur firmior iam & certior factus, attestante sc. dictis Prophetarum ipsâ caelestis Patris voce, firmior inquam seipso, non autem Patris caelestis aut Apostolorum sermone. Eo ferè modo exponit Oecumenius. Sed hac ratione dicendum fuisset Petro. Propterea nunc habemus firmiorem sermonem Propheticum. 6. Erasmus, ut iam antè monuimus, planè novam profert expositionem. Per sermonem enim Propheticum intelligit ipsam Patris caelestis vocem è caelo allatam, cùm Pater ipse caelesti illâ voce quodammodo Filii sui Propheta fuerit ac praeco. Hic sermo Propheticus, inquit, h. e. vox Patris caelestis firmior erat sermone Prophetarum, quos illi venerabantur, quem sensum Erasmus putat esse huius loci germanum, eundemque in Paraphrasi sequitur. Sed ex contextu manifestum, per sermonem Propheticum non intelligi vocem Patris caelestis, sed sermonem Prophetarum V. T. in scriptis eorum comprehensum. 7. Lyranus existimat, sermonem Propheticum Davidis ( Psal. 2. vers. 7.Filius meus es tu, ad quem Apostolus hîc provocet) dici firmiorem, quàm reliquorum Prophetarum sermonem, propterea quòd David fuerit eximius prae reliquis Propheta. Alii Prophetae veritatem sibi revelatam in visionibus imaginariis viderunt, David autem per intellectum sine talibus imaginibus. Atqui Petrus hîc non in specie de unius Prophetae, Davidis scilicet sermone loquitur, sed in genere de toto sermone Prophetico in scriptis Prophetarum annotato. 8. Simplicissimè igitur respondetur, sermonem Propheticum i. e. Testimonium Vet. Test. Prophetarum in eorum scriptis comprehensum dici firmius, non quidem ipsâ voce Patris caelestis in transfiguratione Christi auditâ, sed testimonio Apostolico de illa voce Patris caelestis ac de Christi transfiguratione; nec dici eo verius, sed duntaxat firmius; nec dici firmius in se ac per se, nec absolutè & simpliciter, sed respectu habito ad eos, ad quos Apostolus scribit, quâ de re sic habendum. Firmum aliquid dicitur vel in se, quia immobilis & immutabilis est veritatis, hac ratione omne DEI verbum est aequè firmum, sive â Prophetis in V. sive ab Apostolis in Nov. Test. proferatur; vel in mente hominis veritati illi assentientis, aut de ea adhuc disquirentis. Hoc posteriore modo sermo Propheticus erat firmior Apostolorum testificatione illis, ad quos Apostolus hoc loco scribit. Erant enim inter illos conversi ex Iudaismo, apud quos Prophetarum scripta erant in summa autoritate, utpote tot seculorum consensu firmata ac roborata; Apostolorum verò praedicatio nondum ad sublime illud autoritatis fastigium apud ipsos pervenerat, unde Petrus postquam veritatem doctrinae Christianae probaverat voce Patris, in transfiguratione CHRISTI caelitus allatâ, & â se ac duobus CoApostolis Iacobo & Iohanne auditâ, non contentus hoc domestico testimonio provocat ad sermonem Prophetarum, quem vocat firmiorem, quia apud illos, ad quos scribit, erat maioris autoritatis & venerationis.

Hanc expositionem confirmat. 1. Perpetuus mos Christi & Apostolorum in Nov. Test. quo doctrinam suam ex Vet. Test. oraculis confirmant, quoties ipsis cum Iudaeis fuit negotium, ut superiùs vers. 12. ostendimus. Chrysostomus homil. 52. in cap. 26. Actor. Paulus, ne videatur ipse doctor esse, adducit Prophetas ac Mosen. Et paulò antè. Quoniam Solus vidit, denuò Prophetarum autoritate dicta sua confirmat. Autoritas autem probans semper maior est autoritate probandâ, saltem apud eos, quorum causâ probatio instituitur. 2. Berhoënses hoc nomine â Spiritu sancto commendantur, Actor. 17. vers. 11. quòd auditâ Apostolorum praedicatione quotidiè scrutati fuerint Scripturas (utique Propheticas) an haec ita se haberent, prout â Paulo ac Sila praedicabantur.Ἀνακρίνοντες ponitur ibi pro συγκρίνοντες, quia contulerunt cum doctrina Pauli Scripturas Propheticas, ut ex mutua illa collatione colligerent consensum. Chrysost. in comm. illius loci. οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἀλλὰ μετ' ἀκριβείας ἀνηρεύνον τὰς γραφάς. Τοῦτο γὰρ ἔστι τὸ ἀνέκρινον βουλόμενοι ἀπ' αὐτῶν πληροφορίαν μᾶλλον περὶ τοῦ πάθους λαβεῖν.Non simpliciter sed cum diligentia scrutabantur Scripturas: hoc enim sibi vult illud, diiudicabant, volebant enim â seipsis plenam persuasionem comparare de passione. Theophyl. in h. l. Scrutantes, an reperirenturτῶν παλαιῶν Προφητῶν λόγοις συνάδοντα. 3. Eandem expositionem confirmant pii Veteres. Aug. tract. 35. in Iohann. Quia nos non ibi (in monte sancto) fuimus, & istam vocem de caelo (in transfiguratione ad Christum delatam) tunc non audivimus, ait ad nos ipse Petrus. Et habemus certiorem Propheticum sermonem. Praevidens enim Dominus Iesus Christus, impios quosdam futuros, qui miraculis eius calumniarentur, magicis artibus ea tribuendo, Prophetas antè praemisit. Idem serm. 27. de verbo. Apost. Quis nostrûm non miretur, delatâ voce de caelo certiorem Propheticum sermonem ab Apostolo dictum esse? Certiorem sanè dixit, non meliorem. Tàm enim verus ille sermo de caelo, quàm sermo Propheticus; tàm bonus, tàm utilis. Quid est ergo certiorem, nisi in quo magis confirmetur auditor. Beda in comm. h. l. Si quispiam nostro testimonio discredendum putaverit, quod in secreto gloriam Redemtoris nostri conspeximus divinam, quòd vocem Patris ad eum factam audierimus, certè sermoni Prophetico nemo contradicere, nullus de hoc ambigere audebit, quem divinis Scripturis iam olim insertum omnes verum esse testantur. Humbertus Cenormanensis Sylvae Candidae Episcopus in lib. de azymo. Autoritatem V. T. primus Magister Ecclesiae profitetur firmiorem esse illâ voce, quam super Dominum transfiguratum factam audivit. Firmiorem verò intelligamus dixisse, non quidem simpliciter, sed ratione eorum, qui Veteri tantùm Testamento credebant. Eandem expositionem amplectuntur Thomas de Aquino, Hugo Cardinalis, Lyranus, Dionysius Carthusianus & quidam ex recentioribus Pontificiis. Caietanus in Opusc. Tom. 2. tract. 1. cap. 1. duo asserit, primò, Petrum suo testimonio tanquam humano firmius & certius addere voluisse Propheticum tanquam divinum (quod tamen non est eo sensu accipiendum, quasi testimonium Petri in se & absolute fuerit merè humanum; sed quod ab illis, ad quos scribebat, pro tali haberi potuerit, ac propterea ad Propheticum sermonem, tanquam ad firmiorem, respectu scil. auditorum eosdem ablegaverit) Secundò divino testimonio non humano certitudinem haberi, debere in decernendo iudicialiter res fidei. Confer eundem in comm. h. l. Erasmus in Recogn. annotat. testatur, se nequaquam repugnaturum, si cui magis arrideat Augustini de hoc loco sententia. Salmero in h. l. Sermo Prophetarum dicitur firmior quàm visio transfigurationis, quia quae tunc Apostoli apud Iudaeos fideles vel faciebant, vel dicebant, non erant tantae autoritatis, quantae veteres Scripturae, quae confirmatae & comprobatae erant, & in summum autoritatis fastigium evectae. Barradius Tom. 1. Concord. Evang. lib. 1. cap. 17. Sermo Propheticus firmior est Apostolico, non quidem cum revelatione, sed cum hominibus, qui ad fidem vocantur, comparatus. Veram enim fidem esse colligunt, quae tot Prophetarum antiquissimis & receptis testimoniis confirmatur. Lorinus in comm. Act. 26. v. 22.Petrus Propheticum sermonem, quàm ipsius Christi transfigurationem, quam viderat, firmiorem dicit h. e. aptiorem ad convincendos Iudaeos, qui Prophetas recipiunt. Similia occurrunt apud Gretserum Tom. 1. Defens. Bellarm. in tract. de agnosc. Script. Canon. cap. 7. p. 1908. & Estium in comm. h. l. Apostolici.

Q. 3. Anλόγου Προφητικοῦnomine Apostolus intelligat certum aliquod dictum V. T. Propheticum? Beda & ex eo Lyranus, Gagnaeius & Cornelius â Lapide statuunt, Petrum hoc nomine respicere ad oraculum DavidicumPsal. 2. v. 7.Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Sed rectius dicitur, Petrum in genere loqui de omnibus Mosis & Prophetarum vaticiniis, quae de persona, officio & beneficiis promissi Messiae agunt. Salmero in h. l. Non produxit Petrus ullum aliquem locum, quia passim Scriptura id testabatur.

Q. 4. Quid per diem illucescentem & Phosphorum orientem intelligatur? Resp. 1. Per diem illucescentem plerique Veterum intelligunt diem extremi iudicii & novissimi adventus Christi, quaeκατ' ἐξοχὴνvocaturἡ ἡμέρα,dies illa, quippe quae nobis incipiet, sed non finietur; quae illucescet, sed nunquam tenebrescet; quam nulla sequetur nox; post quam etiam nullus erit dies alius, sed mera aeternitas.Matth. 7. v. 22.cap. 24. v. 36.cap. 26. v. 29.Luc. 21. v. 34.2. Thess. 1. v. 10.2. Tim. 1. v. 18.2. Tim. 4. 18. ubi vocatur ἡμέρα ἐκείνη;1. Thess. 5. vers. 4.Hebr. 10. v. 25.ubi simpliciter vocaturἡ ἡμέρα. Basilius in cap. 13. Esai. p. 464. Dies illa peculiariter dicitur dies propter continuam unionem sui status & perpetuae tranquillitatis. Nullâ enim intercipietur nocte, non vespera ulla certo circumscribet eam limite, quòd eo die, quo hactenus delituerant, occulta tenebrarum, in apertam lucem depromentur. Iuxta hanc hypothesin, quod de sermone Prophetico hîc dicitur, etiam de sermone Apostolico, adeoque de tota Scriptura sacra accipiendum, ut sit sensus, totum praesentis vitae tem pus esse obscuram quandam noctem, errorum, & ignorantiae tenebris circumseptam, Deum verò ex immensa misericordia Scripturae Sacrae lumen nobis accendisse, cuius ductum ac lucem tamdiu sequi debeamus, donec succedat tempus futuri seculi, ac dies illa augustissima, beatissimae aeternitatis initium, in qua non ampliùs Scripturae & lucis in ea accensae adminiculo indigebimus, sed ad intuitivam & beatificam DEI visionem provehemur. 1. Cor. 13. v. 12.Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate, tunc autem â facie ad faciem. 2. Huic expositioni inservit, quòd nomen φωσφόρου in Syriaca versione redditur per [שמשא] quod Solem significat, quodque teste Suida Graecis φωσφόροςSolem denotet, quippe cuius est φωσφορεῖνillucere & diem inferre. Christus enim verus ille Sol iustitiaeMal. 4. v. 2. ac stella splendida & matutinaApoc. 22. v. 16. in die illa novissima in gloria sua veniens meridianum divinae cognitionis iubar & lucem diei clarissima-electis afferet: ac sicut lux Luciferi & aurorae promanat â Sole: sic gloria beatorum promanabit â gloria Christi, quin & in novissimo illo Christi ad iudicium adventu beati incipient fulgere in caelo quasi stellae & Luciferi.Dan. 12. v. 3.Apoc. 2. v. 28. &c. 3. Eandem expositionem sequuntur pii veteres: Augustinus in Psal. 51. Quamdiu ad lucernam ambulamus, necesse est, ut cum timore vivamus; cùm autem venerit dies noster, id est, manifestatio Christi, tunc & nos apparebimus cum ipso in gloria. Idem tract. 35. in Iohann. Quia in comparatione illius lucis, ad quam venturi sumus, adhuc nox est, etiam dies, in quo sumus, audi Petrum Apostolum &c. Habemus, inquit, certiorem Propheticum sermonem, cui benefacitis attendentes sicut lucernae lucenti in obscuro loco, donec dies luce scat & Lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. Quando ergo Dominus noster Iesus Christus venerit, & sicut dicit etiam Apostolus Paulus, illuminaverit occulta tenebrarum &c. tunc praesente tali die lucernae non erunt necessariae.

Non legetur nobis Propheta, non aperietur Codex Apostoli, non requiretur testimonium Iohannis, non ipso indigebimus Evangelio. Ergo omnes Scripturae tostentur de medio, quae nobis in huius seculi nocte tanquam lucernae accendebantur, ne in tenebris remaneremus. Idem serm. 237. de temp. In die ambulamus comparatione infidelium; comparatione verò illius diei, quando resurgent mortui, adhuc nox sumus. Beda in comm. h. l. In huius seculi nocte tenebrosis tentationibus plena, ubi difficilè quis quam invenitur, qui non offendat, quid essemus, si lucernam Prophetici sermonis non haberemus? Sed nunquid lucerna semper erit necessaria? non utique. Donec, inquit, dies lucescat. Mane enim astabo & contemplabor. Ad lucernam interim nocturnam pertinet, quòd filii DEI sumus, & nondum apparuit, quid erimus. Et in comparatione quidem impiorum dies sumus, Paulo dicente. Fuistis aliquando tenebrae, nunc autem lux in Domino. Sed si comparemur illi vitae, in qua futuri sumus, adhuc nox sumus & lucernâ indigemus. Quis verò est Lucifer iste, de quo Apostolus dicit, & Lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris? Si dominum dicas, parum est. Luciferipse clarus noster intellectus est. Ipse enim oritur in cordibus nostris: ipse illustrabitur, ipse manifestabitur. Dilectio erit, qualem nunc optamus, & quoniam non est, suspiramus; & qualis erit, singuli in singulis videbimus, quomodo nunc facies nostras alterutrûm videmus: quae Bedae verba adducit Glossa ordinaria in h. l. Augustini & Bedae vestigiis insistens Caietanus ad h. l. sic commentatur. Petrus universum statum huius vitae assimilat loco caliginoso, egenti lucernae lumine, quod est Scriptura sacra: futura vita assimilatur diei claro, quo Lucifer h. e. Christus oritur non corporaliter, sed spiritualiter in cordibus hominum. 4. Sed per diem illucescentem & Phosphorum orientem rectiùs intelligitur uberior, perfectior, clarior & magis explicata Christi & mysteriorum divinorum cognitio. Ut enim Paulus Rom. 13. v. 12.tempus V.
