Verùm Angelus DEI salvos facit eos; & conterunt ad parietem, qui est Christus, pedem insidentis; & ita interdum evenit, ut simpliciores vitae suae exemplo corripiant superiores. (Tales olim plurimi fuerunt & adhuc sunt in Papatu, quorum aures puriores, quàm labia docentium, ut frustra quaeratur, ubi fuerit Ecclesia sub Papatu ante exortam Evangelii lucem.)

Ἐκδίησις. 1. Vulgata versio v. 15. habet secuti viam Balaam ex Bosor, ac si Bosor esset nomen loci, cùm tantùm in Graeco sit τοῦ Βοσόρ, sensu eo, quod Balaam fuerit filiusΒοσόρ. Pontificii, quibus vulgata versio in Concil. Trident. facta est authentica, ut eius autoritatem tueantur, evincere conantur, Βοσόρ fuisse loci nomen, sed in duas diversas abeunt sententias. 1. Quidam statuunt, per Βοσόρdenotari illum locum, qui Hebraeis diciturבצרDeut. 4. v. 43.Ios. 20. v. 8.1. Paral. 6. v. 78. quod LXX. reddiderunt Βοσόρ.Idem nomen loci etiam extat1. Maccab. 5. v. 26. Sed haec sententia non congruit circumstantiis Historiae de Balaamo. בצר enim seu Βοσόρ in textibus adductis est nomen loci in terra Canaan tribus Rubeniticae. Balaam autem ex Pethor urbe Mesopotamiae oriundus dicit Deut. 23. v. 4.Num. 22. v. 5. unde de seipso dicit, Num. 23 v. 7.de Aram i e. Syria eduxitme Balac, ubi Abulensis insigni errore nomine Aram intelligit Haran sive Charras, Abrahae patriam. Urbem enim illam, in qua Abraham habitavit, Hebraei scribunt per ח in initio ן in fine חרן Sed Aram, ex qua Balaam evocatus, scribunt per א in principio & ם in fine ארם quo nomine Aramae a sive Syria Hebraeis vocatur. 2. Quidam ergo existimant, Βοσόρesse illius loci nomen, quiNum. 22. v. 5.diciturפתורquae civitas fuit patria Balaami. Congruentiam autem Hebraicae vocis פתור cum Graeco Βοσόρ, hoc modo demonstrant, quod Iudaeiתraphatum sive aspiratum communiter ut S blaesum pronuncient, ac proinde proפתורPetrum legisseΒεσόρ,& commutato scheva, quod ut e brevissimum legitur in oΒοσόρ, quod aliàs apud veteres fieri notat Weigenmeierus in tabb. pag. 5. 3. Sed enim quia non tam de vulgatae versionis autoritate, quàm de textus Graecil, qui solus est authenticus, integritate solicitos nos esse convenit, & verò nulli Codd. Graeci legunt ἐκ τοῦ Βοσόρ, sed simpliciter τοῦ Βοσόρ, ideò certum esse debet, per voculam Βοσόρ non alicuius loci nomen, sed Balaami parentem denotari. 4. Neque pugnat cum hac sententia, quod parens Bileami,Num. 22. v. 5.Mich. 6. vers. 5.non Bosor, sedבעורBeor vocetur. Ut enim nihil dicamus de eo, quod Augustinus q. 48. super Numer. recitans hunc Petri locum, ac Syriaca versio â Pococke in lucem edita, itidem h. l. iuxta Hebraicam V. T. pronunciationem legant Beor, quo modo etiam in Lutheri versione, in quibusdam editionibus legitur, responderi potest, vel parentem Bileami fuisse διώνυμονbinominem &בעור sc. & βοσόρ appellatum (quod in scripturis frequens. Confer. Gen. 26. v. 34. cum Gen. 36. v. 2. Item Iudic. 6. v. 32. cum. 2. Sam. 11. v. 21. Item 1. Sam. 21. v. 2. cum Marc. 2. v. 26. Item. 1. Paral. 2. v. 6. cum Ios. 7. v. 1. Item 2. Reg. 24. v. 6. cum 1. Paralip. 3. v. 16. & Ierem. 22. v. 24.) vel בעור ab Interprete mutatum esse in Βοσόρ, cuiusmodi mutationes in nominibus, praesertim propriis, saepè accidunt, ut Tiglath Pileser & Tilgath Pilneser. 2. Reg. 15. vers. 19.1. Paral. 5. v. 6. Abigal & Abigail 2. Sam. 17. v. 25.1. Paral. 2. v. 16. Aram & Ram 1. Paral. 2. v. 9.Matth. 1. v. 3. Timnath-seres & Timnath-sera. Iud. 2. v. 9.Ios. 24. v. 30. Bethbara & Bethabara. Iud. 7. v. 24.Ioh. 1. v. 28. Quin & hoc ipso in loco, quem Moses Num. 22. v. 5. & seqq. vocat Bilhamum, illum Petrus & Iudas v. 11. vocant Balaamum. Syrus Belhamum. 5. Inde Salmero veritatis fulgore coactus â vulg. vers. hoc loco discedit. Beda, inquit, putatΒοσόρesse nomen civitatis, quam habitabat Balaam. Quia tamen Graecè diciturΒαλαάμ τοῦ Βοσόρ,significatur Balaam fuisse filium Bosor, licetNum. 22.dicatur filius Beor, & aut hîc posita est vox Bosor pro Beor, aut utroque nomine vocabatur.

2. Abulensis Num. 22. q. 10. rectè refellit Hebraicum delirium Rabinorum de decem rebus, quae creatae sint in vespera Sabbathi in occasu Solis post formationem hominis, ex quibus tertio loco numerant os asinae Balaam ad loquendum.

Observationes 1. Usitatum est in Scripturis, idololatriam & falsam doctrinam comparari adulterio & scortationi, ac proinde etiam falsos doctores meretricibus ad libidinem alios pellicientibus. Apoc. 9. v. 8.cap. 17. v. 1. &c. Beda in h. l. Pellices appellari solent meretrices sumto vocabulo â pollutione, vel â pellis suae formositate, quâ incautos illiciunt. Pelliciunt ergo animas instabiles, quieas malè docendo erroneis variorum dogmatum sectis quasi constuprantium luxuribus subdunt.

2. Scortatio Spiritualis ac corporalis plerunque sunt coniunctae. Diabolus est mendax.Ioh. 8. vers. 44. & Spiritus immundusLuc. 11. v. 24. impellit ergò ad mendacia haeresium spargenda, & impuras libidines sectandas, quos laqueis suis tenet constrictos. Sed & quomodo fidem coniugi servaret, qui DEO non servat fidem.

3. Faecundum est peccatum, non ibi desinit, ubi incipit. Sequens peccatum plerunque est antecedentis poena, & peccatum antecedens, est sequentis causa.

4. Cumprimis verò luxuriam & otium, lascivia & obscoenae libidines consequi solent. Prov. 30. vers. 15.Luxuria nunquam dicit, sufficit.Os. 4. v. 10.Fornicati sunt & non cessaverunt. De Messalina Iuvenalis Satyr. 6. Et lassata viris nondum satiata recessit.

5. Qui in fidei doctrina nondum sunt satis confirmati ac fundati, illi â falsis doctoribus facili negotio seducuntur. Eph. 4. v. 14.Non simus parvuli fluctuantes & circumrotati omni vento doctrinae in nequitia hominum &c.2. Tim. 3. v. 6.Semper discentes, nunquam ad scientiam veritatis pervenientes.

6. Falsâ doctrina plerumque ad aucupia pecuniarum est comparata. Luth. in l. contra falsò dictum statum Spiritualium tom. 2. f. 115. Was Menschen Ding ist/ das trägt Geld/ Gottes Wort träget nichts denn das Kreutz.

7. Homines avari sunt maledictionis filii. Act. 8. v. 20. foenus pecuniae avaris fit funus animae. Prosper. lib. 2. de vita contemplat. cap. 13. Qui divitias habere volunt, sine difficultate non inveniunt, sine curanon servant, sine anxia delectatione non possident, sine dolore non perdunt.

8. Qui viam veritatis in verbo monstratam relinquunt, in varia errorum avia abripiuntur.

9. Sicut de Balaamo hoc loco dicit Petrus, quòd mercedem iniquitatis amaverit, ita quoque de Iuda proditore Lucas Actor. 1. v. 18. pronunciat, quod acquisiverit agrum de mercede iniquitatis. Uterque avaritiâ impulsus & excaecatus in grav issimum peccatum fuit prolapsus.

10. Beda in comm. h. l. etiam nomen Balaami falsis doctoribus ac commodat. Sed & nomen, inquit, ipsius Balaam, qui vanus populus sive praecipitans eos interpretatur, talibus convenit. Qui enim agnitam veritatis viam sponte ipsi deserunt, quid nisi vanus sunt populus? quid nisi in praecipitium suos mittunt auditores, quibus non salutaria, quae corrigant, sed quae illos delectent, erronea praedicant.

11. Asina Bileami, vocem humanam edens, docet, Deum non esse alligatum causis secundis, sed posse etiam supra Naturam, imò contrà Naturam agere.

12. Qui in ore asinae vocem humanam formare potuit, is potest confessoribus suis, etiamsi sint ἰδιῶται καὶ ἀγράμματοιAct. 4. v. 13. dare στόμα καὶ σοφίαν, cui non possint contradicere & resistere omnes adversarii. Luc. 21. v. 15.

13. Qui DEUM in verbo secum Ioquentem audire nolunt, quandoque ab asinis obiurgantur. Sic motiones quandoque Principum; simpliciores peccata & errores Pastorum arguunt.

14. Augustinus q. 50. in Num. loquelam asinae mysticè interpretatur de stultis mundi, quos electurus erat DEUS, ut confunderet sapientes.1. Cor. 1. v. 27. Ambrosius in cap. 19. Luc. de populo gentili, qui sub adventu magni Angeli, cùm antè esset asinus, loqui debebat.

15. Gregorius parte 3. Curae Pastoralis admon. 13. Insanus homo â subi galimuto corripitur, quando elata mens humilitatis honum, quod tenere debeat, ab afflicta carne memoratur, Caro per aegritudinem ad cognitionem sui mentem revocat, ut illam, quam plerunque sanus homo abiicit, infirmitatis memoriâ reformet.

## 2:15-16
Connection. He illustrates the avarice of false teachers by the example of the false prophet Balaam, who once allowed himself to be hired for a reward to speak evil against the Israelite people.

Exposition of the text. Καταλιπόντες τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδόν ἐπλανήθησαν. Vulg. Forsaking the right way; they have gone astray. The Greek properly has After they have forsaken the right way or having forsaken the right way they have gone astray. By the right way, he understands the true and saving doctrine divinely revealed in the word, which he calls the right way by a common phrase of Scripture Esdr. 8. v. 21. Just as he had called it in v. 2. the way of truth, that is, the true way. Elsewhere it is called the way of the Lord Gen. 18. v. 19. Iud. 2. v. 22. Actor. 18. v. 25. the way of peace Psal. 14. v. 3. Luc. 1. v. 70. the way of wisdom, Prov. 4. v. 11. the way of life, Prov. 10. v. 17. the way of justice Prov. 16. v. 31. the way of salvation Actor. 16. v. 17. because, namely, it leads to θεογνωσίαν, wisdom, justice, peace, and salvation.

The word ετιαραλανήφησαν expresses: 1. a deviation from the right way to the pathless regions of errors, as the opposition εὐθεῖας ὁδοῦ καὶ τῆς πλάνης shows; 2. uncertainty in doctrine. For just as the true and royal way is one, but there are many erroneous ways: so those who have declined from the royal way of heavenly truth wander through various errors, and have nowhere to stand, but now embrace this, now that; 3. the seduction of others, because the word πλανᾶν signifies not only to err, but also to lead others into error with oneself; Matth. 24. v. 5. Marc. 13. v. 5. Ioh. 7. v. 12. etc. Hence Paul describes false teachers thus 2. Tim. 3. v. 13. πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι A place parallel to this of ours is Jude v. 12. νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων περιφερόμεναι As clouds without water they are carried about by winds: Thus those seducers fluctuate like a ship wandering in the middle of the sea, and are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Eph. 4. v. 14. But especially pertinent here is that Iudas v. 13. calls such false teachers ἀστέρας πλανήτους wandering stars, on account of the instability which is born from the fact that they are outside the firmament of the true faith: or even will-o'-the-wisps, because they not only err themselves, but also make others err.

Ἐξακολουθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ βαλαὰμ τοῦ Βοσόρ. Vulg. following the way of Balaam of Bosor, in which way also Bede reads in his commentary, as if Bosor were the name of a place. But in the Greek it is τοῦ Βοσόρ, by which periphrasis with proper names added, paternity is accustomed to be designated, so that the sense may be, who was the son of Bosor, namely son, which opinion the Syriac version confirms, which for the sake of ἐξηγήσεως added the name [בר]. But the Apostle asserts that false teachers followed the way of Balaam, who was the son of Bosor, because just as Balaam was so desirous of money that he allowed himself to be hired for a reward by Balac, King of the Moabites, to curse the people of Israel, whom he knew to have been blessed by God, as is known from Num. 22. 23. & 24.: so also those false teachers insist upon the footsteps of Balaam & Simon Magus, who when he saw that the Holy Spirit was given by the Apostles through the laying on of hands, offered them money, so that he too might obtain the power of giving the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands Acts 8. v. 18. & 19. but was forced to hear from Peter, May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. v. 20. This way of Balaam chosen by the false teachers the Apostle opposes to the straight way abandoned by them, which seems to be taken from Num. 22. v. 32. where the Angel of the Lord says to Balaam Your way is before me ירט perverse.

Ὅς μισθόν ἀδικίας ἠγάπησεν. Vulg. who loved the reward of iniquity. The Greek ἀδικίας properly signifies of injustice. But Balaam is said to have loved the reward of injustice, because when he was invited by the promise of gifts by Balac, King of the Moabites, through ambassadors, to curse the people of Israel, whom he knew to have been blessed by God, he offered himself prompt & ready for that, and although warned by God, he did not go with the ambassadors the first time, yet when Balac sent more and more honorable princes to him, and through them promised him the highest honors and most ample rewards, he went with them, so that he might comply with the will of the King. Num. 22. v. 5. & following. That reward, therefore, which the Moabite ambassadors carried with them in their hand is called v. 7. reward of injustice, because Balaam hoped that it would be counted out to him for an unjust & impious work.

Ἔλεγξιν δέ ἔχειν ἰδίας παρανομίας. Vulg. But he had a rebuke for his madness. The Greek words properly have, But he had a rebuke for his own transgression, i. e. he was rebuked on account of his transgression, because when the will of God was known concerning not cursing the people of Israel, he nevertheless strove for the contrary. Num. 22. v. 19.cap. 23. v. 13. & 29. Some think that the Latin Interpreter read ἀδικίας as παρανομίας or παραφροσύνης, but the Greek codices consistently read παρανομία,, which little word is more suitable for this passage, since mention of παραφροσύνης is made only in the following words. The Syriac in this passage likewise has the noun [עברנותא], which signifies transgression, sin, etc. from the root [עבר], he passed over, he transgressed. Luther Er hat eine Straffe seiner Ubertretung.

Ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον ἐκώλυσε τὴν τοῦ Προφήτου παραφροσύνην. The Syriac version joins this clause with the preceding one, in this way: But the mute donkey was a corrector to him of his transgression, which spoke with the voice of men, [and] prohibited the folly of the Prophet. But in the Greek text this clause is separated from the preceding one, although as regards the sense it is joined, for it explains the former clause, namely, what kind of ἔλεγξιν of his transgression Balaam had. Therefore, the causal conjunction γὰρ,, which the Hebrews often omit, must be understood. Luther inserts the little word ἐξηγήσεως nemlich.

ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον. The Vulgate rendered it, a mute beast of burden. But in the Greek ζῶον, is not added, just as it is not included in all Latin codices in the word ὑποζύγιον,, since there is no ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον that is not an animal. Furthermore, it is manifest from the History of Balaam Num. 22. v. 21. that by ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον in this passage is understood אטון, a donkey, which name the Syriac also uses in this passage. A corrector to him was [אתנא] a donkey, just as also elsewhere the name of the genus ὑποζύγιον beast of burden is used for the name of the species, namely donkey or ass ( אתון is female, חמור is male and female; for both the LXX put ὑποζύγιοι ) Iudic. 5. v. 10.Zach. 9. v. 9.Matth. 21. v. 5. & elsewhere in the O.T. generally, which some think was done by the LXX Interpreters for this reason, lest it should seem absurd to Ptolemy, King of the Egyptians, under whose auspices the Greek version was adorned, that Moses, the Prophet of the Lord, the liberator of the Israelite people, and other honored men, had been carried by donkeys.

Ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον. Some Latin codices they render, speaking in the voice of a man, in which way also Bede reads in his commentary & Gregory in part 3 of the Pastoral Care, admonition 13, citing this passage. But the preposition ἐν by a customary Hebraism abounds in this place. Luther elegantly. Das stumme lastbare Thier redet mit Menschen Stimme.

Ἐκώλυσε τὴν τοὺ Προφήτου παραφροσύνην. For truly it was great madness to set out against the will of GOD by the impulse of avarice to curse that people, whom it was established had been blessed by GOD. The word κωλύειν the Syrian expressed by [קלא] he restrained, he coerced, from which the very κωλύειν seems to be derived. A place parallel to this one of ours is held in the Epistle of Jude, verse 11. Woe to them, who have walked in the way of Cain (i. e. they have followed the example of Cain, who went away from the face of the Lord, that is, he was the first to make a divorce from the Church of God) and have been poured out in the error or deception of the reward of Balaam (that is, deceived and impelled by the avarice of the example of Balaam, who allowed himself to be hired for a reward to curse the Israelite people, they carry themselves into every wickedness) and have perished in the contradiction of Korah (they exist as the cause of perdition for themselves, while they excite seditions and dissensions by the example of Korah and his followers.)

Latin:

Connexio. Avaritiam falsorum doctorum illustrat exemplo Pseudoprophetae Bileami, qui mercede se passus olim fuit conduci ad male dicendum populo Israëlitico.

Textus expositio. Καταλιπόντες τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδόν ἐπλανήθησαν. Vulg. Derelinquentes rectam viam; erraverunt. Graeca propriè habent. Postquam derelinquerunt rectam viam vel relictâ rectâ viâ aberraverunt. Per rectam viam, intelligit veram & salutarem doctrinam divinitus in verbo patefactam, quam vulgatâ Scripturae phrasi vocat viam rectam Esdr. 8. v. 21. Sicut eam in v. 2. vocaverat viam veritatis, h. e. veram. Alibi vocatur via DominiGen. 18. v. 19.Iud. 2. v. 22.Actor. 18. v. 25.via pacisPsal. 14. v. 3.Luc. 1. v. 70.via sapientiae,Prov. 4. v. 11.via vitae,Prov. 10. v. 17.via iustitiaeProv. 16. v. 31.via salutisActor. 16. v. 17. quia sc. ad θεογνωσίαν, sapientiam, iustitiam, pacem, & salutem deducit.

Verbum ετιαραλανήφησαν exprimit. 1. deviationem â viâ recta ad errorum avia, ut ostendit oppositio εὐθεῖας ὁδοῦ καὶ τῆς πλάνης 2. incertitudinem in doctrina. Quemadmodum enim via vera ac regia est una, sed erroneae viae dantur complures: ita qui â regia caelestis veritatis via declinarunt, per varios errores vagantur, nec habent, ubi consistant, sed modò hoc, modò illud amplectuntur 3. aliorum seductionem, quia verbum πλανᾶν significat non solùm errare, sed etiam alios in errorem secum ducere;Matth. 24. v. 5.Marc. 13. v. 5.Ioh. 7. v. 12. &c. inde falsos doctores Paulus sic describit 2. Tim. 3. v. 13.πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι Locus huic nostro parallelus est Iudae. v. 12. νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων περιφερόμεναιUt nubes aqua carentes ventis circum aguntur: Sic seductores illi instar navis in medio mari errantis sluctuant, & omini vento doctrinae circumferuntur. Eph. 4. v. 14. Cumprimis verò hûc pertinet, quod Iudas v. 13. eiusmodi falsos doctores vocat ἀστέρας πλανήτουςsidera errantia, ob instabilitatem, quae ex eo nascitur, quod sunt extra verae fidei firmamentum: vel etiam ignes fatuos, quia non solùm ipsi errant, sed etiam alios errare faciunt.

Ἐξακολουθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ βαλαὰμ τοῦ Βοσόρ. Vulg. secuti viam Balaam ex Bosor, quo modo etiam legit Beda in comm. ac si Bosor esset nomen loci. Sed in Graeco est τοῦ Βοσόρ, quâ periphrasi nominibus propriis adiectâ paternitas designari consuevit, ut sit sensus, qui fuit Bosor, sc. filius, quam sententiam confirmat versio Syriaca, quae ἐξηγήσεως causâ nomen [בר] adiecit. Ideò verò viam Balaami, qui fuit filius Bosor, falsos doctores secutos esse Apostolus asserit, quia quemadmodum Balaam pecuniarum tàm fuit cupidus, ut pateretur â Balac Moabitarum Rege mercede sese conduci ad maledicendum populo Israëlitico, quem sciebat â Deo esse benedictum, ut ex Num. 22. 23. & 24. notum: ita quoque falsi illi doctores Balaami & Simonis Magi vestigiis insistunt, qui cùm videret, per impositionem manuum dari ab Apostolis Spiritum sanctum, obtulit illis pecuniam, ut ipse quoque obtineret potestatem per manuum impositionem dandi Spiritum sanctum Actor. 8. v. 18. & 19. sed â Petro audire cogebatur, Pecunia tua sit tecum in perditionem, quoniam donum Dei existimasti pecunia possideri.v. 20. Hanc viam Balaami â falsis doctoribus electam opponit Apostolus viae rectae ab ipsis derelictae, quod desumptum videtur ex Num. 22. v. 32. ubi Angelus Domini dicit Bileamo Viae tua est coram meירטperversa.

Ὅς μισθόν ἀδικίας ἠγάπησεν. Vulg. qui mercedem iniquitatis amavit. Graecum ἀδικίας propriè significat iniustitiae. Dicitur autem Balaam amasse mercedem iniustitiae, quia cùm promissione munerum â Balaco Moabitarum Rege per Legatos invitaretur, ut populo Israëlitico, quem â Deo benedictum noverat, malediceret, promtum & paratum ad illud sese offerebat, ac quamvis monitus â Deo, prima quidem vice cum Legatis non abiret, tamen cùm Balac plures & honoratiores Principes ad ipsum mitteret, ac per illos honores summos & praemia amplissima ipsi promitteret, abiit cum illis, ut Regis voluntati morem gereret. Num. 22. v. 5. & seqq. Dicitur ergo merces illa, quam Legati Moabitici secum portabant in manu sua. v. 7.merces iniustitiae, quia Balaamus pro opere iniusto & impio eam sibi numeratum iri sperabat.

Ἔλεγξιν δέ ἔχειν ἰδίας παρανομίας. Vulg. Correptionem verò habuit suae vesaniae. Graeca propriè habent, Redargutionem verò habuit propriae trangressionis, i. e. corripiebatur propter suam trangressionem, quod cognita Dei voluntate de non maledicendo populo Israëlitico in contrarium nihilominus nitebatur. Num. 22. v. 19.cap. 23. v. 13. & 29. Quidam existimant, Latinum Interpretem proἀδικίαςlegisseπαρανομίαςvelπαραφροσύνης sed Graeci Codd. constanter legunt παρανομία, quae vocula magis huic loco convenit, cùm in sequentibus demùm verbis παραφροσύνης fiat mentio. Syrus h. l. itidem habet nomen [עברנותא] quod transgressionem, peccatum &c. significat â rad. [עבר]transivit, transgressus est. Lutherus Er hat eine Straffe seiner Ubertretung.

Ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον ἐκώλυσε τὴν τοῦ Προφήτου παραφροσύνην. Syriaca versio hoc membrum cum praecedente coniungit, hoc modo. Correptrix autem fuit illi transgressionis suae asina muta, quae cum voce hominum locuta est, prohibuit stultitiam Prophetae. Sed in Graeco textu hoc membrum â praecedente seiungitur, quamvis quoad sensum sit coniunctum, explicat enim prius membrum, qualem sc. ἔλεγξιν suae transgressionis Balaamus habuerit. Subintelligenda igitur coniunctio causalis γὰρ, quam Hebraei saepe omittunt. Luth. inserit voculam ἐξηγήσεωςnemlich.

ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον. Vulg. reddidit, subiugale mutum animal. Sed in Graeco non additur ζῶον, uti nec in omnibus Latinis Codd. includitur enim in voce ὑποζύγιον, cùm nullum sit ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον quod non sit animal. Caeterum ex Historia Balaami Num. 22. v. 21. manifestum, per ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον h. l. intelligi אטוןasinam, quo nomine etiam Syrus h. l. utitur. Correptrix illi fuit[אתנא]asina, sicut etiam aliàs nomen generis ὑποζύγιον subiugale usurpatur pro nomine speciei, videlicet asina vel asino ( אתון est femina, חמור mas & femina, pro utroque LXX. ponunt ὑποζύγιοι) Iudic. 5. v. 10.Zach. 9. v. 9.Matth. 21. v. 5. & in V. T. alibi passim, quod â LXX. Interpp. quidam ideò factum censent, ne Ptolomaeo Aegyptiorum Regi, cuius auspiciis Graeca versio fuit adornata, absurdum videretur, Mosen Prophetam Domini, populi Israëlitici liberatorem, & alios viros honoratos asinis, fuisse vectos.

Ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον. Quidam Codd. Latini reddunt, in hominis voce loquens, quo modo etiam legunt Beda in comm. & Gregorius part. 3. Curae pastoralis adm. 13. hunc locum adducens. Sed praepositio ἐν usitato Hebraismo hoc loco abundat. Luth. eleganter. Das stumme lastbare Thier redet mit Menschen Stimme.

Ἐκώλυσε τὴν τοὺ Προφήτου παραφροσύνην. Verè enim magna erat dementia contra DEI voluntatem impulsu avaritiae proficisci ad maledicendum illi populo, quem constabat à DEO esse benedictum. Verbum κωλύειν Syrus expressit per [קלא]cohibuit, coërcuit, ex quo ipsum κωλύειν videtur deductum. Locus huic nostro parallelus habetur in Epist. Iudae vers. 11. Vae illis, qui viâ Cain incesserunt (i. e. secuti sunt exemplum Caini, qui à facie Domini abiit, h. e. primus ab Ecclesia Dei divortium fecit) & errore seu deceptione mercedis Balaam effusi sunt (h. e. avaritiâ decepti & impulsi exemplo Balaami, qui ad maledicendum populo Israëlitico mercede se conduci passus fuit, in omne scelus sese efferunt) & contradictione Core perierunt (perditionis sibi causa existunt, dum exemplo Core & asseclarum eius seditiones ac dissensiones excitant.)

## 2:17
Connection. He touches upon two other vices of false teachers, namely pride and empty speech, which latter vice he illustrates with two similes, while he compares those arrogant and empty-speaking teachers to fountains lacking water, and to clouds driven and dissipated by whirlwinds of winds.

Exposition of the text. οὗτοι εἰσι πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι. Vulg. These are fountains without water. Augustine in his book on faith and works, chapter 25, reads dry fountains. However, by fountains in this place are understood the receptacles of fountains, which, with their veins obstructed, are destitute of waters, for fountains properly so called do not lack water.

Νεφέλαι ὑπολαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι Vulg. And clouds driven by whirlwinds. In the Greek the copulative καὶ, is not added, which omission of the copulative particle does not lack emphasis; and νεφέλαι properly signifies clouds, not mists, which are the matter of clouds.

Λαίλαψ is a violent storm and an impetuous whirlwind, a conflict of many winds. Aristotle in his book on the world says that λαίλαπα is πνεύμα βίαιον καὶ εἱλούμενον κάτωθεν ἄνω a violent wind, which is suddenly rolled from below upwards. Varinus describes it thus. λαίλαψ ἔστι σκότος μετὰ συστροφὴ μετ' ὑετοῦ. The Evangelists use this word in describing the storm of the sea, miraculously calmed by Christ, Mark 4. v. 37.Luke 8. v. 23. The LXX for סער whirlwind Job 38. v. 1.Jeremiah 25. v. 32. The Syrian in this place rendered it by [מן לעל] But Amira teaches that [לעל] with the preposition [מן] becomes an adverb, and admits no noun after itself and signifies from above, so that the sense may be: Clouds which are driven from above. Etzelius rendered it by a whirlwind, either because he regarded the Greek text more than the Syriac; or because for [לעל] he read [עלעלא] which signifies a whirlwind.

Ἐλαυνοῦσθαι, signifies to be agitated, to be driven, to be whirled around. Luc. 8. v. 29. it is used concerning the impulse and agitation of a Demon, by whom those false teachers, if not indeed corporally, yet nevertheless spiritually are obsessed. Iacob. 3. v. 4. it is used concerning the agitation of ships by strong winds. The Apostolic similitude seems to be taken from Prov. 25. v. 14. as clouds and wind without rain, or not producing rain: so is a man who boasts of a lying gift.

A parallel passage exists in Jude v. 12. οὗτοι εἰσιν νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων, περιφερόμεναι clouds without water that is, light and sterile, which indeed promise rain, yet do not pour it out, but being driven around by the winds, are dissipated in the air. By rain in the Scriptures is denoted salutary doctrine refreshing the souls of men Deut. 32. v. 2. it is signified, therefore, that false teachers indeed promise the rain of salutary doctrine, yet in reality exhibit it not at all. Clouds ἄνυδροι lifted up on high promise rains to the parched earth, but they depart into the breezes, the serenity of the sky being returned to men, which they had taken away for a time.

Moreover, Jude adds three other similitudes before he subjoins the threat of destruction, which in Peter is immediately subjoined to the first similitude. For he compares false teachers first to trees φφινοταιστροις withering in autumn, which some refer to flowers, some more correctly to fruits. The Vulgate rendered it, autumnal trees, that is, of the extreme autumn. For some trees are accustomed to bloom at the end of autumn contrary to the reason of the season, which farmers judge to be a sign that they will shortly die. Some explain it thus ὧν φθίνει ἡ ὀπώρα, whose fruit withers, which indeed bear some fruit, but corrupt and withered, which either from juice and nourishment failing, or from worms exceeding, falls off before maturity. Some φθανοπώρινον think it to be the same as τό μετόπωρον after autumn, that is, the winter season. Plutarch in Sympos. 8. ἔοικε δὲ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ περιϊόντος οἷον γῆρας εἶναι τὸ φθονόπωρον.. This explanation can easily be reconciled with the preceding, for the extremity of autumn is the beginning of winter. Moreover, the speech rises in the Apostle. First he calls them δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ, which are next absent from καρποφόροις or τελεοκαρποῦσι, then ἄκαρπα altogether, thirdly ἀποθανόντα, lastly ἐκριζωθέντα Nor is it lacking in emphasis, because he calls them δενδρα δὺς ἀποθανόντα. For a twofold kind of death is noted, one to which they, like all others, are subject by Nature, the other which they have drawn upon themselves by their own impiety; or because, more elegantly, it is signified that they are spiritually dead through sins, and will at some time fall into eternal death; or because, having been once freed from the death of sin through Baptism, they have relapsed into the same death through apostasy. Δένδρα ἐκριζωθέντα they are called, both because they are deprived of all spiritual communion with CHRIST and his mystical body; and because so certain a destruction hangs over them, as over trees cut out by the roots, and from them, as if from trees torn up by the roots, no fruits can any longer be hoped for.

Secondly, he compares them to the waves of the sea. For he calls them κύματα ἄγρα θαλάσσης wild waves of the sea, so that the epithet may refer to the waves, not to the sea. ἐπαυρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας, foaming out their own shames, by which similitude is denoted of false teachers. 1. Inconstancy, because like the sea they perpetually fluctuate in their dogmas. 2. Seditious motions, because like the effervescing sea they cannot rest. 3. Turpitude and impudence, because they glory in their shameful crimes, because they boast of their crimes and filth like the sea, which casts its waves into mire and mud, whose waves overflow into trampling and mud. Esai. 57. v. 20.

Thirdly, he compares them to wandering stars. For he calls them ἀστέρας πλανήτας. Some take this of meteors, which are called ignes fatui, by which travelers are seduced. But others of stars, which are called planets, i.e., wanderers, although in reality they do not wander, nor have uncertain motions, but are only so called by the opinion of the common people. This similitude fits false teachers beautifully, who wish to be seen as most bright stars, and great lights of the Church: but they are wandering stars, because by their doctrine they do not illuminate the minds of men, but rather seduce them and make them err. But let us return to our Petrine text, in which it further follows.

Οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται. The Vulgate rendered, to whom the mist of darkness is reserved. But in the Greek is added, εἰς αἰῶνα forever. Estius considers the Latin version here to be more sincere, than the Greek text, since that εἰς αἰῶνα seems to have been transferred here from the Epistle of Jude and inserted into the Greek Codices: But he proves this conjecture of his with no reason. The most ancient Greek Codices, both in this place and in Jude, have that εἰς αἰῶνα added.

That the relative, to whom, is to be referred not to the nearer, namely either to clouds, or to springs, but to the more remote, namely to the pronoun οὗτοι those, i.e., the false teachers, is evident from the Greek text in which is held the masculine οἷς, which can be construed neither with πηγαῖς, nor with νεφέλαις. The same thing appears from the parallel passage of Jude v. 13, where that νεφέλαις is used, and with three other similitudes interposed, finally that prediction of destruction is subjoined.

By ζόφον τού σκότους in the Hebrew phrase is understood darkness of gloom, i.e., most dense darkness, which Matth. 8. v. 12.cap. 22. v. 13.cap. 25. 30. are called outer darkness, i.e., the outermost, most remote from the region of light. Dionysius the Carthusian in his commentary establishes that the darkness of darkness is called the most dark darkness, just as the rose is called the flower of flowers. Thus the right hand of power is the right hand powerful in virtue Matth. 26. v. 64. the body of death is the mortal body Rom. 7. v. 24. the holiness of truth is true holiness Ephes. 4. v. 24. Jude in the parallel passage v. 13. repeats the same in as many words, except that he prefixes the article to the noun αἰῶνος, οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετήρηται. Thus therefore he again repeats the commination of destruction, and inculcates it upon those false teachers. The little word τετήρηται looks back to the punishment of the Angels, described by the same v. 4. because the false teachers have that punishment in common with the evil Angels.

Latin:

Connexio. Duo alia falsorum doctorum vitia perstringit, superbiam sc. & vaniloquentiam, quod posterius vitium 1. Illustrat duabus similitudinibus, dum comparat fastuosos & vaniloquos illos doctores fontibus aquâ carentibus, & nubibus â turbinibus ventorum agitatis ac dissipatis.

Textus expositio. οὗτοι εἰσι πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι. Vulg. Hi sunt fontes sine aquâ. Augustinus lib. de fide & operibus cap. 25. legit fontes siccos. Intelliguntur autem hoc loco per fontes receptacula fontium, quae venis eorum obstructis, aquis destituuntur, fontes enim propriè sic dicti non carent aquâ.

Νεφέλαι ὑπολαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι Vulg. Et nebulae turbinibus agitatae. In Graeco non additur copulativa καὶ, quae praetermissio particulae copulativae non caret emphasi; ac νεφέλαι propriè significat nubes, non nebulas, quae sunt nubium materia.

Λαίλαψ est procella vehemens & impetuosus turbo plurium ventorum conflictus. Aristoteles lib de mundo dicit, λαίλαπα esse πνεύμα βίαιον καὶ εἱλούμενον κάτωθεν ἄνωventum violentum, qui infernè sursum versus repentè convolvitur. Varinus eum sic describit. λαίλαψ ἔστι σκότος μετὰ συστροφὴ μετ' ὑετοῦ. Evangelistae hac voce utuntur in describenda tempestate maris, miraculosè â Christo sedata, Marc. 4. v. 37.Luc. 8. v. 23. LXX. pro סערturbineIob. 38. v. 1.Ierem. 25. v. 32. Syrus h. l. reddidit per [מן לעל] Docet autem Amira [לעל]praeposito[מן]adverbiascere, nullumque post se nomen admittere ac significare desuper, ut sit sensus. Nubes quae desuper agitantur. Etzelius reddidit â turbine, vel quia Graecum textum magis respexit, quam Syriacum; vel quia pro [לעל] legit [עלעלא] quod turbinem significat.

Ἐλαυνοῦσθαι, significat agitari, impelli, circumrotari.Luc. 8. v. 29. usurpatur de impulsu & agitatione Daemonis, â quo falsi illi doctores, si non quidem corporaliter, sed tamen spiritualiter sunt obsessi. Iacob. 3. v. 4. usurpatur de agitatione navium per ventos validos. Similitudo Apostolica desumta videtur ex Prov. 25. v. 14.ut nubes & ventus sine pluvia, vel pluviam non gignentes: sic vir, qui se iactat de dono mendaci.

Locus parallelus extat Iudae v. 12. οὗτοι εἰσιν νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων, περιφερόμεναιnubes sine aqua h. e. leves ac steriles, quae pluviam quidem promittunt, non tamen fundunt, sed â ventis circumactae, in aëre dissipantur. Per pluviam in Scripturis denotatur salutaris doctrina animas hominum refocillans Deut. 32. v. 2. significatur igitur, quod falsi doctores pluviam salutaris doctrinae quidem promittant, reipsa tamen minimè exhibeant. Nubes ἄνυδροι sursum elatae pluvias arenti terrae pollicentur, sed in auras abeunt, redditâ hominibus caeli serenitate, quam ad tempus abstulerant.

Caeterùm Iudas adhuc alias tres similitudines addit, antequam exitii comminationem subiiciat, quae apud Petrum primae similitudini statimsubiungitur. Comparat enim falsos doctores primò arboribusφφινοταιστροιςautumno marcescentibus, quod quidam ad flores, quidam rectius ad fructus referunt. Vulg. reddidit, arbores autumnales, h. e. extremi autumni. Solent enim nonnullae arbores extremo autumno praeter temporis rationem florere, quod agricolae iudicant esse signum, illas brevi emorituras. Quidam sic exponunt ὧν φθίνει ἡ ὀπώρα,quorum fructus marcescit, quae fructum quidem aliquem ferunt, sed corrupium & marcidum, qui vel succo nutrimentoque deficiente. vel vermibus excedentibus ante maturitatem decidit. Quidam φθανοπώρινον putant esse idem quod τό μετόπωρονpost autumnum, h. e. tempus brumale. Plutarch. in Sympos. 8. ἔοικε δὲ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ περιϊόντος οἷον γῆρας εἶναι τὸ φθονόπωρον.. Haec explicatio cum praecedente sacile conciliari potest, autumni enim extremitas est brumae initium. Assurgit autem apud Apostolum oratio. Primò illos vocat δένδρα φθινοπωρινὰ, quae proximè absunt à καρποφόροις sive τελεοκαρποῦσι, de inde ἄκαρπα prorsus, tertiò ἀποθανόντα, postremò ἐκριζωθέντα Nec caret emphasi, quod vocat eos δενδρα δὺς ἀποθανόντα. Notatur enim duplex mortis genus, unum cui isti, sicut caeteri omnes obnoxii sunt à Natura, alterum quod sibi suâ impietate attraxerunt; vel quod concinniùs, significatur illos per peccata spiritualiter esse mortuos, & in aeternam mortem aliquando prolapsuros; vel quod per Baptismum à morte peccati semel liberati, in eandem mortem per apostasian sint relapsi. Δένδρα ἐκριζωθέντα vocantur, tùm quia omni communione spirituali cum CHRISTO & corpore eius mystico sunt privati; tùm quia tàm certus ipsis imminet interitus, ac arboribus radicitus excisis, tum ex illis tanquam ab arboribus radicitus evulsis, nullis amplius sperari possit fructus.

Secundò comparat eos fluctibus maris. Vocat enim illos κύματα ἄγρα θαλάσσηςfluctus feros maris, ut epitheton referatur ad fluctus, non ad mare. ἐπαυρίζοντα τὰς ἑαυτῶν αἰσχύνας,despumantes sua ipsorum dedecora, quâ similitudine denotatur falsorum doctorum. 1. Inconstantia, quod instar maris in suis dogmatibus perpetuò fluctuent. 2. Seditiosi motus, quod instar maris effervescentis quiescere non possint. 3. Turpitudo & impudentia, quod glorientur de pudendis suis flagitiis, quod flagitia & sordes suas iactitent instar maris, quod fluctus suos in cenum ac lutum eiicit, cuius fluctus in conculcationem & lutum redundant. Esai. 57. v. 20.

Tertiò comparat illos stellis erraticis. Vocat enim eos ἀστέρας πλανήτας. Quidam hoc accipiunt de meteoris, quae vocantur ignes fatui, per quos viatores seducuntur. Quidam verò de sideribus, quae planetae, h. e. errones vocantur, quamvis reverâ non vagentur, nec incertos habeant motus, sed vulgi tantum opinionè sic appellentur. Pulchrè haec similitudo convenit falsis doctoribus, qui videri volunt lucidissima sidera, & magna Ecclesiae lumina: sed sunt stellae erraticae, quia per doctrinam suam non illuminant hominum mentes, sed potiùs eos seducunt & errare faciunt. Sed redeamus ad textum nostrum Petrinum, in quo porrò sequitur.

Οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται. Vulg. reddidit, quibus caligo tenebrarum reservatur. Sed in Graeco additur, εἰς αἰῶναin aeternum. Estius sinceriorem hîc arbitratur versionem Latinam, quàm textum Graecum, cùm illudεἰς αἰῶναex Epistolae Iudae huc translatum & Codd. Graecis insertum videatur: Sed coniecturam hanc suam nullâ probat ratione. Codd. Graeci antiquissimi tàm hoc loco, quàm apud Iudam illud εἰς αἰῶνα habent adiectum.

Relativum, quibus, non ad propinquius, videlicet vel ad nubes, vel ad fontes, sed ad remotius, videlicet ad pronomen οὗτοιilli, sc. falsi doctores referendum esse, patet ex textu Graeco in quo habetur masculinum οἷς, quod nec cum πηγαῖς, nec cum νεφέλαις construi potest. Id ipsum apparet ex loco parallelo Iudae v. 13. ubi illud νεφέλαις & tribus aliis similitudinibus interpositis tandem subiicitur illa interitus praedictio.

Per ζόφον τού σκότους phrasi Hebraicâ intelligitur caligo tenebricosa h. e. tenebrae densissimae, quae Matth. 8. v. 12.cap. 22. v. 13.cap. 25. 30. vocantur tenebrae exteriores, h. e. extimae, â regione lucis remotissimae. Dionys. Carthus. in comm. caliginem tenebrarum statuit dicicaliginem caliginosissimam, sicut rosa dicitur flos florum. Sic dextra virtutis est dextra virtute pollens Matth. 26. v. 64.corpus mortis est corpus mortale Rom. 7. v. 24.sanctitas veritatis est sanctitas vera Ephes. 4. v. 24. Iudas in loco parallelo v. 13. eadem totidem verbis repetit, nisi quod nomini αἰῶνος articulum praefigit, οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετήρηται. Sic ergo denuò exititii comminationem repetit, & falsis illis doctoribus inculcat. Vocula τετήρηται respicit ad supplicium Angelorum, eâdem descriptum v. 4. quia cum malis Angelis falsi doctores supplicium illud commune habent.

## 2:17-19 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Why are false teachers compared by the Apostle to fountains without water? Resp. It is denoted by this similitude.

1. That false teachers have left the fountain of living water and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water Ierem. 2. v. 13. that is, that having left the word of God they have turned themselves to traditions and human dreams.

2. That they promise many things in words, but in reality perform nothing, as is said a little later v. 19. They promise liberty to others, when they themselves are slaves of corruption. A fountain lacking water invites those weary from a journey to drink, but when they have approached closer, they see themselves deluded. They boast that they wish to give drink to the thirsty, but they do not have the water of saving wisdom. Thus false teachers promise truth and happiness to their hearers, when they themselves, being immersed in vices on both ears, are destitute of both goods. Jerome lib. 2. contra Iovin. They open as it were fountains of knowledge, which do not have the water of doctrines; they promise rain like prophetic clouds, to which the power of God might arrive, and they are agitated by the whirlwinds of demons and vices: which words, with a few things changed, Bede brings forward in comm. h. l. They open, he says, as it were fountains of knowledge, because they do not have the doctrine, they promise rain, like clouds of prophecy to which the truth of God might arrive and they are agitated by the whirlwinds of demons and vices.

3. That their doctrine does not provide firm, living, and efficacious consolation, because by water consolation is mystically denoted in the Scriptures. Zach. 9. v. 11. Luc. 16. v. 24.

4. That they carry before them an outward appearance of holiness, learning, and piety, but in reality are destitute within. 2. Tim. 3. vers. 5. Ἔχοντες μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας, τὴν δὲ δύναμιν αὐτῆς ἠρνημένοι. Augustine in the book on faith and works, chapter 25. He calls them fountains, because they have received the knowledge of our LORD JESUS CHRIST, but dry because they do not live accordingly. It seems therefore that Peter is alluding to the Prophetic saying. Jerem. 15. vers. 18. Your hand has become to me like a lie of unfaithful waters.

Q. 2. Why are the same compared to clouds driven by the storms of winds? Resp. By this similitude, those false teachers are denoted.

1. Inconstancy, because like clouds agitated by a whirlwind, they yield now to this, now to that opinion, and are finally constant in their levity. Looking to this, Paul Eph. 4. vers. 14. warns us, that we be not carried about with every wind of doctrine.

2. Fraudulence, because they entice and deceive men with false promises, just as in a time of drought clouds sometimes make a show of rain, but are scattered by the winds. To this can be referred that the Apostles are compared to clouds Isa. 5. v. 6. chap. 60, v. 8. but fruitful ones, irrigating the souls of men with the rain of saving Evangelical doctrine. False teachers therefore αντιθετιχῶς are called clouds driven by winds, that is, sterile and indeed promising rain, yet not bringing it, because they call themselves Apostolic, and yet do not teach Apostolic things.

3. Vanity. Clouds hanging in the air have a great appearance outwardly, but are suddenly dissipated by the winds: nothing is vainer than the boastful promises of false teachers.

Q. 3. In what sense are false teachers called servants of corruption? Resp. 1. by reason of guilt, because they are servants of sin, of which servitude of sin these parallel sayings speak John 8. v. 34. Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin. Rom. 6. v. 6 that we should no longer serve sin. v. 12 Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey its lusts. v. 17. you were the servants of sin, v. 19. you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity. vers. 20. When you were the servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. 2. By reason of punishment, because they are servants of the Devil and of death. For he who is a servant of sin, he is also a servant of the Devil and of death; of the former, because when the Devil overcomes a man through sin, he reduces him into his own snares and into his own power; of the latter, however, because the wages of sin is deathRom. 6. v. 23. and the Devil has the power of deathHebr. 2. v. 14.dominating those who through their whole life are subject to slavery by the fear of death. vers. 15.

Ἐναντιοφάνεια. The eternal punishment of the damned is described by the gloom of darknessv. 17. And yet the damned will be tormented by fire, which is not gloomy, but bright. Resp. 1. Augustine in book 20 of The City of God, ch. 16, rightly says, What kind that infernal fire is, I think no man knows, unless perhaps one to whom the divine Spirit has shown it. Therefore it is not yet exactly certain whether that infernal fire will be corporeal, visible, and devoid of all matter? Compare the treatise on Hell §. 68. 2. Those who posit an infernal fire that is corporeal and material think that the power of shining will be separated from it by divine power, with only the power of burning left for the torment of the impious.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Whatever the Apostle attributes to false teachers in v. 17., all those things apply to Papal teachers. For they, having abandoned the fountain of living water, namely the Holy Scriptures, pursue the cisterns of human traditions outside the Word; their doctrine does not provide firm and solid consolation; the same are inconstant in their opinions, and disagree among themselves in various ways. Luther in the book against the falsely so-called state of the Spirituals, vol. 2, fol. 112: A Bishop without the duty of preaching is a fountain without water, a cloud without rain; he holds the Episcopal seat, but performs nothing of those things which are incumbent upon a Bishop, just as πηγή ἄνυδρος he is in the place of a fountain, but does not provide water. The same in the commentary on this place, in the same volume, f. 409: Teachers are called fountains in the Scriptures, as those from whom saving doctrine ought to spring forth, by which souls may be refreshed. For this office Bishops are anointed. But what do they do? Absolutely nothing; only the title alone remains.

2. The Apostle expressly asserts in v. 18. that through the vain talk of false teachers, even those are seduced who ὄντως had truly escaped from those who live in error. It is therefore false, what the Calvinists teach with the Anabaptists, that true faith once had cannot be lost by any crimes from that the Holy Spirit can be lost or cast out from those who are truly reborn. The exception is also frivolous, that those who are said to have lost faith, had it only δοκήσει in their own opinion and that of others, because the Apostle says they did not have οἰομένως but ἄντως faith. Athanasius, oration 4 against the Arians, volume 1, page 270, Commelin edition, ὅτε γοῦν ἐκπίπτει τις ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος διὰ τίνα κακίαν, ἡ μέν χάρις ἀμεταμέλητος μένει τοῖς βουλομένοις, κἄν τις ἐκ πεσῶν μετανοῇ, οὐκετι δὲ ἐν τῷ θεῷ ἐστιν ἐκεῖνος ὁ πεσῶν, διὰ τὸ ἀποστῆναι ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τὸ ἐν τῷ θεῷ ἅγιον καὶ παράκλητον πνεῦμα ἀλλ' ἐν ἐκείνῳ ἔσται, ᾧ ἑαυτὸν ὑπέταξε ἁμαρτάνων, with which words he refers to this very Apostolic passage.

Objection 1. Piscator in his commentary on this passage: that Peter's statement must be understood κατὰ τι according to the judgment of charity, which considers everyone in the external assembly of the Church as believers. The same author in chapter 10 of Hebrews, scholium 29, page 1345: apostates are said to be sanctified not κατ' ἀλήθειαν but κατὰ δόξαν. Others express the same thing thus: this must be understood δόξαστικῶς, κατὰ χρηστικῶς in the face of the Church, according to the preconceived opinion of those who fall away and of others concerning them. Response 1. Nay, the Apostle expressly asserts that they ὄντως had truly escaped from those who live in error. This cannot be said of those who are such only by the judgment of charity, because charity believes all things, hopes all things. 1 Cor. 13:7 2. If those things which are proposed in the Scriptures to be believed are allowed to be κατὰ δόκησιν, nothing more certain can be gathered from the Scriptures. Marcion, as witnessed by Tertullian in his book on the flesh of Christ, when Catholics were proving the truth of the flesh of Christ from the fact that he was born, suffered, died, was buried, etc., used to reply φανταστικῶς καὶ κατὰ δόξαν that these things were done, and by these devices, says Tertullian, he was destroying all the original instruments of Christ. 3. Heb. 6:4 certain apostates are described thus, that they were enlightened, that they tasted the heavenly gift and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, verse 5, that they tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come. These certainly cannot be taken in the sense that they were only κατὰ τὸ δοκεῖσθαι such.

2. Tossanus objects that the statement of the Apostle must be taken concerning those who had known the truth and had withdrawn from idolatry, even though they were not truly reborn and endowed with true faith. Response 1. In the following verse, the Apostle asserts that those of whom he speaks had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of Christ. Therefore, not only by historical faith, but they were also endowed with true and saving faith. For historical faith does not provide this, that through it we may escape the pollutions of the world. 2. If those who are endowed only with historical faith can be said to have escaped the pollutions of the world, it would follow that it could also be said of the Devil that he has escaped the pollutions of the world, since he also knows the truth of the heavenly doctrine. 3. It could also be said of hypocrites serving the world that they have escaped the pollutions of the world, since they too are endowed with historical faith. 4. The Apostle compares those who are again entangled in the pollutions of the world, which they had escaped vers. 22., to swine returned to the wallowing in the mire, and to dogs re-consuming what they had vomited. But how can these comparisons be applied to those who were not previously purged from the pollutions of the world by true faith?

3. There is also this exception of Tossanus, that the Apostolic statement must be understood of those who are seduced by false teachers, but are again converted by GOD. Resp. 1. That they were again converted to God after their relapse, there is nothing of that in the Apostle. 2. And even if they were indeed converted again, nevertheless before their conversion they were destitute of true faith, which they had nevertheless possessed when they were escaping the pollutions of the world. 3. To temporal, one should not oppose true, but permanent; and to true, one should not oppose temporal, but false. Faith is either true or false. True faith is either temporal or permanent; temporal from the vice of men; permanent from the grace of God, not indeed absolute, but ordained. Indeed, true is said in three ways. First, true κατ' οὐσίαν, to the Scholastics is true of essence or existence, when a thing has whatever pertains to its essence, and can exercise its own acts; to this is opposed false, feigned, apparent, or putative. Secondly, something is said to be true κατ' ἐπιμονὴν & ἐπίτευξιν or in respect of the end, when namely it actually attains its end, to which it is ordained, however much it may meanwhile be interrupted in its course at some time; by some it is called true of permanence or perseverance; to this is opposed vain, frustrated, and useless. Thirdly, it is said to be true κατ' ἐπίτασιν, true of tenacity of solitude, of fixed firmness; to this is opposed weak and feeble. When it is asked whether true faith can fall away, then the question must be taken concerning the first, not the second or third signification.

4. Others object that certain Greek Codices read ὀλίγον, who have escaped a little, so that the sense is, that neophytes not yet sufficiently confirmed in religion are more easily seduced by pseudo-teachers. Resp. We have explained above what is to be determined concerning this reading.

3. The Apostle says that false teachers are slaves of corruption, which he confirms with this reason, because by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also addicted as a slave. From this we gather against the Synergists and Papists that man after the fall is a slave of sin, since he has been overcome and defeated by sin; and therefore the will of man in spiritual matters is no longer free, but a slave of sin. Augustine in Enchir. cap. 30. Man, using free will badly, destroyed both himself and it. For just as he who kills himself, certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself he does not live, nor will he be able to resurrect himself when he has killed himself: so when it was sinned by free will, with sin as the victor, free will was lost; for by whom anyone is defeated, to him he is also addicted as a slave. For this is the sentiment of the Apostle Peter, which since it is true, what kind of liberty, I ask, can an addicted slave have, except when it delights him to sin. For he serves liberally who does the will of his Master freely; and by this he is free to sin, who is a slave of sin. Basil of Seleucia homil. 2. on Adam, calls man after the fall αἰχμάλωτον ἅρματος οἰκείου a captive of his own chariot. And afterwards. παραδοϊς τή ῥαθυυίᾳ τήν δεσποτείαν γίνεται δούλος παθῶν, having betrayed his master through sloth, he becomes a slave of the affections. Bellarmine objects lib. 5. de grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 29. resp. ad 4. testim. Servitude and liberty taken generally are without doubt opposed, but not any servitude is opposed to any liberty, otherwise the Apostle would not say Rom. 6. vers. 20. that those who are slaves of sin are free from righteousness, and on the contrary those freed from sin are slaves of righteousness. Therefore the servitude of sin is opposed to liberty from sin, not to the liberty of Nature, which is properly called free will. For he who is a slave of sin cannot by his own powers shake off the yoke of sin, and arrive at the liberty of righteousness, yet he can through free will with GOD helping be freed from sin, and he can, if he wishes, remain by himself in the servitude of sin: Just as also on the contrary the servitude of Nature, that is, natural determination to one thing, such as is in cattle, is opposed to the liberty of Nature, that is, the free will of the will, but not to liberty from sin; indeed those which lack the liberty of Nature, by this very fact that they lack it, cannot in any way to serve sin. Similar things occur in Estius in the annotations to Rom. 6. v. 22.

Resp. 1. Bellarmine confuses freedom from coercion with freedom of rectitude; the freedom of the subject with the freedom of the object. If by freedom of Nature he understands the very essence of the human will, or the freedom of the subject, or freedom from coercion, we willingly concede that it was not lost through the fall, for man still acts freely in evil, coerced by no one. But if by freedom of Nature he understands the freedom of rectitude or the freedom of the object, by which the will of man holds itself equally to choosing good or evil, to which it seems to look that he defines servitude as opposed to the freedom of Nature by determination to one, we say that it was entirely lost through the fall. 2. Scripture teaches the same with us, and the pious ancients teach it. Augustine, On Grace and Free Choice, chapter 15, explains the whole matter vigorously thus: The will is always free in us, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness, when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin, when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But by the Grace of God it is always good, and through this it comes to pass that a man is of a good will, who was previously of an evil will. Bernard, sermon 81 on the Song of Songs: It was pressed by a yoke, yet by no other than that of a certain voluntary servitude, and it was indeed miserable on account of the servitude, but inexcusable on account of the will. For it is the will that, when it was free, made itself a slave to sin by assenting to sin; nevertheless, it is the will that keeps itself under sin by serving voluntarily. 3. Nor can the contrary be proven from Bellarmine's distinction. For Bellarmine viciously opposes free choice to determination to one, implying that determination to one does not consist with the free choice of man or with the freedom of Nature, when nevertheless he is forced to confess, nay, he laboriously argues in book 3, On Grace and Free Choice, c. 16: that God is of free choice, whose will, however, is determined to one, namely to the good. Bernard, in the book On Grace and Free Choice, says very well: Let no one think that free choice is so called because it is occupied with equal power or faculty in good and evil, otherwise neither God nor the Angels, whether good or evil, would be said to be of free choice, but rather it is called free choice because it makes the will equally free, whether in good or in evil. 4. The servitude of sin, to which all men after the fall before their conversion are subject, does not take away the freedom of Nature, if by it is understood that inclination prone to evil, implanted and innate in all through corrupt Nature. however, it does take away the freedom of Nature, if by it is understood the freedom of rectitude concreated and originally implanted in human Nature, by which the will was occupied with an equal faculty between good and evil. 5. The Apostle calls them free from righteousness μεταφορικώς emancipated from the rule of righteousness or void of righteousness. But those void of righteousness are not free toward righteousness, but only toward unrighteousness, nor toward good, but only toward evil. But in this place the question is not about freedom or voidness of righteousness, but about the freedom of the will toward righteousness, or toward good without grace. And indeed the thing itself teaches that the freedom of righteousness for the Apostle is nothing other than the depravity of Nature and the proneness toward unrighteousness. When therefore Bellarmine fights for the freedom of righteousness, that is, for freedom toward good, in reality he fights for the depravity of Nature and the proneness toward unrighteousness. 6. It is said insidiously, that an unregenerate man can, through free will, with GOD helping, be freed from sin. For if that assertion is understood in this way, that the help of GOD excites the dormant powers of free will, so that the grace of GOD and the will of man are associate causes of conversion, (in which sense Bellarmine puts it forward) then the assertion is false; but if it is explained in such a way that man differs from a brute in that he is still endowed with a will after the fall, into which, as into a subject, the grace of conversion can fall, which does not fall into cattle, it is rightly said. Therefore, one must distinguish between ἐνέργειαν active toward good, and between the passive capacity for conversion. The former we deny to man after the fall, but the latter we grant.

4. In Papal doctors this is also fulfilled, that they bring forth things that are turgid and haughty, which are nevertheless vain and empty. Luther in his commentary on this place The whole Papacy is stuffed with such haughty and vain boastings. Let the encomiums be considered, which they attribute to their Pope, that he is the Vicar of Christ, the Monarch of the Church, that he has one Consistory with Christ, that he has all laws in the cabinet of his breast, that he cannot err, and other things of this kind. Let the encomiums be considered, which they attribute to Bishops. They say the Episcopate is a state of perfection, and yet their Bishops do almost nothing else than that, having neglected the souls of their care and having omitted the duty of teaching, they luxuriate and indulge their own genius. If they desire to perform any part of a sacred duty, they chant Masses, consecrate temples and altars, veil Nuns, baptize bells, etc. Let the praises be considered which they attribute to Monasticism, because those established in it can not only fulfill the law perfectly, but also perform works of supererogation, and communicate the same to others. By the entry into Religion that is by the profession of Monasticism they say a man is so cleansed from sins, as he was cleansed by Baptism; they say that works which are done in this state, even the vilest, are to be preferred to the highest works of piety which are done by the married. Let the praises be considered which they attribute to their traditions, that they contain certain abstruse mysteries, not to be revealed indiscriminately to all; that they are either to be preferred to the written word of GOD, or certainly to be made equal to it. Let the praises be considered which they attribute to the Mass, to votive offerings, to pilgrimages, to holy water, to rosaries, etc., and it will clearly appear that all these things, since they are invented besides and outside, nay even against Scripture, are ὑπερογκα ματαιότητος.

5. But this also is fulfilled in the Papal doctors, that by their doctrine they entice men to the desires and lusts of the flesh. The Pope by the prohibition of marriage has filled the world with lusts and horrendous carnal crimes, says the marginal Gloss in this place. We see, says Luther in the book against the false so-called spiritual state, vol. 2, fol. 115. b. that the Ecclesiastical state is very wide, those who live in it are all bound by the vow of celibacy, and yet Scripture together with experience testifies that virginal continence is a singular and supernatural gift, which was given to few even from the order of distinguished Saints: but they themselves make this gift as common as daily bread, they entice the younger ones into that Ecclesiastical and Monastic state, who afterwards stick in impurity throughout their whole life. Let the fruits therefore be considered, which arise from forced celibacy, namely the monstrous and nefarious lusts of the Mass-priests and Monks. Let those egregious emblems of the Papist writers be weighed, that a Priest marrying a wife sins more gravely than if he kept a hundred concubines at home; that second marriages are more illicit for Priests than adultery; that it is better to be tormented by the flames of burning than to contract marriage, if indeed one has made a vow of celibacy. Let eyes also be turned to the brothels, which in more populous cities are publicly built and fortified with privileges and are exposed to the sight of all.

6. That also agrees with the Apostolic prophecy, that Papal doctors promise freedom from sin through indulgences and Masses purchased with money, through works of supererogation communicated by the intervention of a certain price, through Papal Bulls granting dispensation in prohibited degrees, etc.

7. Moreover, all other doctors of the Church should be suspected who promise abstruse mysteries with a certain vain grandiloquence, not content with the simplicity of Scripture, such as were once the Simonians, Nicolaitans, Gnostics (who, as the very boastful name implies, claiming knowledge for themselves alone regarding abstruse matters, trifled with no less vanity than pride) and others of this bran: but in our own century those fanatics who boasted of revelations and called themselves heavenly Prophets; likewise the Anabaptists and especially the Enthusiasts, Methists, Weigelians, etc., whose doctrine relies in large part on feigned and fictitious revelations.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Estius, in order to reconcile the Vulgate version in vers. 18. with the Greek text, determines that it is likely; that Peter wrote and the Latin Interpreter read not ασελγείαις, in the dative plural, but ασελγείας in the genitive singular. 1. Since Jerome in book 2 against Jovinian reads of luxury; Augustine on faith and works chapter 25, of unchastity. 2. Nor are there lacking Greek Codices in which the same case is read. 3. Since the change of this reading into the other is very easy, with only an iota added. 4. And finally, the common reading of the Greeks does not receive a convenient sense unless a conjunction is added, and with lasciviousness. The same pleases Lorinus in his commentary on this place.

But there is not such strength in these arguments that we are therefore forced to posit some error in the Greek Codices. For 1. both Jerome and Augustine frequently cite the Vulgate version. 2. The Greek Codices that read thus are more recent, conformed to the Latin version. 3. No change can be proven to have been made here. 4. We are forced by no necessity to add the conjunction καὶ, because the preposition ἐν takes its place, ἐν ἐπιθυμίαις σαρκός, ἐν ἀσελγείαις i.e. εἰς ἐπιθυμίας σαρκός καὶ ἀσελγείας. Therefore Estius is in vain solicitous about the exposition of the word luxury placed in the genitive, because, namely, it must be referred either to the closer one, as flesh of luxury by the phrase In Hebrew it is the same as luxurious and lascivious flesh, that is, inclined toward luxury and lasciviousness: or more remotely, so that the desires of luxury are spoken of, insofar as they have libidinous pleasure as their object; the desires of the flesh, insofar as they arise from the sensitive part not obeying reason.

2. The same Estius on v. 19 annotates thus. This passage fits (promising them liberty, etc.) the heretics of our time, who promise salvation to men from faith alone, and that it is to be obtained most certainly, with no obstacles from the sins which anyone might have committed after faith has once been received. Lorinus in the same way in his commentary on this place. The heretics who demand only faith offer the greatest liberty; indeed, they do not fear to place holy men among the reprobate because they have not served the desires of the flesh.

Resp. 1. If Estius wishes these things to be understood of the Calvinists, who maintain that faith once received cannot be lost by any sins, it is nothing to us, who detest that error. 2. We, however, distinguish between sins of infirmity and of malice or those committed against conscience. We say that the former can consist with faith, but the latter by no means. 3. We do not preach liberty to sin or carnal license, but we teach that spiritual liberty from the servitude of sin and from the guilt of condemnation has been obtained through Christ for those who flee with true faith to Christ the liberator, John 8. v. 36. At the same time, however, we require from those who are reborn and believe in Christ the mortification of the flesh, that is, of depraved concupiscences; and the sanctification of the Spirit, expressly teaching that faith and the Holy Spirit are cast out through sins against conscience. 4. We also expressly teach that true and living faith cannot be separated from good works, but exerts itself through good works required in the law of God. 5. It is therefore falsely attributed to us that we promise salvation to men from faith alone, that is, separated from good works, with no obstacles from the sins which anyone might have committed after faith has once been received. For thus speaks the Augustan Confession, art. 12. They condemn (our churches) the Anabaptists, who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit.

Observations. 1. False teachers are wells without water and clouds without rain, because they do not bring forth effective consolations from the Word by which terrified and afflicted consciences might be refreshed, nor do they, like fountain and rain water, render hearers fertile in good works.

2. The interlinear gloss and from it John Huss on this passage Where there is a fountain without water, there is mud and mire: thus in these there is no water of overflowing grace, but the mud of defiling malice. Nor is it a wonder, because they have abandoned the fountain of the water of life. They are therefore fountains not overflowing, but rather defiling, not calming the heat of pleasure, but more truly stirring it up; not refreshing, but infecting; not sanctifying, but polluting.

3. As false teachers are compared to fountains without water and clouds without rain: so on the contrary pious teachers are compared to clouds, fruitful with salutary rain. Isa. 60. v. 8. Moses, the teacher of the Israelite people, prayed that his doctrine might grow as the rain, and flow as the dew, as the shower, as the drops.Deut. 32. v. 2. For the Hebrews, not without mystery, one and the same word ירה signifies both he taught and it rained.Joel 2. v. 23. He will give us the Teacher of righteousness, and will make the morning rain descend to us.

4. That false teachers are compared to clouds driven by the wind, Bede in his commentary on this passage explains it thus, that they are agitated by the whirlwinds of demons and vices, because false doctrine is the doctrine of demons1 Tim. 4. v. 1. and a seedbed of various sins. John Huss on this passage: Clouds driven by winds stir up a storm and obscure the splendor of the Sun: thus heretics disturb the peace of minds, stir up seditions, and with the darkness of errors obscure the Sun of righteousness.

5. The punishment of the damned is described through the gloom of darkness, through the storm of darkness Jude v. 13. they are said to dwell in the land of darkness and the shadow of death or death-bearing Job 10. v. 21. there are attributed to them outer darkness i.e. extremeMatt. 8. v. 12.ch. 22. v. 13.ch. 25. v. 30. Through this darkness is denoted not only the deprivation of natural light, because hell is a dark and horrible prison, a place of darknessJob 38. v. 19. but also and especially 1. Spiritual gloom, blindness of mind, ignorance of GOD. Isa. 42. v. 2.Luke 1. v. 79.John 1. v. 5. because the damned dwell in extreme lack of salutary θεογνωσίας, they are destitute of the light of divine knowledge, they have a blinded heart, and thus are mere darkness. Eph. 5. v. 8. etc. 2. Perversity of will, cast-off impiety, sins of every kind, which are works of darkness. Eph. 5. v. 11. because in the damned the perversity of the will is not healed, in which and with which they were once dead. 3. Calamities, afflictions, and miseries of every kind 2 Sam. 22. v. 26.Ps. 18. v. 29. etc. because hell is the bilge of all miseries.

4. The kingdom of the Devil, which is called the power of darknessEph. 6. v. 12.Col. 1. v. 13. because the Devil will obtain full and absolute dominion over the damned. 6. Wicked men in this life walk in the darkness of sins, from there they are cast down from the darkness of vices into the darkness of torments. Dionysius the Carthusian in his commentary on this place.

7. Tertullian in his Prescription against Heretics, chapter 41, speaks thus about heretics in general. They are all puffed up, they all promise knowledge, the catechumens are perfect before they are taught. The heretical women themselves, how bold they are! Who dare to teach, to contend, to perform exorcisms, to promise cures, perhaps even to baptize. Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian. The Apostolic discourse described Jovinian speaking with puffed-out cheeks and weighing inflated words.

8. The Holy Spirit also graphically depicts this arrogant empty-talking of false teachers and hypocrites elsewhere. 1. Sam. 2. v. 3.they multiply to speak lofty things boasting.Psal. 12. v. 5.they magnify their tongue.Psal. 73. v. 9.they set their mouth against the heavens.Psal. 131. v. 1.they walk in great and wonderful things above themselves.

9. Many are entangled again by false dogmas and wicked deeds in the snares of sins, from which they had been extricated by the grace of God. Luke 11. v. 26.

10. True Christian liberty is not a carnal license to do anything with impunity according to one's pleasure, as the followers of Epicurus persuade themselves; for such carnal liberty is rather a most shameful slavery. The pious are free, that is, liberated from the slavery of sin, from the power of the Devil, from the curse of the law, and from the yoke of Mosaic ceremonies John 8. v. 32.Rom. 6. v. 18.Gal. 5. v. 1. but they must not abuse this liberty for a license to sin, but as servants of God they must serve Him in righteousness and holiness Luke 1. v. 75.Rom. 6. v. 19.Gal. 5. v. 13.

11. There is no slavery more shameful and detestable than to freely indulge in sins and the lusts of the flesh. Origen, in homily 23 on Genesis, examining that Apostolic passage Coloss. 2. verse 14.Blotting out the handwriting &c. writes thus. That handwriting was a security for our sins, for each one of us in those things which he commits is made a debtor and writes the letters of his own sin. Augustine on the honest woman, chapter 30. What great iniquity, that a lustful man should sell and hand over to the Devil, for the delight of one hour, the soul which Christ redeemed with His own blood? of which sale the written bond by his own subscription he delivers the sinner fortified to the Devil. tract. 41. on John Your will shall be free, if it shall be pious, you shall be free, if you shall be a slave; free from sin, a slave of righteousness. serm. 13. on the words of the Apostle A free will is not to be spoken of, as long as it is subject to conquering and binding desires.

12. Sin is called corruption, both because it corrupts, defiles, and contaminates the nature of man: and because it deprives man of the highest good: and because it leads man to eternal corruption.

13. Captivity under the Devil is a just punishment for sin. For because the Devil overcame our first parents through sin, from that they with all their descendants became slaves of sin and captives of the Devil. Augustine in Epist. 28. to Jerome rightly warns, that the souls of men, inasmuch as they are rational, are not delivered to the servitude of Demons in the same way as pigs, which are brute and by nature far inferior to the Angelic, but that sin necessarily intervenes here. For although man is mortal, yet he is also rational and capable of GOD, and therefore he is not a slave of the Angels, but a fellow-servant, and he renders service to GOD not through the Angels, but by himself. Wherefore that the Devil is named Prince of this world John 14. v. 30. and is said to hold men captive to his will 2. Tim. 2. verse 26. and that we need the work of Christ, so that we may be freed from the power of Satan, cannot draw its origin from anywhere else than from sin.

14. Ephrem tom. 1. serm. exhort. to piety gathers from this Apostolic passage the vileness of sin, and of all created things, if they are compared with GOD; vehemently wondering, if there is anyone who prefers to serve the creature, rather than GOD the creator Rom. 1. v. 25. not only by venerating idols, but by perpetrating any more serious sin.

15. Augustine lib. 5. against Julian. chap. 13. proves from this passage that one sin is the punishment of another sin. When it is said, he says, that a man is delivered to his desires, he becomes guilty from that, because deserted by GOD he yields to them, and consents, is overcome, is dragged, is captured, is possessed: for by whom anyone has been defeated, to him he is also assigned as a slave; and the consequent sin becomes for him the punishment of the preceding sin.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quare falsi doctores ab Apostolo fontibus sine aqua comparentur. Resp. Denotatur hac similitudine.

1. Quòd falsi doctores fontem aquae vivae reliquerint & foderint sibi cisternas dissipatas, quae continere non valent aquasIerem. 2. v. 13. hoc est, quòd relicto Dei verbo ad traditiones & somnia humana se converter int.

2. Quòd verbis multa promittant, reipsâ verò nihil praestent, sicut paulò pòst dicitur v. 19. Libertatem aliis promittunt, cùm ipsi sint servi corruptionis. Fons aquâ carens defessos ex itinere invitat ad bibendum, sed ubi propiùs accesserint, se delusos vident. Iactitant se potum dare velle sitientibus, sed non habent salutaris sapientiae aquam. Sic falsi doctores veritatem ac felicitatem auditoribus suis promittunt, cùm ipsi utpote vitiis in utramvis aurem immersi utroque bono destituantur. Hieronymus lib. 2. contra Iovin. Aperiunt quasi fontes scientiae, qui aquam non habent doctrinarum; promittunt imbrem velut nubes Propheticae, ad quas perveniat virtus Dei, ac turbinibus exagitantur Daemonum atque vitiorum: quae verba paucis mutatis adducit Beda in comm. h. l. Aperiunt, inquit, quasifontes scientiam, quia quem non habent doctrinam, promittunt imbrem, velut nubes Prophetiae ad quas perveniat veritas Dei & turbinibus exagitantur Daemonum atque vitiorum.

3. Quòd doctrina ipsorum non praebeat firmam, vivam & efficacem consolationem, quia per aquam mysticè in Scripturis denotatur consolatio. Zach. 9. v. 11.Luc. 16. v. 24.

4. Quod externam sanctitatis, eruditionis, ac pietatis speciem prae se ferant, sed reipsâ interiùs destituantur. 2. Tim. 3. vers. 5.Ἔχοντες μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας, τὴν δὲ δύναμιν αὐτῆς ἠρνημένοι. Augustinus libro de fide & operibus cap. 25. Fontes vocat, quòd acceperint cognitionem DOMINI nostri IESUCHRISTI, siccos autem quia non congruenter vivunt. Videtur ergò Petrus alludere ad dictum Propheticum. Ierem. 15. vers. 18.Facta est mihi manus tua quasi mendacium aquarum infidelium.

Q. 2. Quare iidem comparentur nubibus â procellis ventorum agitatis? Resp. Denotatur hac similitudine falsorum istorum doctorum.

1. Inconstantia, quod instar nubium â turbine exagitatarum modò in hanc, modò in illam concedant opinionem, ac constantes tandem sint in levitate sua. Eò respiciens Paulus Eph. 4. vers. 14. praemonet nos, ne circumferamur omni vento doctrinae.

2. Fraudulentia, quod falsis promissis homines lactent & decipiant, sicut tempore ficcitatis nubes quandoque speciem pluviae faciunt, sed â ventis disiiciuntur. Hûc referri potest quod Apostoli comparantur nubibus Esai 5. v. 6.cap. 60, v. 8. sed fecundis, pluviâ salutaris doctrinae Evangelicae hominum animas irrigantibus. Falsi ergo doctores αντιθετιχῶς vocantur nubes â ventis agitatae, hoc est, steriles & pluviam quidem promittentes, non tamen afferentes, quia Apostolicos sese vocant, & tamen non docent Apostolica.

3. Vanitas. Nubes in aëre pendentes exteriùs magnam habent speciem, sed â ventis subitò dissipantur: sic falsorum doctorum gloriabundis promissionibus nihil vanius.

Q. 3. Qùo sensu falsi doctores dicantur servi corruptionis? Resp. 1. ratione culpae, quia sunt servi peccati, de qua peccati servitute loquuntur haec dicta parallela Ioh. 8. v. 34.Qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati.Rom. 6. v. 6ut ultrà non serviamus peccato.v. 12Non regnet peccatum in mortali corpore vestro, ut oboediatis concupiscentiis eius. v. 17. fuistis servi peccati, v. 19. exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiae & iniquitati ad iniquitatem. vers. 20. Cùm servi essetis peccati liberi fuistis iustitiae. 2. Ratione poenae, quia sunt servi Diaboli & mortis.
