3. Because we are prone by Nature to errors and sins after the fall of our first parents, thence we are in need of frequent reminders and exhortations, so that, having shaken off the torpor of the flesh, we may progress in faith, hope, and charity.

4. Uncorrupted sincerity most befits the truly pious, to which the Apostle exhorts them 1. Cor. 5. v. 7. and proposes his own example to them. 2. Cor. 1. v. 12. In simplicity of heart and sincerity of GOD we have conducted ourselves. Bernard, Epist. 334. to Roland. Let dove-like simplicity act for you, and let serpent-like prudence war against the wiles of the malignant and ancient serpent.

5. Whatever we have perceived either from the preaching or the reading of the word, let us piously mindful of them confer them for our own utility, namely for the promoting of our piety and salvation.

6. We are built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone. Eph. 2. v. 20. The Prophets and Apostles are those two Cherubim, who look toward Christ the only propitiatory. Rom. 3. v. 25. This very thing confirms the truth of Christian doctrine, because it is confirmed by the testimony of the Prophets and Apostles.

7. Against the enemies of sound doctrine and holy life, the safest fortification and most efficacious remedy can and ought to be sought from the Prophetic and Apostolic writings. For sacred Scripture, or, which is the same thing, the word of GOD reduced to letters, is the instrument of our conversion and illumination, the storehouse of all salvific knowledge and wisdom, and the armory against enemies of every kind.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Antequam contra irrisores novissimum Christi ad iudicium adventum negantes eos, ad quos scribit, praemoneat atque praemuniat, denuò scriptionis huius suae scopum indicat, quod iam antè fecerat, cap. 1. v. 12. videlicet, ut confirmet eos in doctrina Christi, in qua utpote Prophetarum & Apostolorum testimoniis confirmata constanter permanere debeant.

2. Sic ergo brevibus repetit summam eorum, quae in cap. 1. â. v. 16. usque ad finem capitis proposuerat, nam & ibi tùm Apostolorum tùm Prophetarum testimoniis doctrinam Evangelii confirmaverat.

Textus expositio. Ταύτην ἤδη ἀγαπητοὶ δευτέραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπιστολὴν. Vulg. Hanc ecce vobis, carissimi, secundam vobis scribo Epistolam. Graeca propriè habent. Hanc iam, dilecti, secundam vobis scribo Epistolam. Pro ἤδη Interpres legit ἰδοὺEcce. Sed Graeci Codd omnes constanter legunt ἤδη, quod etiam Syrus expressit [כדו] Nomen ἁγαπητοὶ Syrus reddidit, [חביבי]dilecti mei, ac si in Graeco est, ἁγαπητοὶ μου. Ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν. Vulg. in quibus vestram excito in commonitione sinceram mentem. Verbum διεγείρεινcap. 1. vers. 13. reddiderat per suscitare, hîc rectius exprimit per excitare, ex veterno sc torporis, teporis & oblivionis.

In praecedentibus habetur nomen singulare ἐπιστολὴν, cum eo non videtur convenire nomen plutale εν αις. Beda in comm. sic respondet. In quibus, in Epistolis dicit sive in eis, ad quos Epistolas scribit. Sed posterius quilibet videt esse coactum. Quidam ergò putant hîc subesse aliquidσολοικοφανὲς ad quod evitandum verba Petri sic vertunt. Has secundas vobis scribo literas. Sed absit, ut Spiritui sancto per Petrum loquenti & scribenti soloecismum tribuamus. Notandum igitur, quod ad sensum, non ad verba referatur constructio. Qui enim secundam Epistolam se scribere asserit, primam â se scriptam esse praesupponit, & sic reipsâ duarum Epistolarum mentionem facit. Subintelligendum igitur aliquid hoc modo. Hanc iam secundam post priorem, vel praeter primam vobis scribo Epistolam. ἐν αἷς scil. ἐπιστολαῖς,in quibus, h. e. in quarum utraque sinceram vestram mentem excito.

Εἰλικρινὴς est sincerus, purus, infucatus, q. d. τῇ εἴλῃ vel ad εἴλην κρινόμενοςad Solis splendorem examinatus & diiudicatus, quia ad εἴλην τὰ μεμιγμένα καὶ τὰ ἀμιγῆ facili negotio διακρίνεται.1. Cor. 5. vers. 8. coniunguntur εἰλικρίνεια καὶ ἀλήθεια veritas omni fuco opposita. 2. Cor. 1. v. 12.ἁπλότης καὶ εἰλικρίνεια, quod enim sincerum, illud est simplex & impermixtum. Syrus reddidit per [שפיר]elegans, pulchrum, bonum; quod enim sincerum & purum, illud etiam est pulchrum. Tribuitergò Apostolus illis, ad quos scribit εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν, quia persuasus erat, ipsos esse sincerae mentis & aperti animi. Vocula ὑπομνήσεως ostendit, quòd Apostolus statuat, illos non tàm uberiori informatione, quàm seriâ commonefactione indigere, id quod verbis magis disertis sic exprimit cap. 1. vers. 12.Non negligam vos semperὑπομιμνήσκεινcommonere de his, & quidem scientes & confirmatos in praesenti veritate. Ponitur autem ἐν ὑπομνήσει pro δι' ὑπομνήσεως per commonitionem, quippe quae erat medium excitationis & exhortationis ad constantiam in fide. Glossa interlinearis videtur accepisse activè ut vos commoneam & alios vos commoneatis. Eodem modo Thomas, ut moniti monere possitis2. Cor. 1. v. 6. Sed propriè & directè de sua admonitione Apostolus loquitur. Syrus reddidit [בעוהדנא] quod Pococke vertit in recordationePhil. 1. v. 3.2. Tim. 1. v. 5. Sed potest etiam verti in commonitione, sive per revocationem in memoriam, quia [עהד] in Aphel significat facere recordari, vel in memoriam revocare. Erasmus pro ἐν ὑπομνήσει legit ἐν ἐπιγνώσει eodem etiam modo Lutherus videtur legisse, sic enim reddidit. In welcher ich erwecke und erkenne euern lauteren Sinn.

Μνησθῆναι τῶν προειρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων Προφήτων Vulg reddidit, ut memores sitis eorum, quae praedixi verborum â sanctis Prophetis. Pervertit & obscuravit Interpres sensum, qui in Graeco textu est satis perspicuus. Vocula enim τῶν προειρημένων non referenda est ad Petrum scribentem, quod fecit Vulgatus Interpres, sed ad Prophetas, hoc modo. Ut memores sitis eorum, quae â sanctis Prophetis praedicta sunt verborum, quo modo etiam Syrus reddidit, ut recordemini verborum[דקדמי אתאמרי]quae antè dicta, sive praedicta sunt â Prophetis. Quin & ipsemet vulgatus Interpres locum parallelum Iudae v. 17. eodem modo reddidit. Vos autem, carissimi, memores estote verborumτῶν προειρημένων ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων,quae praedicta sunt ab Apostolis Domini nostri Iesu Christi.

Καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολῆς τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος. Vulg. Et Apostolorum vestrorum praeceptorum Domini & Salvatoris. In voce ἡμῶν mutavit personam primam in secundam. Quia enim Petrus ipse est in numero Apostolorum, ideò absurdum ipsi visum fuit vertere Apostolorum nostrorum, proinde mutavit in pronomen secundae personae vestrorum. Sed Graeci Codd. omnes, Complutensi excepto, constanter legunt ἡμῶν in prima persona. Mutavit etiam singulare τῆς ἐντολῆς in plurale τῶν ἐντολῶν, cùm tamen singulare itidem in omnibus Codd. Graecis legatur. Vocula ἐντολῆς hoc loco generaliter accipitur pro doctrina, sicut Hebr. תורה itidem in genere doctrinam notat.

Caeterum de genuina textus Graeci versione & sensu tres occurrunt sententiae.

1. Quidam eum sic reddunt. Ut memores sitis praecepti Domini & Salvatoris, â nobis Apostolis vobis traditi. Illi textum sic ordinant & complent.

Καὶ τῆς τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος ἐντολῆς (δοθείσης vel προειρημένης ὑπὸ) τῶν ἡμῶν Ἀποστὸλων. Hunc sensum expressit Syrus, qui locum hunc sic reddidit. Ut memores sitis mandati Domini & Servatoris nostri[דביד]quod fuit per manum Apostolorum h. e. quod ministerio Apostolorum vobis traditum.

2. Quidam sic vertunt. Ut memores sitis praecepti, tùm ab Apostolis, tùm â Domino & Salvatore vobis traditi. Illi textum sic ordinant. Καὶ τῆς τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος ἐντολῆς (καὶ) τῶν ἡμῶν Ἀποστόλων sc. ἐντολῆς. quò referri potest, quod Graeca Scholia dicunt, τὸ ὑπὸ servire tribus, sc, τῶν προφητῶν Ἀποστόλων, Κυρίου Ιησοῦ.

3. Erasmus sic reddendum censet. Ut memores fitis mandati nostri, qui sumus Apostoli Domini & Salvatoris, h. e. ut memores sitis mandati quod accepistis â nobis Domini & Salvatoris Apostolis. Iuxta hanc expositionem textus sic ordinandus: καὶ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος, quo modo etiam Lutherus reddidit, Daß ihr gedencket an unser Gebot / die wir sind Apostel des Herrn und Heilandes.

4. Ad hanc explicationem proximè accedit ea, quâ pronomen ἡμῶν coniungitur cum genitivis κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος hoc modo, Ut memores sitisτῆς ἐντολῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλοων τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν,mandati (sc. quod accepistis) ab Apostolis Domini & Salvatoris nostri (Iesu Christi.)

Probamus hanc expositionem, tertio loco allatam, ex eo, 1. quòd nullam vim infert textui, sed tantùm verborum quandam traiectionem, in Scripturis, praesertim etiam in Epistolis Petrinis non infrequentem, statuit. Confer 1. Petr. 1. v. 11.cap. 3. v. 21.2. Petr. 1. v. 19.

2. Quòd exactè convenit cum membro priore, in quo mentio fit verborum â Prophetis praedictorum, ut hac ratione Prophetarum & Apostolorum de doctrina Evangelii testimonia coniunguntur, sicut etiam in cap. 1. v. 16. & seqq. fuerant coniuncta.

3. Quòd congruit loco parallelo Iudae v. 17. μνήσθητε τῶν ῥημάτων τῶν προειρημένων ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Res ipsa testatur, locum illum esse huic nostro parallelum, nisi quòd Iudas duntaxat Apostolorum mentionem facit, Petrus autem pro ratione instituti sui Prophetas iisdem coniungit.

Estius agnoscit, hanc expositionem textui Graeco maximè congruere, quam proinde, nuncio vulgatae versioni misso, amplectitur. Bartholomaeus Petrus, Estii in professione successor, qui additiones ad eiusdem commentarios scripsit, conatur versionem vulgatam ad eundem sensum reducere, sed non sine vi manifesta eidem illata. Accedit, inquit, ad hunc sensum, quod est in nostra vulgata, si sic ordinemus & distinguamus. Ut memores sitis eorum verborum â sanctis Prophetis enunciatorum, quae praedixi in hac ipsa Epistola; memores item sitis praeceptorum, quae nos Apostoli vestri vobis dedimus, eadem praecepta Domini & Salvatoris. At cui, quaeso, vulgatam versionem legenti hic sensus in mentem venit?

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quare Apostolus dicat, se in hac & priore Epistola sinceram ipsorum mentem per commonefactionem excitare? Resp. ut benevolentiam sibi conciliet, & tacitae obiectioni occurrat. Poterantenim illi, ad quos scribebat, obvertere. Non adeò opus erat, nos ad constantiam in fide Christiana animari & excitari, cùm sincero corde huic doctrinae addicti simus. Respondet Apostolus. Praeclarè quidem novi, vos esse sinceri cordis & candidi pectoris, neque quidquam sinistri de vobis suspicor, interim tamen tùm ratione officii mei Apostolici, tùm ratione periculi, â falsis doctoribus & Epicuraeis irrisoribus vobis metuendi, literis hisce meis ad constantiam in doctrina vos excitare volui, imò etiam debui.

Q. 2. Quodnam praeceptum Petrus hoc loco intelligat? Resp. 1. Salmeron exitimat, intelligi praecepta de dilectione DEI & proximi, ad quae reliqua omnia referuntur. Sed ex collatione cap. 1. huius Epistolae manifestum est, Apostolum non solum ad vitae sanctitatem, in dilectione DEI & proximi consistentem, sed etiam ad custodiendam doctrinae sinceritatem eos, ad quos scribit, exhortari & commonefacere voluisse. 2. Quidam in specie accipiunt de praecepto constantiae, quod in fidei Christianae professione constantes persistere, & ab omnibus Pseudo Prophetis, qui ab ea conantur illos abducere, solicitè sibi cavere debeant, quod praeceptum in cap. 1. & 2. illis inculcaverat. 3. Sed quia Apostolus in genere mentionem facit eorum, quae â Prophetis & Apostolis dicta, ideò rectiùs praecepti nomen accipitur de tota doctrina Christiana, testimonio Prophetarum & Apostolorum confirmata, quam vivâ voce ipsis priùs praedicatam in memoriam eis revocat. ἐντολή enim respondens Hebraeorum מצוה significat doctrinam.cap. 2. vers. 21. 4. Verùm enim verò inter has duas posteriores sententias non est magna differentia. Ideò enim ea, quae â Prophetis & Apostolis pro confirmatione doctrinae Christianae dicta, in memoriam ipsis revocat, ut in doctrina Christiana & fidei professione sint constantes. 5. Ex loco parallelo Iudae v. 18. videri posset colligi, per hanc ἐντολὴν Apostolicam intelligi debere exhortationes Paulinas de cavendis doctrinis Daemoniorum 1. Tim. 4. v. 1. & fugiendo impiorum circa finem mundi futurorum consortio 2. Tim. 3. v. 1. Sed Iudae locus non aequè latè patet, ac hic noster.

Ἐναντιοφανεία.Apostolus dicit, se hanc secundam Epistolam scribere. Atqui Apostoli non acceperunt â Christo mandatum scribendi, sed praedicandi.Marc. 16. v. 15. Resp. in loco parallelo Matth. 28. v. 19. iubentur docere omnes gentes, iam verò docendi munus non tantùm vivae vocis praedicatione, sed etiam scriptione peragitur. Adde quòd omnes etiam secuturi temporis gentes docere iubeantur, ut constat ex v. 20. id quod vivâ voce absque scripto praestare minimè poterant. Confer Exeg. tom. 1. loc. 1. §. 23. & seqq.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Ex verbis Petri, hanc secundam vobis scribo Epistolam, falsitatis convincitur Erasmi opinio, quâ statuit, Petrum ante duas illas Epistolas, quae adhuc hodie extant, aliam adhuc Epistolam ad eosdem scripsisse, quae temporum iniurià perierit. id quod cupidè amplectuntur, qui Scripturae imperfectionem ex amissis quibusdam scriptis divinis & Canonicis evincere satagunt. Atqui si ante priorem Epistolam Petrus aliam scripsisset, non secundam, sed tertiam â se scribi dicere debuisset. Meritò igitur Estius ad h. l. sic annotat. B. Petrus secundam hanc nominans Epistolam ad eos scriptam, satis utique significat, se priùs adeosdem, non duas, nec plures, sed unam Epistolam dedisse.

2. Quod Petrus non solùm praecepta Apostolica, sed etiam verba Prophetica iis, ad quos scribit, commendat, opponendum est Anabaptistis & Photinianis, qui minoris autoritatis censent ea, quae â Prophetis in V. T. scripta, quàm ab Apostolis in N. T. Schmalzius in refutat. Smiglecii p. 79. Parùm curandum est, quid dicat de cultu Dei Propheta V. foederis. Theoph. Nicolaides adversus Midzibezium. p. 68. Recipitur quidem hoc testimonium sed plus valuisset, si Apostolus dixisset.

3. Cùm Apostolus hunc finem assignet utriusque â se scriptae Epistolae, ut memores sint verborum, quae praedicta sunt â Prophetis, & mandati sui, ex eo colligitur, Prophetas & Apostolos eandem prorsus doctrinam, quam vivâ voce tradiderunt, literis consignasse. Illis enim non tantùm fideles, qui ipsorum tempore vixerunt, de doctrina sua commone facere voluerunt, sed eandem etiam ad posteritatem transmittere, ut qui circa extrema mundi tempora victuri erant, haberent certam & immotam veritatem, quam olim vivâ voce tradiderunt.

4. Petrus hoc loco docet, verum & unicum salutis fontem esse Dei verbum in Propheticis & Apostolicis scriptis comprehensum. quod opponendum Swencfeldianis, Anabaptistis; Weigelianis, qui spreto verbo externo interiores revelationes & Enthusiasmos expectant.

5. Petrus Christum absolutè vocat Κύριον καὶ σωτῆρα. Est ergo verus Deus, quia vox κύριος respondet in N. T. Hebraeorum IEHOVAH, quod est solius veri Dei proprium, & αὐποκρατορικῶς salvare itidem est opus solius veri Dei proprium, Esai. 45. v. 11. Extra me non est Salvator. Opponendum hoc Photinianis Deitatem Christi negantibus.

Ἐκδίκησις. Pontificii ex verbo ὑπομνήσεως colligunt, Scripturae finem proprium & praecipuum non esse, ut esset regula fidei, sed ut esset commonitorium quoddam utile ad conservandam doctrinam ex praedicatione acceptam. Quid verò respondendum sit, exposuimus, superiùs cap. 1. v. 12.

Observationes. 1. Magnum DEI beneficium est, quòd homines non solùm voce, sed etiam scriptis animi sui sensa invicem communicare possunt. Aristot lib. περὶ ἑρμην. part. 1. cap. 1. ἔστι μὲν τὰ ἐν τῇ φωνῇ τῶν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ παθημάτων σύμβολα; καὶ τὰ γραφόμενα τῶν ἐν τῇ φωνῇ,

2. Longè verò maximum DEI beneficium est, quòd sanctum suum verbum per Prophetas & Apostolos non solùm vivâ voce praedicari, sed etiam in literas redigi voluerit. id quod requirebat vitae humanae brevitas, hominum numerositas, custodiae â traditione expectandae in fidelitas, memoriae humanae imbecillitas, caelestis doctrinae stabilitas & haereticorum perversitas. Confer. Exeges. tom. 1. Loc. 1. §. 19.

3. Quia ad errores & peccata post lapsum primorum nostrorum parentum per Naturam sumus proni, indè crebris commone factionibus & exhortationibus indigemus, ut excusso carnis torpore, in fide, spe & caritate proficiamus.

4. Sinceritas incorrupta maximè decet verè pios, ad quam Apostolus eos hortatur 1. Cor. 5. v. 7. ac suum illis proponit exemplum. 2. Cor. 1. v. 12.In simplicitate cordis & sinceritate DEI conversati sumus. Bernhardus Epist. 334. ad Rolandum. Pro te faciat columbina simplicitas, & adversùs maligni & antiqui serpentis astutias militet prudentia serpentina.

5. Quae vel ex praedicatione vel lectione verbi percepimus, illorum piè memores ea in nostram utilitatem, videlicet ad promovendam nostram pietatem & salutem, conferamus.

6. Extructi sumus super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, lapide angulari existente Christo Iesu.Eph. 2. v. 20. Prophetae & Apostoli sunt duo illi Cherubim, qui Christum unicum propitiatorium respiciunt. Rom. 3. v. 25. Hoc ipsum doctrinae Christianae veritatem confirmat, quòd Prophetarum & Apostolorum testimonio sit confirmata.

7. Adversùs sanae doctrinae & sanctae vitae hostes tutissimum munimentum & efficacissimum remedium ex Propheticis & Apostolicis scriptis peti potest ac debet. Scriptura enim sacra, sive, quod idem est, verbum DEI in literas redactum est nostrae conversionis & illuminationis organum, omnis salvificae scientiae ac sapientiae promtuarium, & adversùs omnis generis hostes armamentarium.

## 3:3
Connection. 1. In the preceding chapter 2, the Apostle had forewarned those to whom he writes, that they should beware of false teachers, lest they be seduced by them into destructive heresies. From this forewarning he passes to another related one, that they should beware of Epicurean mockers, who are about to deny the last coming of Christ to judgment and the destruction of the world; for an equal danger to the faith threatens from false teachers and from Epicurean mockers.

2. Moreover, he shows the necessity of this forewarning, when he says, that they ought to know this first as a principal and most necessary matter.

Exposition of the text. Τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες. Vulg. knowing this first. πρῶταν here denotes not so much order, as dignity. Because it behooves them to know this as a primary matter and most necessary for the sake of caution. In that sense some determine πρῶτον to be used Rom. 3. v. 2. so that it regards not so much the order of speech, as the prerogative and dignity of rank. Thus στόλη πρώτη Luc. 15. v. 22. is the principal robe. The Syrian rendered this in this place by [לוקדם] first.

Τὸ γινώσκοντες has respect to the word ἀγαπητοὶ in v. 1. It includes, however, a precept, that they ought to know this first and before all things, as is gathered from the parallel passage 2. Tim. 3. v. 1. τοῦτο γίνωσκε, that in the last days hard times shall come. To this, therefore, pertains the rule: Among the Greeks, active participles are taken for verbs of the indicative or imperative mood. 1. Petr. 3. v. 1. Wives ὑποτασσόμεναι be subject to your husbands. v. 7. Husbands συνοικοῦντες be dwelling together or dwell together according to knowledge. The Syrian rendered it. When you have known this first. Luth. with the copulative particle added. Und wisset das auffs erste.

Ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ' ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται. For ἐσχάτου some Greek Codices read ἐσχάτων, without any variation of sense. The Vulg. rendered it, that there shall come in the last days mockers in deception. But in the Greek there is not held anything which corresponds to that προσδιορισμῷ in deception, just as neither in Oecumenius, nor in the parallel passage Iudae v. 18. which has it thus. Ἔλεγον ὑμῖν (οἱ Ἀπόστολοι) ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ ἔσονται ἐμπαῖκται.

Ἐμπαῖκται, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐμπαίξειν are called mockers, deriders, to whom it is a game and a joke, whatever is taught concerning the last coming of Christ, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning the final judgment, concerning the consummation of the age, concerning eternal life and death, and who also mock others by this name, because they have faith in these dogmas, which in their opinion are absurd and paradoxical. Luth. in the margin gloss. ἐμπαίκται are our Epicureans and Sadducees, who believe neither this nor that, they institute life according to their own pleasure, they walk according to their own lusts, as Peter speaks; who think it is permitted to them, whatever they please, whose examples are encountered everywhere before our eyes. The LXX Interpreters use for תעלולים little ones, because the root, עלל among other things signifies also to mock, whence by ἐμπαίζειν is turned more often. Ex. 10. v. 2.Num. 22. v. 29.Iud. 19. v. 25. Such ἐμπαῖκται Psalm. 1. v. 1. are called לצים scoffers, whom the LXX there call λοιμοὺς plagues, because those Epicurean mockers are truly pestilent men, plagues of religion and piety. The Syrian in this place rendered it [מבזחין] from the root [בזח] he mocked, he derided, to which is cognate the root [בזה] he despised, he contemned, because such scoffers are despisers of God and men.

Ἐπ' ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐλεύσονται. That in the parallel passage of Jude vers. 18. is expressed thus. Ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ ἔσονται. Gen. 49. vers. 1. באחרית הימים in the last of the days; so also the Syrian in this place rendered it. [בחרתא דיומתא] in the extremity or end of the days, that is, in the last days. The Petrine phrase is such as in the preceding chapter 2. v. 18. they will speak ὐπέρογκα ματαιότητος swollen vanities.

In the word ἐλεύσονται John Huss observed an emphasis in his Commentary: He does not say that they will be sent, because they will come not by divine authority, but by their own usurpation.

Κατἀ τὰς ἰδίας αὑτῶν ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι. The Vulgate: walking according to their own concupiscences. The Greek has, going according to their own concupiscences, just as Augustine also reads in book 20 of the City of God, chapter 18. Jerome in book 1 against Jovinian translates in this way, walking according to their own desires. Jude in the parallel passage v. 18. repeats these in almost as many words, except that with the word ἰδίας omitted, he adds the noun ἀσεβειῶν. Κατὰ τὰς ἑαυτῶν,, he says, ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῶν ἀσεβειῶν. They are, however, ἐπιθυμίαι ἀσεβειῶν most impious desires, because the genitive plural is used in this way among the Hebrews, and has the force of a superlative. Thus Daniel is called a man of desires, i. e., most desired. Dan. 10. v. 11. The Messiah is called a man of sorrows, i. e., affected by the most grievous sorrows, Esa. 53. v. 3. The Syrian has the noun [רגיגתא] concupiscence, desire, cupidity. When therefore Peter and Jude prophesy that those scoffers will walk according to their own concupiscences, it is signified that the empaectae These men, having cast off the fear of GOD and having set aside the word from their eyes, are about to indulge in the depraved concupiscences of their corrupt flesh, especially gluttony and lust, and are about to surrender themselves entirely to those vices.

The little word ἰδίας is emphatic. For it signifies that such depraved concupiscences are implanted in man by Nature after the fall, and that they are opposed to the adventitious gifts of GOD. The word walking denotes, as it were, new progressions in impiety, and as Paul speaks concerning seducers 2. Tim. 3. v. 13. progressing for the worse.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. In praeced. cap. 2. praemonuerat Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit, ut sibi caverent â falsis doctoribus, ne ab illis in haereses exitiales seducerentur. Ab hac praemonitione transit ad aliam cognatam, ut sibi caveant ab Epicuraeis irrisoribus, qui novissimum Christi ad iudicium adventum & mundi interitum negaturi sint; aequale enim periculum fidei imminet â falsis doctoribus & ab Epicurae is irrisoribus.

2. Ostendit autem praemonitionis huius necessitatem, quando dicit, hoc primùm tanquam rem praecipuam & maximè necessariam ipsos debere scire.

Textus expositio. Τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες. Vulg. hoc primùm scientes.πρῶταν hîc non tàm ordinem, quàm dignitatem notat. quod hoc tanquam rem praecipuam & cautelae ergo maximè necessariam ipsos scire oporteat. Eo sensu quidam πρῶτον usurpari statuunt Rom. 3. v. 2. ut non tàm sermonis ordinem, quàm praerogativam & dignitatem grad ûs respiciat. Sic στόλη πρώτηLuc. 15. v. 22. est praecipua vestis. Syrus hoc loco reddidit per [לוקדם]priùs.

Τὸ γινώσκοντες respectum habet ad vocem ἀγαπητοὶ in v. 1. Includit autem praeceptum, quòd cumprimis & ante omnia hoc scire debeant, ut colligitur ex loco parallelo 2. Tim. 3. v. 1.τοῦτο γίνωσκε,quòd in novissimis diebus instabunt dura tempora. Hûc ergo pertinet regula: Apud Graecos participia activa pro verbis indicativi vel imperativi modi accipiuntur. 1. Petr. 3. v. 1. Uxores ὑποτασσόμεναι subditae sint maritis. v. 7. Viri συνοικοῦντεςcohabitantes sint sive cohabitent secundùm scientiam. Syrus reddidit. Cùm priùs hoc noveritis. Luth. additâ copulativâ particulâ. Und wisset das auffs erste.

Ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ' ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται. Pro ἐσχάτου quidam Codd. Graeci legunt ἐσχάτων, sina ulla sensûs variatione. Vulg. reddidit, quod venient in novissimis diebus in deceptionem illusores. Sed in Graeco non habetur aliquid, quod respondeat illi προσδιορισμῷ in deceptionem, uti nec apud Oecumenium, nec in loco parallelo Iudae v. 18. qui sic habet. Ἔλεγον ὑμῖν (οἱ Ἀπόστολοι) ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ ἔσονται ἐμπαῖκται.

Ἐμπαῖκται, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐμπαίξειν dicti, sunt illusores, irrisores, quibus ludus & iocus est, quicquid de novissimo Christi adventu, de resurrectione mortuorum, de iudicio extremo, de consummatione seculi, de vita & morte aeterna docetur, quique etiam aliis hoc nomine illudunt, quòd dogmatibus hisce, ipsorum opinione absurdis & paradoxis, fidem habeant. Luth. in gloss. margin. ἐμπαίκταιsunt nostri Epicuraei & Saducaei, qui nec hoc, nec illud credunt, vitam pro lubitu suo instituunt, iuxta suas concupiscentias ambulant, ut Petrus loquitur; qui licere sibi putant, quicquid libet, quorum exempla oculis nostris passim obversantur. LXX. Interpp. utuntur pro תעלוליםparvuli, quia rad, עלל inter alia significat etiam illudere, unde per ἐμπαίζειν saepiùs vertitur. Ex. 10. v. 2.Num. 22. v. 29.Iud. 19. v. 25. Eiusmodi ἐμπαῖκταιPsalm. 1. v. 1. vocantur לציםderisores, quos LXX. ibi vocant λοιμοὺςpestes, quia Epicuraei illi irrisores verè sunt homines pestilentes, religionis & pietatis pestes. Syrus h. l. reddidit [מבזחין] â rad. [בזח]illusit, irrisit, cui cognata est radix [בזה]sprevit, contemsit, quia tales irrisores sunt Dei & hominum contemtores.

Ἐπ' ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐλεύσονται. Illud in loco parallelo Iudae vers. 18. sic effertur. Ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ ἔσονται.Gen. 49. vers. 1.באחרית הימיםin novissimo dierum; sic & Syrus h. l. reddidit. [בחרתא דיומתא]in extremitate vel sine dierum h. e. in novissimis diebus. Phrasis Petrina talis est, qualis in cap. praeced. 2. v. 18. loquentur ὐπέρογκα ματαιότητοςpraetumidas vanitates.

In verbo ἐλεύσονται emphasin observavit Iohann. Huss in Comm. Non dicit, quod mittentur, quia non autoritate divinâ, sed usurpatione propriâ venient.

Κατἀ τὰς ἰδίας αὑτῶν ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι. Vulg. iuxta proprias concupiscentias ambulantes. Graeca habent, secundùm proprias suas concupiscentias euntes, quomodo etiam Augustinus legit lib 20. de Civ. Dei cap. 18. Hieronymus lib. 1. contra Iovinianum vertit hoc modo, iuxta propria desideria ambulantes. Iudas in loco parallelo v. 18. fermè totidem verbis haec repetit, nisi quòd omisso vocabulo ἰδίας addat nomen ἀσεβειῶν. Κατὰ τὰς ἑαυτῶν, in quit, ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῶν ἀσεβειῶν. Sunt autem ἐπιθυμίαι ἀσεβειῶν cupiditates impiissimae, quia genitivus pluralis hoc modo apud Hebraeos usurpatur, ac vim habet superlativi. Sic Daniel vocatur vir desideriorum i. e. desideratissimus. Dan. 10. v. 11. Messias vocatur vir dolorum, i. e. gravissimis doloribus affectus, Esa. 53. v. 3. Syrus habet nomen [רגיגתא]concupiscentia, desiderium, cupiditas. Quando ergo Petrus & Iudas vaticinantur, irrisores illos secundùm proprias concupiscentias ambulaturos, significatur, quòd empaectae isti excusso DEI timore & verbo ex oculis seposito pravis corruptae carnis suae concupiscentiis, cumprimis gulae & libidini sint indulsuri ac vitiis illis sese totos tradituri.

Vocula ἰδίας est emphatica. Significat enim, eiusmodi concupiscentias pravas post lapsum homini â Natura esse infitas, easque adventitiis DEI donis opponi. Ambulandi verbum denotat novas veluti in impietate progressiones, ac ut Paulus de seductoribus loquitur 2. Tim. 3. v. 13.profectus in peius.

## 3:3-7 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place: 1. Whether by ἐμπαῖκτας are impostors more correctly understood than mockers or deriders? Estius determines this in his commentary on this place. ἐμπαῖκτας, he says, you would more correctly translate it as deriders, who are instructed in the art of deceiving, called so by the Hebrews from the property of the language, because while they deceive men they expose them to the mockery of others; nay, even those whom they deceive, they deride in their heart as simpletons and ignorant of guile, often even laughing at them among themselves with guffaws. To which he accommodates that which Matth. 2. v. 16. Herod is said to have been mocked by the Magi, that is, deceived. But ἐμπαίζειν properly signifies to mock; as appears from Matth. 20. v. 19. cap. 27. v. 29. and 31. cap. 27. v. 41. Marc. 10. v. 34. cap. 15. v. 31. Luc. 14. v. 29. cap. 18. v. 32. cap. 22. v. 63. cap. 23. v. 11. and 36. which proper signification of this verb fits this place most excellently, as is evident from their own words, which μιμητικῶς are subjoined by the Apostle, and from parallel places. Bede on this place: Mockers will come in the last days, mocking, namely, the faith and hope of Christians, because they promise in vain that the time of the resurrection will be for them.

Q. 2. What is that promise, of which those mockers speak? Salmeron raises this question, and answers it, that it is to be understood as the promise which Christians expect concerning the promised kingdom of Christ, and concerning the renewal of the world, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. The Vulgate Latin translation gave occasion for the question, in which the coming of Christ is distinguished from the promise. But the Greek text does not allow us to doubt that the promise is understood concerning the second or final coming of Christ to judgment, which not only the Patriarchs and Prophets in the Old Testament, but also Christ himself and the Apostles in the New Testament foretold it several times, and indeed the Angels themselves, as witnesses of the truth, promised the same. Acts 1. v. 11.

Q. 3. What ἐμπαῖκται did they mean by this χλευαστικῂ question? Bede thinks that they intended to signify by it only the delay of Christ's coming to judgment. He rebukes, he says, Peter, and calls those mockers who assert that the coming of the Lord and the promises are delayed: Paul restrains 2. Thess. 2. v. 1. & seqq. those who suppose that the day of the Lord is at hand: whence it is evident to all who love his coming, that the mind must be restrained more temperately in this opinion, so that we may not suspect that the same day of the Lord is coming either near, or sooner, or on the other hand later, but that we may only diligently ensure this, that whether he comes sooner or later, he may find us prepared when he has come. This exposition could be confirmed.

1. From Prophetic passages. Isa. 5. v. 19. Woe to those who say: Let him make haste, let him speed his work, that we may see; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, and we shall know. Jer. 17. v. 15. Behold, they say to me, Where is the word of the Lord? let it come now. Ezek. 12. v. 22. What is that proverb you have in the land of Israel, saying: The days will be prolonged, and every vision will fail.

2. From Evangelical Parables. Matt. 24. v. 47. If that evil servant says in his heart, My Lord delays to come v. 48. and begins to strike his fellow servants &c. v. 49. The Lord of that servant will come in a day that he does not expect, and in an hour that he does not know. Compare Luke 12. v. 45. & seqq.

3. From the Apostle's opposing refutation. For Peter answers these ἐμπαῖκταις thus v. 9. The Lord does not delay the promise, as some count delay. But it is said more correctly that ἐμπαῖκτας they, by this question, simply went about to deny the final coming of Christ to judgment, so that the sense of the question here is: The hope concerning Christ's coming to judgment is vain and fruitless. For besides the fact that it is most common in the Scriptures for questions formed by the particles Is it, who, how &c. to deny simply, Gen. 18. v. 14. & 17. Ps. 113. v. 5. Matt. 12. v. 26. & 34. Luke 14 v. 5. John 3. v. 4. Rom. 3. v. 3. &c. especially pertinent here are questions formed by the particle איה ποῦ, having the force of insulting. Psalm 42. verse 4. My tears have been to me My bread has been my food day and night, while they say to me daily, Where is your God?Psalm. 79. v. 10.Why should the nations say, Where is their God? that is, there is no one who takes care of them, they cry out in vain to their God, seeking help from him. Tob. 2. v. 22. the wife of Tobias insults her husband, ποῦ αἱ ἐλεημοσύναι σου. You receive no fruit from your alms. So also in this place, Where is the promise of his coming? that is, it is nowhere, it has vanished, it is a lie.

They confirm this exposition. 1. The following words of theirs ἐμπαίκτων. Since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were.

2. The Apostolic refutation opposed to those mockers, in which he dissolves their fig-tree argument, and confirms the certainty of the Lord's coming.

3. Those mockers brought forward the delay of the coming as an argument that Christ would never return for judgment, just as also in the cited Prophetic passages and Evangelical parables, impious men wished to infer from the delay of fulfillment the vanity of a promise, or even of a threat.

Q. 4. Did those mockers deny the coming of Christ to judgment in order to take away from the pious the hope of future reward and glory, or indeed to remove from themselves and others the fear of future judgment? A. Some affirm the former, and they prove it from the word promise, which leads us to the heavenly rewards promised to the pious, the hope of which they wished to weaken in their minds. But some establish the latter, moved by the argument that they gave themselves entirely to the pursuit of pleasures, and wished to free their followers from the fear of judgment to that end, so that they themselves might also securely immerse themselves in the mire of gluttony and lusts. But these opinions are not opposed, but rather subordinated. For by denying the return of Christ to judgment, by denying the resurrection of the dead, by denying the final judgment, the rewards of the pious and the punishments of the impious are denied. Tertullianus lib. de resurr. carnis cap. 11. p. 318. No one lives so carnally as those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, for those who deny it despise punishment and discipline.

Q. 5. Could ἐμπαῖκται these men have been refuted from their own words? Estius thinks, ἐμπαῖκταις that they contradicted themselves and could have been refuted from their own words, inasmuch as they used such a word, by which their impious opinion could be refuted, since by sleeping the hope of a resurrection of bodies to happen at some time is insinuated, according to that of the Psalm. 40. Shall he who sleeps not add, that he may rise again. Resp. 1. We do not deny that in the vicissitude of sleep and waking a certain mirror of the resurrection from death is proposed. For just as sleep is not a certain perpetual rest, but at a certain time we are awakened again and the vigor of the mind, of the senses, and of the body returns more lively: so we shall not remain perpetually in death, but the hour will come, in which all who are in the monuments will hear the voice of the son of man &c. Dan. 12. vers. 2. Iohann. 5. vers. 28. Beda in Mark. The Christian custom has prevailed, that the dead, who are not doubted to be about to rise again, are called sleeping. 2. But the saying of the Psalmist Psal. 41. v. 9. is brought in impertinently to prove that. For there are described the nefarious counsels of the enemies concerning Christ being utterly oppressed, and extirpated, and his resurrection being hindered. For thus the fountains of truth have it. A word of Belial poured out upon him, and he who has lain down, let him not add, that he may rise that is, let him never rise. ἐμπαῖκται

3. But also from the bare little word of falling asleep ἐκοιμήθησαν they could hardly be effectively refuted, since they could answer, that even the Gentiles denying the resurrection of bodies, call death sleep, and use the vocabulary received among Christians, although they do not assent to the dogma, which Christians deduce from it. 4. Nay, in the word they seem to express their Epicurean security, for this they wish to say: Long since those ought to have been awakened, whom you say are not so much dead, as resting in the sepulcher. 5. The same judgment [applies] to that which some establish, that by the word κτίσεως, used by ἐμπαίκταις, their Epicurean mockery could likewise be refuted. For that which has a beginning of its origin, that it has an end, παράδοξον is not; and he who acknowledges the world created, must confess, that the creator can again abolish and dissolve that which he created, nay reduce it into nothing, so that now it is not to be asked, whether the world can be finished, but whether God wills, that it ought to be finished. But indeed they seem to have used even this κτίσεως word through mockery from the hypothesis of the Christians.

Q. 6. Should the little word κτίσεως be translated more correctly as 'creation', or rather as 'creature'? Resp. Erasmus thinks the little word κτίσεως should be translated as creation, that is, that primal production of creatures, in which sense Piscator, Tossanus, and the Photinians accept this word Rom. 1. v. 20. But it is more correctly rendered as creature or created things, in which way also the Syrian, the Latin Interpreter, and Luther rendered it. For 1. κτὶσις in the Holy Scriptures is not used concerning the action of creation, but concerning created works; nor concerning the act, but concerning the effect, that is, the very substance of creatures. Nor is this word accepted otherwise Rom. 1. v. 20. as was shown in the Exegesis vol. 1. Loc. 2. §. 74. 2. In the Scriptures these two are ἰσοδυναμοῦντα, κτίσεως & ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κόσμου, as appears from the collation of Mark 13. v. 19. with Matt. 24. v. 21. 3. When Christ in Mark at the said place uses this phrase ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως, he notably adds ἧς ἔκτισεν ὁ θεὸς, which compels us to accept this word concerning the creatures themselves, not concerning the action of creation. 4. If Peter had wished the act of creation to be understood by κτίσιν he would not have said ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως, but ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, with which phrase, in that signification which Erasmus urges, Scripture uses Matt. 13. v. 35.chap. 25. v. 34.Luke 11. v. 50.Heb. 4. v. 3.chap. 9. v. 26.Rev. 13. v. 8. 5. It is more consistent with the context of this passage that κτίσις be accepted concerning the creature, rather than concerning creation, because those mockers were urging this, that created things had always remained in the same state. 6. Erasmus himself rendered this phrase Mark 13. v. 19. as from the beginning of the creature, when both in this place and Mark 10. v. 6. he had rendered it from the beginning of the creation.

Q. 7. Should the adverb ἔκπαλαι in v. 5 be accepted concerning the primal creation of the world, or rather concerning the times of Noah? Resp. Piscator determines that it must be accepted concerning the times of Noah, moved by the argument that in the following verse it is said, ὁ τότε κόσμος, which was then the world, namely in the time of Noah. But the Apostle in this little verse is not yet dealing with the destruction of the world by the flood, but with the primal creation of the world, as Piscator himself acknowledges in the ἀναλύσει of the text, for he says that Peter's aim is that in this verse he wishes to show that it is possible for GOD to destroy the world, which he confirms by reasoning from a like case. GOD was able by His word, that is, by His command, to create the world. Therefore He will be able to destroy the same by His word.

And if the Apostle is dealing with the primordial creation of the world, then certainly το ἔκπαλαι must be understood not of the times of Noah, but of the first beginning of created things. The same appears from the words immediately following, in which he asserts that the earth was compacted by the word of God out of water and through water, which no one can deny was done in the primordial creation.

Q. 8. What is to be determined concerning the reading of certain Latin Codices, which Bede brings forward in his commentary on this place. Another, he says, edition has, the heavens were of old consisting of water and through water; which Rupert also has, book 1 on Genesis, chapter 50. Resp. 1. In this reading, earth is omitted, of which explicit mention is made in the authentic Greek text. 2. The singular number is changed into the plural, συνεστῶσα is rendered by consisting. 3. That which the Apostle predicates of the earth is attributed to the heavens. 4. Bede himself departs from that reading and follows ours.

Q. 9. Whether by water in this place is understood prime matter? Salmero affirms it, for thus he annotates on this place. How were the heavens made out of water, when they are superior and are not seen to have such a generation, that water existed before the heavens themselves, and of whose matter they could have been composed. It can be answered that by the name of water in the beginning of Genesis comes the whole of prime matter, for thus it is said. Darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters. For water easily receives an offered form, and for that reason it rightly represents prime matter, which is receptive of all forms. Just as therefore prime matter Gen. 1. v. 1. is called earth void and empty, on account of its vileness, and darkness of the abyss on account of the privations of forms: so also it is called water on account of the ease of inducing any form whatsoever, because it easily becomes circular and square and triangular, and finally receives every kind of figure according to the proportion of the vessel in which it is placed. From that water, therefore, were both the heavens and the very Elemental earth, which we tread upon.

Resp. 1. Salmero presupposes that the Apostle says that the heavens were created out of water, but we have taught in the exposition of the text that the Apostle does not say this. 2. By heaven, earth, and the abyss of waters Gen. 1. v. 1. is understood the rude and undigested mass, the confused and not yet disposed and adorned bulk, by a certain πρόληψιν by reason of the term to which, of the consequent and the end, by the name of heaven and earth called. Some call it primary matter, but differing greatly from the Aristotelian primary matter. The author of the book Wisd. ch. 11. v. 18. calls it ὕλην ἄμορφον, not because it was entirely destitute of every form, but because it was rude, unformed, destitute of that complete and ultimate form, which it obtained in the following days. August. book 1 on Genesis against the Manichaeans, ch. 7. Heaven and earth are called primary matter here, for the reason that from it on the second day heaven, and on the third day earth was to be produced. Just as if, considering the seed of a tree, we say that the roots and trunk and branches and fruits and leaves are there, not because they are already, but because they are to be. 3. Salmeron is refuted in this question by his own followers. Estius in his commentary on this place. Some wish primary matter to be signified by the name of waters, but in a sense alien to the Scriptures. Cornelius à Lapide on this place. Take heavens and earth properly, but not primary matter, as Augustine seems to wish to mean book 1 on Genesis against the Manichaeans, ch. 7. for primary matter was not created unformed, but with the form of the heavens and the earth. 4. Therefore, by the name waters properly accepted, the Apostle understands the very Element of water, in which signification he also accepts it in the verse immediately following, when he says, the ancient world perished being flooded with water.

Q. 10. In what sense is the earth said to be constituted out of water and through water? Resp. 1. Some explain the former ἐξ ὕδατος thus, that the earth consists of water as if from a part of itself, since water is still enclosed in the channels of the earth, and therefore it is said to consist of water, inasmuch as it still constitutes one globe with it, just as a gold ring, which has a gem enclosed, is said to consist of gold and gem. They explain the latter, δι' ὕδατος thus, that they establish that it is placed for ἐν ὕδατι, ἐν μέσῳ ὕδατος, in the sense that the earth floats in water; or that it is said to consist through water as through a foundation, upon which it rests Ps. 24. v. 2. Ps. 136. v. 6. 2. But it is more correctly said that Peter refers us to the creation of the earth made on the third day of the hexaemeron and described by Moses Gen. 1. v. 9. and 10., as we warned above in the exposition of the text. It is said therefore out of water, viz. to have emerged, when previously water covered the whole earth, and through water to have been compacted and constituted. 3. For although the earth emerged from the waters, and was separated from the waters, nevertheless some amount of water was still required for the consistency of the earth, so that it would not crumble and disperse into dust, and so that it would be suitable for the production and conservation of mixed bodies, whence immediately after the formation of the earth God said Gen. 1. v. 11. Let the earth bring forth the green herb, and such as may seed. For this reason these two members are joined with the best logic, because the water emerged from the earth, and yet the earth was solidified and compacted by the water. 4. The opinion of some of the ancients is the same. Philo in his book on the creation of the world argues, on the third day of the six days of creation, whatever was salty in the water, which would be harmful to the fertility of the earth, flowed together into one place, with the sweet moisture left in the earth, both as a glue for the joining together of the earth, and for the production of plants and animals. Bede in his commentary on this passage The earth consists of water, because in the beginning of creatures God said, Let the waters be gathered together into one gathering, and let the dry land appear, and it was so. It consists through water by the word of GOD, because by divine dispensation it is entirely full of veins of water within, just as we see the body of living creatures overflowing with veins of blood, so that it would not fail from dryness, if the irrigation of the waters were to cease: finally we see that in the heat of summer lands, having consumed their moisture, wither and are soon turned into dust, which the wind casts away. Oecumenius on this passage The earth from water indeed as from a material principle, but through water as through a perfecting principle. For water contains the earth like a certain glue, which is present to it, which if it did not happen to it, it would be necessary for it to be dissolved and turned into air. 5. Parallel passages of Scripture serve to confirm this exposition, in which θαυματούργημα of the third day is described. Iob. 38. v. 8. Who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke forth, as if it were coming out of the womb (an infant with great effort) coming forth? v. 9. when I made a cloud the garment thereof, and wrapped it in a thick mist as in swaddling bands? v. 10. and I set my bounds around it, and made a bar and doors, v. 11. and said: Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further (so that you may cross,) and here thou shalt break thy swelling waves. Psal. 24. v. 2. He hath founded it upon the seas, and hath prepared it upon the rivers, (with which the passage Psal. 136. v. 6. who stretched out the earth above the waters. agrees. But a certain diversity occurs in the exposition. Some interpret that founding of the earth upon the waters thus, that the earth was made higher, superior and more eminent than the waters, which previously enveloped it. Beza on this passage: The earth is said to be founded upon the waters, partly because the Lord so arranged the waters, that nevertheless if you consider only the shores, the land seems higher and in a way placed upon them; partly because, surrounded by the Ocean and irrigated by so many rivers springing up everywhere, it is truly said to be founded and stabilized in the waters themselves. Some explain it thus.

Just as Noah is said to have been saved δι' ὕδατος through the midst of the waters1 Pet. 3:20so also the earth is said to be founded upon the water i.e., through the midst of the waters. Some warn that the words of David are not to be understood concerning the whole element of water or earth, but concerning those waters which complete their courses through subterranean channels. Some establish that the particle על does not signify upon, but at, or near, so that the conjunction of both elements, namely water and earth, may be shown through it, sinceJob 26:7the earth is said to be suspended על בלי־מה upon nothing, because the earth, similar to a ball, resting on no support, hangs such a heavy burden in the balanced air. Drusius, book 9, Praeterit., page 387: The earth is not founded upon the seas or rivers, but near them. Moreover, that 'upon' is taken for 'near', 'close to', 'alongside', etc., is better known than it needs to be proven.Ps. 1:4like a tree planted upon the rivers of waters i.e., near the rivers, etc. Ps. 104:6You covered the earth with the abyss as with a garment, the waters stand above the mountainsv. 7at your rebuke they fled, etc. (On the first day, the earth was covered by the abyss as with a garment, but by the command of GOD, the earth was laid bare and separated from the waters.) v. 9You have set a boundary for them, that they may not pass over, that they may not return to cover the earth.Prov. 8:29He set His decree for the sea, that the waters should not pass His shore, when He was describing or establishing the foundations of the earth.Jer. 5:22I have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance, and it shall not pass it, and they shall move you (the waters of the sea) and they shall not prevail; its waves shall swell, and they shall not pass over it.

Q. 11. What is to be understood by the world, which is said to have perished, having been inundated by waters? Resp. 1. Some understand by the name world the human race. Estius in his commentary on this passage: Do not understand 'world' here as heaven and earth, as many interpret, but the human race, which acceptance of 'world' is most common in the Scripture of the New Testament. A parallel passage in chapter 2 of this Epistle serves to prove this position v. 5GOD did not spare the original world. 2. Others prefer to understand the earth, which is a part of the world, which was miserably devastated and corrupted by the waters of the flood. The scope of the Apostle serves to prove this exposition, which directly and principally aims at proving that this machine of the world will one day perish by fire, which ἐμπαῖκται denied: as does the opposition between τὸν τότε κόσμον, and τοὺς νῦν οὐρανοὺς in v. 6 and 7. 3. But neither exposition is opposed to the history of the flood or to the analogy of faith, therefore both can be joined, because in the flood both the globe of the earth was miserably devastated, and the men living on the earth, with the exception of eight souls, all perished submerged by the waters.

Q. 12. Of which heavens is the Apostle speaking in v. 7. ? Resp. 1. Augustine, book 20 of The City of God, chapter 18, understands it of the aerial heavens. We understand, he says, those aerial heavens, whose place and space the water had then (at the time of the flood) surpassed by rising. Therefore the whole or almost the whole of this windy air, which he calls heaven or rather heavens, but those lowest ones, not those supreme ones where the Sun and Moon and Stars are established, had been converted into a humid quality, and in this way when the earth had perished, the former face of which earth had indeed been deleted by the flood etc. Therefore the heavens and the earth which i.e. which world, for that world which perished by the flood, is stored up by the same water, it is reserved for fire at the last day of judgment. Ludovicus Vives in his commentary on this passage rightly warns that the sense is not so obscure as the context of the words. For thus Augustine concludes from the Apostolic text. Those heavens which formerly perished by the waters in the flood, those will perish by fire at the consummation of the age. But those heavens which perished by the waters in the flood are the aerial ones. Therefore. Following the footsteps of Augustine, as he is accustomed, Bede also insists here, writing thus. By the name of heavens the Apostle signifies this humid and turbid air, for Scripture is accustomed to call this heaven and sometimes heavens. 2. Among the Papists, Estius determines the same thing at this passage v. 5, commenting thus. Here and especially in the following verses the Apostle intends only to speak of the aerial heaven, and not of all of it, but of that part which contains the lowest and middle region of the air, from which the birds of the heaven and the clouds and the rains are called of the heaven. For to these regions of the heaven and no higher did the waters of the flood reach. Whence those who contend that this whole passage ought to be understood of the superelementary heaven are violent Interpreters, there the aerial heaven is understood here not only by almost all later Theologians, as well the sententiaries as the commentators of this Epistle, but also by Augustine and Bede. The same at v. 7. The heavens, which he says are reserved for fire, it is necessary that the same be understood as above, viz. the aerial ones, in respect of which he says, which now are; but not the star-bearing ones, as some wish. For nowhere does Scripture signify that the celestial orbs and the stars, which themselves are a certain fire, are to be burned and dissolved by the fire of the conflagration, which is said here of the heavens; as neither are they naturally susceptible to such a passion. Therefore the opinion of those who refer or extend this conflagration to the superelementary heavens, whether you consult Theology, they are destitute of authority; or Philosophy, of reason. The same is the opinion of Lorinus in his commentary on this passage & of Hieronymus Magius in book 2 of his work on the burning of the world, chapter 5. 3. Among the Calvinists, Piscator establishes the same in his scholia on this passage. There is in this place, he says, on verse 5, a discourse concerning the lowest heaven, namely the air, inasmuch as it perished for a time through the flood. 4. But it is more correctly established that the ethereal heavens are to be understood, which we confirm with the following arguments. First, in verse 10 & 12 following he distinguishes those heavens, which he says are reserved for fire on the day of judgment and will pass away, from the Elements & from the earth. Therefore, they cannot be understood as the aerial heavens, inasmuch as they are contained under the name of the Elements. Second, he opposes new heavens and a new earth to the heavens and earth that will perish by fire v. 13. But the new heavens and the new earth are not opposed only to the aerial, but also to the ethereal heavens. Those words, We expect new heavens, are not to be explained concerning the air, but also concerning the superior heavens, says Barradius in book 9 of his Concordance of the Gospels, chapter 11, p. 592. Therefore, the former words also, the heavens are reserved for fire, the heavens will perish, are to be accepted not only concerning the air, but also concerning the superior heavens. Third, just as it is correctly gathered from the creation of a new earth that the former is going to perish: so from the creation of a new heaven it is likewise correctly inferred that the former is going to pass away: Fourth; the Apostle asserts that those heavens will perish by fire, which the Holy Spirit also confirms in other places of Scripture will perish. But the Holy Spirit confirms that not only the aerial, but also the ethereal heavens will perish. Job 14, verse 12. Man will not rise again, until the heavens are not. Psalm 72, verse 7. In the kingdom of the Messiah a multitude of peace will flourish, until there is no more Moon. Psalm 102, verse 26. In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. v. 27. They themselves will perish, but you remain. (Lest anyone think that only the aerial heavens, and not the ethereal; only the inferior, and not the superior are going to perish, therefore the universal particle כלם all will grow old, is added, namely as many as are the works of your hands, as many as were created by GOD, as appears from verse 26.) The emphasis of this saying moved Augustine, so that in book 20 of The City of God, chapter 24, he wrote thus. It is possible in the Apostolic text 2 Peter 3 that the aerial heavens are understood as going to perish, etc., while those superior ones are saved and remain in their integrity, in whose firmament the stars are established, etc.; but this which I have mentioned from the Psalm seems to leave no heaven which is not going to perish he did not say that they exist. For where it is said, the works of your hands are the heavens, they themselves shall perish, just as none of them is separated from the work of GOD, so none of them is separated from destruction. Isa. 34. v. 4. All the host of the heavens shall melt away (The Sun, Moon, and stars, like a certain battle line arranged in a fixed order by the heavenly Commander, are called the host of the heavens or the heavenly host; of that the Prophet says that it shall melt away or dissolve) and the heavens shall be folded up like a book (where regard is had to the form of books, which the Hebrews used, different from ours. The books of the Hebrews consisted of one long and continuous page, which was rolled around a piece of wood. Just as the creation of the heaven is compared to the stretching out of a skin or a tabernacle Ps. 104. v. 2. Isa. 40. v. 22. so its destruction is most aptly compared to the folding up of a book or scroll. But lest anyone should think that the heaven is to be rolled up or folded in such a way that the stars remain fixed to it, just as the characters of letters in a folded book, therefore the Prophet adds) all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falls from the vine, and as it falls from the fig tree. Isa. 51. v. 6. The heavens shall vanish like smoke, and the earth shall grow old like a garment. Isa. 65. v. 17. Behold I create new heavens, and a new earth, and the former shall not be remembered, nor shall they come upon the heart. Matt. 5. v. 18. chap. 24. v. 35. Mark 13. v. 31. Luke 16. v. 17. chap. 21. v. 33. Heaven and earth shall pass away. Rev. 20. v. 11. from the face of him who sits upon the throne the earth and heaven fled away, and no place was found for them. chap. 21. v. 1. I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more. Fifth, from this also Augustine, even if he understood the aerial heavens by the name of the heavens in Peter, nevertheless did not wish to define that the ethereal heavens would be free from the conflagration of fire on the day of judgment. For thus he writes, as cited by Bede in his commentary on this place. The aerial heavens certainly perished, being near to the earth, according to which they are called the birds of the heaven. There are, however, he says, also the heavens of the heavens above the firmament; But whether they too are to perish by fire, or only these, which also perished by the flood, is sometimes (somewhat) a more scrupulous debate among the learned. (The passage of Augustine exists in his enarrations on Ps. 101.) But also Estius, after he had argued with great effort that in the Apostolic text the aerial heavens are to be understood, finally at verse 13. he comments thus. We do not deny that Peter's doctrine has truth, even concerning the higher heavens, in which the heavenly lights are fixed, not because those bodies are to be purged by fire, which do not need purging, but because And they themselves will undergo a transformation for the better. 5. Many among the Papists embrace the same opinion with us, that the ethereal heavens are to be understood here, as Estius himself admits in his commentary on verse 5. Ambrosius Catharinus in his commentary on 2 Peter 3 writes thus: That Peter speaks of the heavens properly, and not of the air, is clear. For after he said, in which the heavens shall be dissolved with a great noise, he added, But the elements shall be dissolved with heat, which seems to pertain to the air and to the water, which are to be dissolved by fire. But concerning the earth he says particularly, the earth and the works that are in it shall be burned up. Salmero, Disp. 4 on 2 Peter, discourses thus: Bede and other interpreters interpret the heavens in this place as the aerial ones. But this exposition seems to be forced for two reasons. First, because although heaven is sometimes taken for the air, according to that, the birds of the heaven, who covers the heaven with clouds, etc., yet the heavens in the plural number are never taken for the air, but here we read in the plural number, the heavens and the earth. Then, even if the text had heaven in the singular, where however it is said absolutely heaven and earth, the name of heaven is always accustomed to be taken for the true heaven, where the earth is opposed to it, as the Apostle does here. For heaven and earth is a sphere with a center, and therefore it signifies by synecdoche the whole universe. That if anyone should object that it is the usage of the Hebrew language to be plural rather than singular, because it is said שמים to explain the multitude of the heavens, I answer first, that such a word is not plural, but dual, which designates no more than two heavens. Then, even if I were to grant that by that word the heavens are taken also for the air and for the true heaven, yet the seventy interpreters and the Apostle Peter in this place and our interpreter have established a difference between the singular and the plural of this name οὐρανοὺς. For in the singular it can be taken for the air and for the true heaven, but in the plural it is always taken for the true heaven and not for the air; to which thing it serves, that when there is speech about those supreme bodies, etc., it is called the heaven of heaven and the heaven of heavens. Likewise when there is speech about those supreme and heavenly waters, they are always called the waters that are above the heavens. And afterwards: The air itself does not come under the appellation of the heavens, as some wish, and whatever is lower under the orb of the Moon, etc. Therefore the Apostle speaks in this place of the true heavens, of which David said: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, namely by fire, but you remain: and all shall grow old like a garment, where he shows that the true heavens and the true earth shall truly perish. And again: In this second example of the destruction of the world by fire, Peter teaches that the heavens themselves, which once remained unharmed and safe from the flood, etc., which the Philosopher he places them as unbegotten and incorruptible, they will not be able to escape the force and efficacy of fire, for they will perish utterly and will grow old and will be renewed. ibid. page 138. That some of the Fathers interpret the words of Peter not as to be understood of the highest and true heavens, but of the airy and watery ones, they are refuted even by the reason of the text itself. For we have shown first that the airy and elemental heavens are never accepted under the name of heavens in the plural number; and Peter, after the heavens have been named, adds, the Elements will be dissolved with heat. And afterwards. The elements will melt with the burning of fire, which seems to regard the air, and water, and the sphere of fire. Therefore, those three Elements cannot be accepted through the heavens, since he distinguishes the heavens twice from the Elements. All these things Salmero, which although they are not all of equal strength, yet they bear clear testimony concerning the consensus. Blasius de Viegas in comm. Apoc. 21. p. 812. confesses, in the words of Peter,v. 10.the heavens will pass away with a great rush, the celestial bodies themselves are understood. Therefore, the same are also understood in v. 7.. Cornelius à Lapide on chapter 34 of Isaiah v. 4. That exposition, by which some in the Apostolic passage 2 Pet. 3. understand the air through the heavens, does not sufficiently agree v. 10. & 12. where the Apostle opposes the heavens to the Elements. Therefore, he understands not the airy, but the sidereal heavens through the heavens. He also says, the heavens will pass away with a great rush, the Elements will be dissolved with heat; and more effectively v. 12. The heavens burning will be dissolved, and the Elements will melt with the burning of fire, where they themselves are forced to accept the highest ether through the heavens, but through the Elements the air, water, and fire, which are on the earth or around the earth. The same to this Petrine passage. The heavens signify not only the air, as Bede and others wish, but also the true heavens. And afterwards to v. 10. St. Justin, St. Jerome, Theodoret, St. Ambrose, Hilary, Nyssen, Oecumenius, and of the modern Catholics Salmeron and Serarius, have thought that the sidereal heavens will perish by fire with Basil lib. 3. hexaem. and they prove it vigorously on this passage. Hieronymus Magius, Franciscus Valesius, Ludovicus Molina and others. 6. To the argument which is brought forward for the contrary opinion, we respond that the Apostle by no means concludes in that way. The heavens perished in the flood, Therefore they will also perish at the end of the world, but in a far different way, which we explained above in the connection. But also the antecedent of this argument nowhere occurs in Peter, just as it does not agree with the History of the flood, since neither the airy nor the ethereal heavens perished in the flood. That the ethereal heavens did not perish in the flood, all concede, but that the airy heavens perished in the flood, they prove from the fact that the water increased and occupied that whole capacity where the birds fly, and thus the heavens perished according to the quantity and spaces of the air of this. But from the fact that water occupied the lowest and middle region of the air, it cannot yet be inferred that the air or the aerial heavens perished in the flood.

Q. 13. How does the Apostle infer the destruction of the heavens and the earth on the day of judgment from the fact that the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and through the water by the word of GOD. Resp. 1. Estius in comm. v. 6. establishes the force of the conclusion as follows. Since it is established from the Scriptures that the heaven was already of old, and also the earth standing out of the waters, and consisting through the waters, and that these things were done not by any power of created Nature, but by the word of GOD: yet after so many centuries, that is, after one thousand six hundred years, such a change of the same followed, that with the prior order disturbed, the heaven was mixed with the earth, the celestial waters indeed covering the whole earth again, whence it happened that the human race, suffocated by the waters, perished. It ought not, therefore, to seem incredible if it is said that even after many centuries, of the world that now is running its course, there will at some time be such a great change of heaven and earth, which will bring about the consummation of the world. 2. But it is more correctly said that the Apostle in vers. 5. & 6. brings forward two distinct arguments. In v. 5. he opposes ἐμπαίκταις the creation of the world. Whatever has been created by the word of GOD, that can be destroyed again by the word of the same GOD, however long it may have lasted, and remained in the same state. In vers. 6. the Apostle proceeds not so much κατασκευαστικῶς, as ἀνασκευαστικῶς, nor does he act so much as one arguing, as one responding. He denies in that verse the assumption in the argument ἐμπαίκτων, that the world has always remained in the same state, unvaried. For he shows that at the time of the flood a great change of things was made, and the world, which then was, being inundated by water, perished in the flood. In v. 6. from the brought forward ἐνστάσει, concerning the particular corruption of the world through the flood, he deduces the truth of the prediction concerning the destruction of the world by fire. Where, however, it is to be well noted that the Apostle does not conclude in this way: The world perished by the waters of the flood; therefore it will at some time perish by the conflagration of fire, but τὸ he is only able to urge against ἐμπαῖκτας them in this way: If GOD could destroy the world by waters particularly, certainly He could also at some time destroy it by fire universally. And this very thing was sufficient for the purpose of the Apostle; for εμπαιηται they concluded ἀδύνατον that it is impossible for the world to be destroyed, since it has remained in the same state for so long. From which it also easily appears that a comparison is not to be instituted. between the parts of the world which perished in the flood, and between those parts of the world which will perish by fire at the end of the world, since the latter destruction, being universal, embraces more parts than the former, which was only particular.

Q. 14. In what sense are the heavens and the earth said to be stored up as if in a treasury by the word of God? Resp. 1. Some take τῷ λόγῳ in the meaning of the dative case, so that the sense may be: God preserves these heavens and this earth by His word, command, and will, so that He may at some time do with them what pleases Him. 2. Others, however, take τῷ λόγῳ in the meaning of the ablative case, so that the sense may be: These heavens and this earth are preserved by the word and divine power as if in a certain treasury, not so that they may remain forever, but so that they may be destroyed at the appointed time. The word of God is as it were a certain treasury, from which He draws forth all things. Thus the treasuries of the winds Psal. 135. v. 7. Ierem. 10. v. 13. cap. 51. v. 16. the treasuries of the deeps Psalm. 33. v. 7. are their hidden receptacles, as also of the fountain Numer. 20. v. 6. of the water of rain Deut. 28. v. 12. of snow, of hail, Iob. 38. v. 22. 3. But the matter comes to the same thing in both cases. The Apostle seems to look to those places of Scripture in which God is said to open His treasury when He exercises particular judgments against the impious in this life Deuter. 32. v. 24. Is it not hidden with me, sealed up in my treasuries? v. 35. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, where it is treated of the final destruction of the Jewish people. Ierem. 50. vers. 25. God has opened His treasuries, and has brought forth the weapons of His wrath, where the discourse is about the destruction of the Babylonians. Roman. 2. v. 2. According to your impenitent heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath. Iacob. 5. v. 3. you have treasured up wrath for yourselves in the last days. Just as a treasury is acquired by the daily addition of coins, according to that common saying: Add a little to a little, you will accumulate a great heap: so the impious accumulate divine wrath by their daily sins, so that at length the whole may be drawn forth like a treasury. Just as a treasury is kept in secret: so the impious do not see the destruction prepared for them. For just as the sinner treasures up guilt for himself: so God treasures up punishment for him; He has in the treasuries of His providence, omnipotence, and justice infinite kinds of punishments with which He may punish the sins of men. Thus, therefore, because GOD will exercise universal judgment against the whole human race when He destroys heaven and earth, therefore Peter says, heaven and earth by the word of God as if in a treasury are hidden away, so that in their own time they may be consumed by the conflagration of fire. 4. Conforming to this exposition is what Augustine teaches in book 1 against the adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, that treasures are the hidden dispositions of God, so that He may punish, and that which the sinner deposits daily little by little and bit by bit, he will find later as a huge mass and heap. In his enarrations on Psal. 49. he says, that the guilt of sins is so called, because the evils which a man does, God keeps for him, bringing them forth in His own time for his vengeance.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. The earth in this place is said to have been constituted out of water and through water.v. 5.ButPsal. 24. v. 2.Psal. 136. v. 6.it is said to be stretched out and founded upon the waters. Resp. A reconciliation can be sought from the things said in q. 10.

2. The world, which was at the time of the flood, is said to have perished, being inundated with waterv. 6.But neither did all parts of the world perish by water, nor did all men in it perish, for eight souls were saved in the ark; nor did the men who perished in the flood perish according to both of their parts, because their souls were immortal.

Resp. 1. For the world to be said to have perished, it suffices that a certain part of the world, namely the earth, was miserably destroyed and lost. For that which is appropriate to a part is attributed to the whole according to that part. Bede on this passage: The earth perished, because being submerged and covered by waters, it not only lost for so long a time the state of bringing forth fruit that was implanted in it, but also received in many places a face unlike that which it had first received. 2. The preservation of eight men in the ark at the time of the flood does not prevent the whole human race from being said to have perished in the flood, because the denomination is made from the greater part, and that preservation of a few in the ark was an extraordinary miracle, without which, had it occurred, even they would have perished by the waters in the sea. 3. According to that part of themselves, men are said to have perished by the waters in the flood, which is mortal and corruptible, i.e., according to their bodies; their souls will experience their perdition and second death in Gehenna. In the same sense, Peter in v. 7. attributes to impious men ἀπώλειαν or perdition. August. book 20 of the City of God, ch. 18: He does not hesitate to speak of the perdition of men also on account of a certain great change, when nevertheless their nature is to remain, even if in eternal punishments.

3. Οι νυν ουρανοι says the Apostle v. 7. And yet the same heavens, which now are, have been from the very beginning of creation.

Resp. 1. Those who understand v. 5. & 7. as aerial heavens, which the Apostle says perished by water in the flood and will perish by fire at the end of the age, respond that regard is had not to the diversity of substance, but of accidents. Estius on this passage: The Apostle calls them the heavens and earth which are now, in distinction to the heavens and earth which were before or of old, not because they differ from them in total substance or in all qualities, but because they are different in a good part on account of the change interposed by the flood of waters, by which they perished in a certain manner, the waters changing everything. 2. Furthermore, Lorinus, from the very fact that the Apostle calls them τοὺς νῦν οὐρανοὺς,, attempts to prove that in v. 5 & 7 one must understand aerial heavens. Because, he says, heavens taken properly, namely the celestial orbs, retain their same course and natural qualities perpetually, according to that Ps. 119. v. 81. therefore by heavens in this place and v. 7. must be understood the whole region of the air, which it is agreed is subject to many changes, and at the time of the flood a very great one happened to it, etc. But we showed above that Peter nowhere says that the heavens perished in the flood. 3. The thing itself testifies that the particle νῦν in vers. 7. does not have reference to v. 5. but to v. 6. immediately preceding. For thus the Apostle's words hold. By which ὁ τότε κόσμος being flooded with water, perished, οἱ δὲ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ γῆ but the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire. The sense therefore is: As the antediluvian world perished by water, so the present world will perish by fire, from which, however, it cannot be gathered either that the heavens perished at the time of the flood, or that the heavens today are different than they were before the flood, nay rather, the Apostle notably says the world perished in the flood by water, not the heavens, so that he may absolve the heavens from that particular destruction made in the flood. He also notably says the heavens will perish by fire at the end of the age, so that he may include them in that universal destruction of the world which is to be at the end of the age. For that proposition, the ancient world perished of old by the flood, is verified in this proposition, The earth and its inhabitants perished in the flood, therefore lest anyone should think that even at the end of the age only the earth and its inhabitants, and not the heavens, are to be consumed by fire, for that reason the Apostle notably says that the heavens which are now, together with the earth, are reserved for fire. 4. Osiander from vers. 5. repeats, the heavens which were of old, and which are now, are reserved for fire, so that the sense may be: Although the heavens did not perish in the flood, and the earth emerged again from the waters, and after drying was again adorned with herbs, trees, and fruits: yet it is not to be established that the world will endure perpetually: but as the earth was once preserved in the waters until the watery flood: so now the heavens and the earth are preserved for a fiery flood.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Both the Papists and the Calvinists and especially the Photinians attack the articles of faith from natural principles, in which part they follow the footsteps of these ἐπαίκτων. Estius on v. 5: The Apostle opposes Holy Scripture to the reasoning of those mockers, taken from the perpetual course of things, which was a certain physical little argument, and that a fallacious one, since God is the author and Lord of Nature.

2.
