7. Antiquum est Diaboli artificium, Naturae cursum verbo DEI & eius promissionibus opponere, cùm tamen DEUS sit Naturae autor, qui eam pro arbitrio tùm evehere, tùm mutare, tùm planè evertere potest.

8. Sicut ignorantia invincibilis errorem & peccatum quodammodo minuit: sic affectata & voluntaria magis aggravat.

9. Qui vel in fide errant, vel in vita peccant, à Scriptura semper, quandoque etiam à conscientia sua erroris & peccati arguuntur. Matth. 22. v. 29.Erratis, nescientes Scripturas, nec virtutem Dei.Tit. 3. v. 11. quidam haeretici dicuntur αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

10. Omnipotente Dei verbo caelum visibile & corporeum in primaeva creatione est formatum; veracissimo Dei verbo caelum invisibile & spirituale credentibus est promissum. Iohan. 14. vers. 2.

11. Verbum Dei est caeli & terrae non solùm ἀρχιτεκτονικὸν sed etiam ἑδραίωμα basis & columna, cui utrumque aedificium innititur. Hebr. 1. v. 3.Portat omnia virtutis suae. Pari ratione fidei nostrae basis & fundamentum est Dei verbum.

12. Aquae in unum locum congregatio & à terra separatio est evidens divinae potentiae ac sapientiae demonstratio, quod θεούργημα praedicant dicta Scripturae superiùs citata Iob. 38. v. 8. & seqq. Psal. 104. v. 5. & seqq. Tota nostra in his terris vita nihil aliud est, quàm perpetua quaedam ab aquis diluvii in arca conservatio ac transitus per mare rubrum. Divinâ enim virtute atque imperio adhuc hodie fit, quod terra ab aquis suâ Naturâ altioribus non obruitur.

13. Stabilitas terrae itidem ut singulare divinae potentiae opus commendatur 1. Paral. 16. v. 30.Psal. 75. v. 4.Ps. 104. v. 6.Eccl. 1. v. 4. Eadem de firmitate divinarum promissionum nos admonet. Portatur terra omnipotente Dei verbo: Sic in Christo verbo Dei hypostatico omnes Dei promissiones sunt Amen. 2. Cor. 1. v. 20.

14. Inundatio diluvii quâ priscus mundus interiit, confirmat comminationum divinarum veritatem, irae divinae adversùs peccata severitatem, Dei potentiam & maiestatem, quâ omnes creaturas contra impios armare potest.

15. Verbo Dei terra ex aqua & per aquam fuit compacta & eodem consistit: verbo Dei & aquis eadem terra in diluvio fuit destructa. Ut in regno naturae verbum Dei non solùm creat & conservat, sed etiam diruit ac destruit: sic in regno gratiae verbum Dei est quibusdam odor vitae ad vitam, quibusdam odor mortis ad mortem2. Cor. 2. v. 15.

16. Horribile fuit diluvium aquae, quod arbores eradicavit, montes & aedificia diruit, totam terram miserè devastavit, & omne, in quo erat Spiritus vitae suffocavit: sed longè horribilius erit diluvium ignis, quo totum hoc universum in fine seculi conflagrabit.

17. Flagrantes prisci mundi libidines Deus aquâ extinxit, emortuam effaeti mundi caritatem igne conflagrationis accendet.

18. Habet Deus thesaurum gratiae, ex quo beneficia; habet thesaurum iustitiae & irae, ex quo supplicia depromit.

19. Dies iudicii erit impiis dies exitii; piis verò dies salutis.

20. Iudicia particularia, quae Deus in hoc seculo adversus impios quandoque exercet, sequetur iudicium universale in die iudicii, ac proinde quae impiorum scelera in hoc seculo non puniuntur temporaliter, in futuro seculo certissimè punientur in omnem aeternitatem.

## 3:4
Connection. 1. The Apostle recites μιμητικῶς the argument of those mockers, by which they are about to oppose the certainty of the coming of Christ for judgment and the destruction of the world, which holds thus. If the world has stood unmoved and unchanged for so many centuries, it is a consequence that it is about to endure forever hereafter, and therefore Christ is never about to return to institute judgment and to destroy the world. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also.

Exposition of the text. Καὶ λέγοντες, ποῦ ἔστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ. The Vulgate, with the conjunction ηαι, omitted but the disjunctive particle ἡ, inserted and the genitive παρουσίας changed into the nominative, rendered it thus. Saying, where is the promise or his coming? But the Greek properly has. And saying, where is the promise of his coming? in which way Lyranus also reads, from which it can be gathered that this reading existed in slightly older Latin Codices.

The little word Παρουσίας signifies both presence 2. Cor. 7. vers. 10. Phil. 2. v. 12. and coming Matth. 24. v. 3. 27. 37. 39. 1. Cor. 15. v. 23. etc. Augustine in the same place accepts it in the former signification, for thus he alleges this passage. Where is the promise of his presence? But it is more correctly accepted in the latter signification, in which it is also used in chapter 1 of this Epistle v. 16. and cap. 3. vers. 12. just as the Syrian also rendered it here by [מתיתה]. Moreover, as often as the noun παρουσίας is accepted concerning the return of Christ to judgment, which is most frequent in the Scriptures of the N. T., it is more correctly rendered by coming, than by presence. Promise Moreover, adventus is called the promised advent by the same phrase by which ὑπέρογκα ματαίοτητος cap. 2. v. 18. & ἔσχατον ἡμερῶν cap. 3. v. 3. the Apostle had spoken. Some explain it thus: Where is the promise of his advent, that is, where is the fulfillment of the promise concerning his advent? But the former exposition is simpler, with which, however, the latter agrees as to sense. By advent is understood the final advent of Christ for judgment, which, with respect to his first advent in the flesh, is accustomed to be called the second, from Hebr. 9. v. 28. Christ (in his first advent) was offered once to take away the sins of many, ἐκ δευτέρου the second time (in his second advent) he will appear without sin to those who wait for him for salvation. It is also called the glorious and majestic advent, with respect to the first advent, which was humble and despised.

The relative pronoun αὐτοῦ looks back to vers. 2. in which mention is made of Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος, that is, CHRIST JESUS, to which the rule can be accommodated: The Hebrews often keep silent about the subject, and leave it to be understood as if it were common and known to everyone. It could also not absurdly be thought that those Epicurean mockers, whose words the Apostle recites, did not even wish to express the name of Christ in explicit words through ἐξουθενισμὸν.

Ἀφ' ἧς γὰρ οἱ πατέρες ἐκμοιμήθησαν, πάντα οὕτω διαμένει ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως. Vulg. For since the Fathers fell asleep, all things continue so from the beginning of the creation. In the Greek, around ἀφ' ἧς, the noun ἡμέρας, must be understood, from which day the Fathers fell asleep. Von dem (Tage) an / da die Väter entschlaffen. Luther rendered it thus: Nachdem die Väter entschlaffen sind.

By τοῦς πατέρας are understood not only the Patriarchs and Prophets of the Old Testament, from whose prophecies the Christians living in the time of the Apostles were confirming the second advent of Christ for judgment, as is evident from Epist. Iudae v. 14. where the prophecy of the Patriarch Enoch is brought forward: but also the Apostles of the New Testament Fathers, from whose prophecies the Christians who will live a little before the end of the world will demonstrate the final advent of Christ for judgment. For we showed above that the Apostle is dealing directly and principally here with ἐμπαίκταις, who will live a little before the end of the world.

By τὸ ἐκοιμήθησαν fell asleep, ἐμπαίκται they understand the death of those Fathers, as it is the common of Scripture, both of the Old and New [Testament].

In the Testament, the phrase obdormitio or somnus is used Deut. 31. vers. 16.2. Sam. 7. v. 12.1. Reg. 2. v. 10.Esai. 26. v. 20. cap. 56. v. 14. Dan. 12. vers. 2.Matth. 9. v. 24.Ioh. 11. v. 11.

Πάντα οὗτω διαμένει, all things thus remain and persevere, that is, in the same state. Although so many centuries have passed, we see nothing of this world changed or abolished, but the same machine of the world remains intact according to all its parts, the same appearance of the heavens, the earth, and all parts of the world remains. Creatures acquire eternity for themselves through the propagation of the species, which they cannot obtain in individuals that perish daily. Ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως. Some think that οἷα ἦν as they were from the beginning of the creation should be understood, in which way Luther also rendered it, Es bleibet alles / wie es von Anfang der Creaturen gewesen. But we are compelled by no necessity to posit an ellipsis here, for the sense is complete, which holds as follows. From the time the Fathers fell asleep, all things thus remain, that is, in the same state from the very beginning of the creation or of created things.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Recitat Apostolus μιμητικῶς argumentum illorum irrisorum, quo certitudinem adventûs Christi ad iudicium & interitus mundi sint oppugnaturi, quod sic habet. Si mundus per tot secula immotus & invariatus perstitit, consequens est, quòd inposterum etiam semper duraturus sit, ac proinde Christus nunquam rediturus sit ad iudicium instituendum & mundum destruendum. Sed verum prius. Ergo etiam posterius.

Textus expositio. Καὶ λέγοντες, ποῦ ἔστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ. Vulg. omissâ copulâ ηαι, insertâ verò particulâ disiunctivâ ἡ, ac genitivo παρουσίας mutato in nominativum, sic reddidit. Dicentes, ubi est promissio aut adventus eius. Sed Graeca propriè habent. Et dicentes, ubi est promissio adventus eius? quo modo etiam Lyranus legit, ex quo colligi potest, in Codd. Latinis paulò antiquioribus hanc lectionem extitisse.

Παρουσίας vocula significat tùm praesentiam2. Cor. 7. vers. 10.Phil. 2. v. 12. tùm adventumMatth. 24. v. 3.27.37.39.1. Cor. 15. v. 23. &c. Augustinus d. l. accipit in priore significatione, sic enim locum hunc allegat. Ubi est promissum praesentiae eius? Sed rectiùs accipitur in posteriore significatione, in qua etiam usurpatur cap. 1. huius Epist. v. 16. & cap. 3. vers. 12. sicut & Syrus hîc reddidit per [מתיתה] Quinimò quoties παρουσίας nomen de reditu Christi ad iudicium accipitur, quod in Scripturis N. T. est frequentissimum, rectiùs per adventum, quàm per praesentiam redditur. Promissio autem adventus dicitur promissus adventus eadem phrasi, quâ ὑπέρογκα ματαίοτητοςcap. 2. v. 18. & ἔσχατον ἡμερῶνcap. 3. v. 3. Apostolus dixerat. Quidam sic exponunt. Ubi est promissio adventus eius h. e. ubi est complementum promissionis de ipsius adventu. Sed prior expositio est simplicior, cum qua tamen posterior quoad sensum convenit. Per adventum intelligitur novissimus Christi ad iudicium adventus, qui respectu primi in carnem adventus dici solet secundus, ex Hebr. 9. v. 28.Christus (in primo suo adventu) semel oblatus est ad multorum exhaurienda peccata,ἐκ δευτέρουsecundo (in secundo suo adventu) sine peccato apparebit expectantibus se in salutem. Vocatur etiam adventus gloriosus & maiestaticus, respectu primi adventus, qui fuit humilis & contemtus.

Pronomen relativum αὐτοῦ respicit ad vers. 2. in quo fit mentio Κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος h. e. CHRISTI IESU, quò accommodari potest regula. Hebraei suppositum saepe reticent, & illud quasi vulgatum & notum cuique subaudiendum relinquunt. Posset etiam haud absurdè cogitari, Epicuraeos illos irrisores, quorum verba Apostolus recitat, per ἐξουθενισμὸν ne quidem nomen Christi disertis verbis exprimere voluisse.

Ἀφ' ἧς γὰρ οἱ πατέρες ἐκμοιμήθησαν, πάντα οὕτω διαμένει ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως. Vulg. Ex quo enim Patres dormierunt, omnia sic perseverant ab initio creaturae. In Graeco circa ἀφ' ἧς sub intelligendum nomen ἡμέρας, ex quo die Patres dormiverunt. Von dem (Tage) an / da die Väter entschlaffen. Lutherus sic reddidit. Nachdem die Väter entschlaffen sind.

Per τοῦς πατέρας intelliguntur non solùm Patriarchae & Prophetae Vet. Test. ex quorum vaticiniis Christiani, tempore Apostolorum viventes, secundum Christi ad iudicium adventum confirmabant, ut patet ex Epist. Iudae v. 14. ubi Enochi Patriarchae vaticinium adducitur: sed etiam Apostoli Nov. Test. Patres, ex quorum vaticiniis Christiani, paulò ante mundi finem victuri, novissimum Christi ad iudicium adventum demonstrabunt. Ostendimus enim superiùs, Apostolum directè & principaliter hîc agere de ἐμπαίκταις, paulò ante mundi finem victuris.

Per τὸ ἐκοιμήθησανobdormiverunt,ἐμπαίκται mortem illorum Patrum intelligunt, quippe quae vulgatâ Scripturae tum V. tum N.

Test. phrasi obdormitio sive somnus vocatur Deut. 31. vers. 16.2. Sam. 7. v. 12.1. Reg. 2. v. 10.Esai. 26. v. 20. cap. 56. v. 14. Dan. 12. vers. 2.Matth. 9. v. 24.Ioh. 11. v. 11.

Πάντα οὗτω διαμένει,omnia sic permanent & perseverant, sc. in eodem statu. Quamvis tot secula praeterierint, nihil tamen huius mundi mutatum vel abolitum videmus, sed manet eadem mundi machina secundùm omnes partes integra, manet eadem caeli, terrae & omnium mundi partium facies. Creaturae per speciei propagationem aeternitatem sibi acquirunt, quam in individuis quotidiè intereuntibus obtinere non possunt. Ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως. Quidam sub intelligendum censent οἷα ἦνqualia fuerunt ab initio creaturae, quo modo etiam Lutherus reddidit, Es bleibet alles / wie es von Anfang der Creaturen gewesen. Sed nullâ necessitate cogimur, ellipsin hîc statuere, sensus enim integer est, qui sic habet. Ex quo Patres obdormiverunt, omnia sic manent, h. e. in eodem statu iam inde â creaturae sive rerum creatarum initio.

## 3:5
Connection. The Apostle refutes the argument ἐμπαίκτων, brought forward in the verse immediately preceding, by denying first the connection of the major proposition, which was formed thus. If the world has persisted unmoved and unchanged for so many centuries, it follows that it is also going to endure forever in the future. The Apostle answers that the connection is null. The duration of a state does not secure eternity for the world, nor does it prevent the creator of the world from being able to destroy it again. For however long a time the world may have endured, and persisted in the same state, it was nevertheless created at a certain time. And if GOD was able to create the world by His word, certainly He will also be able to destroy it by His word. The former is so certain that ἐμπαίκται they are convicted in their own conscience of its truth.

Exposition of the text. Λανθάνει γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοῦτο θέλοντας. Vulg. For this escapes them by their own will, that is, out of affected and gross ignorance they do not want to know what they in reality know, or certainly ought to know and can know. The pronoun τοῦτο has respect to the following, just as also in the preceding

v. 3. he had said, τους πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, that, namely, which he was immediately subjoining. Gagnaeus refers the pronoun τοῦτο to all the following things, and consequently also to the future destruction of heaven and earth, of which the Apostle treats in v. 7. It is not, he says, to be thought that Peter is saying that these things alone escape them, which they could not be ignorant of from Scripture itself; but this escapes them, that just as then the air and earth were flooded by the deluge, and the world that then was perished: so the heavens that now are, and the earth, have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire against the day of judgment. But it is more correctly said that the pronoun τοῦτο is to be referred only to those things which are brought forward from the Scriptures in v. 5. & 6. concerning the creation of the world and its destruction through the deluge.

Ὅτι οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι. Vulg. that the heavens were of old. The Apostle looks back to the first chapter of Genesis, in which the primeval creation of the heavens and the earth, and of all things that are in them, is described, and thus he opposes Holy Scripture to the reasoning of his adversaries drawn from the natural course of things. He says, therefore, that the heavens were ἔκπαλαι already of old, that is, [מן קדים] from antiquity, as the Syrian rendered it, already from the very first beginning of all things (for ἐκ has the force of intensifying, 2. Petr. 2. v. 3.) existed, understand κτισθέντας created by the word of God. For thus the Mosaic Scripture has Gen. 1. v. 6. God said, let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters v. 7. And GOD made the firmament.

Καὶ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι' ὕδατος συνεστῶσα τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ. Vulg. And the earth consisting out of water and through water by the word of God. In the Greek is the aorist συνεστῶστα compacted, concreted, constituted, as Augustine reads in book 20 of the City of GOD, chapter 18, and that ἐξ ὕδατος, is more correctly translated, out of water.

Certain Latin Codices read consisting in the plural, so that this participle may refer equally to the heavens and to the earth, in which way Oecumenius also seems to have read συνεστῶτα in the plural in the Greek, writing thus on this passage: And just as the deluge came unexpectedly upon the heaven and earth constituted out of water: so also now it is decreed that the corruption of the universe should happen through fire, with which the impious also will perish. But the Greek Codices consistently read συνεστῶσα in the singular, in which way not only Augustine in the aforementioned work, but also Jerome in his commentary on chapter 65 of the Psalms

they cite this passage. The Syriac likewise has the singular [קמת] substitit. Cornelius à Lapide in this place retains the singular consistens, and nevertheless refers it to the heavens and the earth. The consistens, he says, regards not only the earth, but also the heavens through a Hebrew syllepsis. For the Hebrews make an adjective agree with the nearer substantive, even though it may also refer to the more remote one. But no necessity compels us to establish such a syllepsis in this place, since the participle συνεστῶσα is used by the Apostle concerning the earth alone.

Leonhardus Lessius, on the divine attributes, book 13, chapter 20, establishes a transposition in the Apostolic text. The de aqua he refers to the heavens; But τὸ per aquam he refers to the earth, and explains it concerning the division of the waters above from those below, so that the sense may be: The heavens were constituted out of water, because GOD at the beginning of the world made the firmament, that is, the heaven, which would consist in the middle, and would divide the waters above from those below, and thus it would stand out from both, and would consist separately from both: but the earth was constituted through water, when he gathered the waters which were under the firmament into one place, and through the midst of the waters the dry land appeared. Cornelius à Lapide judges this exposition to be genuine. But the same presupposes that the little word συνεστῶσα must be referred not only to the earth, but also to the heavens, which is false.

When, however, the Apostle says that the earth consists out of water and through water, he sends us back to the creation of the earth made on the third day of the hexaemeron and described by Moses, just as in the preceding words, by the consensus of all interpreters, he had sent us back to the creation of the heaven, described v. 6. & 7. That formation of the earth, however, is described by Moses thus: Gen. 1. v. 9. And God said, Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so. v. 10. And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas. The sense, therefore, of the Apostolic statement is this, καὶ γῆ i.e., ἦν (which must be repeated from the preceding) ἐξ ὕδατος i.e., out of water, namely it emerged, it stood forth, so that ἐξ ὕδατος is the same as ἐκτος ὕδατος; or it was separated from the waters, since previously water covered and enveloped the whole earth; ηαι διυδατος συνεστῶσα and through water it was constituted, compacted, solidified, consisting.

What is finally added τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ, that not only to the nearer, namely to γῆν, nor only to the more remote, namely but it must be referred to both οὐρανοὺς,, in that sense, that both the heavens already long ago existed, namely created by the word of God; and that the earth already long ago was established and compacted by the word of God out of water and through water. For Moses testifies to both; the former, when he writes, God said, let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters: the latter, when he writes, God said, let the waters be gathered into one place, that the dry land may appear, to which pertain the parallel passages, in which all things and thus not only heaven and earth, but also water are said to have been created by the word of God. Psal. 33. v. 9.Psal. 148. v. 5. The following v. 7. requires the same exposition, in which the heavens, which now are, and the earth are said to be reserved by the same word, where ὁ λόγος (certainly τοῦ θεοῦ ) is likewise referred to both. Therefore we cannot prove that Piscator establishes a transposition here, and connects those words τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ with those ὅτι οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι, such a transposition as he says occurs in Apoc 13. v. 8. in which place, just as in this one of ours, we deny that that feigned transposition of words must be established.

Latin:

Connexio. Refellit Apostolus argumentum ἐμπαίκτων, in versu proximè praecedente adductum, negando primùm connexionem maioris propositionis, quae sic informata erat. Si mundus per tot secula immotus & invariatus persitit, consequens est, quod inposterum etiam semper duraturus sit. Respondet Apostolus, connexionem esse nullam. Diuturnitas status non conciliat mundo aeternitatem, nec impedit, quò minùs mundi creator eundem iterum destruere possit. Quanto cunque tempore mundus duraverit, inque eodem statu perstiterit, tamen certo tempore est creatus. Atquisi DEUS verbo suo potuit mundum creare, utique etiam verbo suo eundem poterit destruere. Prius tàm certum est, ut ἐμπαίκται in conscientia sua de eius veritate convincantur.

Textus expositio. Λανθάνει γὰρ αὐτοὺς τοῦτο θέλοντας. Vulg. Latet enim eos hoc volentes, hoc est ex affectata & crassa ignorantia scire nolunt, quod reverâ sciunt, vel certè scire debent & possunt. Pronomen τοῦτο respectum habet ad sequentia, sicut etiam in praeced.

v. 3. dixerat, τους πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, illud sc. quod statim subiiciebat. Gagnaeus pronomen τοῦτοadomnia sequentia refert, ac proinde etiam ad futurum caeli terraeque interitum, de quo Apostolus agit v. 7. Non est, inquit, putandum, quod dicat Petrus, haec illos tantummodò latere, quae ex ipsa Scriptura nescire non poterant; sed hoc eos latet, quod sicut tunc aër & terra inundaverunt diluvio, & mundus qui tunc erat periit: ita caeli, qui nunc sunt, & terra, eodem verbo repositi sunt, igni reservati in diem iudicii. Sed rectiùs dicitur, pronomen τοῦτο tantùm ad ea referendum, quae in v. 5. & 6. de mundi creatione, eiusque per diluvium destructione ex Scripturis adducuntur.

Ὅτι οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι. Vulg. quòd caeli erant priùs. Respicit Apostolus ad primum caput Geneseos, in quo caeli & terrae, atque omnium, quae sunt in eis, primaeva creatio describitur, sicque ratiocinationi adversariorum ex naturali rerum cursu petitae opponit Scripturam sacram. Dicit ergò, caelos fuisseἔκπαλαιiam olim hoc est, [מן קדים]ab antiquo, ut Syrus reddidit, iam inde â primo rerum omnium initio ( ἐκ enim habet vim intendendi, 2. Petr. 2. v. 3.) extitisse, sub intellige κτισθέντας creatos per Dei verbum. Sic enim habet Scriptura Mosaica Gen. 1. v. 6.Dixit Deus, fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, & dividat aquas ab aquis v. 7. Et fecit DEUS firmamentum.

Καὶ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι' ὕδατος συνεστῶσα τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ. Vulg. Et terra de aqua & per aquam consistens Dei verbo. In Graeco est aoristus συνεστῶστα compacta, concreta, constituta, ut legit Augustinus lib. 20. de Civ. DEI cap. 18. ac illud ἐξ ὕδατος, rectiùs vertitur, ex aqua.

Quidam Codd. Latini legunt consistentes in plurali, ut aequè ad caelos ac ad terram participium hoc referatur, quo modo etiam in Graeco συνεστῶτα in plurali legisse videtur Oecumenius, in h. l. sic scribens. Et quemadmodum caelo ac terra ex aqua constitutis diluvium inopinatò supervenit: ita & nunc statutum est, ut per ignem fiat universi corruptio, cum quo impii quoque peribunt. Sed Graeci Codd. constanter legunt συνεστῶσα in singulari, quo modo etiam non solùm Augustinus d. l. sed etiam Hieronymus in comm. cap. 65 Psai.

locum hunc citant. Syrus itidem habet singulare [קמת]substitit. Cornelius â Lapide in h. l. retinet singulare consistens, ac nihilominus ad caelos ac terram illud refert. Tò consistens, inquit, nont tantùm terram, sed etiam caelos respicit per syllepsin Hebraicam. Hebraei enim adiectivum concordant cum substantive proximiori, licet ad remotius quoque referatur. Sed ad statuendam istiusmodi syllepsin hoc loco nulla nos cogit necessitas, cùm de sola terra participium συνεστῶσα ab Apostolo usurpatur.

Leonhardus Lessius de attrib. div. lib. 13. cap. 20. statuit in textu Apostolico traiectionem. Tò de aqua refert ad caelos; Sedτὸper aquam refert ad terram, & explicat de divisione aquarum superarum ab inferis, ut sit sensus. Caeli constituti sunt ex aquis, quia DEUS initio mundi fecit firmamentum, puta caelum, quod medium consisteret, divideretque aquas superas ab inferis, itaque ex utrisque extaret, & ab utrisque separatim consisteret: terra verò constituta fuit per aquam, quando aquas, quae erant sub firmamento, congregavit in unum locum, & per medium aquarum apparuit arida. Hanc expositionem Cornelius â Lapide iudicat esse genuinam. At eadem praesupponit voculam συνεστῶσα non solùm ad terram, sed etiam ad caelos referendam esse, quod falsum.

Quando autem terram ex aqua & per aquam consistere dicit Apostolus, remittit nos ad creationem terrae die tertio hexaëmeri factam & descriptam â Mose, sicut in praecedentibus verbis omnium Interpp. consensu remiserat nos ad creationem caeli, descriptam v. 6. & 7. Illa verò terrae formatio â Mose sic describitur. Gen. 1. v. 9.Et dixit Deus. Congregentur aquae de sub caelis ad locum unum, ut conspiciatur arida, & factum est ita. v. 10. Et vocavit Deus aridam, terram, & congregationem aquarum vocavit maria. Sensus igitur dicti Apostolici hic est, καὶ γῆ sc. ἦν (quod repetendum ex praecedentibus) ἐξ ὕδατος i. e. ex aqua, scilicet emersit, extitit, ut ἐξ ὕδατος sit idem, quod ἐκτος ὕδατος; vel ab aquis separata est, cùm priùs aqua totam terram operiret atque involveret; ηαι διυδατος συνεστῶσα& per aquam constituta, compacta, solidata, consistens.

Quod postremò subiicitur τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ, illud non solùm ad propinquius, videlicet ad γῆν, nec solùm ad remotius, videlicet ad οὐρανοὺς, sed ad utrumque reserendum est, sensu eo, quod & caeli iam olim extiterint verbo Dei scil. creati; & quod terra iam olim verbo Dei ex aqua & per aquam constituta fuerit atque compacta. Utrumque enim testatur Moses; prius, quando scribit, Dixit Deus, fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum: posterius, quando scribit, Dixit Deus, congregentur aquae in locum unum, ut appareat arida, quò pertinent loca parallela, in quibus omnia & sic non solùm caelum & terra, sed etiam aqua dicuntur verbo Dei creata. Psal. 33. v. 9.Psal. 148. v. 5. Eandem expositionem requirit sequens v. 7. in quo caeli, qui nunc sunt & terra eodem verbo dicuntur repositi, ubi ὁ λόγος (utique τοῦ θεοῦ) itidem ad utrumque refertur. Probare igitur non possumus, quod Piscator hîc traiectionem statuit, ac verba illa τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγῳ cum illis, ὅτι οὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι connectit, qualem traiectionem occurrere dicit Apoc 13. v. 8. in quo loco aequè ac in hoc nostro confictam illam verborum traiectionem statuendam esse negamus.

## 3:6
Connection. 1. Just as in the preceding verse the Apostle had denied the connection in the argument of the scoffers, so now furthermore he denies the assumption of the same. This assumption was: The world has remained unmoved and unchanged for so many centuries ever since its first creation. The Apostle denies this, showing that the ancient world perished in the inundation of waters in the flood. For although the world was not utterly destroyed in the flood, yet the whole orb of the lands was miserably devastated and corrupted, and the face of things changed and deformed, so that it cannot truly be said that all things have remained perpetually unchanged in the same state from the beginning. Certainly, that the whole world perished with the exception of eight souls is not for all things to persevere in the same tenor.

2. Therefore the Apostle also recalls the minds of the pious to the destruction of the world by the flood, because without doubt even before the flood there existed such scoffers, who mocked Noah preaching about the destruction of the world and building the ark, saying: If the world stood for one thousand and six hundred years in water, is it to be feared that it will be overwhelmed by the waters?

Exposition of the text. Δι' ὧν ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο. Vulg. By which the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished. But obscurely and ambiguously, as will be evident from what is to be said. The initial words δι' ὧν. 1. some, among whom are Beza, Piscator, Tossanus, etc., determine that they are to be translated illatively, wherefore, for which reason; they wish the genitive to be placed for the accusative, διὰ but with the accusative signifies because of Ioh. 6. v. 57. δι' ἐμὲ because of me. Rom. 3. v. 25. δια τὴν παρέσιν because of the remission. In the same signification they take these little words δι' ὧν in chapter 1 of this Epistle v. 4. so that the sense may be: Because the earth did not exist of itself, but was created by the word of God: therefore the world, which then was, perished overflowed with water. Or, because the earth consists out of water and in water, thence it happened that it was overwhelmed by the waters in the flood, the waters surely reclaiming their ancient seats, by the command of Him, by whose order they had once receded from the earth. But 1. concerning this signification of the words δι' ὧν it is deservedly doubted, since it has not yet been confirmed by suitable examples. 2. The creation of the earth was not the cause of the flood. 3. Nor was this properly the cause of the flood, that the waters enveloped the earth before they departed by the command of creation; but the sins of men were solely the cause of the flood. 4. In the flood not only were the fountains of the great deep broken up, but also the windows of heaven were opened and a huge rain descended. Gen. 7. v. 11.

2. Some think that B. Luther rendered the words δι' ὧν in an adversative sense. For thus he rendered it: Dennoch ward zu der Zeit die Welt mit der Sündfluth verderbet. But the thing itself testifies that B. Luther did not take those words δι' ὧν in an adversative sense, which they also nowhere obtain; but for the sake of clarity he inserted an adversative particle, for he rendered those words δι' ὧν thus, Durch dieselbe.

3. Most simply, therefore, δι' ὧν is rendered in the way in which the Vulgate rendered it, namely by which. But soon a question emerges, to which member from the preceding ones is that ὧν to be referred?

1. Some refer it to οὐρανοὺς, so that the sense may be, by the heavens, i.e., by the rains poured out from heaven, the world submerged in waters perished, to which they accommodate the fact that Gen. 7. v. 11. the windows of heaven are said to have been opened, and a huge rain is said to have descended. Estius in his commentary on this place. But it is a harsh catachresis to understand by the heavens the rains poured out from heaven,

2. Bede in his commentary refers to οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν,, for thus he annotates on this passage: By which, he says by the heavens and the earth, which he had named before. For by these lost things the world, which had consisted in these, (had stood) perished. For the flood did not touch the higher parts of the world in the least. Therefore the earth perished, because it was submerged and covered by the waters, etc., and the heavens perished according to the quantity and spaces of this air. Thus, therefore, Bede does not take the relative ὧν as the cause of the destruction, but as the object of the destruction. In almost the same way the interlinear Gloss: by which, that is, in which parts, the air and the earth. Barradius, in volume 3 of the Concordance of the Gospels, book 10, chapter 1, insists on the footsteps of Bede: By which heavens and earth the world was oppressed by the flood. But it perished not by the higher heavens, from which not even a drop of water flowed out, but by the lower air, whose cataracts were opened, and poured out an infinite abundance of waters onto the lands. But the world perished inundated by the earth, because the world was overwhelmed by the flood through the waters which are above the earth, that is, through the waters of the sea and the rest which are included in the bowels of the earth. Gagnaeus explains it in the same way in his commentary. But the earth was the receiving or passive subject of the corruption, but not the acting cause, of which the Apostle treats in this place.

3. Some refer to the heavens, the earth, and the water, of all of which in the preceding verse 5 mention had been made, so that the sense may be: From the heavens, that is, from the air, it rained for forty continuous days; and the lower waters, which were in the bowels of the earth, the earth vomiting them forth, erupted and overflowed. But by the heavens in v. 5. the air is not understood, but the ethereal or starry heaven, as we shall demonstrate a little later. It is also harsh and unusual to say that the world perished by the earth, that is, by the waters poured out from the bowels of the earth.

4. Most simply, therefore, the pronoun ὧν is referred to the word of God and the water, of which mention had been made in the preceding verse, as Blessed Luther explained in the marginal gloss. By which, that is, by the word and the water, so that the sense may be: Just as the world was created from the beginning by the word of GOD: so also it perished in the flood by the word of GOD, that is, by the will and command of GOD. And just as the earth in the first creation emerged from the waters and was separated from them, so that they would no longer envelop the earth: so at the time of the flood, the fountains of the great deep being broken up, the water again overwhelmed the earth, and again occupied its natural place.

Ὁ τότε κόσμος i.e. ὦν or γεγονὸς the world that then was, the ancient world, ὁ κόσμος ἀρχαῖος, as he called it in the preceding chapter, v. 5. For the adverb τότε does not pertain to the verb ἀπώλετο, as some wish, but to the noun κόσμος, which is most manifest from the Greek text, not equally clear from the Latin version.

Ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς inundated with water, overwhelmed, whence the flood is called by the Greeks κατακλυσμὸς. The Syrian rendered it by [טף] from the root [טוף] he was submerged, whence the flood is called by the Syrians [טופנא] Augustine, book 20 de Civ. DEI, chapter 18, cites the passage thus, inundated with water, it perished. But what is to be understood by the verb ἀπώλετο will be clear when we have explained in the questions what is denoted by the word world in this verse.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Sicut in versu praeced. Apostolus negaverat connexionem in argumento irrisorum, ita iam porrò negat eiusdem assumtio nem. Assumtio haec erat. Mundus iam inde â prima sui creatione per tot secula immotus & invariatus perstitit. Negat hoc Apostolus, ostendens, priscum mundum in diluvio aquarum inundatione periisse. Quamvis enim mundus in diluvio non sit penitus destructus, tamen totus terrarum orbis miserè fuit vastatus & corruptus, ac facies rerum mutata & desormata, ut verè dici nequeat, omnia ab initio in eodem statu perpetuò invariata mansisse. Certè totum mundum exceptis octo animabus periisse, non est eodem tenore omnia perseverare.

2. Ideò etiam Apostolus ad destructionem mundi per diluvium animos piorum revocat, quia dubio procul etiam ante diluvium extiterunt eiusmodi illusores, qui Noam de interitu mundi concionantem & arcam exaedificantem irriserunt, dicentes. Si mundus per mille & sexcentos annos in aqua constitit, an metuendum, ut ab aquis obruatur?

Textus expositio. Δι' ὧν ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο. Vulg. Per quae ille tunc mundus aquâ inundatus periit. Sed subobscurè & ambiguè, ut patebit ex dicendis. Verba initialia δι' ὧν. 1. quidam, inter quos Beza, Piscator, Tossanus &c. statuunt vertenda esse illativè, quapropter, quamobrem; genitivum positum volunt pro accusativo,διὰautem cum accusativo significat propterIoh. 6. v. 57.δι' ἐμὲpropter me.Rom. 3. v. 25.δια τὴν παρέσινpropter remissionem. In eadem significatione voculas hasce δι' ὧν accipiunt cap. 1. huius Epist. v. 4. ut sit sensus. Quia terra non extitit â seipsa, sed per Dei verbum fuit creata: ideò mundus, qui tunc erat aquâ inundatus periit. Vel, quia terra ex aqua & in aqua consistit, inde factum, ut aquis in diluvio fuerit obruta, antiquas nimirum fedes aquis repetentibus, mandato illius, cuius imperio olim â terra recesserant. Atqui 1. de hac significatione vocularum δι' ὧν meritò dubitatur, cùm nondum sit idoneis exemplis confirmata. 2. Creatio terrae non fuit diluvii causa. 3. Nec haec fuit propriè diluvii causa, quòd aquae terram, ante quam creationis iussu discederent, obvolverint; sed peccata hominum unicè diluvii causa fuerunt. 4. in diluvio non folùm rupti sunt fontes abyssi magnae, sed etiam apertae caeli fenestrae & ingens pluvia descendit.Gen. 7. v. 11.

2. Quidam existimant. B. Lutherum reddidisse verba δι' ὧνin sensu adversativo. Sic enim reddidit. Dennoch ward zu der Zeit die Welt mit der Sündfluth verderbet. Sed res ipsa testatur, B. Lutherum verba illa δι' ὧν non accepisse in sensu adversativo, quem etiam nuspiam obtinent; sed perspicuitatis gratiâ particulam adversativam inseruisse, verba enim illa δι' ὧν sic reddidit, Durch dieselbe.

3. Simplicissimè igitur δι' ὧν redditur eo modo, quo vulgata reddidit, videlicet per quae. Sed mox emergit quaestio, ad quod membrum ex praecedentibus illudὧνsit referendum?

1. Quidam referunt ad οὐρανοὺς, ut sit sensus, per caelos h. e. imbres caelitus effusos mundum aquis subersum periisse, quò accommodant, quòdGen. 7. v. 11.fenestrae caeli dicuntur apertae, ac ingens pluvia dicitur descendisse. Estius in comm. h. l. Sed durâ est catachresis, per caelos intelligere imbres caelitus effusos,

2. Beda in comm, refert ad οὐρανοὺς καὶ γῆν, sic enim ad h. l. annotat. Per quae, per caelos & terram dicit, quae priùs nominaverat. Per haec enim perdita mundus, qui in his constituerat (constiterat) periit. Nam superiores mundi partes diluvium minimè tangebat. Periit ergò terra, quia submersa & cooperata aquis &c. perierunt & caeli secundùm quantitatem & spacia aëris huius. Sic ergò Beda relativum ὧν non accipit pro perditionis causâ, sed pro perditionis obiecto. Eodem ferè modo Glossa interlin. per quae h. e. in quibus partibus aëre & terra. Bedae vestigiis insistit Barradius tom. 3. Concord. Evang. lib. 10. cap. 1. Per quos caelos & terram mundus diluvio oppressus est. Periit autem non per caelos superiores, ex quibus ne gutta quidem aquae effluxit, sed per inferiorem aërem, cuius cataractae apertae sunt, aquarum copiam infinitam in terras effuderunt. Per terram a. mundus inundatus periit, quia per aquas, quae supra terram sunt, h. e. per aquas maris & reliquas quae terrae visceribus includuntur, obrutus est mundus diluvio. Eodem modo exponit Gagnaeus in comm. Atqui terra fuit subiectum recipiens seu patiens corruptionis, non autem causa agens, de qua Apostolus hoc loco agit.

3. Quidam referunt ad caelos, terram & aquam, quorum omnium in praeced. v. 5. facta erat mentio, ut sit sensus. Ex caelis h. e. ex aëre pluit continuis quadraginta diebus; & aequae inferiores, quae erant in terrae visceribus, evomente eas terrâ eruperunt & exundârunt. Sed per caelos in v. 5. non intelligitur aër, sed caelum aethereum sive stellatum, ut paulò pòst demonstrabimus. Durum etiam atque insolens est dicere, quòd mundus per terram h. e. per aquas ê terrae visceribus effusas perierit.

4. Simplicissimè igitur pronomen ὧν refertur ad Dei verbum & aquam, quorum in vers. praecedente facta erat mentio, quomodo B. Lutherus in glossa marginali exposuit. Per quae h. e. per verbum & aquam, ut sit sensus. Sicut per verbum DEI mundus ab initio fuit conditus: ita quoque per verbum DEI h. e. DEI voluntate & mandato in diluvio periit. Ac sicut terra in prima creatione ex aquis emersit & ab eis separata est, ut non ampliùs terram involverent: ita tempore diluvii, ruptis abyssi magnae fontibus, aqua terram iterum obruit, ac locum suum naturalem iterum occupavit.

Ὁ τότε κόσμος sc. ὦν sive γεγονὸςmundus qui tunc erat, mundus priscus,ὁ κόσμος ἀρχαῖος, ut eum vocavit cap. praeced. 2. v. 5. adverbium enim τότε non pertinet ad verbum ἀπώλετο, ut quidam volunt, sed ad nomen κόσμος, quod ex Graeco textu manifestissimum, ex Latina versione non aequè perspicuum.

Ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶςaquâ inundatus, obrutus, unde diluvium Graecis vocatur κατακλυσμὸς. Syrus reddidit per [טף] â rad. [טוף]submersus est, unde diluvium Syris vocatur [טופנא] August. lib. 20. de Civ. DEI cap. 18. locum sic citat, aquâ inundatus deperiit. Quid autem per verbum ἀπώλετο accipiendum sit, patebit, quando in quaestionibus exposuerimus, quid per mundi vocabulum in hoc versiculo denotetur.

## 3:7
Connection. From the ἐνστάσει, brought forward in the verse immediately preceding concerning the particular corruption of the world through the flood, which the Apostle had opposed to the assertion of the scoffers, that the world had remained unmoved and unchanged from the beginning of the creation for so many ages, he deduces the truth of the prediction concerning the destruction of the world by fire. For he who was able to destroy the world by water particularly and inchoatively, he will also be able to destroy the same by fire universally and completely.

Exposition of the text. Οἱ δὲ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσι. Vulg. But the heavens which now are and the earth by the same word are kept in store, which version is ambiguous. Luth. Also auch der Himmel ietzund. But in the Greek Codices there is an adversative. For those who have not looked into the Greek Codices, in which is held τεθησαυρισμένοι treasured up, hidden in a treasury, they took the participle kept in store in that sense, that the heavens are placed again or restored into their former state. And yet if Peter wished this, he would not add οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ, but would simply say οἱ οὐρανοὶ; for by saying, which now are, he supposes them to be already restored, so that we may pass over the Greek since θησαυρίζειν nowhere signifies a restoration to a former state; rather, it signifies in this place the storing up of the heavens in the treasury of divine providence. Lyranus rendered it, preserved, and adds, because if the preserving power of God were withdrawn from them, they would be reduced to nothing. The Syriac translates it, [אסנין] they are heaped up or they are being heaped up. Luth. Sie werden gesparet.

For >τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ some Greek Codices have >τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ Beza in his annotations on this place says, I read τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ partly from the authority of the old Interpreter, and partly from that of two ancient Codices, for it is a much richer reading than if you read αυτου ηογω. But αὐτοῦ λόγῳ is also held in v. 5. and in that way also the Syriac rendered it [במלתא דילה] by his word, as also Luther. Die Himmel werden durch sein Wort gesparet.

Although there is no certain diversity in the sense, because the word, by which the heavens are preserved as if hidden in a treasury, in a general concept is the same word with that, by which the ancient world perished in the flood, we nevertheless prefer the reading, which has αὐτοῦ λόγῳ, as being conformable to the more approved Codices and to the other ἐμφατικωτέραν, For the pronoun αὐτοῦ has this sense. It is God, who once created the world by his word; it is the same, who once destroyed the world by his word; it is the same, who preserves the world as if in a treasury by his word, so that it may one day be destroyed by fire. Since he himself is omnipotent, therefore he was able to perform all things by his word, or rather by his nod, and by his word, or rather by his nod, he will one day destroy the world Πυρὶ τηρούμενοι, Vulg. reserved for fire. But the Greek τηρούμενοι is of the present tense, are preserved for fire, i.e. so that in their own time they may be consumed by fire, for thus he explains it a little later v. 10.. The Syriac rendered it [לנורא מתנטרין] are reserved for fire. The Apostle therefore opposes the destruction of the world made by water at the time of the flood, and the destruction of the world to come by fire at the time of the final judgment, just as is immediately added.

Εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων. Vulg. for the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men. The sense is, that are kept for the fire until the day of judgment, namely that final and universal one. Some render it of damnation, so that κρίσις is put for κατακρίσει, and they join it with the following noun ἀπωλείας, in this way: Until the day of the damnation and destruction of ungodly men, that is, in which ungodly men will be adjudged to damnation and destruction. But the matter comes to the same thing, since on one and the same day both the universal judgment will be instituted, and ungodly men will be condemned to everlasting destruction. For the Apostle makes notable mention of the perdition of the ungodly for this reason, because just as in the day of judgment fire will consume heaven and earth: so also will the ungodly in that same day of judgment hear that horrible sentence of the judge, Matth. 25. v. 41. Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the Devil and his angels.

Latin:

Connexio Ex allatâ in versu proximè praecedente ἐνστάσει, de corruptione mundi particulari per diluvium, quam Apostolus opposuerat assertioni irrisorum, quod mundus iam inde â principio creaturae per tot secula immotus & invariatus perstiterit, deducit veritatem praedictionis de mundi per ignem interitu. Qui enim mundum per aquam destruere potuit particulariter & inchoativè, ille etiam eundem destruere poterit per ignem universaliter & completivè.

Textus expositio. Οἱ δὲ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσι. Vulg. Caeli autem qui nunc sunt & terra eodem verbo repositi sunt, quae versio est ambigua. Luth. Also auch der Himmel ietzund. Sed in Graecis Codd. est adversativa. Qui enim Graecos Codices non introspexerunt, in quibus habetur τεθησαυρισμένοιthesaurizati, in thesauro reconditi, illi participium repositi acceperunt sensu eo, quod caeli sint iterum positi sive in priorem statum restituti. Atqui si Petrus hoc vellet, non adderet οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ, sed simpliciter diceret οἱ οὐρανοὶ; dicendo enim, qui nunc sunt, supponit iam esse restitutos, ut praetermittamus, Graecum cum θησαυρίζειν nuspiam significare restitutionem in priorem statum; significatur potiùs h. l. repositio caelorum in thesaurum divinae providentiae. Lyranus reddidit, conservati, & addit, quoniam si virtus Dei conservans ab eis retraheretur, in nihilum redigerentur. Syrus vertit, [אסנין]coacervati sunt vel coacervantur. Luth. Sie werden gesparet.

Pro >τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ quidam Codd Graeci habent >τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ Beza in annot. h. l. Legoτῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳpartim ex veteris Interpretis, partim ex duorum vetustorum Codd. autoritate, multò enim est uberior lectio, quàm si legasαυτου ηογω. Sed αὐτοῦ λόγῳ habetur etiam in v. 5. ac eo modo etiam Syrus reddidit [במלתא דילה]in verbo eius, uti etiam Luther. Die Himmel werden durch sein Wort gesparet.

Quamvis verò in sensu non sit quaedam diversitas, quia verbum, quo caeli servantur velut in thesauro reconditi, in generali conceptu est idem verbum cum eo, quo priscus mundus diluvio periit, praeferimus tamen lectionem, quae habet αὐτοῦ λόγῳ, utpote probatioribus Codicibus conformem ac alterâ ἐμφατικωτέραν, Pronomen enim αὐτοῦ hunc habet sensum. Deus est, qui verbo suo olim mundum creavit; idem est, qui verbo suo olim mundum destruxit; idem est, qui verbo suo mundum velut in thesauro conservat, ut per ignem aliquando destruatur. Ipse cùm sit omnipotens, ideò verbo suo, imò nutu omnia praestare potuit, ac verbo suo, imò nutu, mundum aliquando destruet Πυρὶ τηρούμενοι, Vulg. igni reservati. Sed Graecum τηρούμενοι est praesentis temporis, servantur igni, h. e. ut suo tempore igne concrementur, ita namque paulò pòst v. 10. exponit. Syrus redd. [לנורא מתנטרין]ad ignem reservantur. Opponit igitur Apostolus perditionem mundi factam per aquam tempore diluvii, & perditionem mundi futuram per ignem tempore extremi iudicii, sicut statim additur.

Εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων. Vulg. in diem iudicii & perditionis impiorum hominum. Sensus est, quòd serventur ad ignem usque in diem iudicii, sc. extremi illius & universalis. Quidam reddunt damnationis, ut κρίσις ponatur pro κατακρίσει, & coniungunt cum sequente nomine ἀπωλείας, hoc modo. Usque in diem damnationis & exitii impiorum hominum h. e. in quo homines impii damnationi & exitio adiudicabuntur. Sed res eodem redit. siquidem uno eodemque die & iudicium universale instituetur, & homines impii sempiterno exitio damnabuntur. Ideò enim Apostolus notanter meminit perditionis impiorum, quia ut in die iudicii ignis caelum & terram absumet: ita quoque impii in eodem iudicii die audient horribilem illam iudicis sententiam, Matth. 25. v. 41.Discedite â me maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est Diabolo & Angelis eius.

## 3:8
Connection. 1. The Apostle shakes off that ἐμπαίκτων, in the argument that the world has remained in the same state for several ages, from which he inferred that it would remain in such a state perpetually. The Apostle responds that as nothing is great to GOD, so also nothing is long-lasting to Him, since with Him a thousand years are as one day.

2. By a certain prolepsis, he meets both the objection of the mockers and the silent thought of the weak, that the coming of Christ to judgment, and thus also the day of the destruction of the world, is being delayed. The Apostle responds that this should not seem long to anyone, nor should GOD be accused of slowness on this account, since with Him a thousand years are as one day. To us, a thousand years seem a long time, but with the eternal and infinite God, there is a far different method of calculation.

3. Bede on this passage offers such a connection. Therefore the Apostle mentions these things, in order to convict those whom he had previously mentioned as saying, where is the promise of His coming? showing that the Lord is by no means forgetful of His promise or of His coming to judge the living and the dead: but since He so embraces each day of our age in His eternal memory as the circuit of a thousand years: so He surveys a thousand years as the space of one day without labor, it is clearly to be understood that He most certainly knows the end of those very days and of all years, when the brightness of His coming is to be revealed, when the promised rewards are to be rendered to the saints.

4. By the same effort the Apostle confirms the minds of the pious, so that they may not doubt concerning the promised coming of Christ to judgment, even if it seems to be deferred for some time; and he represses the curiosity of idle men, so that they may not inquire into the certain and definite time of that coming, but rather prepare themselves for it at every hour and moment.

5. The Ordinary Gloss hands down such a connection as this. Having proved that the judgment will truly be, he shows how effective it will be. If it is said to you by the Pseudo-Apostles, that you can do what you want, because so much time remains until the day of judgment, that because of the length of time the judge will not be able to know many things, do not believe them, because whatever can be done in a thousand years, he sees just as that which is done in one day. If they say, by repenting for a thousand years you will not obtain forgiveness of sins, do not believe, because one day of true repentance is worth as much as a thousand years, as to the thief. If they say, it is not necessary to labor for so long, you can take a breath for one day, do not believe, because a thousand years of labor do not suffice for life any more than one day. And since the judgment is to be, therefore do not be seduced by the Pseudo-teachers, who say to you, that even if the judgment is to be, it is not however to be feared by you, because since there are so many thoughts and so many acts of men, if they must be discussed one by one, thousands of years will not suffice, since it is said that the judgment will be in one single day, and thus many things will be able to be hidden from the judge. But let this not be hidden from you, that one day is worth as much before God for doing something, as a thousand years for men for doing the same thing.

Exposition of the text. Ἐν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοὶ. Vulg. But let this one thing not be hidden from you, most dear. In the Greek it is, beloved. Two Royal Codices for ἀγαπητοὶ substitute ἀδελφοὶ. The Syrian in his own manner rendered [חביבי] my beloved. By the word λανθάνειν some establish that the Apostle looks to this, that the day of the coming of Christ and of the final judgment is hidden, so that the sense may be. Although the day in which Christ is to come to judgment and is to destroy the world is hidden, this however ought by no means to be hidden from you, but as often as the coming of the Lord seems to you to be deferred, you should always think that, with a comparison made to God and eternity, no time is long. It is more simply established that by the little word λανθάνειν the Apostle looks to verse 5, where concerning ἐμπαίκταις he says, λανθάνει αὐτοὺς τοῦτο θελόντας, so that the sense may be, lest you fall into the same [error] as ἐμπαίκταις lest you fall into ignorance, it must by no means be hidden from you that in the same Scripture of the O. Test. which foretold the coming of Christ to the final judgment and the consummation of the age, it stands noted that a thousand years are with GOD as one day. While indeed he warns that this should not be hidden from them, he wishes that they be certain, and that they thoroughly persuade and believe themselves Acts 26. verse 26.Romans 10. verse 13.1. Thess. 4. v. 13. Ioh. Huss. in comm. h. l. He says less, and signifies more, as if to say: Be certain.

Ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη, καὶ χίλια ἔτη ὡς ἡμέρα μία. This is taken from Psalm 90. v. 4. where David, after he had said, God is from age to age, i. e. is eternal, adds: For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, when it is past, and as a watch in the night. LXX. ὅτι χίλια ἔτη ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς σου Κύριε, ὡς ἡμέρα ἡ ἐχθὲς ἥ τις διῆλθε καὶ φυλακὴ ἐν νυκτὶ. Therefore what David says, in the eyes of God, that Peter expresses thus, with the Lord; and what David says, as yesterday, when it is past, that Peter expresses thus, as one day. The sense in both places is the same, namely that in the eyes and estimation of God, as being immutable, infinite, and eternal, a thousand years, indeed all that succession of past, present, and future time, which extends itself from the origin of the world even to its end, is one day, indeed far less than one day, since between finite time, even the longest, and infinite eternity there is no proportion. The number of a thousand is placed synecdochically for any revolution of times.

The emphasis, however, is in the προσδιορισμῷ added, παρὰ Κυρίῳ as if to say: The Apostle. With us there is a great difference, and a very long interval of time between one day and a thousand years, because we are subject to time, and are measured by it, but with God, who is not subject to the succession and change of time, to whom all things past and future are present, one day and a thousand years as regards the proportion of measure with infinite eternity do not differ in the least. The Syrian παρὰ Κυρίῳ simply rendered [למריא] Lord. By the name Κυρίου here is understood Christ according to the customary phrase of the N. T. 1. Corinth. 8. v. 6. εἷς Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, to whom also elsewhere in this Epistle Peter appropriates the name Κυρίου. c. 1. v. 2.8.11.14. & 16.c. 2. v. 20. cap. 3.

vers. 2.9. 10.15. & 18. which exposition the scope of the Apostle confirms, for he treats of the most recent coming of Christ to judgment, which he confirms against those ἐμπαῖκταις denying it, or certainly calling it into doubt.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Excutit Apostolus illud in argumento ἐμπαίκτων, quòd mundus per aliquot secula in eodem statu permanserit, ex quo inferebat, eum perpetuô in tali statu mansurum. Respondet Apostolus, ut DEO nihil magnum: ita quoque eidem nihil esse longinquum, quippe apud quem mille anni ut dies unus.

2. Per prolepsin quandam occurrit tùm illusorum obiectioni, tùm infirmorum tacitae cogitationi, quòd adventus Christi ad iudicium, & sic etiam mundi interitus dies differatur. Respondet Apostolus, nemini hoc diuturnum deberi videri, nec tarditatis DEUM hoc nomine accusandum esse, cùm apud ipsum mille anni sint sicut unus dies. Nobis mille anni videntur diuturnum tempus, sed apud aeternum & infinitum Deum longè alia computi ratio.

3. Beda in h. l. talem profert connexionem. Ideò haec Apostolus commemorat, ut convincat eos, quos dicere praemiserat, ubi est promissio adventus eius? ostendens, Dominum nequaquam oblitum suae promissionis aut adventus adiudicandum vivos & mortuos: sed cùm ita unumquemque diem seculi nostri aeternâ suâ memoriâ complectatur ut annorum mille circuitus: ita mille annos, ut unius diei spacium sine labore circumspiciat, manifestè intelligendum, quod ipsorum quoque dierum & annorum omnium finem certissimè noverit, quando adventus ipsius claritas revelanda, quando promissa sint sanctis praemta reddenda.

4. Eâdem operâ confirmat Apostolus piorum animos, ne de promisso Christi ad iudicium adventu dubitent, etiamsi aliquandiu videatur differri; ac reprimit hominum otiosorum curiositatem, ne certum & definitum adventus illius tempus inquirant, sed singulis potiùs horis ac momentis ad illum sese praeparent.

5. Glossa ordinaria eiusmodi tradit connexionem. Probato, quodiudicium verè erit. ostendit, quàm efficax fuerit. Si dicitur vobis à Pseudo Apostolis, quod vultis, potestis facere, quia tantum tempus restat usque ad diem iudicii, quod ex longinquitate temporis iudex scire multa non poterit, non credatis eis, quia quicquid potest fieri mille annis, ita videt, sicut illud quod fit unâ die. Si dicunt, mille annis paenitendo non assequimini veniam delictorum, non credatis, quia unus dies verae paenitentiae tantum valet, quantum mille anni, sicut latroni. Si dicunt, non oportet tamdiu laborare, unâ die potestis respirare, non credatis, quia mille anni laboris non plus sufficiunt ad vitam, quàm unus dies. Et quandoquidem futurum est iudicium, ergò nolite seduci per Pseudodoctores, qui dicunt vobis, quod etsi sit futurum iudicium, non tamen vobis timendum, quòd cùm sint tot cogitationes & tot actus hominum, si sigillatim debeant discuti, non sufficient millia annorum, cùm in uno solo die dicatur futurum iudicium, & sic multa poterunt latere iudicem. Sed non lateat vos istud, quod tantum valet apud Deum dies unus ad agendum aliquid, quantum mille anni hominibus ad solam rem faciendam.

Textûs expositio. Ἐν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοὶ. Vulg. Unum verò hoc non lateat vos, carissimi. In Graeco est, dilecti. Regii duo Codd. pro ἀγαπητοὶ substituunt ἀδελφοὶ. Syrus more suo reddidit [חביבי]dilecti mei. Verbo λανθάνειν quidam statuunt Apostolum eo respicere, quod dies adventus Christi & iudicii extremi lateat, ut sit sensus. Quamvis lateat dies, in quo Christus ad iudicium est venturus & mundum destructurus, hoc tamen vos latere minimè debet, sed quoties adventus Domini vobis videtur differri, semper illud cogitetis, comparatione ad Deum & aeternitatem factâ nullum tempus esse longum. Simpliciùs statuitur, voculâ λανθάνειν Apostolum respicere ad vers. 5. ubi de ἐμπαίκταις dicit, λανθάνει αὐτοὺς τοῦτο θελόντας, ut sit sensus, ne in eandem cum ἐμπαίκταις ignorantiam incidatis, latere vos minimè debet, quod in eadem Scriptura V. Test. quae adventum Christi ad iudicium extremum & seculi consummationem praenunciavit, annotatum extat, mille annos esse apud DEUM instar unius diei. Dum verò admonet, ut ipsos hoc non lateat, vult ut certi sint, sibique penitus persuadeant & credant, Actor. 26. vers. 26.Roman. 10. vers. 13.1. Thess. 4. v. 13. Ioh. Huss. in comm. h. l. Minus dicit, & plus significat, q. d. Certisitis.

Ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη, καὶ χίλια ἔτη ὡς ἡμέρα μία. Desumtum hoc ex Psalm. 90. v. 4. ubi David, postquam dixerat, Deum esse à seculo inseculum, i. e. esse aeternum, subiungit. Quoniam mille anni in oculis tuis, sicut hesterna dies, cùm transierit & custodia in nocte. LXX. ὅτι χίλια ἔτη ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς σου Κύριε, ὡς ἡμέρα ἡ ἐχθὲς ἥ τις διῆλθε καὶ φυλακὴ ἐν νυκτὶ. Quod ergò David dicit, in oculis Dei, illud Petrus sic effert, apud Dominum; & quod David dicit, sicut dies hesterna, cùm transicrit, illud Petrus sic effert, sicut dies unus. Sensus utrobique idem est, videlicet in oculis atque aestimatione Dei, utpote immutabilis, infiniti & aeterni mille annos, imò omnem illam praeteriti, praesentis & futuri temporis successionem, quae ab origine mundi ad eius usque finem sese extendit, esse unum diem, imò longè minùs, quàm unum diem, cùm inter tempus finitum etiam longissimum, & infinitam aeternitatem nulla sit proportio. Numerus millenarius Synecdochicè ponitur pro quacunque revolutione temporum.

Emphasis autem est in προσδιορισμῷ adiecto, παρὰ Κυρίῳ q. d. Apostolus. Apud nos magnum est discrimen, & longissimum temporis intervallum inter diem unum & mille annos, quia nos tempori sumus subiecti, & ab illo mensuramur, sed apud Deum, qui non est temporis successioni & mutationi subiectus, cui omnia praeterita & futura sunt praesentia, unus dies & mille anni quoad proportionem mensurae cum infinita aeternitate nihil quidquam differunt. Syrus παρὰ Κυρίῳ simpliciter reddidit [למריא]Domino. Nomine Κυρίου hîc intelligitur Christus iuxta usitatam N. T. phrasin 1. Corinth. 8. v. 6.εἷς Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, cui etiam alibi in hac Epistola nomen Κυρίου Petrus appropriat. c. 1. v. 2.8.11.14. & 16.c. 2. v. 20. cap. 3.

vers. 2.9. 10.15. & 18. quam expositionem confirmat scopus Apostoli, agit enim de novissimo Christi ad iudicium adventu, quem contra ἐμπαῖκταις illum negantes, vel certè in dubium vocantes confirmat.

## 3:8-9 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Why does God defer the perfect punishment of the impious until the day of the final judgment? Resp. 1. Because the measure of iniquities is not yet completed by them in all ways. Gen. 15. v. 16. 2. So that the number of the elect may be completed, who are to be either afflicted or killed by the impious before the day of judgment. Apocal. 6. v. 12. The souls of those killed on account of the word of God under the altar cry out. How long, O Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood from those who dwell on the earth? To them it is said, that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who are to be killed as they were, are completed. Bede on this place, Petrin. Therefore the Lord still defers, so that the sum of the elect, which He decreed with the Father before the ages, may first be fulfilled. Whence also in the Apocalypse the souls of the Martyrs, who thirsted for the day of judgment and resurrection to arrive more quickly, heard that they should rest for a little time yet, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers was completed; which the Ordinary Gloss repeats from Bede. 3. So that space and time for repentance may be granted to sinners, through which they may be freed from eternal destruction, as Peter testifies in this place. 4. So that GOD may prove His μακροθυμίαν καὶ χρηστότητα toward any men whatsoever the more illustriously, by tolerating sinners for so long and inviting them to repentance in various ways.

Rom. 2. vers. 4. τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς μετάνοιαν σε ἀγει. 5. So that the extreme malice of the ungodly who are unwilling to be converted may be rendered more manifest to all, and their punishment may appear most just. Rom. 2. vers. 5.According to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath against the day of judgment.

2. Who are those of whom the Apostle says that they consider the delay of Christ's final coming to judgment to be slowness? Resp. Directly and principally the Apostle treats of ἐμπαίκταις, who were weaving an argument from this delay, by which they utterly denied the final coming of Christ and the last judgment, similar to that wicked servant of whom Matth. 24. v. 47.Luc. 12. v. 45. meanwhile, even to the pious, because of the infirmity of faith, the coming and judgment of Christ sometimes seems to be delayed longer, as is insinuated by the slumbering of the virgins, even the wise ones, by which χρονίζοντος τοῦ νυμφίου they were oppressed Matth. 25. v. 5. and by the cry of the souls under the altar Apoc. 6. v. 10.. Therefore, Peter raises them up at the same time, teaching that that delay of some years, whatever it may be, which in respect of eternity is clearly nothing, is not to be accused by the name of slowness.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. The Lord does not delay the promise, says Peter, but acts patiently, by deferring, that is, the punishments of the ungodly, with which agrees the Apostolic saying Rom. 2. vers. 4. The long-suffering of God invites the ungodly to repentance. But on the contrary Deut. 7. vers. 5. says Moses. The Lord thy God is a faithful God, rendering to them that hate him their reward to their face, and destroying them; he will not delay to him that hateth him; and Syr. c. 35. v. 20.The Most High will judge the just and will do judgment, v. 21. and the Lord will not be slack, and he will have no patience with them, the mighty. If God is long-suffering toward the ungodly and defers punishment so that time for repentance may be granted to them, how does he not delay in inflicting punishment upon the ungodly?

Resp. Βραδύτης or slowness is considered in two ways. 1. ἀνθρωπίνως humanly. Thus slowness among men is called that when someone, either out of forgetfulness, or change of plan, or negligence, or some laziness, neglects the occasion of acting. 2. θεϊκῶς divinely. Thus the slowness of God is nothing other than μακροθυμία and ἀνοχὴ, by which, not out of negligence, but out of mercy and kindness, he tolerates sinners for a long time and defers punishments, so that he may invite them to repentance.

2. The Lord does not delay his promise, says Peter. On the contraryHab. 2. v. 3.Hebr. 10. v. 37.If the Lord should make a delay, wait for him.

Resp. 1. In the Prophet it is immediately added: Coming he will come and will not delay. 2. Therefore it is one thing, as we have also warned above, to make a delay, or to defer; but another thing to delay, i.e., to defer beyond the due and appointed time. Exod. 22. v. 29.you shall not delay to render your tithes and your first fruits, namely at the appointed time. Tob. 9. v. 4.You yourself know that my father counts the days, and if I delay one day more (beyond the defined time of return) his soul is saddened. The former is expressed in the Hebrew text by the verb יתמהמה from the root מהה in Hithpael he hesitated: the latter by the verb יאחר from the root אחר he delayed, which is used in a faulty sense. Gen. 24. v. 56.Prov. 23. v. 30.

3. Peter infers from this that God does not delay the promise, because a thousand years with God are as one day: But this reason does not yet seem to effect this, that with respect to men, among whom a thousand years are a very long time, the divine promise is not delayed.

Resp. 1. Some think that regard is had for the blessed, who have long been living in eternal happiness and glory with God. The Apostle supposes, they say, that death is near at hand for individual men, and because after death the saints are no longer measured by time, but by an age or eternity, therefore he says that God does not delay his promises, i.e., because death approaches everyone; but after death those who enjoy eternal blessedness care little or nothing that the day of judgment is deferred by a thousand years. But Peter is not dealing with those who already enjoy blessedness in heaven, but with those who still live on earth, to whom the day of judgment seems to be deferred. 2. It must therefore be said that although a thousand years considered in themselves and absolutely are a very long time, yet if they are considered comparatively, with regard had to eternity, they are like a most minute point. Because Christ is expected to return from heaven, therefore according to the heavenly clock the years that intervene between the promise of his return and its fulfillment are to be counted.

4. God does not wish some to perish, but all to come to repentance. But many do not return to repentance, but perish eternally. How therefore does the truth of those Prophetic oracles stand?Psal. 135. v. 6.all things that God willed, he has done in heaven and on earth.Esa. 46. v. 10.My counsel shall stand and all my will shall be done.

Resp. GOD wills some things absolutely and simply; some things under a certain condition and by certain means. Θελητά of the first kind, since they are absolute, always come to pass, for who will resist His will?Rom. 9. v. 19. But θελητά of the second kind, since they are circumscribed by a certain condition and by certain means, do not come to pass unless that condition is posited and those means are posited. GOD wills, and seriously wills, the life and salvation of the sinner, but yet He also wills the conversion of the sinner through the word and the Holy Spirit. 1. Timoth. 2. v. 4. But if the sinner rejects that word, Act. 13. v. 46. and resists the Holy SpiritAct. 7. v. 51. and thus by his own fault is not converted, God by a just judgment wills the damnation of the impenitent sinner. Dionys. Carthus. in h. l. God does not will anyone to perish, but all to be saved, speaking of the antecedent will, that is, considering men according to what they are as men, as being of a rational Nature and capable of happiness: but not speaking of the consequent will, as being considering them as such and such. Just as an earthly King wills all his subjects to prosper and live, in so far as they are his subjects, but not in so far as some of them are evildoers and rebels, thieves, murderers, robbers.

Piscator objects in the notes to the treatise of Vorstius on God, note 4, to page 58, thesis 13, If God wills to do certain things under a condition, it follows that God wills them only then, when the condition is fulfilled, and ceases to will them, when the condition ceases to be performed, and consequently that the will of God is mutable, which is what conflicts with the sayings. All my will shall be done. Who will resist His will? Macovius Disp. 3. There is no conditional will of God. Resp. 1. That God wills certain things under a condition can be most evidently proved from the Prophetic saying, Ierem. 18. v. 7. I will suddenly speak against a nation, and against a kingdom, to root out and to pull down and to destroy it. v. 8. If that nation shall repent of their evil, which I have spoken against it, I will repent of the evil, that I thought to do unto it. v. 9. And suddenly I will speak of a nation and of a kingdom, to build and to plant it. v. 10. If it shall do evil in my sight, that it obey not my voice, I will repent of the good, wherewith I said I would benefit it. 2. The same distinction between the absolute will is gathered from manifest sayings of Scripture. For concerning the absolute will of God it is said Esa. 46. v. 10. All my will shall be done. Roman. 9. v. 19. Who will resist His will? But concerning the conditional will it is said, Matth. 23. v. 36. How often would I have gathered you, and ye would not, Luc. 7. v. 30. the Pharisees rejected the counsel of God against themselves.Acts 7. v. 51.You always resist the Holy Spirit. 3. Nor is any mutability of will attributed to God on that account. If God absolutely willed the salvation of all men, then it would finally follow that, with the will changed, he wills the damnation of some. But because he does not will the salvation of all men except in a certain way, under certain conditions, and by certain means, therefore no change of will is to be feared, even if he should most justly will the destruction of some by a just judgment. Thus a householder, without any change of will, wills that all servants work in the vineyard, yet in such a way that if they are unwilling to work, they are thrust into the mill. August. de Spirit. & lit. cap. 33. 4. One must also distinguish between antecedent will & consequent, which distinction Chrysostom approves in homil. 1. in Epist. ad Ephes. p. 954. where he calls the former first, the latter second; and Damascenus in lib. 2. orth. fidei cap. 29. lib. 1. contra haeres. Manich. p. 563. where he calls the former θέλημα προηγούμενον, the latter θέλημα ἑπόμενον. And likewise Anselm in lib. de volunt. where he calls the former the will of mercy, the latter of justice. The antecedent will is that by which God, as a most kind Father, wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth.1. Tim 2. v. 3.The consequent will is that by which God, as a most just judge, finally wills the impenitent and unbelieving to be damned. 5. The Calvinists accuse this distinction of contradiction, but just as mercy and justice in God do not conflict in the least, so also the absolute and conditional will, the antecedent and consequent will, the first and second will, the will of justice and mercy bring no change upon God. Compare the Exegesis in tom. 1. Locor. tract. de Natura Dei §. 271.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Salmero Disp. 4. in 2. Epist. Petri pag. 137. discourses thus: Although the intellect can now scarcely grasp this (that God has had, and has, all past and future years, in act at once and in reality, and therefore one day is with him just as a thousand years) one must stand more by the word of God than by our intellect, which is not capable of divine things. But yet when we shall have been partakers of eternity, we shall grasp this truth, just as many others, as concerning the Trinity, the incarnation, which altogether surpass every faculty of the created intellect, even the angelic. Salmero says all these things most correctly, which are to be opposed to the remaining Papists, who attribute too much to reason in matters of faith, while they not only prove false articles of faith from the principles of reason, but also true ones they repudiate the articles of faith revealed and founded in Scripture, for the reason that they are opposed to reason. But if the mysteries of faith are above reason, it can easily happen that by accident they also become against reason, when, namely, human reason does not contain itself within its own sphere, nor follows the guidance of the word, but rashly takes upon itself judgment concerning those things which are of mere revelation and pure faith, and desires to pronounce upon them not from the prescription of the word, but from its own natural principles.

2. When Peter in this place pronounces, that a thousand years with the Lord are as one day, and one day as a thousand years, then he speaks of Christ, since he is dealing professedly with his most recent coming to judgment. Therefore, there is proposed in this place an evident testimony concerning the eternity of Christ according to his divine Nature, and consequently we conclude from this place against the Photinians thus. He with whom a thousand years are as one day, he is the true, eternal, and immutable God. With Christ the Lord a thousand years are as one day. Therefore Christ the Lord is the true, eternal, and immutable God. The major premise is confirmed by the comparison of this Apostolic place with Psal. 90. from which Peter brings this sentence. v. 1. says Moses. Lord, you have been our refuge from generation to generation. v. 2. Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God. v. 4. For a thousand years before your eyes are as yesterday, which has passed. Here it is manifest from the antecedents that this phrase pertains to the description of eternity, that a thousand years are with God as one day. The minor premise is confirmed by the whole context of this place.

3. God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to repentance, says Peter, to which that of Paul 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. is consonant: God wishes all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Therefore God did not wish that the first men should fall, and through the fall involve both themselves and all their descendants in eternal destruction. For if God does not wish any to perish, therefore he also did not wish the first parents to perish. If God does not wish any to perish, much less does he wish the whole human race to perish, and consequently the first men did not fall by some immutable decree and ordination of God, nor was the human race involved in destruction.

4, God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to repentance. Therefore he is not the cause of sin. For if he were the cause of damnation from a certain absolute decree of reprobation, it would certainly also be the cause of sin, whence the Calvinist proponents of the absolute decree say that God has predestined certain men to damnation and the causes of damnation.

5. God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to repentance. Therefore it is false, what the Calvinists and with them certain Papists teach, that God by a certain absolute decree has reprobated the greatest part of the human race, whom He does not wish to be converted and saved, for whom also Christ has not died. I say certain Papists teach this, for some either reject that absolute decree of reprobation, or wish to appear to reject it. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: Hence it is clear that God wills the salvation of all, and does not will the damnation of anyone, and consequently reprobates no one before his foreseen demerits and death in sin. Which will in God is not only of sign, as some have judged, but also of good pleasure, as Gabriel Vasquez solidly shows. p. 1. q. 19. Disp. 83. c. 2. Lorinus on this passage: Hence is elicited a proof of the better and more common opinion, that grace is always prepared for men in this life sufficient for removing all sins, nor should any exception be placed either in sins or in sinners, however much they may have sinned. And afterwards: It can still be excepted concerning infants and those lacking the use of reason. But for these a mediately sufficient remedy is given through parents, as Prosper teaches lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. Peter speaks in this place of those having the use of reason, who are capable of repentance. It is also a general proposition not to be restricted to the kind of individuals or to the predestined. Beza, Piscator, and others from among the Calvinists except 1. that the saying of our Apostle must be accepted concerning the elect alone. God does not wish any to perish, namely of us, who believe in Christ, and therefore are in the number of the elect, but all to come to repentance, namely all of us, who believe in Christ, which are the words of Piscator in the scholia on this passage.
