The same man in the observations deduced from this place §. 5. writes thus: Peter does not speak here of all men in the universe, but only of all the elect: for he writes to the faithful Jews, whom out of charity he held as elect, therefore he says, He is patient towards us, that is, whom He has called through the Gospel, and even now calls, not wishing any, that is, of us to perish, but all, that is, us, whom He calls, to tend toward repentance. Estius, a Papist, inculcates the same exception in his commentary on this passage: It is understood here, he says, the will of God absolute and properly so called, not however concerning all men, but concerning the elect alone. For he says Peter, God acts patiently because of or towards you, namely the elect. For this Epistle is written to the same ones to whom the first was written, namely to the elect strangers. Thus therefore Peter says that the Lord acts patiently, that is, defers his promised coming and judgment because of the elect, so that they may not perish, but being converted to repentance may be saved, just as Paul says that he endures all things because of the elect, so that they too may obtain salvation, 2. Tim. 2. v. 10. Just as because of the elect those days of great tribulation will be shortened Matth. 24. v. 22. so that, namely, oppressed by the magnitude of the tribulations, they may not fall into despair and perish: so the Lord acts patiently, and defers the time of judgment because of the elect, so that all who still remain to be gathered may be gathered. For if God were to anticipate the time of judgment decreed by himself, some of those whom he chose from eternity for salvation would perish. Resp. 1. We concede that God defers the day of judgment because of the elect, but that he defers it because of the elect alone, and that only the elect are to be understood here when Peter says, God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to repentance, that indeed is what we deny. 2. For Peter writes to the whole assembly of the called, in which there were many reprobates, whose repentance and salvation, however, according to his antecedent or merciful will, God seriously sought, and among other causes he also deferred the final judgment to that end, so that time for repentance might be available to them as well. 3. Thus therefore we conclude. Those whom God wishes to come to repentance, he does not wish any of them to perish by some absolute hatred and decree. But God wishes even the reprobate to come to repentance. Therefore he does not wish any of the reprobate to perish by some absolute hatred and decree. The proposition is Peter's in this text. The assumption is Paul's Rom. 2. v. 4. Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God invites you to repentance? v. 5. but you according to your hardness and impenitent heart treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God. Thus therefore that μαρκροθυμία, of which Peter makes mention, invites even those to repentance who, by securely indulging in sins, gradually heap up divine wrath, so that at length the whole may be drawn forth like a treasure. Hence Hemmingius on this passage annotates the Apostolic text thus. Clearly without any ambiguity of words or sense the Apostle pronounces that God does not wish any to perish, but all to be gathered to repentance. Wherefore let us hold this saying in memory, so that we may fortify ourselves against those who today deny that the grace of GOD is universal. Nor It is that the authority of the new Interpreter moves us, who restricts this saying to the pious, to whom Peter writes. For this manifestly fights with the words of the Apostle, who speaks of those who have not done penance. 4. Therefore, the causes explained above are to be recalled in this place, on account of which God defers the perfect punishment of the impious until the day of judgment, from which it will be established that not only the elect, but also the reprobate are called by God to penance, and consequently it must also be accepted concerning the reprobate that God does not wish them to perish, but to be saved, namely, according to His antecedent will. For that the preaching of penance is universal, manifest sayings of Scripture prove Luke 24. v. 47. Christ commanded that penance and remission of sins be preached in His name unto all nations. Acts 17. v. 30. God announces to all men everywhere that they should do penance. Rom. 11. v. 32. God has concluded all under unbelief, that He may have mercy on all. From those we conclude thus. Those whom God calls to penance, He also seriously seeks the salvation of them. God calls all men to penance. Therefore, He seriously seeks the salvation of all men. 5. The saying of Peter is general. God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to penance. That ought not to be restricted from a preconceived opinion about an absolute decree of reprobation, but rather explained universally from parallel places of Scripture. Ezek. 18. v. 23. chap. 33. v. 11. I do not desire the death of the impious. Matt. 23. v. 37. How often would I have gathered you, and you would not. 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. God wishes all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. c. 4. v. 10. God is the Savior of all men, especially of the faithful. 6. Peter attributes the name of elect to the Churches to which he writes, not by reason of all who were in the external society of the church and in the number of the called, but by reason of the principal members, who were joined to Christ the head in the mystical body by the interior bond of the Spirit, through a Synecdoche customary in the Scriptures. But it cannot be proved from that, when Peter says in this place that God does not wish any to perish, but all to come to penance, that this must be accepted concerning the elect alone. For it could be gathered in the same way that the elect alone ought to be mindful of the words foretold by the Prophets and Apostles chap. 3. v. 2. that the elect alone ought to know that a thousand years are with God as one day v. 8. that the elect alone ought to prepare themselves by holy conversation for the last coming of Christ v. 11. that the elect alone ought to esteem the long-suffering of God as salvation. v. 15.

2. Tossanus objects thus. God does not wish any to perish, namely, so that the blame may reside with Him, so that He may deny the time of conversion to men. Resp. 1. When Peter says, God does not wish any to perish, but that all should come to repentance, then he not only absolves God from blame, but also denies that the cause of the damnation of the impious is to be attributed to an absolute decree of God. 2. Although those who place the foreknowledge of the fall before the decree of reprobation seem to absolve God from the blame of the perdition of men, nevertheless those who derive the very fall of man from an absolute decree of God, which many of the Calvinists do, manifestly attribute to God the blame of cruelty and unmercifulness. For it is a cruel mercy to wish someone to be miserable, so that He may have an occasion of showing mercy. 3. Tossanus himself annotates thus on this v. 9.. God is μακρόθυμος towards us, so that time for repentance may be available to us, and so that the impious may have no excuse, as if the coming of Christ had been too precipitate and hurried. And yet if this is the cause of the delay, certainly God also grants to those very impious ones a space for repentance. Then a little later Tossanus adds. God exhorts all to repentance, even the impious, and grants them time for repentance. Therefore, that they are not converted, the blame for that thing does not reside with God, but with those very ones who abuse the long-suffering and patience of God. Rom. 2. v. 5. From which we gather thus. Those to whom God grants time for repentance, He also wishes to be saved. And yet God grants time for repentance even to the impious and perishing, who abuse the long-suffering of God. Therefore, He also wishes the impious and perishing who abuse the long-suffering of God to be saved, namely, by an antecedent will, as was explained above. 4. The Calvinists see this well, thence they recur to the distinction between the hidden and revealed will; between the will of sign and of good pleasure: and they determine that the Apostolic saying 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. must be accepted διαιρετικῶς concerning kinds of individuals, not συμωληρωματικῶς concerning individuals of kinds. But what is to be answered to such empty evasions was explained in vol. 2 of the Commonplaces, treatise on Providence §. 113, on predestination and reprobation §. 58, 59, 71, in Exeg. vol. 1, Commonplace, treatise on the Nature of God §. 268, 269.

3. Chamier, vol. 3, treatise, book 7, chapter 8, §. 11, objects, that one must distinguish between the will of God and His good pleasure. חפץ he says, in Ezekiel is not simply to will, but to be delighted, to desire, εὐαρεστεῖν.

But who would deny that God can will, and yet not be delighted by the death of a sinner? For it is certain, if He willed it in any way, it would in no way come to pass. Resp. 1. If it is not the good pleasure of GOD that the impious should perish, then certainly He did not reprobate the impious out of some absolute hatred and decree. 2. God wills the salvation of the impious person even as he is perishing, namely, by an antecedent will or one of mercy; He wills the damnation of the same person persisting in impiety, namely, by a consequent will or one of justice. 3. Chamier adds, that death is inflicted upon the impious and impenitent by God the most just judge. Therefore this is the consequent and judiciary will of God, having respect to the final impenitence of the impious.

4. Estius, besides the exception discussed above, brings forward two others: God, he says, does not will that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. 1. Insofar as He has provided and bestowed upon the human race in general certain means and general aids, through which men could be converted to God, although these are by no means sufficient for the conversion and salvation of men without special aids, which are not given to all. 2. Insofar as He wills and causes pious men not to want anyone to perish, but to want or desire that all who are turned away from GOD should return to Him through true repentance. But the former explanation does not satisfy the emphasis of the Apostolic statement. For unless God offered sufficient means of salvation to those very ones who are perishing, it could not truly be said of Him that He does not will that any should perish, but that He wills that all should be saved. Let Estius hear Bellarmine, a man of his own society, in book 2 de grat. & lib. arbit. chapter 5, v. 1. An aid sufficient for salvation is given to all, according to place and time, mediately or immediately. That in that whole chapter 5 he confirms and among other things writes §. Item Wis. 11. You have mercy on all, because You can do all things, and You overlook the sins of men for the sake of repentance &c. These things certainly can hardly be understood, unless we confess that sufficient aid is granted to all. For how does He have mercy on all and spare all, if He does not at least give them the aid by which they might be able to arrive at reconciliation, if they should so will? Nor ought these things to be restricted to the elect: for the reason why God spares all and has mercy on all is rendered in this place from creation, because God created all. But creation is common to all absolutely. §. He likewise brings forward John 1. &c. our Apostolic statement, and joins to it that Pauline one 1 Tim. 2 v. 4. and discourses on both as follows. This was the opinion of Augustine concerning this Apostolic passage, that God wills all to be saved, because He gives to all that from which they might be able to will to believe and be saved, yet in such a way that if they themselves should not will it, they are not saved, but are destined for eternal punishments, which was also the exposition of St. Prosper Book 2 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapters 23, 25, & 28. Item the Commentaries, which are attributed to Ambrose. Item those of Chrysostom, Theophylact & Oecumenius, who say that God wills all to be saved, if they themselves also will it, etc. That item 1 Tim. 4 Who is the Savior of all men, especially of the faithful, can hardly be explained otherwise than as St. Prosper explains it in book 2 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10, namely, that we may understand that God is the Savior of all, because He gives to all that from which they can be saved, but especially of the faithful, because He gives to them not only that they can be saved, but also that they are saved. Finally, that 1 Cor. 15 Christ died for all, and 1 Tim. 2 who gave Himself a redemption for all; and 1 John 2 He is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world, how can it be true if something is not given to all, from which they might be able to become participants in the death of Christ? For since no one can be a participant in the death of Christ and the price of this redemption without a preceding gift, Christ paid the price of redemption for all in vain, if He did not wish to open to all the way by which they could arrive at redemption. Bellarmine explicitly contradicts all these things, Estius.

The later exposition of Estius is clearly foreign to the scope of the Apostle. For it is not the Apostle's purpose to teach what the pious will or do not will from the impulse of the Holy Spirit, but what the Lord, who delays the day of judgment, wills or does not will by Himself. We ask, however, from Estius, whether that will of the pious, by which they seriously seek that all men be converted to God and be saved, is conformable to the divine will or not? If the former, then certainly God Himself also wills by Himself that all men come to repentance and be saved. If the latter, then greater mercy is attributed to the pious than to God, who is charity itself 1 John 4:16 and whose mercy is as great as He Himself is, that is, infinite Sirach 2:23.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. From the fact that a thousand years are said to be like one day before God, and one day like a thousand years, many of the ancients gather that the world will last for six thousand years, since the world was created in six days. Jerome in his epistolary exposition of Psalm 89 to Cyprian, volume 4, page 44: I judge from this passage, and from the Epistle which is inscribed with the name of Peter, that a thousand years are accustomed to be called one day, so that, namely, because the world was fashioned in six days, it is believed to subsist for only six thousand years, and afterwards the seventh and eighth number comes, in which the true Sabbath is practiced, and the purity of Circumcision is restored. Similar things occur in Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho, page 240.

And in book of questions to the nations question 71. page 337. Irenaeus book 5. against heresies chapter 28. page 352. Lactantius book 7. Institutes chapter 7. and 14. page 416. Hilary canon 17. on Matthew. Augustine book 20. on the City of God chapter 7. Fevardentius in notes to Irenaeus book 5. chapter 28. for this opinion cites Justin, Irenaeus, Hilary, Germanus, of Constantinople, the Talmudists, Hydaspes, King of the Medes, Trismegistus, the Sibyls, Hippolytus, Chrysostom, Cyril, Gaudentius of Brescia, Pico della Mirandola. Cornelius à Lapide on verse 8. of this Epistle annotates thus: This opinion (concerning the duration of the world for six thousand years) has more solid foundations, and therefore is that of many Fathers and Doctors, whence it is probable, nor can it be argued of rashness.

But. 1. The same Augustine, who is cited for this opinion, in his exposition of Psalm 89 (according to the Hebrews 90.) refutes those who accommodate the words of the Psalmist to that opinion. Men have dared, he says, to presume the knowledge of times, which the Lord said to the disciples desiring to know. It is not for you to know the times, which the Father has put in his own power, Acts 1 and they have defined that this age can be finished in six thousand years as if in six days, and they did not attend to what was said, as one day which has passed. For not when this was said had only a thousand years passed, and what ought most especially to have warned them, lest they be mocked by the uncertainty of times, is that as a watch in the night. For neither as they seem to have opined something likely concerning six days because of the first six days, in which God perfected his works, so also can those who opine fit six watches, i. e. eighteen hours. 2. Ambrose book 7. Commentary on Luke explaining that of Matthew. After six days Christ was transfigured, indicates that he does not accept such a period of worldly age, because in his times more than six thousand years were being computed. (Sixtus Senensis rightly warns in book 5. of the Holy Library annotation 190. that Ambrose followed a certain calculation of the years of the World peculiar to himself, since according to the calculation of the Hebrew truth in the time of Ambrose four thousand four hundred years had not yet passed, for the Hebrews count from the creation of the world until Christ years 3962.) 3. It was not the purpose of Moses, nor of Peter, to compare the hexaemeron of creation with the duration of the world, but to teach that with God spaces of time are not to be measured by the same moments as with men, since to Him, placed outside all succession of time, all things are most present in a most simple τῷ νῦν. 4. Who will make us certain, that the time of the consummation of the age is to be estimated from the six-day creation of the world. If anything is to be granted to analogy, it will lead us rather to the time of duration than of commencement, namely that in the space of six days the world is to be dissolved again, just as in the space of six days it was founded from the beginning. Compare Sixtus Senensis, book 6, Bibliotheca, annotation 73, and the treatise on the Last Judgment, § 77. 5. Hence some of the Papists themselves repudiate this opinion. Lorinus on this passage: A false opinion must be avoided, Psal. 90. and one leaning upon this passage, concerning the duration of the world for only six thousand years, just as, to wit, the world was made in six days, so that the great day of God consists of a thousand years. Estius on verse 8 of this passage: It is vain that some, relying on this formula, by which a thousand years are reckoned with the Lord as one day and conversely, have attempted to affirm uncertain things for certain, and to interpret certain obscure things by taking days as standing for a thousand years, or even for individual years. As for example, when they take the six days of the creation of the world as an argument that the same world will endure for six thousand years, etc., which are conjectures of superstitiously curious men, entirely uncertain and foreign to the sense of this passage. It is to be noted, however, that this opinion relies on the almost common consensus of the Fathers, which, since it is repudiated by Estius in this question, presents an argument that the consensus of the Fathers does not present an apodictic argument.

2. Bede in his commentary on this passage discourses thus: Some think this sentence (that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years) is to be understood in such a way, as if the day of judgment has such length as the space of a thousand years, not considering that he does not say simply, there will be one day, as a thousand years, but one day, he says, is with the Lord, as a thousand years. Just as it is also evident that the Psalmist equates a thousand years not to the future day of judgment, but to yesterday, which has passed before the eyes of the Creator, nay rather he likens all our years, that is, all the time of this age, to the watch of one night, which is the fourth part of the night: so Blessed Peter equates as it were each day of the present age to a thousand years for each day with the Lord, that is, he asserts them to be of the same measure, because, to wit, he himself beholds all things, both small and great, equally. And indeed Peter, if he wished this to be understood only concerning the day of judgment, that it would truly be of such length as our thousand years are, could certainly have indicated his opinion more openly, nor would there be need to add with the Lord, because that day, if it were of such length, would appear so even to all men, when it had arrived.

3. From the fact that Peter in this place alleges the saying Sirach chapter 35, verse 19 ὁ Κύριος ὀν μὴ βραδύνῃ, a Papist might attempt to reconcile Canonical authority to Sirach. I respond: 1. A bare allegation in the New Testament does not yet prove the Canonical authority of any book, since the sayings of Gentile poets are also alleged by the Apostles, but it is required that all the requirements of Canonical books should agree with any book. 2. Nor is it yet clearly established whether Peter brings these things from Sirach, since a similar sentiment exists in Moses Deut. 7, verse 10 οὐχὶ βραδύνει (ὁ Κύριος..

Observations. 1. Scripture confirms the eternity of GOD elsewhere by a simple and plain assertion Gen. 21, verse 33 Isa. 40, verse 28 chapter 57, verse 15 Dan. 6, verse 26 Rom. 16, verse 26. In this place, as also Ps. 90, verse 5, it establishes it by the negation of time and succession. Justin in Questions and Responses to the Greeks, folio 29, οὐδὲν ἔγχρονον ἔστι παρὰ τῷ θεῷ.. Bede in this place: In the knowledge of divine power, both past and future and present things stand equally, and the courses of times which seem long to us, and which seem short, are certainly of equal space before the creator of times, who beholds all things, both great and small, equally.

2. Ephrem, volume 1, sermon of exhortation to piety: A thousand years of this age in that eternal and incorruptible world have as much comparison as the smallest sand of the sea with the whole sand of the same: which is taken from Sirach 18, verse 8 As a drop of water from the sea, and a grain of sand; so are a thousand years in the days of the age, that is, of eternity. Lyra in this place: By a millennium is understood any revolution of times whatsoever, which is small and of no moment, compared to divine eternity.

3. If, therefore, the most recent coming of Christ to judgment seems to be delayed, let us consider that there is absolutely no comparison between a thousand years and eternity, which is altogether infinite and interminable, and that a thousand years are with GOD as one day. Augustine in Psalm 89: What seems long to you is short before GOD. Bede in this place: Since GOD embraces each day of our age with His eternal memory, as the circuit of a thousand years: so He surveys a thousand years as the space of one day without labor, it is to be clearly understood that He most certainly knows the end of those very days and of all years, when the brightness of His coming is to be revealed, when the promised rewards are to be rendered to the saints.

4. Just as with GOD there is no vicissitude of light and darkness:

(James 1:17. With the Father of lights there is no παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα or shadow of turning i.e. arising from conversion, such as in the visible and corporeal Sun, which in its setting, turning itself to the opposite hemisphere, casts a shadow on the hemisphere which it leaves) so also with God there is no vicissitude of time, as there is with us humans, for whom things past have passed away, and things future are not yet present: but as Augustine speaks of Him in book 4 of De Trinitate, chapter 21. He is without that temporal motion above every creature, without any intervals of times and places, and at once one and the same from eternity to eternity as eternity itself.

5. By the very fact that Peter says, a thousand years with God are as one day, and one day as a thousand years, he tacitly confesses that the day of the final coming of Christ and the universal judgment is unknown to men. Mark 13:32.Acts 1:7. Augustine in book 18 of De Civitate Dei, chapter 53. In vain do we attempt to calculate and define the years that remain for this age, when we hear from the mouth of Truth that it is not for us to know this, etc. He who says, It is not for you to know the times, etc., loosens the fingers of all who calculate about this matter and bids them be still.

6. Μακροθυμίαν of GOD commends that He grants space for repentance to sinners. Isaiah 30:18. The Lord waits, that He may have mercy on you. Wisdom 11:24. You have mercy on all, because You can do all things, and You overlook the sins of men for the sake of repentance. Romans 2:4. the kindness of GOD leads you to repentance. Justin in Apology to Antoninus. The heavenly Father prefers repentance rather than punishment.

7. But let us not abuse this μακροθυμίᾳ and χρηστότητι of GOD for carnal security, but let us recognize the time of our visitation, Luke 19:44. and give thanks to GOD, that He did not immediately destroy us, as we had deserved by our sins, but granted a time of repentance, and while the doors of grace are still open, let us turn to God in true repentance. Sirach 5:8. Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. v. 9. for suddenly His wrath will come. Let us be mindful that death does not delay Sirach 14:12. If God delays it a little, it is because He is long-suffering toward us, not wishing to catch us in sin, but to invite us to repentance.

8. Moreover, God not only delays punishment, but also exhibits benefits, by which He invites and entices the man who has begun to deliver himself to death through sin, so that he may return to his creator, from whom he wickedly he has separated himself, let him convert and obtain salvation. Cypr. book on the good of patience. What and how great is the patience in God, that in insult to His majesty and honor, patiently sustaining the profane temples and earthly figments and sacred sacrileges instituted by men, He makes the day to be born and the light of the sun to rise equally upon the good and the evil? And when He waters the earth with rains, no one is excluded from His benefits? We see, moreover, by the insuperable equality of patience, that at the nod of God the seasons obey, the elements serve, the winds blow, the fountains flow, the abundance of harvests grows, the trees abound with fruits, and when He is exacerbated by frequent, nay continuous offenses, He tempers His indignation, and when He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining, that is, mercifully and deferring, so that, if it can be done, the malice long protracted may at some time be changed.

Latin:

Quaeritur hoc loco. 1. Quare Deus perfectam impiorum punitionem usque ad diem extremi iudicii differat? Resp. 1. quia mensura iniquitatum nondum est ab ipsis modis omnibus completa. Gen. 15. v. 16. 2. Ut compleatur numerus electorum, qui ab impiis ante diem iudicii vel affligendi, vel interficiendi. Apocal. 6. v. 12. Animae interfectorum propter verbum Dei sub altari clamant. Usque quo Domine non iudicas & vindicas sanguinem nostrum de illis, qui habitant in terra? illis dicitur, ut requiescant adhuc modicum, donec compleantur conservi eorum & fratres eorum, qui interficiendi sunt sicut ipsi. Beda in h. l. Petrin. Ideò Dominus adhuc differt, ut electorum priùs summa, quam cum Patre ante secula decrevit, adimpleatur. Unde & in Apocalypsi animae Martyrum, qui diem iudicii & resurrectionis ocyùs adventare sitiebant, audiverunt, ut requiescerent tempus adhuc modicum, donec compleretur conservorum & fratrum eorum numerus; quod ex Beda repetit Glossa ordinaria. 3. Ut peecatoribus spacium ac tempus paenitentiae concedatur, per quam ab aeterno exitio liberentur, ut Petrus h. l. testatur. 4. Ut suam erga quosvis homines μακροθυμίαν καὶ χρηστότητα DEUS eò illustriùs comprobet, peccatores tamdiu tolerando & variis modis ad paenitentiam invitando.

Rom. 2. vers. 4.τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς μετάνοιαν σε ἀγει. 5. Ut manifestior omnibus reddatur extrema impiorum converti nolentium malitia, & iustissima appareat eorum poena. Rom. 2. vers. 5.Secundùm duritiem tuam & impoenitens cor thesaurizas tibi iram in die iudicii.

2. Quinam sint illi, de quibus Apostostolus dicit, quòd dilationem novissimi Christi ad iudicium adventus tarditatem existiment? Resp. directè & principaliter agit Apostolus de ἐμπαίκταις, qui ex hac mora argumentum nectebant, quo novissimum Christi adventum & extremum iudicium penitus negabant, similes servo illi nequam, de quo Matth. 24. v. 47.Luc. 12. v. 45. interim etiam piis ex fidei infirmitate quandoque diutiùs videtur Christi adventus & iudicium differri, ut per dormitationem virginum etiam prudentum, quâ χρονίζοντος τοῦ νυμφίου oppressae sunt Matth. 25. v. 5. & per clamorem animarum sub altari Apoc. 6. v. 10. insinuatur. Illos ergò Petrus simul erigit, docens, qualemcunque illam aliquot annorum moram, quae aeternitatis respectu planè nulla sit, non esse tarditatis nomine accusandam.

Ἐναντιοφανείαι. 1. Non tardat Dominus promissum, inquit Petrus, sed patienter agit, differendo sc. impiorum poenas, cum quo congruit dictum ApostolicumRom. 2. vers. 4.Longanimitas Dei invitat impios ad paenitentiam. Contrà veròDeut. 7. vers. 5.inquit Moses. Deus fidelis est, reddens odio habentibus eum contra faciem eius, ut perdere faciat eum; non tardabit odio habenti eum; & Syr. c. 35. v. 20.Altissimus iudicabit iustos & faciet iudicium, v. 21. & Dominus non tardabit, neque patientiam in illis habebit fortis. Si Deus longanimis est erga impios, ac poenam differt, ut concedatur illis tempus paenitentiae, quomodo non tardat in supplicio impiis inferendo?

Resp. Βραδύτης sive tarditas dupliciter consideratur. 1. ἀνθρωπίνως humanitus. Sic tarditas apud homines dicitur illa, quando quis vel ex oblivione, vel consilii mutatione, aut negligentiâ vel pigritiâ aliquâ occasionem agendi negligit. 2. θεϊκῶς divinitus. Sic tarditas Dei nihil aliud est quàm μακροθυμία & ἀνοχὴ, quâ non ex negligentia, sed ex misericordiâ & benignitate peccatores diu tolerat & poenas differt, ut eos ad paenitentiam invitet.

2. Non tardat Dominus promissum, inquit Petrus. ContrauròHab. 2. v. 3.Hebr. 10. v. 37.Si moram fecerit Dominus, expecta eum.

Resp. 1. Apud Prophetam statim additur. Veniendo veniet & non tardabit. 2. Aliud ergò est, ut superius etiam monuimus, moram facere, sive differre; aliud verô tardare i. e. ultra debitum & constitutum tempus differre. Exod. 22. v. 29.decimas tuas & primitias tuas non tardabis reddere, nempe statuto tempore. Tob. 9. v. 4.Scis ipse, quoniam numerat pater meus dies, & si tardavero unâ die plus (ultra definitum tempus reditus) contristatur anima eius. Prius in textu Hebraeo effertur per verbum יתמהמה à rad. מהה in Hithpaël cunctatus est: posterius per verbum יאחר à rad. אחרtardavit, quod in vitio usurpatur. Gen. 24. v. 56.Prov. 23. v. 30.

3. Petrus ex eo infert, Deum non tardare promissum, quia mille anni apud Deum sunt sicut unus dies: At haec ratio nondum videtur hoc efficere, quod respectu hominum, apud quos mille anni sunt tempus longissimum, promissum divinum non tardetur.

Resp. 1. Quidam existimant, respectum haberi ad beatos, qui iamdum in aeterna felicitate & gloria cum Deo vivunt. Supponit, inquiunt, Apostolus singulis hominibus brevi adesse mortem, & quia post mortem sancti iam non tempore mensurantur, sed aevo aut aeternitate, ideò ait, Deum non tardare promissiones suas, sc. quia unicuique mors appropinquat; post mortem autem illi, qui fruuntur aeternâ beatitudine, parum aut nihil eurant, quod dies iudicii mille annos differatur. Atqui Petrus non agit cum illis, qui in caelo beatitudine iamdum fruuntur, sed qui in terris adhuc vivunt, quibus dies iudicii differri videtur. 2. Dicendum igitur, quòd quamvis mille anni in se & absolutè considerati sint tempus longissimum, tamen si comparatè, respectu ad aeternitatem habito, considerentur, sint instar minutissimi puncti. Quia Christus ex caelo rediturus expectatur, ideò iuxta horologium caeleste anni, qui inter reditus illius promissum & complementum intercedunt, numerandi veniunt.

4. Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire. At multi non revertuntur ad paenitentiam, sed in aeternum pereunt. Quomodo ergò constat veritas oraculis illis Propheticis?Psal. 135. v. 6.omnia, quae voluit Deus, fecit in caelo & in terra.Esa. 46. v. 10.Consilium meum stabit & omnis voluntas meafiet.

Resp. Quaedam DEUS vult absolutè & simpliciter; quaedam certâ conditione ac certis mediis. Θελητά primi generis, cùm sint absoluta, semper fiunt, voluntati enim Dei quis resistet?Rom. 9. v. 19. Sed θελητά secundi generis, cùm sint certâ conditione ac certis mediis circumscripta, non nisi positâ illâ conditione ac positis illis mediis eveniunt. Vult DEUS & seriò vult peccatoris vitam & salutem, sed tamen vult etiam peccatoris conversionem per verbum & Spiritum sanctum. 1. Timoth. 2. v. 4. Quòd si peccator verbum illud repellat, Act. 13. v. 46. & Spiritui sancto resistatAct. 7. v. 51. atque ita propriâ culpâ non convertatur, Deus iusto iudicio vult peccatoris impaenitentis damnationem. Dionys. Carthus. in h. l. Deus non vult quemquam perire, sed omnes salvari, loquendo de voluntate antecedente, h. e. considerando homines secundùm quod homines sunt, utpote rationalis Naturae ac felicitatis capaces: non autem loquendo de voluntate consequente, utpote considerando eos, ut tales & tales. Quemadmodum Rex terrenus vult omnes subditos suos prosperari ac vivere, in quantum sunt subditi sui, non autem in quantum quidam eorum malefici sunt & rebelles, fures, homicidae, latrones.

Excipit Piscator in notis ad tractat. Vorstii de Deo not. 4. ad pag. 58. thes. 13. Si Deus vult quaedam facere sub conditione, sequitur Deum ea tùm demum velle, cùm conditio impletur, & desinere velle, cùm conditio praestari desinit, ac proinde voluntatem Dei esse mutabilem, id quòd pugnat cum dictis. Omnis voluntas mea fiet. Voluntati eius quis resistet? Macovius Disp. 3. Conditionata Dei voluntas nulla est. Resp. 1. Deum quaedam sub conditione velle, evidentissimè probari potest ex dicto Prophetico, Ierem. 18. v. 7.Repentè loquar adversùs gentem, & adversùs regnum, ut eradicem & destruam & disperdam illud. v. 8. Si paenitentiam egerit gens illa à malo suo, quod locutus sum adversùs eam, agam & ego paenitentiam super malo, quod cogitavi, ut facerem ei.v. 9.Et subitò loquar de gente & de regno, ut aedificem & plantem illud. v. 10. Si fecerit malum in oculis meis, ut non audiat vocem meam, paenitentiam agam super bono, quod locutus sum, ut facerem ei. 2. Eadem distinctio inter voluntatem absolutam colligitur ex manifestis Scripturae dictis. De absoluta enim Dei voluntate dicitur Esa. 46. v. 10.Omnis voluntas mea fiet.Roman. 9. v. 19.Voluntati eius quis resistet? Sed de conditionata voluntate dicitur, Matth. 23. v. 36.Quoties volui vos congregare, & noluistis,Luc. 7. v. 30. Pharisaei spreverunt consilium Dei adversus semetipsos.Act. 7. v. 51.Vos semper resistitis Spiritui sancto. 3. Nec ulla voluntatis mutabilitas propterea Deo tribuitur. Si Deus absolutè vellet omnium hominum salutem, tùm demum sequeretur, quod mutatâ voluntate aliquorum velit damnationem. Sed quia non nisi certo modo, certis conditionibus, certis mediis vult omnium hominum salutem, ideò nulla metuenda voluntatis mutatio, si vel maximè iusto iudicio quorundam interitum velit. Sic paterfamilias sine ulla voluntatis mutatione vult, ut omnes servi laborent in vinea, sic tamen, ut si operari noluerint, detrudantur in pistrinum. August. de Spirit. & lit. cap. 33. 4. Distinguendum etiam inter voluntatem antecedentem & consequentem, quam distinctionem approbant Chrysostomus homil. 1. in Epist. ad Ephes. p. 954. ubi illam vocat primam, hanc secundam; & Damascenus lib. 2. orth. fidei cap. 29. lib. 1. contra haeres. Manich. p. 563. ubi illam vocat θέλημα προηγούμενον, hanc θέλημα ἑπόμενον. Itemque Anselmus in lib. de volunt. ubi illam vocat voluntatem misericordiae, hanc iustitiae. Antecedens voluntas est, quâ Deus ut benignissimus Pater, omnes homines vult salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire.1. Tim 2. v. 3.Consequens voluntas est, quâ Deus ut iustissimus iudex finaliter impoenitentes & incredulos vult damnari. 5. Calviniani hanc distinctionem contradictionis accusant, sed sicut misericordia & iustitia in Deo minimè pugnant, ita quoque voluntas absoluta & conditionata, voluntas antecedens & consequens, voluntas prima & secunda, voluntas iustititiae & misericordiae nullam mutationem Deo inferunt. Confer Exegesin tom. 1. Locor. tract. de Natura Dei §. 271.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Salmero Disp. 4. in 2. Epist. Petri pag. 137. sic dissert. Etsi modò hoc vix capere possit intellectus (quod Deus habuit, & habet annos praeteritos omnes & futuros, actu simul ac reipsâ, & proinde unus dies apud ipsum sit perinde atque mille anni) standum magis est dicto Dei, quàm nostro intellectui, qui divinarum rerum capax non est. Sed tamen cùm aeternitatis fuerimus participes, hanc capiemus veritatem, sicut & alias multas, uti de Trinitate, incarnatione, quae omnem prorsus superant facultatem intellectus creati, etiam Angelici. Haec omnia Salmero rectissimè, quae opponenda sunt reliquis Pontificiis, qui rationi in rebus fidei nimiùm tribuunt, dum non solùm falsos fidei articulos ex rationis principiis probant, sed etiam veros fidei articulos in Scriptura revelatos & fundatos repudiant, propterea quod rationi adversentur. Atqui si mysteria fidei sunt supra rationem, facili negotio fieri potest, ut ex accidenti etiam fiant contra rationem, quando scil. humana ratio non continet se intra suam sphaeram, nec sequitur ductum verbi, sed iudicium sibi temerè sumit de illis, quae sunt merae revelationis & purae fidei, ac de illis non ex verbi praescripto, sed ex principiis suis naturalibus pronunciare discupit.

2. Quando Petrus hoc loco pronunciat, mille annos apud Dominum esse sicut diem unum, & diem unum sicut mille annos, tùm loquitur de Christo, quippe de cuius novissimo ad iudicium adventu ex professo agit. Proponitur ergò h. l. evidens testimonium de Christi secundùm divinam Naturam aeternitate, ac proinde contra Photinianos ex hoc loco sic concludimus. Apud quem mille anni sunt sicut dies unus, is est verus, aeternus & immutabilis Deus. Apud Christum Dominum mille anni sunt sicut dies unus. Ergò Christus Dominus est verus, aeternus & immutabilis Deus. Maiorem confirmat collatio huius loci Apostolici cum Psal. 90. ex quo Petrus hanc sententiam adducit. v. 1. inquit Moses. Domine refugium factus es nobis à generatione in generationem.v. 2.Priusquam montes fierent, aut formaretur terra & orbis, à seculo & in seculum tu es Deus.v. 4.Quoniam mille anni ante oculos tuos tanquam dies hesterna, quae praeteriit. Hîc ex antecedentibus manifestum, quod ad aeternitatis descriptionem haec phrasis pertineat, mille annos esse apud Deum, sicut diem unum. Minorem confirmat totus huius loci contextus.

3. Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam pervenire, inquit Petrus, cui consonat illud Pauli 1. Tim. 2. v. 4.Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Ergò Deus non voluit, ut primi homines laberentur, ac per lapsum & se & omnes posteros aeterno exitio involverent. Si enim Deus non vult aliquos perire, ergò etiam non voluit primos parentes perire. Si Deus non vult aliquos perire, multò minùs vult totum genus humanum perire, & per conseq. nec immutabili quodam Dei decreto & ordinatione primi homines sunt lapsi, nec genus humanum exitio involutum.

4, Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire. Ergò non est causa peccati. Si enim esset causa damnationis ex absoluto quodam reprobationis decreto, utique etiam esset causa peccati, unde Calviniani absoluti decreti propugnatores dicunt, Deum ad damnationem & causas damnationis homines quosdam praedestinasse.

5. Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire. Ergò falsum est, quod Calviniani & cum illis quidam Pontificii docent, Deum absoluto quodam decreto maximam generis humani partem reprobasse, quos converti & salvari nolit, pro quibus etiam Christus non sit mortuus. Dico quosdam Pontificios id docere, quidam enim absolutum illud reprobationis decretum vel repudiant, vel quod repudient, videri volunt. Cornelius à Lapide in h. l. Hinc patet, Deum velle omnium salutem, & nolle alicuius damnationem, ac consequenter neminem reprobare ante praevisa eius demerita & mortem in peccato. quae voluntas in Deo non tantùm est signi, ut quidam censuerunt, sed etiam beneplaciti, ut solidè ostendit Gabriel Vasquez. p. 1. q. 19. Disp. 83. c. 2. Lorinus in h. l. Hinc elicitur probatio melioris opinionis, magisque communis, paratam semper hominibus in hac vita gratiam esse sufficientem ad omnia tollenda peccata, nec ullam exceptionem poni debere vel in peccatis, vel in peccatoribus, quantumlibet peccaverint. Et postea. Excipi adhuc potest de parvulis & usu rationis carentibus. Sed pro his mediatè sufficiens remedium datur per parentes, ut Prosper docet lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. Loquitur Petrus hoc loco de rationis usum habentibus, qui sunt capaces paenitentiae. Est etiam generalis propositio non restringenda ad genem singulorum vel ad praedestinatos. Excipiunt 1. Beza, Piscator & alii ex Calvinianis, dictum Apostoli nostri accipiendum esse de solis electis. Deus non vult aliquos perire, scil. ex nobis, qui credimus in Christum, ac proinde in numero electorum sumus, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire, nempe omnes nos, qui credimus in Christum, quae sunt verba Piscatoris in scholiis ad h. l. Idem in observationibus ex hoc loco deductis §. 5. sic scribit. Petrus non loquitur hîc de omnibus in universum hominibus, sed tantùm de omnibus electis: scribit enim ad fideles Iudaeos, quos ex caritate pro electis habebat, ideò ait, patiens est erga nos, vid. quos per Evangelium vocavit, & etiamnum vocat, nolens ullos, vid. ex nobis perire, sed omnes, videl. nos, quos vocat, ad resipiscentiam tendere. Eandem exceptionem inculcat Estius Pontificius in comm. ad h. l. Intelligitur hîc, inquit, voluntas Dei absoluta & propriè dicta, non tamen de omnibus hominibus, sed de solis electis. Dicit enim Petrus, Deus patienter agìt propter vel erga vos, utique electos. Nam haec Epistola scribitur ad eosdem, ad quos prima scripta fuit, sc. ad electos advenas. Sic ergò Petrus dicit, Dominum patienter agere h. e. adventum promissum & iudicium suum differre propter electos, ut ne pereant, sed ad paenitentiam conversi salventur, quomodo Paulus dicit, se omnia sustinere propter electos, ut & ipsi salutem consequantur,2. Tim. 2. v. 10.Sicut propter electos breviabuntur dies illi tribulationis magnaeMatth. 24. v. 22. ne sc. magnitudine tribulationum oppressi in desperationem incidant & pereant: ita patienter agit Dominus, tempusque iudicii differt propter electos, ut omnes, qui adhuc restant colligendi, colligantur. Nam si Deus anticiparet iudicii tempus à se decretum, aliqui perirent eorum, quos ab aeterno ad salutem elegit. Resp. 1. Deum differre iudicii diem propter electos, concedimus, sed propter solos electos illum differre, ac solos electos hîc intelligendos esse, quand o Petrus dicit, Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire, id verò est, quod negamus. 2. Scribit enim Petrus toti vocatorum coetui, in quo multi erant reprobi, quorum tamen paenitentiam & salutem iuxta voluntatem antecedentem sive misericordiae Deus seriò expetebat, & inter causas alias etiam eo fine iudicium extremum differebat, ut ipsis quoque tempus paenitentiae suppeteret. 3. Sic ergò colligimus. Quos Deus vult ad paenitentiam venire, illorum neminem absoluto quodam odio & decreto vult perire. Atqui Deus etiam reprobos ad paenitentiam vult venire. Ergò neminem reproborum absoluto quodam odio & decreto vult perire. Propositio est Petri in hoc textu. Assumtio est Pauli Rom. 2. v. 4.Num divitias bonitatis & patientiae & longanimitatis contemnis, ignorans, quod Dei benignitas invitat ad paenitentiam?v. 5.tu verò secundùm duritiem & impoenitens cor tuum thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae & revelationis iusti iudicii Dei. Sic ergò illa μαρκροθυμία, cuius Petrus meminit, etiam illos ad paenitentiam invitat, qui peccatis securè indulgendo paulatim divinam coacervant iram, ut tandem universa instar thesauri depromatur. Inde Hemmingius ad h. l. Apostolicum sic annotat. Disertè absque omni ambiguitate tum verborum, tùm sensus pronunciat Apostolus, Deum non velle ullos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam colligi. Quare hoc dictum memoriâ teneamus, ut nos muniamus adversus eos, qui hodie negant, gratiam DEI universalem esse. Neque est, quod nos moveat novi Interpretis autoritas, qui hoc dictum restriugit ad pios, quibus Petrus scribit. Nam hoc manifestè pugnat cum verbis Apostoli, qui loquitur de eis, qui non egerunt paenitentiam. 4. Repentendae ergò hoc loco causae superiùs expositae, propter quas Deus perfectam impiorum punitionem usque ad diem iudicii differt, ex quibus constabit, non solùm electos, sed etiam reprobos à Deo ad paenitentiam vocari, ac proinde etiam de reprobis accipiendum, quod Deus non velit illos perire, sed salvari, videl. iuxta voluntatem suam antecedentem. Quod enim concio paenitentiae sit universalis, probant manifesta Scripturae dicta Luc. 24. v. 47. Christus iussit predicari in nomine suo paenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes.Actor. 17. v. 30.Deus annunciat omnibus ubique hominibus, ut agant paenitentiam.Rom. 11. v. 32.Conclusit Deus omnes sub incredulitate, ut omnium misereatur. Ex illis sic concludimus. Quos Deus ad paenitentiam vocat, illorum etiam salutem seriò expetit. Deus omnes homines ad paenitentiam vocat. Ergò omnium hominum salutem seriò expetit. 5. Dictum Petri est generale. Deus non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire. Illud non debet ex praeconcepta opinione de absoluto reprobationis decreto restringi, sed potiùs ex parallelis Scripturae locis universaliter explicari. Ezech. 18. v. 23.cap. 33. v. 11.Nolo mortem impii.Matth. 23. v. 37.Quoties volui vos congregare, & noluistis.1. Tim. 2. v. 4.Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire.c. 4. v. 10.Deus est Salvator omnium hominum, maximè fidelium. 6. Petrus Ecclesiis, ad quas scribit electorum nomen tribuit, non ratione omnium, qui erant in externa ecclesiae societate & in numero vocatorum, sed ratione praecipuorum membrorum, quae interiore Spiritus vinculo Christo capiti in corpore mystico erant coniuncta, per usitatam in Scripturis Synecdochen. Sed ex eo probari nequit, quando Petrus hoc loco dicit, Deum non velle aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire, id de solis electis accipiendum esse. Posset enim eodem modo colligi, quòd soli electi memores esse debeant verborum à Prophetis & Apostolis praedictorum cap. 3. v. 2. quòd soli electi scire debeant, mille annos esse apud Deum instar unius diei v. 8. quòd soli electi debeant sancta conversatione ad novissimum Christi adventum sese praeparare v. 11. quòd soli electi debeant longanimitatem Dei salutem aestimare. v. 15.

2. Tossanus sic excipit. Deus non vult ullos perire, sc. ut penes illum culpa resideat, ut conversionis tempus hominibus deneget. Resp. 1. Quando Petrus dicit, Deus non vult ullos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam venire, tùm non solùm Deum à culpa absolvit, sed etiam causam damnationis impiorum absoluto Dei decreto tribuendam esse negat. 2. Quamvis illi, qui decreto reprobationis praevisionem lapsus praesternunt, Deum à culpa perditionis hominum absolvere videantur, tamen qui ipsum hominis lapsum ex absoluto Dei decreto deducunt, quod multi ex Calvinianis faciunt, manifestè Deo culpam crudelitatis & immisericordiae tribuunt. Crudelis enim est misericordia, velle aliquem esse miserum, ut miserendi occasionem habere possit. 3. Tossanus ipse ad hunc v. 9. sic annotat. Deus estμακρόθυμοςerga nos, ut tempus paenitentiae nobis suppetat, & ut impii nullam habeant excusationem, ac si adventus Christi fuisset nimis praeceps & festinatus. Atqui si haec est causa dilationis, utique etiam Deus illis ipsis impiis spacium paenitentiae concedit. Inde paulò post subiungit Toslanus. Deus omnes ad paenitentiam hortatur, etiam impios, ac concedit ipsis tempus paenitentiae. Quod ergò non convertuntur, eius rei culpa non residet penes Deum, sed penes illos ipsos qui longanimitate & patientiâ Dei pessimè abutuntur.Rom. 2. v. 5. ex quibus sic colligimus. Quibus Deus tempus paenitentiae concedit, illos etiam vult salvos fieri. Atqui etiam impiis & pereuntibus, longanimitate Dei abutentibus, Deus paenitentiae tempus concedit. Ergò etiam impios & pereuntes longanimitate Dei abutentes vult salvos fieri, sc. voluntate antecedente, ut superiùs expositum fuit. 4. Probè hoc vident Calviniani, inde recurrunt ad distinctionem inter voluntatem absconditam & revelatam; inter voluntatem signi & beneplaciti: ac dictum Apostolicum. 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. accipiendum esse statuunt διαιρετικῶςde generibus singulorum, nonσυμωληρωματικῶςde singulis generum. Sed quid ad inania eiusmodi effugia respondendum sit, expositum fuit tom. 2. Locor. tractat de Provident. §. 113. de praedestinat. & reprobat. §. 58. 59. 71. in Exeg. tom. 1. Loc. tract. de Natura Dei §. 268. 269.

3. Chamier. tom. 3. trat. lib. 7. cap. 8. §. 11. excipit, distinguendum esse inter Dei voluntatem & beneplacitum.חפץ inquit, apud Ezechielem non est simpliciter velle, sed delectari, defiderare,εὐαρεστεῖν.

Quis autem neget, posse Deum velle, & tamen non delectari morte peccatoris? Est enim certum, si ullo modo eam nellet, nullo modo eam futuram. Resp. 1. Si non est DEI beneplacitum, ut pereat impius, utique etiam non reprobavit impium ex absoluto quodam odio & decreto. 2. Vult Deus impii etiam pereuntis salutem, sc. voluntate antecedente sive misericordiae; vult eiusdem in impietate perseverantis damnationem, sc. voluntate consequente sive iustitiae. 3. Chamier subiicit, mortem infligi impiis & impoenitentibus à Deo iustissimo iudice. Ergò haec est voluntas Dei consequens, & iudiciaria, ad finalem impii impaenitentiam respectum habens.

4. Estius praeter exceptionem superiùs discussam duas affert alias Deus, inquit, non vult aliquos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam pervenire. 1. Quatenus humano generi in universum media quaedam & auxilia generalia providit & contulit, per quae possent homines ad Deum converti, licet ea ad hominum conversionem & salutem absque specialibus auxiliis, quae non omnibus dantur, minimè sufficiant. 2. Quatenus vult & facit, pios homines nolle quempiam perire, sed velle seu desiderare, ut omnes à DEO aversi ad ipsum per veram paenitentiam redeant. Atqui prior explicatio non satisfacit emphasi dicti Apostolici. Nisi enim sufficientia media salutis Deus ipsis pereuntibus offerret, non posset verè de ipso dici, quod non velit ullos perire, sed velit omnes salvari. Audiat Estius Bellarminum societatis suae hominem lib. 2. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 5. v. 1. Auxilium sufficiens ad salutem pro loco & tempore, mediatè vel immediatè omnibus datur. Illud toto isto capite. 5. confirmat & inter caetera scribit §. Item Sap. 11.Misereris omnium, quia omnia potes, & dissimulas peccata hominum propter paenitentiam &c. Haec certè vix intelligi possunt, nisi fateamur, omnibus tribui sufficiens auxilium. quomodo enim miseretur omnium & parcit omnibus, si non dat saltem eis auxilium, quo ad reconciliationem possint pervenire, si velint? Neque debent haec restringi ad electos: nam ratio, cur Deus omnibus pareat & omnium misereatur, redditur hoc loco ex creatione, quia Deus omnes creavit. At creatio communis est omnibus absolutè. §. Illud item Ioh. 1. &c. adducit dictum nostrum Apostolicum, eique coniungit illud Paulinum 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. ac de utroque sic disserit. Augustini de hoc loco Apostolico haec fuit sententia, Deum velle omnes salvos fieri, quia dat omnibus unde possint velle credere & salvari, sic tamen si ipsi noluerint, non salventur, sed ad supplicia destinentur aeterna, quae fuit etiam expositio S. Prosperi lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. 25. & 28. Item Commentariorum, qui tribuuntur Ambrosio. Item Chrysostomi, Theophylacti & Oecumenii, qui dicunt, Deum velle omnes salvos fieri, si & ipsi velint &c. Illud item 1. Tim. 4.Qui est Salvator omnium hominum, maximè fidelium vix potest aliter exponi, quàm ut exponit S. Prosper l. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 10. ut videl. intelligamus, Deum Salvatorem esse omnium, quia dat omnibus, unde salvari possint, sed maximè fidelium, quia dat illis, non solùm ut salvari possint, sed etiam ut salventur. Denique illud1. Cor. 15.pro omnibus mortuus est Christus, &1. Tim. 2.qui dedit semetipsum redemtionem pro omnibus; &1. Ioh. 2.ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non solùm autem nostris, sed etiam totius mundi, quomodo potest verum esse, si non datur omnibus aliquid, unde Christi mortis participes fieri queant? Nam cùm non possit ullus sine praeveniente dono particeps esse mortis Christi & precii redemtionis huius, frustra Christus pro omnibus precium redemtionis solvit, si noluit omnibus viam aperire, quâ ad redemtionem pervenire possent. Haec omnia Bellarminus, Estio disertè contradicens.

Posterior Estii expositio à scopo Apostoli est planè aliena. Neque enim Apostolo propositum est docere, quid pii ex impulsu Spiritus sancti velint vel non velint, sed quid Dominus, qui diem iudicii differt, per seipsum velit vel non velit. Quaerimus autem ex Estio, an illa piorum voluntas, quâ seriò expetunt, ut omnes homines ad Deum convertantur & salventur, sit divinae voluntati conformis, nec ne? Si prius, utique etiam Deus ipse per seipsum vult, omnes homines ad paenitentiam pervenire & salvari. Si posterius, tùm maior misericordia tribuitur piis, quàm Deo, qui est ipsa caritas. 1. Ioh. 4. v. 16. & cuius misericordia tanta est, quantus ipse, h. e. infinita. Sirac. 2. v. 23.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Ex eo, quòd mille anni dicuntur apud Deum esse instar unius diei, & unus dies instar mille annorum, multi ex veteribus colligunt, mundum per sex mille annos duraturum, cùm mundus sex diebus conditus sit. Hieronymus in Epistolari expositione Psal. 89. ad Cyprianum, tom. 4. p. 44. Ego arbitror ex hoc loco, & ex Epistola, quae nomine Petri inseribitur, mille annos pro una die solitos appellari, ut sc. quia mundus in sex diebus fabricatur, sex millibus tantùm annorum credatur subsistere, & postea venire septenarium & octonarium numerum, in quo verus exercetur Sabbatismus, & Circumcisionis puritas redditur. Similia occurrunt apud Iustinum in Dial. cum Tryphone p. 240.

& in l. qq. ad gentes q. 71. pag. 337. Irenaeum lib. 5. adv. haeres. cap. 28. pag. 352. Lactantium lib. 7. Institut. cap. 7. & 14. pag. 416. Hilarium can. 17. in Matth. Augustinum lib. 20. de C. Dei cap. 7. Fevardentius in notis ad Irenaeum lib. 5. cap. 28. pro hac opinione adducit Iustinum, Irenaeum, Hilarium, Germanum, Constantinopolitanum, Thalmudicos, Hydaspen, Medorum Regem, Trismegistum, Sibyllas, Hippolitum, Chrysostomum, Cyrillum, Gaudentium Brixianum, Picum Mirandulanum. Cornelius à Lapide ad v. 8. huius Epist. sic annotat. Haec opinio (de duratione mundi per sex millia annorum) solidiora habet fundamenta, ideoque multorum est Patrum & Doctorum, unde probabilis est, nec temeritatis argui potest.

Atqui. 1. Idem Augustinus, qui pro hac opinione adducitur, in enarrat. Psalm. 89. (secundùm Hebraeos 90.) eos, qui verba Psalmographi ad illam opinionem accommodant, refellit. Ausi sunt, inquit, homines praesumere scientiam temporum, quod scire cupientibus discipulis Dominus ait. Non est vestrûm scire tempora, quae Pater posuit in sua potestate,Actor. 1.& definierunt hoc seculum sex annorum millibus tanquam sex diebus posse finiri, nec attenderunt, quod dictum est, tanquam dies unus, qui praeteriit. Non enim, quando hoc dictum est, soli mille anni praeterierant, & quod eos maximè debuit admonere, ne temporum luderentur incerto, illud est sicut vigilia in nocte. Neque enim sicut de sex diebus aliquid verisimile videntur opinati propter sex dies primos, quibus Deus perfecit opera sua, sic etiam sex vigilias, i. e. horas decem & octo possunt illi opinatini coaptare. 2. Ambros. lib. 7. Comment. in Lucam explicans illud Matthaei. Post dies sex transfiguratus est Christus, indicat, se non recipere talem mundanae aetatis periodum, quia temporibus suis plusquam sex annorum millia computarentur. (Rectè verò monet Sixtus Senensis lib. 5. Biblioth. sanct. annotat. 190. Ambrosium supputationem quandam annorum Mundi sibi peculiarem secutum fuisse, cùm secundùm Hebraicae veritatis calculum Ambrosii tempore nondum praeterierint anni quatuor mille quadringenti, numerant enim Hebraei à conditio mundo usque ad Christum annos 3962.) 3. Nec Mosi, nec Petro propositum fuit hexaëmeron creationis cum duratione mundi conferre, sed docere, quòd apud Deum spacia temporis non sint iisdem momentis metienda, quo apud homines, cùm ipsi extra omnem temporis successionem posito omnia sint in simplicissimo τῷ νῦν praesentissima. 4. Ecquis nos certos reddet, quod tempus consummationis seculi aestimandum sit ex creationis hexaëmero. Si analogiae aliquid dandum, potiùs ad durationis, quàm inchoationis tempus ea nos deducet, quod videlicet sex dierum spacio mundus iterum sit dissolvendus, sicut sex dierum spacio ab initio fuit conditus. Confer Sixt. Senens. libro 6. Biblioth. annot. 73. & tract. de Extrem. Iudic. §. 77. 5. Inde quidam ex ipsis Pontificiis hanc opinionem repudiant. Lorinus in h. l. Cavenda est falsa opinio,Psal. 90.& huic loco innixa, de mundi per sex duntaxat annorum millia duratione, sicut scil. sex diebus mundus factus est, ita ut dies Dei magnus ex mille constet annis. Estius ad v. 8. h. l. Vanum est, quòd quidam freti hac formulâ, quâ mille anni apud Dominum censentur tanquam dies unus & contrà, conati sunt incerta pro certis affirmare, & obscura quaedam interpretari dies accipiendo pro mille annis, aut etiam pro annis singulis. Ut exempli causâ, cùm sex dies creationis mundi pro argumento sumunt, eundem mundum per sex millia annorum duraturum &c. quae coniecturae sunt hominum superstitiosè curiosorum prorsus incertae, & alienae à sensu huius loci. Notandum verò, hanc opinionem niti communi fermè Patrum consensu, qui, cùm ab Estio in hac quaestione repudietur, argumentum exhibet, quòd Patrum consensus non exhibeat apodicticum argumentum.

2. Beda in comm. h. l. sic disserit. Quidaem hanc sententiam (quod unus dies apud Dominum ut mille anni) ita intelligendam putaent, quasi dies iudicii tantam habeat longitudinem, quantum mille annorum spacium, non considerantes, quia non ait simpliciter, erit unus dies, sicut mille anni, sed unus, inquit, dies apud Dominum, sicut mille anni. Sicut etiam constat, quia Psalmista mille annos non diei futuro iudicii, sed diei hesterno, qui praeteriit ante oculos conditoris adaequat, imò omnes annos nostros, hoc est, seculi huius omne tempus custodiae noctis unius, quae est quarta pars noctis assimilat: ita B. Petrus quasi unumquemque diem seculi praesentis mille annos unicuique diei apud Dominum aequiparat, id est, eiusdem mensurae asseverat, quia videlicet omnia & parva & magna aequaliter ipse conspicit. Et quidem Petrus, si hoc de die iudicii vellet tantùm intelligi, quod verè tantae esset longitudinis, quantae sunt mille anni nostri, poterat utique apertiùs suam indicare sententiam, neque opus esset addere apud Dominum, quia ille dies, si tantae esset longitudinis, etiam hominibus cunctis, ubi advenisset, appareret.

3. Ex eo, quod Petrus h. l. allegat dictum Siracidis cap. 35. v. 19.ὁ Κύριος ὀν μὴ βραδύνῃ posset Pontificius conari autoritatem Canonicam Siracidi conciliare. Resp. 1. Nuda allegatio in Nov. Test. nondum probat Canonicam alicuius libri autoritatem, cùm etiam gentilium Poetarum dicta ab Apostolis allegentur, sed requiritur, ut omnia Canonicorum librorum requisita alicui libro conveniant. 2. Nec dum liquidò constat, an Petrus ex Siracide haec adducat, cùm similis sententia extet apud Mosen Deut. 7. v. 10.οὐχὶ βραδύνει (ὁ Κύριος.)

Observationes. 1. DEI aeternitatem confirmat alibi Scriptura simplici & plana asseveratione Genes. 21. v. 33.Esa. 40. v. 28. cap. 57. v. 15. Daniel. 6. v. 26.Rom. 16. v. 26. Hoc loco ut & Psal. 90. v. 5. eam stabilit temporis & successionis negatine. Iustinus in qq. & Respons. ad Graecos fol. 29. οὐδὲν ἔγχρονον ἔστι παρὰ τῷ θεῷ. Beda in h. l. In cognitione divinae virtutis & praeterita & futura & praesentia aequaliter constant, & quae longa nobis, & quae brevia videntur temporum curricula, aequalis utique sunt spacii apud conditorem temporum, qui omnia aequaliter & magna & parva conspicit.

2. Ephrem tom. 1. serm. adhortat. ad piet. Mille anni huius seculi in aeterno & incorruptibili illo mundo tantam habent comparationem, quantam minima arena maris cum tota arena eiusdem: quod desumtum exSirac. 18. vers. 8.Ut gutta aquae è mari, & calculus arenae; sic mille anni in diebus seculi, h. e. aeternitatis. Lyranus in h. l. Per millenarium intelligitur quantacunque revolutio temporum, quae modica est & nullius momenti, comparata divinae aeternitati.

3. Quòd si ergò novissimus Christi ad iudicium adventus videatur differri, cogitemus, nullam planè esse comparationem inter annos mille & aeternitatem, infinitam prorsus atque interminabilem, ac mille annos esse apud DEUM ut diem unum. August. in Psal. 89. Quod tibi videtur longum, breve est apud DEUM. Beda in h. l. Cùm DEUS unumquemque diem seculi nostri aeternâ suâ memoriâ complectatur, ut annorum mille circuitus: ita mille annos, ut unius diei spacium sine labore circumspiciat, manifestè intelligendum, quod ipsorum quoque dierum & annorum omnium finem certissimè noverit, quando adventus ipsius claritas revelanda, quando promissa sint sanctis praemia reddenda.

4. Sicut apud DEUM non est vicissitudo lucis & tenebrarum:

(Iac. v. 17. Apud Patrem luminum non estπαραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα aut obumbratio conversionis i. e. ex conversione orta, qualis in Sole visibili & corporeo, qui in occasu suo ad oppositum haemisphaerium se convertens obumbrat haemisphaerium, quod relinquit) ita quoque apud Deum nulla est vicissitudo temporis, sicut apud nos homines, quibus praeterita transierunt, futura nondum praesto sunt: sed ut Augustinus de ipso loquitur lib. 4. de Trinit. cap. 21. Est sine illo temporali motu super omnem creaturam, sine ullis temporum & locorum intervallis, & simul unum atque idem ab aeternitate in aeternitatem tanquam ipsa aeternitas.

5. Eo ipso, quod Petrus dicit, mille annos apud Deum esse sicut diem unum, & diem unum, sicut mille annos, tacitè fatetur, diem novissimi adventûs Christi & universalis iudicii esse hominibus incognitum. Marc. 13. v. 32.Act. 1. v. 7. Augustinus lib. 18. de C. Dei cap. 53. Frustra annos, qui huic seculo remanent, computare ac definire conamur, cùm hoc scire non esse nostrum ex veritatis ore audiamus &c. Omnium hac de re calculantium digitos resolvit & quiescere iubet ille, qui dicit. Non est vestrum, nosse tempora &c.

6. Μακροθυμίαν DEI commendat, quod paenitentiae spacium peccatoribus concedit. Esai. 30. v. 18.Expectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri.Sap. 11. v. 24.Misereris omnium, quia omnia potes & dissimulas peccata hominum propter paenitentiam.Rom. 2. v. 4.benignitas DEI ad paenitentiam te adducit. Iustinus in Apolog. ad Antoninum. Paenitentiam mavult Pater caelestis quàm poenam.

7. Hac verò DEI μακροθυμίᾳ ac χρηστότητι non abutamur ad securitatem carnalem, sed tempus visitationis nostrae agnoscamus,Luc. 19. v. 44. ac DEO gratias agamus, quòd non, ut peccatis eramus promeriti, statim nos perdiderit, sed tempus paenitentiae concesscrit, ac dum sores gratiae adhuc patent, ad Deum in vera paenitentia convertamur. Sirac. 5. v. 8.Non tardes converti ad Dominum, & ne differas de die in diem. v. 9. subitò enim veniet ira illas. Memores simus, quòd mors non tardatSirac. 14. v. 12.Si Deus aliquantulum illam differt, id inde est, quia longanimis est erga nos, nolens in peccato nos comprehendere, sed ad paenitentiam invitare.

8. Quinimò Deus non solùm differt poenam, sed etiam beneficia exhibet, quibus hominem, qui per peccatum sese coepit morti tradere invitat atque allicit, ut sese ad creatorem suum, à quo nefariè se separavit, convertat & salutem consequatur. Cypr. lib. de bono patient. Qualis & quanta patientia est in Deo, quod in contumeliam suae maiestatis & honoris instituta ab hominibus prophana templa & terrena figmenta & sacra sacrilegia patienter sustinens, super bonos & malos aequaliter facit diem nasci & lumen solis suboriri? & cùm imbribus terram rigat, nemo à beneficiis eius excluditur? Videmus, insuperabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus & innoxiis, religiosis & impiis, gratias agentibus & ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, Elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, exuberare pomis arbusta, & cùm crebris, imò continuis exacerbetur offensis, indignationem suam temperat, & cùm habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens sc. clementer & differens, ut, si fieri potest, multùm malitia protracta aliquando mutetur.

## 3:9
Connection. 1. The Apostle explains the cause why Christ defers his coming to judgment, and thus also the final judgment and the destruction of the world, namely, that because he seriously seeks the salvation of all, space for repenting may be given to men, and thus their salvation may be promoted.

2. This true cause ἀντιθετικῶς he opposes to the false cause, which some were suspecting, namely, that the promised coming is deferred out of a certain slowness.

3. By this reason προληπτικῶς he meets the doubt, why the coming of Christ to judgment is deferred for so long, which delay ἐμπαῖκται they interpret thus, that Christ is never to return to judgment.

Exposition of the text. Οὐ βραδύνει ὁ Κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας. The Latin codices vary here. Some have, the Lord does not delay the promise. But others, the Lord does not delay in his promises, in which way Pelagius cites this passage in his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 2, as if for τῆς ἐπαγγελίας in Greek there were ταῖς ἐπαγγελιαις. Again other codices, the Lord does not delay his promise, which agrees more with grammar than the promise does not delay, unless one wishes to construe the genitive with the noun Lord.

The word βραδύνειν is sometimes placed intransitively 1. Tim. 3. vers. 15. ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνω, but if I should delay, if any delay should be cast upon my coming. In the same way it is used Genes. 43. v. 10. εἰ μὴ ἐβραδύναμεν. Deuter. 7. vers. 10. οὐχὶ βραδύνει (ὁ Κύριος) Sirac. 35. vers. 19. ὁ Κύριος οὐ μὴ βραδύνῃ. Thence some think that also in this place it ought to be taken intransitively, and therefore they join the little word τῆς ἐπαγγελίας with the word Κύριος, so that the sense may be, the Lord of the promise, i. e. the promiser, He who promised, does not delay, in the way that Augustine also reads, because the Hebrews join the word באל in that way with a substantive placed in the genitive, so that they describe the author and possessor of some thing, one skilled in some thing, one having some thing, one who has obtained or is endowed with some thing. Thus, the Lord of words Exod. 24. v. 14. is he who contends in judgment, as the Targum explains; the Lord of the wing Prov. 1. vers. 17. is one having wings; the Lord of dreams Genes. 37. v. 9.is a dreamer; the Lord of the oath Neh. 6. v. 18. he who has sworn; the Lords of the covenant Gen. 14. v. 13. are those allied by covenant συνωμόται, as the LXX rendered it.

But because the word βραδύνειν also occurs used transitively Esa. 46. vers. 13. σωτηρίαν τῶν παρ' ἐμοῦ οὐ βραδύνω, therefore that τῆς ἐπαγγελίας is more correctly joined with the word βραδυνει, so that the sense may be, the Lord does not delay or defer the promise. Estius indeed says that he does not find where the word βραδύνειν is taken transitively, and governs an accusative after it, which he opposes to those who think that for τῆς ἐπαγγελίας one should read τάς ἐπαγγελίας: but we have brought forward a clear passage from Esa. 46. vers. 13. In that way the Syrian also rendered it. The Lord does not delay [במולכונהי] in his promises; as also Luther. Der HERR verzeucht nicht die Verheissung. Nor is there any reason for one to object that the word βραδύνειν is nowhere found used with a genitive. For besides the fact that ἑτέρωσις of cases is not infrequent for the Greeks, it can be said that the particle ἕνεκα, is to be understood, the Lord does not delay τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ἕνεκα, such an ellipsis occurs Actor. 17. vers. 47. The Lord does not delay, as it pertains to the promise, that is, he does not defer the promise. There are those who think that an illative conjunction also ought to be understood οὖν. The Lord therefore does not delay the promise, that is, he does not defer the fulfillment of his promise further than is fitting. For the Hebrews often conceal illative conjunctions, and leave them to be understood. But even if the illative conjunction is not added at all, the sense nevertheless remains whole, which, as is evident from the connection of this verse with the preceding ones, tends toward this, that the slowness or swiftness of the coming of Christ to judgment, and consequently of the punishment to be inflicted upon the impious therein, should not be weighed so much by the clock of our time, or by human estimation, as by divine eternity and providence, to whom all times and the moments of times are present, and before whose eternity this whole time does not deserve the name of any delay. But Peter also intends this, that there is a distinction between to be slow, and to defer, or to make a delay. For he who defers and makes a delay does not immediately act slowly, but he finally acts slowly who defers beyond the due time what is to be done, and whose delay comes into just reproach, which itself is gathered from the Prophetic saying Hebr. 2. v. 3. If the Lord should make a delay, wait for him, coming he will come, and will not be slow.

Ὥς τινες βραδύτητα ἡγούνται. Vulg. As some think. But in the Greek the noun of the preceding verb is repeated, As some think slowness. In the same way also the Syrian rendered it, as men [שווחרא] think hesitation.

Ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ἡμᾶς. Vulg. But he acts patiently because of you, or as other Codices read more correctly, towards us. In the Greek it is properly, he is long-suffering towards us, or towards us, just as the Vulgate Interpreter himself rendered the noun μακροθυμίας in this chapter v. 15. by long-suffering. The verb μαηεοθυμείυ is used elsewhere with the preposition ἐπὶ Matth. 18. vers. 26. & 29. Luc. 18. v. 7. Iac. 5. v. 7. Sirac. 18. vers. 10. cap. 29. v. 11. cap. 35. v. 19. & with the preposition πρός, 1. Thessal. 5. vers. 14. but here it is joined with the preposition εἰς. The Syrian, having followed the Vulgate version rather than the Greek text, rendered it. But it is [מגררוחה מטלתכון] with contracted Spirit because of you. For he who restrains anger contracts his spirit, just as also among the Hebrews μακρόθυμος is called ארך אפים long of angers, who neither is easily angered, nor immediately punishes Ex. 34. v. 6. Num. 14. v. 18. on the contrary, however, קצר אפים short of angers, short of nose. Likewise קצר רוח ὀξόθυμος, who is easily irritated. Therefore the Apostle in this place attributes κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν to God μακροθυμίαν, because he defers the final judgment, and consequently the vengeance to be taken on the impious in it, which long-suffering men are accustomed to do. He alludes to the Prophetic saying Esa. 30. v. 18. The Lord waits, that he may have mercy on you, and therefore he will be exalted sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment.

Regarding the relative pronoun added, the Greek codices vary. The Regius and another codex read εἰς ὑμᾶς,, another Regius δι' ὑμᾶς in the second person, in which way the Vulgate interpreter also translates. But the more approved and more numerous codices read εἰς ἡμᾶς in the first person, in which way Luther also rendered it, Er hat Gedult mit uns /, for which reason in the words of Peter it is ἀνακοίνωσις,, which also occurs elsewhere in his own epistles. 1. Epist. 4. v. 3.

Μὴ βουλόμενος τινάς ἀπολέσθαι. Vulg. not willing any to perish. The Greek words properly have, not willing any to perish, between which two a certain distinction intervenes, it can be gathered from Psal. 5. v 5. Thou art not a God willing iniquity. For sins are not committed with God simply unwilling or against his will, for no one can force God, nor can anything be done with God hindering and resisting; much less are they committed with God simply willing, because God in no way wills or approves what is evil, but they are committed with God not willing. This, however, is the distinction between to be unwilling and not to will, that the former has a privation of will and of an active principle together with repugnance and contrary action; the latter, however, has only στέρησιν that without violent reluctance. Lombard 1. sent. dist. 46. F Evils are not done with God willing or unwilling but not willing, because it is not subject to the will of God that evil be done or not be done, but that he permits it to be done, because it is good to permit evils to be done, and certainly willing he permits, not willing the evils, but willing to permit he permits that they themselves be done, because neither are evils good, nor is it good that they either be done or exist.

The Greek βουλόμενος in this place corresponds to the Hebrew חפץ he was delighted, he had good pleasure; the Syrian has the verb [צבא] which is of the same meaning entirely, it pleased, it was well-pleasing, the sense therefore is that God is not delighted by the destruction and ruin of any man, so that this seems to be taken from Ezech. 18. v. 23. Do I החפץ אחפץ by willing will, that the wicked should die? Do I delight in the death of the wicked? which is repeated cap. 33. v. 11.

Ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι Vulg. but all to return to repentance. The verb χωρῆσαι Erasmus translates actively, to receive all to repentance, understand, God wills. But χωρεῖν used actively signifies to contain, Matth. 19. v. 11. Marc. 2. v. 2. Iohan. 2. v. 6. c. 21. v. 25.

It is therefore more correctly accepted in a neutral signification. God wills all to approach, to come to repentance, in which way the Syrian also rendered it by [אתא] to come, by which same word he uses in the beginning of the following verse concerning the coming of the Day of the Lord. Luther in the same way. Sondern daß sich jederman zur Busse kehre. This exposition is confirmed by the antithesis between τό ἀπολέσθαι & χωρῆσαι of which since the former is neutral, it is left that the latter also must be accepted in the same kind, in which signification the word χωρεῖν is used Matth. 15. v. 17. Euripid. χώρει σύ δεῦρο Approach hither, come hither. Some think χωρῆσαι should be translated to be aggregated, to be gathered, so that it may be hinted, that God acts patiently and the time of judgment is deferred on account of the elect, so that all who still remain to be gathered may be gathered and aggregated to repentance. To which they accommodate that of Oecumenius in his commentary on this place, who says, the time of the consummation is deferred, so that the number of those to be saved may be completed. But in this signification the word χωρῆσαι is nowhere used in the sacred scriptures, nor will examples of that signification easily occur among profane writers.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Exponit Apostolus causam, cur Christus suum ad iudicium adventum, & sic etiam extremum iudicium & mundi destructionem differat, nimirùm, ut, quia omnium salutem seriò expetit, hominibus resipiscendi spacium detur, & sic salus eorum promoveatur.

2. Veram hanc causam ἀντιθετικῶς opponit causae falsae, quam aliqui suspicabantur, videl. quod ex quadam tarditate promissus adventus differatur.

3. Hac ratione προληπτικῶς occurrit dubitationi, quare adventus Christi ad iudicium tamdiu differatur, quam dilationem ἐμπαῖκται sic interpretantur, quod Christus nunquam ad iudicium sit rediturus.

Textus expositio. Οὐ βραδύνει ὁ Κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας. Codices Latini hîc variant. Quidam habent, non tardat Dominus promissi. Quidam verò, non tardat Dominus promissis, quomodo locum hunc citat Pelagius in comm. Epist. Rom. cap. 2. ac si pro τῆς ἐπαγγελίας in Graeco esset ταῖς ἐπαγγελιαις. Rursus alii Codices, non tardat Dominus promissionem suam, quod Grammaticae magis congruit, quàm non tardant promissi, nisi genitivum cum nomine Dominus quis construere velit.

Verbum βραδύνειν quandoque ponitur intransitivè1. Tim. 3. vers. 15.ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνω,si autem tardavero, si quae mora adventui meo iniicietur. Eodem modo usurpatur Genes. 43. v. 10.εἰ μὴ ἐβραδύναμεν.Deuter. 7. vers. 10.οὐχὶ βραδύνει (ὁ Κύριος)Sirac. 35. vers. 19.ὁ Κύριος οὐ μὴ βραδύνῃ. Inde quidam censent, etiam hoc loco intransitivè debere accipi, ac proinde voculam τῆς ἐπαγγελίας coniungunt cum voce Κύριος, ut sit sensus, Dominus promissi, i. e. promissor, qui promisit, non tardat, quo modo etiam Augustinus legit, quia Hebraei vocemבאלeo modo cum substantivo in genitivo posito coniungunt, ut rei alicuius autorem & possessorem, rei alicuius peritum, habentem rem aliquam, re aliquâ potitum aut praeditum describant. Sic Dominus verborumExod. 24. v. 14.est is, qui in iudicio contendit, ut exponit Targum; Dominus alaeProv. 1. vers. 17.est habens alas; Dominus somniorumGenes. 37. v. 9.est somniator; Dominus iuramentiNeh. 6. v. 18.qui iuraverit; Domini foederisGen. 14. v. 13.sunt confoederatiσυνωμόται,ut LXX. reddiderunt.

Sed quia verbum βραδύνειν etiam transitivè usurpatum occurrit Esa. 46. vers. 13.σωτηρίαν τῶν παρ' ἐμοῦ οὐ βραδύνω, ideò illud τῆς ἐπαγγελίας rectiùs coniungitur cum verbo βραδυνει, ut sit sensus, Dominus non tardat vel differt promissum. Estius quidem dicit, se non invenire, ubi verbumβραδύνεινtransitivè sumatur, & accusativum post se regat, quod opponit illis, qui pro τῆς ἐπαγγελίας legendum censent τάς ἐπαγγελίας: sed adduximus locum perspicuum ex Esa. 46. vers. 13. Eo modo etiam Syrus reddidit. Non cunctatur Dominus[במולכונהי]in promissionibus suis; uti etiam Lutherus. Der HERR verzeucht nicht die Verheissung. Neque est, quòd quis regerat, verbumβραδύνεινnuspiam inveniri cum genitivo usurpatum. Praeterquam enim, quòd ἑτέρωσις casuum Graecis non sit infrequens, dici potest, subaudiendam esse particulam ἕνεκα, non tardat Dominus τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ἕνεκα, qualis ellipsis occurrit Actor. 17. vers. 47.Non tardat Dominus, quod ad promissionem attinet, hoc est, non differt promissum. Sunt, qui existimant, subaudiri etiam debere coniunctionem illativamοὖν.Non ergò tardat Dominus promissum, h. e. non ultrà, quàm oportet, promissi sui complementum differt. Hebraei enim coniunctiones illativas saepè dissimulant, & intelligendas relinquunt. Sed si vel maximè illativa coniunctio non addatur, sensus tamen integer manet, qui, uti constat ex connexione huius versiculi cum praecedentibus eò tendit, quòd tarditas aut celeritas adventus Christi ad iudicium, & consequenter supplicii impiis in eo irrogandi, non tàm ex nostri temporis horologio, aut ex humana aestimatione pensitanda sit, quàm ex divina aeternitate & providentia, cui omnia tempora, & temporum articuli sunt praesentîa, ac coram cuius aeternitate universum hoc tempus non meretur alicuius morae nomen. Sed & hoc Petrus intendit, discrimen esse inter tardare, & differre sive moram facere.
