Neque enim qui differt, ac moram facit, statim tardat, sed is demùm tardat, qui ultra debitum tempus, quòd agendum est, differt, ac cuius mora in iustam reprehensionem venit, quod ipsum colligitur ex dicto Prophetico Hebr. 2. v. 3.Si moram fecerit Dominus, expecta eum, veniens veniet, & non tardabit.

Ὥς τινες βραδύτητα ἡγούνται. Vulg. Sicut quidam existimant. Sed in Graeco repetitur nomen praecedentis verbi, Sicut quidam tarditatem existimant. Eodem modo etiam Syrus reddidit, sicut homines[שווחרא]cunctationem existimant.

Ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ἡμᾶς. Vulg. Sed patienter agit propter vos, vel ut alii Codices rectiùs legunt, erga nos. In Graeco propriè est, longanimis est in nos, sive erga nos, sicut ipse vulgatus Interpres nomen μακροθυμίας in hoc cap. v. 15. per longanimitatem reddidit. Usurpatur aliàs verbum μαηεοθυμείυ cum praepositione ἐπὶMatth. 18. vers. 26. & 29.Luc. 18. v. 7.Iac. 5. v. 7.Sirac. 18. vers. 10.cap. 29. v. 11.cap. 35. v. 19. & cum praepositione πρός,1. Thessal. 5. vers. 14. sed hîc coniungitur cum praepositione εἰς. Syrus vulgatam potiùs versionem, quàm Graecum textum secutus reddidit. Sed est. [מגררוחה מטלתכון]contracto Spiritu propter vos. Qui enim iram cohibet, spiritum contrahit, sicut etiam apud Hebraeos μακρόθυμος vocatur ארך אפיםlongus irarum, qui nec facilè irascitur, nec statim punit Ex. 34. v. 6.Num. 14. v. 18. contrà verò קצר אפיםbrevis irarum, brevis nasi. Item קצר רוחὀξόθυμος, qui facilè irritatur. Ideò verò Apostolus hoc loco κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν Deo tribuit μακροθυμίαν, quia differt extremum iudicium, & consequenter ultionem in illo ab impiis sumendam, quod solent homines longanimes facere. Alludit ad dictum Propheticum Esa. 30. v. 18.Expectat Dominus, ut misereatur vestri, & ideò exaltabitur parcens vobis, quia Deus iudicii Dominus.

Circa pronomen relativum adiectum variant Codd. Graeci. Regius & alter Codex legunt εἰς ὑμᾶς, al. Regius δι' ὑμᾶς in secunda persona, quo modo etiam vertit vulgatus Interpres. Sed probatiores ac plures Codices legunt εἰς ἡμᾶς in prima persona, quo modo etiam Lutherus reddidit, Er hat Gedult mit uns / quâ ratione in verbis Petri est ἀνακοίνωσις, quae etiam alibi in ipsius Epistolis occurrit. 1. Epist. 4. v. 3.

Μὴ βουλόμενος τινάς ἀπολέσθαι. Vulg. nolens aliquos perire. Graeca propriè habent, non volens aliquos perire, inter quae duo discrimen aliquod intercedere, colligi potest ex Psal. 5. v 5.Non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es. Peccata enim non fiunt Deo simpliciter nolente vel invito, nemo enim Deum cogere potest, nec quidquam Deo impediente & repugnante fieri potest; multò minùs fiunt Deo simpliciter volente, quia Deus nullo modo vult vel approbat, quod malum est, sed fiunt Deo non volente. Hoc autem inter nolle & non velle est discrimen, quod illud habet privationem voluntatis & principii activi unà cum repugnantia & actione contraria; hoc autem habet tantum στέρησιν illam absque violenta reluctatione. Lombardus 1. sent. dist. 46. F Non Deo volente vel nolente sed non volente fiunt mala, quia non subest Dei voluntati ut malum fiat vel non fiat, sed ut fieri sinat, quia bonum est sinere mala fieri, & utique volens sinit non volens mala, sed volens sinere sinit, ut ipsa fiant, quianec mala sunt bona, nec ea vel fieri esse bonum est.

Graecum βουλόμενος hoc loco respondet Hebraeorum חפץdelectatus fuit, beneplacitum habuit; Syrus habet verbum [צבא] quod est eiusdem omninò significationis, placuit, complacuit, sensus igitur est, quod Deus nullius hominis interitu atque exitio delectetur, ut hoc desumtum videatur ex Ezech. 18. v. 23.Nunquidהחפץ אחפץvolendo volo, ut moriatur impius? Nunquid delector morte impit? quod repetitur cap. 33. v. 11.

Ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι Vulg. sed omnes ad paenitentiam reverti. Verbum χωρῆσαι Erasmus vertit activè, omnes ad paenitentiam recipere, subintellige, Deus vult. Sed χωρεῖν activè usurpatum significat capere,Matth. 19. v. 11.Marc. 2. v. 2.Iohan. 2. v. 6.c. 21. v. 25.

rectiùs igitur accipitur in significatione neutrali. Deus vult omnes ad paenitentiam accedere, venire, quo modo etiam Syrus reddidit per [אתא]venire, quo eodem verbo in princ. seq. vers. de adventu Diei Dominicae utitur. Lutherus eodem modo. Sondern daß sich jederman zur Busse kehre. Confirmat hanc expositionem antithesisinter τό ἀπολέσθαι & χωρῆσαι quorum prius cùm sit neutrale, etiam posterius in eodem genere accipiendum esse relinquitur, in qua significatione verbum χωρεῖν usurpatur Matth. 15. v. 17. Euripid. χώρει σύ δεῦροHuc accede, huc veni. Quidam censent, χωρῆσαι vertendum aggregari, colligi, ut innuatur, Deum patienter agere ac tempus iudicii differri propter electos, ut omnes, qui adhuc restant colligendi, colligantur & ad paenitentiam aggregentur. quò accommodant illud Oecumenii in comm. h. l. qui dicit, consummationis tempus differri, ut numerus salvandorum compleatur. Sed in hac significatione verbum χωρῆσαι in sacris literis nuspiam usurpatur, nec apud prophanos Scriptores exempla illius significationis facilè occurrent.

## 3:10
Connection. 1. Here begins the latter part of this chapter, in which the Apostle describes the manner of Christ's coming to judgment and the destruction of the world, and from it deduces a serious exhortation to the pursuit of piety.

2. He describes the manner of Christ's coming to judgment thus, that the day of the Lord will come, as a thief in the night that is, unexpectedly. He describes the manner of the destruction of the world through an enumeration of the parts to be destroyed.

3. The Apostle had made mention of the divine μακροθυμίας, through which the day of judgment is still deferred. But lest anyone abuse this μακροθυμίᾳ of God for carnal security, and promise himself many years yet to come, the Apostle adds that Christ will come unexpectedly to judgment, and that that day of judgment, because of the destruction of this world that will follow in it, will be exceedingly horrible and tremendous.

Exposition of the text. ἥξει δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα Κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ. Vulg. But the day of the Lord will come, as a thief. The Greek adds in the night, which the Vulgate Interpreter omitted.

By τὴν ἡμέραν Κυρίου he understands the day in which Christ to judgment to exercise judgment and to destroy the world, whence the prefixed article is deservedly held to be emphatic. That day of the Lord, great, i.e., as Jude calls it v. 6. Parallel to this place of ours are those in which that day is called ἡ ἐκείνη ἡμέρα Matth. 7. v. 22c. 24. v. 36.c. 26. v. 29.Luc. 21. v. 34.2. Thess. 1. v. 10.2. Tim. 1. v. 18. ἐξοχικῶς καὶ ἐξαιρέτως, because it is that great day which will put an end to all the days of this age, in which all the dead will rise again, all men will be set before the tribunal of Christ. Item, in which this day is called great day of the Lord and very terribleIoël. 2. v. 11.day of the Lord, in which there will be darkness and not lightAmos. 5. v. 18.that great day of God AlmightyApoc. 16. v. 14.day of Jesus Christ, day of the Lord Jesus1. Cor. 1. v. 8.c. 5. v. 5.2. Cor. 1. v. 14.Phil. 1. v. 6. & 10.c. 2. v. 16. because in it the Son of man will be revealed from heaven Luc. 17. v. 30. The Syrian expressed that emphasis in this way [יומה] that day.

Ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ. Thieves are accustomed to break into the houses of others unexpectedly, and to observe the time when they think they are least expected. Because therefore the day of judgment also will come unexpectedly Matth. 24. v. 44.At the hour in which you do not think, the Son of man is to come, therefore his arrival is compared to the clandestine and unlooked-for arrival of a thief. Peter took this simile from the mouth of his Master Christ Jesus Matth. 24. v. 43.But know this, that if the householder knew at what hour the thief was to come, he would surely watch, and would not suffer his house to be dug through.v. 44.Therefore be you also ready, because at the hour you do not think, the Son of man is to come. which is repeated Luc. 12. v. 39. & 40. Paul used the same comparison for this matter 1. Thess. 5. v. 2.For you yourselves know exactly, that the day of the Lord as a thief in the night, so will it come; and John in the person of Christ Apoc. 3. v. 3.If you will not watch, I will come to you as a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come to you. which is repeated Apoc. 16. v. 15.

Ἐν ἧ οἷ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται. Vulgate in which the heavens will pass away with great violence. He had already said before v. 7.the heavens, which now are, and the earth by the word of God stored up in the treasury to be kept for fire; he now explains that more fully, and recounts the manner of the destruction of this universe by parts.

Ῥοιζηδὸν The Vulgate rendered it, with great violence. Erasmus translates, in the manner of a storm. It can also be rendered with a hissing and a crash, with a vehement sound;

ῥοιζεῖν indeed is to hiss with a shrill sound, ῥοῖζος, is a shrill sound & an impetus, or an impetus with a shrill sound, such as is the hissing of things which are moved most swiftly, as of arrows, of winds, Sap. 5. v. 13. in the flight of birds the wind is said to be cleft βίᾳ ῥοίζου, by the force of a shrill sound. Supplement. Daniel. cap. 14. v. 35. The Angel is said to have carried the Prophet Habakkuk to Babylon ἐν τῷ ῥοιζῷ τοῦ πνεύματος in the impetus of his Spirit. 2. Maccab. 9. v. 7. the chariot was carried ῥοίζῳ with impetus & great speed. Ezech. 47. v. 5. it is used concerning the impetus of a torrent flowing past swiftly. Homer Iliad. π. ὀϊστῶν ῥοῖζον calls it the shrill sound of arrows. Plutarch in his book on listening to poems πνευμάτων ῥοῖζον called it the shrill sound of winds. Budaeus says ῥοῖζον that it is used by Plutarch concerning the impetus of soldiers running forward at the beginning of a battle, who are accustomed to give forth a great shout. The Syriac renders [מנשלי] which Pococke rendered, suddenly, from the root [שלי] he ceased, he rested, whence [שליא] tranquillity, which with the prefix particle [מן] becomes an adverb and signifies ἐξαίφνης quickly, suddenly, Luc. 2. v. 13. Act. 2. v. 2. Dionysius in his commentary on the Syriac paraphrase explains it with a shout. Luth. Mit grossem krachen/ for that which is destroyed with great force and sudden impetus gives forth a great crash, which is metaphorically called a shout.

Peter took the word παρελεύσονται from the mouth of his Master Christ Matth. 24. v. 35.Marc. 13. v. 31.Luc. 21. v. 33. ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται. The same word is used concerning the destruction of the world Matth. 5. v. 8.Luc. 16. v. 17.Apoc. 21. v. 1. στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσονται. Vulgate But the elements shall be dissolved with heat. For the noun heat in the Greek is held καυσούμενα burning, seized by fire, for which Augustine in that place reads burning, just as the Vulgate Interpreter himself in verse 1. 2. rendered that participle καυσούμενα, with the heat of fire. The sense therefore is that the elements are to be consumed by the heat of fire, and through that combustion are to be dissolved and dissipated. The word λύειν is used for destruction Ioh. 2. v. 19. λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον. Act. 27. v. 42. πρύμνα ἐλύετο the ship was destroyed by the force of the waves 1. Ioh. 3. v. 8. The Son of God came ἵνα λύσῃ that he might destroy the works of the Devil. Luther rendered this passage thus. Die Elementa werden für Hitze zerschmeltzen.

Καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα κατακαήσεται. Vulg. But the earth, and the works that are in it, shall be burned up. In the Greek there is not an adversative particle, but a copulative καὶ, which also agrees more with the context. For the elements are not opposed to the heavens in the destruction by fire, but rather are joined, as appears from v. 12. οἱ οὐρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται. Thus, therefore, in describing the destruction of the world, the Apostle, having started from the heaven, descended through the intermediate elements even to the earth, so that he might signify that the whole machine of heaven and earth is to be destroyed. For κατακαήσεται the Syrian has [לא תשתכח] shall not be found, which seems to be taken from Apoc. 20. vers. 11. from the face of him who sat upon the throne, heaven and earth fled away, and there was no place found for them.

Latin:

Connexio. 1. Hîc incipit posterior huius capitis pars, in qua Apostolus modum adventus Christi ad iudicium & destructionis mundi describit, atque ex eo seriam ad pietatis studium exhortationem deducit.

2. Modum adventus Christi ad iudicium sic describit, quod dies Domini venturus sit, sicut fur in nocte h. e. ex improviso. Modum destructionis mundi describit per enumerationem partium destruendarum.

3. Mentionem fecerat Apostolus divinae μακροθυμίας, per quam dies iudicii adhuc differatur. Ne quis verò hac Dei μακροθυμίᾳ abutatur ad carnalem securitatem, & multos sibi annos adhuc polliceatur, subiicit Apostolus, Christum ex improviso ad iudicium venturum, ac diem illum iudicii ob destructionem huius mundi in eo secuturam, fore perquàm horribilem & tremendam.

Textus expositio. ἥξει δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα Κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ. Vulg. Adveniet autem dies Domini, ut fur. Graeca addunt in nocte, quod vulg. Interp. omisit.

Per τὴν ἡμέραν Κυρίου intelligit diem, in qua Christus ad iudicium exercendum & mundum destruendum venturus, unde articulus praefixus meritò habetur emphaticus. Illa dies Domini, magna sc. ut eam vocat Iudas v. 6. Loco huic nostro parallela sunt, in quibus dies illa vocatur ἡ ἐκείνη ἡμέραMatth. 7. v. 22c. 24. v. 36.c. 26. v. 29.Luc. 21. v. 34.2. Thess. 1. v. 10.2. Tim. 1. v. 18.ἐξοχικῶς καὶ ἐξαιρέτως, quia est magna illa dies, quae omnibus huius seculi diebus finem imponet, in qua omnes mortui resurgent, omnes homines tribunali Christi sistentur. Item, in quibus haec dies vocatur magnus dies Domini & terribilis valdeIoël. 2. v. 11.dies Domini, in quo erunt tenebrae & non luxAmos. 5. v. 18.dies illa magna Dei omnipotentisApoc. 16. v. 14.dies Iesu Christi, dies Domini Iesu1. Cor. 1. v. 8.c. 5. v. 5.2. Cor. 1. v. 14.Phil. 1. v. 6. & 10.c. 2. v. 16. quia in ea Filius hominis de caelo revelabitur Luc. 17. v. 30. Syrus emphasin illam expressit hoc modo [יומה]dies illa.

Ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ. Solent fures ex improviso in aedes alienas irripere, ac tempus observare, quo minimè se expectari putant. Quia ergò etiam dies iudicii ex improviso veniet Matth. 24. v. 44.Horâ quâ non putatis, Filius hominis venturus est, ideò adventus eius clandestino & inopinato furis adventui comparatur. Hanc similitudinem desumsit Petrus ex ore Magistri sui Christi Iesu Matth. 24. v. 43.Illud autem scitote, quoniam si sciret Paterfamilias, quâ horâ fur venturus esset, vigilaret utique, & non sineret perfodi domum suam.v. 44.Ideò & vos estote parati, quia quâ non putatis horâ, Filius hominis venturus est. quod repetitur Luc. 12. v. 39. & 40. Eadem comparatione hanc ad rem usi fuêre, Paulus 1. Thess. 5. v. 2.Ipsi enim exactè scitis, quia dies Domini sicut fur in nocte, ita veniet; ac Iohannes in persona Christi Apoc. 3. v. 3.Si non vigilaveris, veniam ad te tanquam fur, & nescies, quâ horâ veniam ad te. quod repetitur Apoc. 16. v. 15.

Ἐν ἧ οἷ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται. Vulgata in quo caeli magno impetu transient. Iam antè dixerat v. 7.caelos, qui nunc sunt, & terram verbo Dei in thesauro repositos igni servari; illud iam uberiùs explicat, & modum destructionis huius universi per partes recenset.

Ῥοιζηδὸν Vulg. reddidit, magno impetu. Erasmus vertit, in morem procellae. Potest etiam reddi cum stridore & fragore, vehementi sonitu;

ῥοιζεῖν enim est sibilare cum stridore,ῥοῖζος, est stridor & impetus, sive impetus cum stridore, qualis est sibilus rerum, quae velocissimè moventur, ut sagittarum, ventorum, Sap. 5. v. 13. in volatu avium ventus dicitur scindi βίᾳ ῥοίζου,vi stridoris. Supplem. Daniel. cap. 14. v. 35. Angelus dicitur Prophetam Habacuc transtulisse Babylonem ἐν τῷ ῥοιζῷ τοῦ πνεύματοςin impetu Spiritus sui.2. Maccab. 9. v. 7.currus ferebaturῥοίζῳimpetu & magnâ celeritate.Ezech. 47. v. 5. usurpatur de impetu torrentis celeriter praeterlabentis. Homerus Iliad. π. ὀϊστῶν ῥοῖζον vocat stridorem sagittarum. Plutarchus lib. de audiend. poëm. πνευμάτων ῥοῖζονstridorem ventorum dixit. Budaeus ῥοῖζονà Plutarcho usurpari dicit de impetu procurrentium militum in pugnae initio, qui magnum solent edere clamorem. Syrus redd. [מנשלי] quod Pococke reddidit, derepente, à rad. [שלי]cessavit, quievit, unde[שליא]tranquillitas, quod praefixâ particula [מן] adverbiascit & significat ἐξαίφνηςcitò, derepente,Luc. 2. v. 13.Act. 2. v. 2. Dionysius in comment. ad Syriacam paraphrasin explicat cum clamore. Luth. Mit grossem krachen/ quod enim magnâ vi ac repentino impetu destruitur, magnum edit fragorem, qui metaphoricè vocatur clamor.

Verbum παρελεύσονται desumsit Petrus ex ore Magistri sui Christi Matth. 24. v. 35.Marc. 13. v. 31.Luc. 21. v. 33.ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται. Idem verbum de mundi interitu usurpatur Matth. 5. v. 8.Luc. 16. v. 17.Apoc. 21. v. 1.στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσονται. Vulg. Elementa verò calore solventur. Pro nomine caloris in Graeco habetur καυσούμεναaestuantia, igni correpta, pro quo Augustinus d. l. legit ardentia, sicut etiam ipse vulgatus Interpres vers. 1. 2. participium illud καυσούμενα reddidit, ignis ardore. Sensus igitur est, quòd Elementa ignis ardore sint comburenda, & per combustionem illam dissolvenda ac dissipanda. Verbum λύειν pro destructione usurpatur Ioh. 2. v. 19.λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον.Act. 27. v. 42.πρύμνα ἐλύετοpuppis destruebatur à vifluctuum1. Ioh. 3. v. 8.Filius Dei venitἵνα λύσῃut destruat opera Diaboli. Lutherus hunc locum sic reddidit. Die Elementa werden für Hitze zerschmeltzen.

Καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα κατακαήσεται. Vulg. Terra autem, & quae in ipsa sunt opera exurentur. In Graeco non est particula adversativa, sed copulativa καὶ, quae etiam magis congruit contextui. Neque enim in destructione per ignem Elementa caelis opponuntur, sed potiùs coniunguntur, ut apparet ex v. 12. οἱ οὐρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται. Sic ergò in describenda mundi destructione Apostolus à caelo exorsus per Elementa intermedia ad terram usque descendit, ut totam caeli terraeque machinam destruendam esse significet. pro κατακαήσεται Syrus habet [לא תשתכח]non reperientur, quod videtur desumtum ex Apoc. 20. vers. 11.à conspectu sedentis super thronum fugit caelum & terra, & locus non est inventus eis.

## 3:10-12 Questions and observations
It is asked in this place. 1. Why is the day of the last coming of Christ for judgment and the consummation of the age called the day of the Lord? Resp. 1. Whatever is great, august, and excellent, that is accustomed to be attributed to God in the Scriptures, as being the supreme Being. Thus the mountains of God, the cedars of God, the winds of God, etc., are called such on account of their magnitude. Because therefore the day of judgment is that great day, of which Ioël 2. v. 11. to which there is no equal Ier. 30. v. 7. in which all men will be set before the tribunal of Christ, therefore κατ' ἐξοχὴν καὶ ἐξαιρέτως it is called the day of the Lord and the day of God, in v. 10. and 12. 2. Because this day is peculiarly destined by God for miraculous, extraordinary, and plainly divine works, namely for the resurrection of the dead, the transformation of the living, the presentation of all men before the tribunal of Christ, the administration of the final judgment, the destruction of the world, the glorification of the pious, and the damnation of the impious, whence it is called That great day of God Almighty Apoc. 16. v. 14. and in the Targum Ps. 1. יום דינא רבא the day of the great judgment. Lyranus in this place: It is called the day of the Lord, because then His will shall be done in all things in the punishment of the wicked and the rewarding of the good. Dionys.

Carthus. in h. l. The day of judgment is specially called the day of the Lord, because in it he will especially declare his omnipotence, wisdom, and justice, will effect his operation, and will complete his will. 3. Because after this day there will be no other, this day will not have a sunset, but mere eternity will follow, which is the property of God alone. Wherefore, since this day is the beginning of eternity, it is therefore deservedly called the day of the eternal God. 4. All days that have been from the beginning of the world, that still are, and that will be in the future on earth, were made for the sake of men, therefore they were men's days, who disposed of them as they wished, whether well or badly, but God also reserved a day for himself, namely this day of judgment, in which the freedom of acting will be taken away from men, but the time of rewarding will follow.

Q. 2. Why is the day of the Lord said to be coming like a thief in the night? Resp. Oecumenius in h. l. He signified the uncertainty of the Lord's coming, like an assault, when it will be least expected, by the thief and the night. By the night indeed, because of the uncertainty, for whatever things are in the night are uncertain; but by the thief, because he is not expected. For no one will be robbed who expects a thief, but those who least expect him, they will be robbed. It is signified therefore by this comparison, that the coming of Christ to judgment will be 1. to most men unforeseen and unexpected. Matth. 24. v. 44. Luc. 12. v. 40. just as thieves are accustomed to come at the time in which they are least expected. 2. By reason of the moment itself uncertain, just as the master of the house does not know at what hour the thief is to come. Marc. 13. v. 35. 3. Sudden, Matth. 24. v. 27. just as a thief accomplishes his purpose with as much speed as he can. 4. Destructive to the impious Luc. 21. v. 35. just as the thief does not come except to steal, slaughter, and destroy. Ioh. 10. v. 10.

Q. 3. Whether the world is to perish according to substance, or indeed according to qualities? 1. We assert the former, which we have proven with many arguments in vol. 9 of the Commonplaces, treatise on the consummation of the age, §. 39. and following. 2. From this Apostolic passage we conclude thus. If the heavens and the earth are reserved for fire, the heavens will pass away with a great noise and force, the elements will be dissolved by heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up, the heavens kindled by fire will be dissolved, and the elements will melt with the heat of fire, it follows that the world is to perish not only according to qualities, but also according to substance. But the former is true, as is evident from vers. 7. 10. and 12. Therefore also the latter. Connection is proved, both from the enumeration of all and singular parts of the world, which are the heavens, the earth, the Elements; and from the emphasis of the words by which the destruction of them all is described. Certainly, whatever shall pass away in such a manner that it is inflamed, burned up, dissolved, melted, conflagrated, consumed, that thing sustains not merely a change of qualities, but the abolition of its very substance. Now, indeed, the Holy Spirit uses those emphatic forms of speaking concerning the heaven and the earth, not only in this place, but also in other parallel places of Scripture. Ps. 102. v. 27.Esai. 34. v. 4.cap. 65. v. 17.Luc. 21. v. 33.Apoc. 20. v. 11. etc. 3. We have warned, however, in the said treatise §. 37. and 38. that we do not deny that many of the pious ancients concede to that opinion, that the world is merely κατὰ ποιότητας to be changed, but not κατ᾽ οὐσίαν to perish; and therefore the opinion concerning the final φθορᾷ of the world is not defended by us as an article of faith, simply necessary for salvation to be known and believed, but is judged by us to be more conformable to the emphatic sayings of Scripture; We have also warned of that, that a charge of heresy ought not to be written against those who, having followed orthodoxy in other matters, describe the destruction of the world through ἀλλοίωσιν, many also of our own in this question preferring ἐπέχειν and to commit the matter to future experience or event, rather than to rashly determine anything certain, and indeed some of our own establish that the world is to perish only by a change of qualities. 4. Most Papists contradict this our opinion concerning the substantial φθορᾷ of the world, yet some of them rise to our opinion, as we showed in the said treatise §. 47. In this place it pleases to note the candid confession of Cornelius à Lapide in his commentary Esai. 34. v. 4. Many, he says, Fathers and recent authors, who wish philosophy to be required for sacred letters, not the contrary, wish that heaven and earth will perish even as to substance, and be changed into another new heaven, and another new earth. For that is seen to be said most clearly here Esai. 34. v. 4. and elsewhere, as cap. 51. v. 6.cap. 65. v. 17.Apoc. 6. v. 14.cap. 21. v. 1.Ecclesiastici 17. v. 30.Psal. 102. v. 27.Matth. 24. v. 35.2. Petr. 3. v. 7. and 12. where note, that sacred Scripture speaks far more effectively concerning the change of the heavens and the Elements, than of blessed bodies in the resurrection, and clearly signifies that there will be a far greater change of those than of men, because that will be substantial, this only accidental. It is added that the heavens were made from the abyss and waters, as I have taught Gen. 1. v. 8. Therefore they are not plainly incorruptible according to form, but according to matter- -matter, according to which they are said to have remained into eternity. The same thing is confirmed from the fact that in the year 1572, a new star was seen in Cassiopeia, which disappeared after two years. Many such changes in the heavens note-modern astronomers etc. Again, since light naturally flows from the essence of the heavens, and since it will be far greater and nobler, it seems likewise that it will flow from another nobler substantial form. For light as great as it will then be is not connatural to the form of the Sun, which now exists. The same, namely that heaven and earth are to perish according to substance, is taught at length by Hieronymus Magius, book 2, on the burning of the world, chapter 6 and 7, Valesius, Sacred Philosophy, chapter 89, and our Molina, treatise on the work of the six days, Disputation 3, etc. Finally he concludes, that both opinions (concerning the destruction of the world according to substance, and concerning destruction according to qualities) are probable, and have weighty authors, yet the former is more conformable to Holy Scripture, the latter to Aristotelian Philosophy.

Q. 4. Whether something concerning the destruction of the world was also known to the Gentiles? Resp. Entirely, as we showed from the oracles of the Sibyls, from Plato and Sophocles, from the Stoics, etc., in the treatise on the consummation of the age, §. 13, whence Theophilus of Antioch, book 2 to Autolycus, writes thus: Regarding the conflagration of the world, the philosophers, willing or unwilling, agree with the Prophets, although in respect of time they are much younger than these. Compare Sixtus of Siena, book 3, Bibliotheca sancta, page 178. It is to be noted, however, concerning this suffrage of the sounder Gentiles: 1. That they did not draw this opinion so much from the light of Nature, as they perceived it from the School of Moses and the Prophets in Egypt, drawing their dogmas from the true source, as Theophilus of Alexandria speaks, book 1 against the Gentiles. 2. That in this assertion they were not perpetually consistent with themselves, but fluctuated in both directions, whence Lactantius, book 7 of the Institutes, chapter 1, pronounces concerning them, that they did not grasp the truth, but only lightly scented it, so that they in no way perceived from where that scent of wisdom, so sweet, so pleasant, had breathed upon them. 3. That (as Salmero rightly warns, Disputation 4 on 2 Peter, page 139) the saying of Peter is not confirmed by those sayings of the Philosophers and Poets, but rather the opinions of the Philosophers are confirmed by this testimony of Peter. 4. That Aristotle, being ignorant of both the creation and the destruction of the world, departed in this question from the authority of his elders, namely the rest of the Philosophers, especially Plato his teacher.

Q. 5. What kind of fire will that be παντολέθριος, by which the whole machine of the world will burn up on the day of judgment? Resp. The Scholastics dispute many things. 1. Concerning the nature and condition of that fire, whether it will be elemental, or truly entirely new and supernatural. 2. Concerning the origin and generation of that fire. 3. Concerning its effects and operation. 4. Concerning its time and duration. But those disputes 1. are more curious than fruitful. 2. and those arguments by which they strive to define them are sought not from the foundations of the sacred scriptures, but from the categories of human reason. We, with Augustine, say in book 20 of the City of God, chapter 16: What kind of fire that is, and in what part of the world or of things it will be, we think no man knows, unless perhaps he to whom the divine Spirit shows it. Compare the treatise on the consummation of the age, §. 21. and following.

Q. 6. Why are the heavens said to be about to pass away with a hissing and a crash? Resp. Because of their sudden and horrible destruction. For just as the upper stories of a building set on fire collapse with a great crash, and indeed with a greater one the more august and lofty the building is: so this entire building of the heavens, set on fire by the final fire, will collapse with a great crash. Just as a man sometimes dies with a cry or a groan drawn from the innermost recess of his heart: so when the preserving and sustaining power of GOD, which is as it were the soul of the world, shall depart from the macrocosm, it will emit a final crash or hissing, and will collapse like a lifeless corpse.

Q. 7. What are those works on the earth which the Apostle asserts will be burned up? Resp. 1. Estius in his commentary on this passage maintains that by the works which are on the earth, Peter wished to signify earthly acts, that is, the works of sinners. Which exposition he proves with the following arguments. First, Paul says in the contrary sense concerning good works Phil. 3. v. 20. that our conversation is in heaven; ibid. v. 19. those who walk according to the flesh are said to mind earthly things. Secondly, Peter in the following words exhorts the faithful; that since all these things are to be dissolved, they should apply themselves to holy conversations and pieties, as if to heavenly works, expecting and hastening unto the coming of that day, lest if they acted otherwise, their works, as if earthly, might be burned up together with the earth, and they themselves might perish, or at least suffer loss. Thirdly, Peter, by saying that the works which are on the earth are to be burned up, seems to insinuate that which was more expressly said by Paul 1. Cor. 3. If anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, for there also he speaks of the same fire of conflagration and the discourse is of purgation, which is treated here. Fourthly, there is also another antithesis in that which follows. But we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. For he seems to oppose this righteousness, which will dwell in the new earth, to the works which are in this earth, that is, to sins. He says that he has Oecumenius as the author of this exposition, although others do not mention it. But it is not Peter's purpose in this place to treat of the burning up of earthly acts or sins, but of the burning up of those things which pertain to the system of the world. For the scope is to teach that the whole machine of the world, the whole system of the world with all its parts and contents, with the sole exception of men, is to perish by fire, whence he descends from heaven, as the supreme part of the world, through the elements as intermediate, to the earth, the lowest part of the world; and because there are various works on the earth, he therefore shows that they also are to be burned up. Estius's arguments can be answered if it is observed that this consequence is null; Sins are elsewhere in the Scriptures called earthly works. Therefore, also in this place, by the works which are on the earth, sins are understood. 1. Cor. 3. it is not a question of the same fire as in this place, but of the fire of temptation and the cross. What the connection of the Apostolic text is, or what the Apostle's collection is, has already been explained before, and we shall explain it more fully a little later. 2. Some, therefore, by works, which are on the earth, understand works made by the hand and art of man, namely buildings, cities, fortresses, bulwarks, and all furniture, and every kind of bodily instrument. 3. Most accept, of those works which naturally have their origin on the earth from the primordial institution of GOD, of mixed bodies, beasts, trees, plants, of gold, silver, and all minerals, all of which are to be burned up by that final fire of conflagration. These two expositions can be joined, because works of both kinds will be consumed by that fire πανολεθρίῳ. Lyranus in this place, Not only the earth, but also all things which have been made in it, and produced from it, will be burned up.

Q. 8. What is the force of the connection in the Apostolic text. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conversations and godlinesses? Resp. 1. Estius establishes Peter's reasoning to be such. The world, which was created for our sake, will be dissolved, purged, and renewed by fire, so that it may become a receptacle for us, that is, for the elect and the just; how much, therefore, does it behoove us ourselves to be pure and holy, so that we may be received into that dwelling? We shall be such, however, if in all things we are holy and let us conduct ourselves piously, fleeing the corruption of desire which is in the worldcap. 1. v. 4. And yet that hypothesis concerning the accidental renovation of the world, if not false, is nevertheless still doubtful and uncertain: nor does the Apostle draw an argument from the condition of the new dwelling, but from the destruction of that old domicile in which we dwell. 2. Another force of connection must therefore be sought, which can be such: Since the whole machine of the world, heaven, earth, and all things that are in it, are at some time to perish, therefore, withdrawing our heart from the inordinate love of the world, let us burn with the desire and love of heavenly goods 1. Cor. 7. v. 20. & seqq. 1. Iohan. 2. v. 15. & 17. Gregory of Nazianzus in the tract on the journeys of life. Therefore it has been ordained that all things of this life should be uncertain and unstable, so that we may burn with the love and desire of firm and stable things. Augustine serm. 245. de temp. If it is the end of the world, one must migrate from this world, the world must not be loved. Since the heavens and the earth are at some time to pass away with a great and horrible crash, because of that destruction let us be seized by filial fear of GOD, lest at the time of the destruction itself we be uselessly terrified. Since the world is at some time to perish, therefore while we are still in the world, let us rightly use worldly goods to relieve the poverty of others, and from transitory and perishing things let us acquire for ourselves a non-perishing treasure. August. Epist. 80. All earthly things will perish, but good works do not perish, which are done from transitory goods. Since on the same day on which the world is to be destroyed, Christ is to come to judgment, and we are all to be stationed at his tribunal, therefore let us live in the true fear of GOD, let us serve him in holiness and justice, let us solicitously beware of sins, etc. Ephrem serm. on the final judgment and compunction. Nothing will profit us in that hour, except the good works which we have carried from here. For it is to be that each one of us will bring his own words and deeds before the tribunal of the incorrupt and tremendous judge. Chrysostom homil. 38. in Iohan. Let us always have this judgment before our eyes, so we shall always be able to be free for virtue. For just as he who forgets that day is carried into a precipice as if a bridle were applied, so he whom this continuous fear strikes, enters upon a modest way of living. Lyranus in h. l. If such severity of the judge shall appear in the sensible Elements, men capable of merit and demerit, of good and evil, ought to be solicitous as to how they may be prepared at the advent of the judge. 3. The Papists themselves prove this force of connection. Salmero Disput. 4.

On this Epistle, regarding the question of why the Apostle concludes thus, seeing that all these things are to be dissolved, what manner of persons ought you to be in holy conversations, he answers, that the Apostle exhorts from the aforementioned to good morals, so that we may be able to meet Christ coming, clothed in the garment of holy conversion, and exercised in the works of piety and mercy, that we may with a generous spirit despise all things, as being about to perish shortly, and that we may cheerfully supply the goods that are present for the uses of others, and store up for ourselves a treasure in heaven from the perishing goods, and be solicitous about the unexpected advent of the Lord, so that when He comes and knocks, we may immediately open to Him. Hieronymus Baptista de la Nuza in his Evangelical treatise, treatise 2, part 3, § 26, n. 482, comments on this Petrine passage thus: All things are to be dissolved; you, therefore, who know this, gather from it what manner of person you ought to be, and to what things you are bound to attend, and how solicitous you ought to be in holy pieties, that is, in alms and works of mercy, transmitting all your things through the hands of the poor to where you are finally to be led. St. Augustine elegantly encompassed these things in sermon 50 on the times, noting two sentences of Christ. The first is, heaven and earth shall pass away. This is the voice of one predicting what will infallibly happen. The second, Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth. This is the voice of one admonishing, which follows from the former. Therefore, if you believe the one predicting, says Augustine, if you do not despise the one admonishing, let that be done which He says. He does not deceive you who gave such counsel. You will not lose what you have given, but what you have sent will follow. Therefore I give counsel; give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. You will not remain without treasure, but what you have on earth solicitously, you will have in heaven securely; I give counsel of saving, not of losing. If an architect were to tell you that your house was about to fall, would you not move out before you perished? The builder of the world tells you that the world is about to fall, and do you not believe? Hear the voice of the one predicting, heaven and earth shall pass away; hear the counsel of the one admonishing, Do not store up for yourselves treasure on earth. Lorinus on this passage, The Apostle urges an exhortation from the things said, that we may prepare ourselves quickly and studiously for the judgment which we await, certainly that God will not spare sinners, who has determined to purge even creatures devoid of sense, because of some stain contracted in a certain way from the sins of men, by a general burning, etc.

Q. 9. By what reason we ought to hasten unto the coming of the day of the Lord. Resp. 1. By the example of the prudent virgins with lamps let us hasten with burning hearts to meet the heavenly Bridegroom Matt. 25. verse 1. most greedily desiring His advent and saying with the Bride; Come Lord Jesus. Apoc. 22. verse 20. Lift up your heads, says Christ Luke 21. v. 28. which Gregory homily 1. on the Gospel interprets thus, Exhilarate your hearts. 2. Through a holy conversation of life, a strenuous course in the stadium of piety, and an ardent desire for eternal life, let us prepare ourselves daily for His advent Phil. 3. v. 11. and following. For he who diligently applies himself to pious works shows that he loves the Lord's advent and is hastening toward it, by the example of servants who await with desire the return of their masters whom they love while absent, being meanwhile diligently intent upon the work committed to them: Theodoret on 2. Tim. 4. v. 8. He loves the advent of God, who follows His laws, and institutes his life from them. Interlinear Gloss, hastening unto the advent etc. by doing well so that you may be such, for whose sake the Lord may come to judgment to save them. Lyranus in this place awaiting with security and hastening with hilarity. 3. We ought to hasten unto the advent of the Lord, as if looking to this one thing, doing this one thing. He who completes one thing maturely, he hastens; he who begins many things at once, and does not complete them, he is in a hurry. 4. Watch at all times praying, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of man. Luke 21. v. 36. He who always watches and watchfully awaits the Lord's advent, he hastens unto the advent of that day.

Ἐναντιοφάνεια. The Apostle says, The elements shall be dissolved with heat, but the earth, and the works that are in it, shall be burned up. v. 10. But since the earth is contained under the name of the elements, why therefore does he set forth its destruction separately? Resp. 1. he repeats the earth for this reason, that he might add something else which pertains to it, namely that not only it itself, but also the works which are in it, are to be burned up. 2. when in v. 12. he had said again that the elements would be liquefied by the heat of fire, he adds nothing concerning the dissolution or burning up of the earth. 3. Although στοιχεῖον signifies as it were a primordial foundation, which most especially befits water and earth: nevertheless Aristotle and other philosophers call them the four elements.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Again here we have an illustrious testimony concerning the destruction of the world, ἐμπαίκταις and to be opposed to all who deny it.

2. An evident argument can also be elicited from this Apostolic passage, that the world is to be changed not only according to qualities, but is also to perish according to substance, must be opposed to all who deny the substantial destruction of the world. We showed the nerve of the argument above in q. 3.

They object, 1. that this is to be understood not of the act, but of the power, that GOD can, if He wills, utterly annihilate the world. Salmero Disp. 4. on this Epistle p. 140. Although the heavens and the earth and all things are to be crushed, and afterwards to be reformed for the better, GOD nevertheless wished to declare through Peter and through other Prophets that all things are to perish and to be reduced almost to nothing, so that we may acknowledge His omnipotence, by which He was able not only to create the world, but also to destroy it and reduce it to ancient chaos, and what is even greater, to turn it into nothing, which nevertheless would seem to us to be entirely impossible to happen. Barradius lib. 10. Concord. Evang. cap. 1. The heavens shall perish, that is, they can perish, if GOD wills; they shall grow old like a garment, i.e., they shall be able to grow old. Resp. 1. This explanation of Scripture is too cold; Scripture speaks expressly not only of the power, but also of the act of destruction and corruption. 2. For in the same sense and respect in which it is said in the opposite member that GOD remains and is always the same, Psal. 102. vers. 27. 28. in the same sense and respect are the heavens said to perish and grow old. Now, however, GOD is said to remain and be always the same not only in the sense and respect that He can remain and be always the same, but that He remains and is the same by the very act itself. Therefore, the heavens are also said to be about to perish in that sense and respect, not that they can merely perish if GOD wills, but also that they are truly and by the very act itself to perish at the time divinely appointed. 3. In Prophetic prophecies, words are not to be taken only of power, but of the act itself, otherwise there would be no certainty of them, no use: but in those sayings of Scripture which treat of the destruction of the world, a prophecy is proposed. Therefore. Compare the article on the consummation of the age §. 40.

2. Lorinus on v. 13. of this chapter objects, sometimes it is affirmed by hyperbole that heaven and earth will perish, or under a tacit condition, if they were to perish, yet the truth and event would not be lacking to those things which are said. Resp. nay rather, neither by hyperbole, nor hypothetically, but simply and absolutely does Scripture assert this destruction of heaven and earth, as the emphatic sayings of Scripture enumerated in their place show.

3. Furthermore, from this Apostolic passage it can be proved, not only the elements and the earth, but also the heavens themselves, will burn with fire on the day of judgment, which must be opposed to those Papists who except the heavens from the matter of that universal and final conflagration. Barradius, lib. 9, Concord. Evang., cap. 11, p. 592: Which heavens will the fire purge? Is it those in which the stars shine? By no means. Similar things occur in Gregorius de Valent., tom. 4, comm. in Thom., z277; Blasius de Viega in comm. Apoc. 21., pag. 812; Estius in comm. h. l.

They except: 1. In the words of Peter, the ethereal heavens are not to be understood, but the aerial ones. Barrad. d. l.; Estius in h. l.; Sixtus Senens., lib. 6, Biblioth., annot. 340. Response: We have demonstrated the contrary above in Expos. v. 7, not only from the Apostolic text and parallel passages of Scripture, but also from the Papists themselves, Ambrosius Catharinus, comm. Hebr. 1; Salmeron, Disp. 4, in hanc Epistol.; Cornelius à Lapide in comm. Esai. 34; Blasius de Viega in cap. 21, Apocal.

2. By the passing away of the heavens is not to be understood their change according to substance, but only a change into a more excellent state through the transition from motion to rest. Blasius de Viega d. l. Response: The emphatic words of Scripture, by which the destruction of the heavens is described, show the contrary. For if the heavens will perish and will grow old like a garment, Psal. 102. v. 27. they will be rolled up like a scroll, Esai. 34. v. 4. they will vanish like smoke, Esai. 51. v. 6. they will pass away, Luc. 21. v. 33. and indeed with a great noise, as Peter teaches in this place v. 10., if being set on fire they will be dissolved, v. 21. If they will recede like a scroll rolled up, Apoc. 6. v. 15. If they will so flee from the face of him who sits upon the throne that no place is found for them, cap. 20. v. 11., then certainly they will not only cease from motion, but will also perish according to substance. But that is so. Therefore this is also so. Hence some of the Papists themselves refute this interpretation. Ambrosius Catharinus comments on our Apostolic passage thus: I have warned the reader that the exposition of the Scholastics, who wish that the heavens will suffer nothing but will only cease from motion, is otherwise too forced, which certainly contradicts these words of Blessed Peter and the prophecies of the ancients. The passage to which Catharinus refers the reader is found in comm. Hebr. 1., where, weighing those words Psal. 102. The heavens are the works of your hands, they themselves will perish, etc., he writes thus: How will the heavens perish? Most say, as regards local motion. But this is not to perish, nor to grow old, which tends toward destruction, as the Apostle says below, and what grows old is near to destruction. Furthermore, Blessed Peter Epist. 2, gives this testimony concerning heaven he left. The heavens shall pass away with a great rush, the heavens burning shall be dissolved, but we look for new heavens. Furthermore, the beloved in the Apocalypse. I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth passed away. And Isaiah, Lift up your eyes to the heavens, for the heavens shall melt away like smoke. And our Lord himself, Heaven and earth shall pass away. From these testimonies of the Scriptures, therefore, unless we wish to do violence to the words, we are compelled to confess that there will truly be some great alteration of the heavens by fire, and not merely a cessation of motion alone, through which alteration the heavens will be in a certain way founded anew, and will become far more beautiful than they now are. Lucianus the Benedictine Monk in his annotations on Chrysostom not only defends the same assertion, but also contends to draw Chrysostom into the same opinion, as reported by Sixtus Senensis in book 6 of the Bibliotheca Sancta, annotation 340. Salmero establishes the same thing in Disputation 4 on this Epistle of Peter, writing thus on page 138: That some interpret this passing away as a cessation of the heavens from motion seems to me clearly violent and forced. For to dissolve the heavens by fire through a cessation from motion is in my judgment something else, and far less, than to be dissolved by being set on fire, and it signifies rather through alteration and corruption that the heavens perish. For whatever fire seizes, it is accustomed by its power and efficacy to convert into ashes, like wood and stones, etc. When the Apostle says, they shall pass away with a great rush, it seems to be similar to that which the Lord says, Heaven and earth shall pass away, to which he opposes, but my words shall not pass away. Therefore they shall not pass away in such a way that they remain only without motion, but they shall pass away entirely, so that they cease to be, etc. Nor content with these, Peter repeats and inculcates the same thing, through whom the heavens burning shall be dissolved. You see, therefore, that this repetition is a confirmation of the prior statement, so that it cannot admit that gloss. Suarez in part 3, volume 2, Disputation 58, section 3 (who otherwise constantly maintains that by the name of heavens Peter in this chapter understood the air) considers it probable that the celestial orbs themselves also, at the final judgment, when the world shall be renewed, are to be moved more swiftly, so that they may carry the aerial heavens with them, and at the conflagration of the universe may concur both by that swifter motion of theirs and furthermore by their influence and action. Cornelius à Lapide in his commentary on this place, on verse 10: Distinguished Theologians and Philosophers assert that the sidereal heavens will burn and melt through the fire of the conflagration, inasmuch as they are compacted, constricted, and as it were glued together from water, so that they may be purged from all filth and dregs, and become purer and more subtle. For the holy Peter and Isaiah say this expressly herechapter 34, verse 4.chapter 51, verse 6.and among the more recent ones Our Tannerus discusses at length concerning the heavens q. 11. And afterwards. If fire acts by the power of God upon Spirits, for instance upon Demons and damned souls, why does the same not act by the same power upon the corporeal heavens?

3. By the passing away of the heavens is to be understood only their purgation and the change of their qualities. Salmero on this passage. With the forms of the heavens corrupted under the same matter, which is eternal, new heavens will be formed. Estius on v. 12. It is not signified here that the change of the heavens and Elements is according to substance, but according to qualities, just as the change of wax occurs according to shape, melting, and softness. The same on v. 13. Celestial bodies are not to be purged by fire, but will only receive a transmutation for the better. Resp. 1. Some of the ancients rise up to this opinion, whence we do not reject it simply as contrary to the analogy of faith. Oecumenius on this passage. The world will not tend entirely toward corruption, but toward renewal, just as we are accustomed to melt certain corporeal things with fire, not that we might attribute absolute destruction to them, but that we might provide purity and sincerity to them. Gennadius in the book on Church dogmas, chap. 70. Let us not believe that heaven and earth are to be abolished by fire, but to be changed for the better, the figure of the world also, that is, the image, not the transitory substance. 2. Meanwhile, we judge the opinion which establishes that not only the earth, but also the heavens will perish according to substance, to be more conformable to the emphatic description of the worldly destruction noted in the Scriptures, and therefore we repeat here the same argument which we opposed to the immediately preceding exception. 3. Nor is this opinion destitute of the suffrage of the ancients. Sixtus Senensis in book 6 of the Bibliotheca, annotation 340, establishes Clement of Rome and Hilary as patrons of this opinion. Clement, he says, in the second volume of the Recognitions introduces Peter the Apostle teaching two heavens, one higher and invisible, perpetual and eternal, which blessed Spirits inhabit; the other lower, visible, distinguished by various stars, corruptible and to be dissolved at the consummation of the age, and entirely to be abolished, so that with the veil of its corpulence removed, that heaven higher than these might appear to those who are worthy of its sight. Embracing this opinion of Clement, Hilary Can. 4 on Matthew says, we judge heaven and earth, the greatest Elements, to be dissolved. and in the explanation of Psal. 122. explaining the same thing more fully, he says. This heaven, which is subject to our sights through the matter of itself, which has received both the nature and the name of the firmament as if it were solidified smoke, will pass away and will not be: but the seat of the Lord, namely the heaven in which GOD dwells, remains forever. These of Hilary And it is the opinion of Clement, which Jerome, in book 14 on Isaiah, reports to have been approved by some through the present testimony of Peter: The heavens, which now are, and the earth are reserved for fire, etc., and again by the prophecy of Isaiah crying out: The heavens shall melt like smoke, which Aquila and Symmachus translated, the heavens shall be reduced to nothing, and shall be ground down like salt and shall vanish. Jerome also notes that this was the opinion of certain philosophers, who thought that all things which we see are to perish by fire. All these things Sixtus Senensis, who although he falsely asserts that the opinion of Augustine, that in the said passage of Peter not the sidereal but the aerial heavens are to be understood, is more reasonable and more conformable to the words of Peter, yet it suffices for us that he grants us the suffrage of some from antiquity. Then the same Senensis, having abandoned the opinion of Augustine, passes over to the camps of those who accept the passage of Peter concerning the sidereal heavens indeed, but accept their destruction either as a cessation of motion or a change for the better, concerning which exposition what is to be judged is clear from what has been said.

4. From this Apostolic passage it can be proven that not only the earth, but also the remaining Elements are to perish on the day of judgment. For the Apostle expressly says στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα λυθήσονται v. 10. and στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα τακήσεται. This must be opposed 1. to those who except the Element of fire from the final πανολεθρία of the whole world. Gregor. de Valent. tom. 4. comm. in Thom. p. 2276. Fire, which will be in its natural sphere, since it does not have any foreign qualities mixed in there, will not be altered by that fire of the conflagration, but only the remaining Elements and some fires, which will then be found impure in the lower places. Lorinus on v. 10. h. l. The Elements will not be corrupted, but will undergo alteration and purification. All things pertain to the integrity of the universe. And since the heavens and the earth are to remain, it does not seem fitting that the air, contrary to the earth and necessary for occupying the empty space up to the earth, should be removed, nor the fire, whose place is above the air, and which in its most pure sphere does not even have need of purification, and is of the same Nature as the fire which will purify or corrupt other things; nor the water, concerning which Scripture does not hand down that it is to be dried up or renewed entirely. Estius on v. 10. h. cap. It does not appear how fire consumes fire, the Elemental fire of the conflagration, and all of it, especially since the Element of fire is not in foreign matter, which can be consumed by another fire, for thus a greater fire is accustomed to consume a lesser one, by feeding upon its foreign matter. Add that with it consumed, the space which it now occupies, which is indeed most amply given to it by the Peripatetics, and rightly so, or it would be left a vacuum, or it would have to be filled by another body.

Resp. 1. Scripture says in general that the world is to pass away, the age is to be completed, the end of all things is approaching, etc. 2. Peter in this place says absolutely and indefinitely that the elements are to be dissolved by heat, but we can by no means exclude fire from the number of the elements. 3. Fire, if it is deprived of fuel, consumes itself, and thus perishes. 4. The hypothesis of this opinion, if not false, is nevertheless doubtful and uncertain, namely that the fire of the conflagration has only the power of purging the elements, but not of abolishing and destroying them. 5. Estius's arguments are very frivolous, to which we oppose that of Salmeron, Disput. 4 on this Epistle, p. 138. Peter seems to have said these things (concerning the destruction of the heavens and the elements) to overturn the opinion of Aristotle. It is agreed that Aristotle, through that principle, From nothing nothing is made, denied the creation of the world, and posited the eternity of the world, and by certain reasons and demonstrations, as he himself thinks, proved it; he also hesitated concerning the immortality of the soul according to the opinion of many Greek Fathers. But what can you hope for from a Philosopher denying such clear and open dogmas? Certainly, to tell the truth, I cannot bear with a patient mind when I see some so superstitiously and tenaciously defending the dogmas of Aristotle, that they would rather twist many texts of Scripture with violent glosses and meanings than strike against Aristotle in one thing. For more is to be attributed to one place of Scripture, through which the Holy Spirit speaks, than to all philosophers, constantly saying one and the same thing. All these things Salmeron. 6. Bede in his commentary on this place explains the opinion of Peter in general concerning all the elements, although he maintains that two of them are to be abolished, and only two are to be repurged. There are four, he says, elements of which this world consists, fire, air, water, and earth, all of which that greatest fire will consume, yet it will not consume them all to such an extent that they do not exist at all, but it will consume two to such an extent, but it will restore two to a better appearance, etc. It is certain for sure, because those consumed by fire, with the fire absent, will soon resume a more pleasing appearance, etc. But concerning fire and water we read nothing of the sort, but rather we have in the Apocalypse, And the sea is no more; we have in the Prophets, And the light of the lamp will not shine for you anymore. 7. Lorinus on this place at v. 10 comments thus. Andreas of Caesarea, Arethas, Anselm, Haymo, and Rupert incline toward the opinion of Bede concerning the destruction of all water and fire in c. 21 of the Apocalypse. And afterwards at v. 13. To the opinion, which from the middle He removes all the Elements (after the resurrection and judgment) Philippus Solitarius seems to have adhered to this, Dioptra chapters 6 and 7.

2. To those who except the upper region of the air from this conflagration and destruction of the world. Barradius, book 9, in Conc. Evang., chapter 11, p. 592. It is asked, how far is the fire (of the conflagration) to ascend? The interlinear Gloss answers 2 Pet. 3. The fire of judgment will ascend as much as the water of the flood ascended. But the water of the flood ascended fifteen cubits above the mountains Gen. 7. the fire will ascend just as much. The ordinary Gloss 2 Thess. 1. There will be fire in the world, which will precede Christ, occupying as much space of the air as the water occupied in the flood. The opinion of the Master and the Scholastics is the same. Estius on this passage at verse 10. The opinion of Bede, by which he explains this Petrine passage concerning the four Elements, does not please, because the conflagration of the world to come by fire, of which the Scriptures speak, will only be of this lowest world, which once perished by the flood, whence Augustine and others, among whom is Bede himself, judge that that fire will not ascend higher than where the waters of the flood reached. Therefore, others, omitting the element of fire, think that the three remaining ones, which are commonly best known, are signified by the name of Elements; air, water, and earth, for these perished by the waters of the flood in the sense explained above, wherefore they will also be, as is said here, to be dissolved by the fire of the conflagration. But because he has already named the heavens i.e., the air, Peter in the former member, saying that they will pass away, and again in the following verses he separates the heavens i.e., the air from the Elements, therefore others more correctly think that the earth and water alone are comprehended in this part by the name of Elements, especially since an Element in Greek στοιχεῖον signifies as it were a primordial foundation, which most especially befits those thicker ones, earth and water. And afterwards at verse 12. The thing itself teaches that the earth and water alone are comprehended by the name of Elements, the air having been named before and separately (in the word of the heavens) having been named.

Resp. 1. Peter says absolutely that the Elements are to be dissolved by the heat of fire, not merely certain parts of the Elements. 2. Who has made them certain that the fire of the conflagration of the world is not to ascend higher than the waters of the flood once ascended? 3. Estius and Barradius understand by the heavens that will perish by fire the aerial heavens. But the Psalmist expressly says Ps. 102. v. 27. all the heavens will perish: Therefore he signifies that the whole and entire space of air interposed between the celestial orbs and the earth is to perish. 4. The destruction of the world by the cataclysm was partial, the destruction of the world by fire will be total. Therefore the reason for both is not equal.

5. The hypothesis is false, that by the heavens in the Apostolic text the aerial heavens are understood.

3. To those who except the sea from this πανολοθρία and destruction of the world by fire. Ribera on chapter 21 of the Apocalypse, verse 1. The sea is not going to perish according to its substance, but is to be renewed, so that it may have a much more beautiful appearance. And afterwards. The sea must remain for the integrity and beauty of the universe. Barrad. book 10, Commentaries, chapter 1, page 611. Water in the new world will be like crystal. Estius on this place. Understand the dissolution of the Elements (water and earth), not in that they are resolved into prime matter, which alone is their material principle (for this dissolution is impossible, or at least by no means suitable for the renewing world) but through which, with all impurity removed and as it were boiled away, they are rendered entirely pure, as if examined and tested by fire. Cornelius à Lapide on this place. Bede thinks that two Elements, namely fire and water, are clearly going to perish on the day of judgment, etc., but it is far truer that the Elements are only to be altered, so that they are changed for the better, but not indeed to be corrupted, for all things pertain to the integrity of the universe.

Resp. 1. The words of the Apostle are sufficiently clear and perspicuous. The elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire. If we except fire, air, and water from destruction, what then shall we understand by the name of elements? Peter could have, while the hypothesis of the Papists stands, clearly omitted the mention of the elements, for he says separately concerning the earth, the earth, and the works that are in it, will be burned up. 2. What is clearer than the Apocalyptic passage cap. 21. v. 1. The sea is no more? 3. Weighing the evidence of which saying, Andreas of Caesarea in his commentary on that place writes thus. It is to be noted that concerning the heaven and the earth he indeed says, it has passed away, that is, it has been changed, but concerning the sea, the sea will not be anymore. For what is the utility of the sea, when there is no need for men to navigate it? 4. Bede in his commentary on 2 Peter 3 says that water just as much as earth is to be consumed to such an extent, that it is not at all. 5. Primasius in his commentary on Apoc. 21. v. 1. following Augustine book 20, de C. D. chapter 16, leaves the abolition of the sea in the middle. Whether, he says, the sea is dried up by that greatest heat, or whether it itself is also turned for the better, I would not easily say. For we read that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, but not also a new sea. Haymo in his commentary on the same Apocalyptic place is likewise doubtful. Lorinus on this place of Peter Fire will also rage against the water, drying and consuming it. Apoc. 16. v. 12. 6. It is frivolous, what Ribera suspects, that it is said concerning the sea for this reason, that it is no longer Let it be future, because perhaps it is to be renewed in such a way that it does not even seem to retain its own substance, just as the earth and the heaven, especially if it is true, what some say, that water will not be fluid after the end of the world, but consolidated and gathered together like a sphere. But that which is changed only according to qualities, it cannot be said of it that it is no longer. Therefore, Ribera seeks another escape. Perhaps, he says, we will answer better and more expeditiously if we say that in those words, I saw a new heaven and a new earth, the water and the other elements are also signified as renewed, and when he says, the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, then the sense is that they have been renewed and have ceased to be, namely, such as they were before, therefore it is to be understood similarly, what is added. And the sea is no longer, namely, that which had been before. But these do not attain the emphasis of the text. For how the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, that is explained in other places of Scripture, especially in the preceding chapter 20, verse 11, concerning their substantial destruction. From the face of him who sits upon the throne, the earth and the heaven fled, and no place was found for them. 6. It is not far from a blasphemous denial of divine omnipotence, what Estius says, that the dissolution of the elements, by which they are resolved into prime matter, is impossible. For if it was possible for God to induce the form of the elements into prime matter, nay, to create prime matter from nothing, certainly it will also be possible for Him to resolve the elements into prime matter, nay, to annihilate them. How much more correctly Salmero in this place, p. 140: It is given by the Apostle to fire that it may act upon the heavens themselves, nor is there need to add any power to the fire anew so that it may be able to act. But if the fire could not, then we would grant that that fire as an instrument of GOD could act.

4. To those who except the interior parts of the earth from this conflagration of the universe. Estius in his commentary on this place, v. 10: He attributes the burning of the earth as an element, for the rest, thick and material, in which the force of the fire may appear more vehement: although this is not to be accepted concerning the whole globe of the earth, as if the fire were to penetrate the whole, but concerning the exterior parts, which serve human uses, and which, having been in a certain way infected and contaminated by the sins of men, will stand in need of the purgation which is made through fire. Lorinus in this place: The burning of the earth was according to the surface, or according to that part which is sufficient for its purgation, etc. Because the element of earth, according to the common opinion, is to be in the world after the judgment, nor of a different species, it would be in vain for the whole to be corrupted and produced anew, when purgation and perfection without corruption could suffice.

Resp. 1. The Apostle speaks absolutely, the earth and the works that are in it shall be burned up; he does not say that only certain parts of the earth are to be burned. 2. Hence Ephrem, in his book on penance, chapter 4, maintains that the whole earth will be consumed by fire. We shall see, he says, a fiery river, flowing from the rising of the sun even to its setting and, like a sea raging with waves, devouring mountains and valleys, and burning up the whole earth, and whatsoever things are in it. 3. Barradius, in book 10 of the Concordance of the Gospels, 611, argues that the whole earth after the consummation of the age will be transparent, except for the tartarean caverns, so that the whole world may be visible to the eyes of the blessed, and nothing may lie hidden. Therefore, even the interior parts of the earth will be changed through renewal. 4. Estius concedes that water, with all impurity removed and boiled away, must be rendered entirely pure, as if examined and tested by fire. But one could argue in the same way. Water is not infected and contaminated by the sins of men, therefore it also does not stand in need of purification by fire.

5. Moses Bar-Cepha, who in his book on Paradise, chapter 18, excepts the earthly Paradise from the fire of the conflagration of the world. Concerning this earthly Paradise, certain of the Papists maintain that it is to be preserved for little children, so that after the judgment they may dwell in it for all eternity. But Cornelius à Lapide, in his commentary on this passage, rightly warns that both are improbable. The former, because Paradise perished, having been overwhelmed by the waters of the flood; the latter, because the whole earth, and all things that are in it, shall be burned up. Lorinus, on this passage, in almost the same way: No reason persuades that the earthly Paradise should be exempted from the general law of the conflagration.

6. Cornelius à Lapide, who in his commentary on this passage discourses thus concerning the wood of the cross: The wood of the cross of Christ will be immune from the fire of the conflagration, and that it is to be brought into the heavens as if it were the triumphal trophy of Christ, the Sibyl sings, book 6 of the Poems, saying,

O happy wood, on which GOD himself hung! Nor did the earth contain you, but you shall see the signs of the heavens, when the renewed fiery face of GOD shall shine.

Christ hints the same Matth. 24. v. 30. Then the sign of the Son of man shall appear, which Saint Chrysostom explains as the very cross of Christ in his homily on the cross and the thief, Waldensis, volume 3 on the Sacraments, title 20, chapter 158, and Saint Cyril hints at this in Catechesis 13, Saint Ephrem in his sermon on true penance, chapter 4, and Gretser, book 1 on the cross, chapter 92, and Suarez, part 3, volume 2, Disputation 57, section 2, judge it to be probable. Similar things occur in Lorinus in his commentary on this passage

Resp. 1. Anselm in the Elucidations, Abulensis, and Jansenius take the saying of Christ Matt. 24. v. 30. concerning the sign of the cross formed in the air. 2. However much we may not disapprove of the opinion of the pious ancients concerning the cross that is to appear on the day of judgment, we nevertheless deny that it can be established with apodictic certainty, and therefore we commit that whole matter to the future event. 3. But it can be affirmed far less as certain and indubitable what the Papists say, that that wood of the cross to which Christ was affixed, and which is now divided into very small particles and proposed to be viewed among relics in many places, is to be divinely reformed and to appear in heaven; and not only the wood of the cross, but also other instruments and monuments of the Lord's passion, such as the column, the nails, the ropes, the crown of thorns, etc., are then to be carried by Angels and demonstrated to the world, etc. Likewise, that that wood of the cross, when Christ comes, will precede him as a standard, and will remain set up in the judgment itself before the judge, so that it may be recognized, and will be immune from the fire of the conflagration, and is finally to be brought into heaven. Compare Harmon. Evang. chap. 161.

5. An evident argument for asserting the divinity of Christ can also be gathered from this passage, to be opposed to the Photinians who deny it. The Apostle calls the day of the final judgment the day of the Lord v. 10. & the day of GOD v. 12. just as Paul also Tit. 2. v. 13. says, waiting for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great GOD and our Savior Jesus Christ. where it is well to be noted that the name great GOD in that Pauline passage, which is clearly parallel to this one of ours, is expressly attributed to Christ. For if the name τοῦ θεοῦ were to be understood of the Father, then it should have been said καὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος, with the article placed before it: but because the article is omitted in the latter name σωτῆρος, it is manifest from that, that one and the same person, namely Christ Jesus, is called both God and our Savior. Compare 2. Cor. 1. v. 3. Eph. 1. v. 3. Add that ἐπιφάνεια in the N. T. is nowhere attributed to the Father, but to the Son alone. 2. Thess. 2. v. 8. 1. Timoth. 6. v. 14. 2. Tim. 1. v. 10. chap. 4. v. 1. & 8. Therefore, what Cassianus, weighing the Apostolic passage Rom. 9. v. 5., writes in book 3 on the incarnation, When Paul says that Christ is God, this suffices for Christians, but when he adds that he is God over all, by that he excludes every blasphemy of treacherous assertion, we can also accommodate that same thing to the passage Tit. 2. v. 13.. When Paul says that Christ is God, this suffices for Christians: but when he adds that he is the great God, by that he excludes every blasphemy of treacherous assertion.

6. Finally, because the time of the final judgment is called a day both in this place and elsewhere throughout the Scriptures, therefore it is most false what the Muhammadans trifle, that the time of judgment will last for fifty thousand years, as is evident from the book on the doctrine of the Turks.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. Estius suspects that προσδιορισμὸν in v. 10 ἐν νυκτὶ does not pertain to the integrity of the text, but was transcribed here from 1. Thess. 5. v. 2. where it is said, You yourselves know exactly that the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night.

Resp. 1. With the same ease it can be said that this προσδιορισμὸν was omitted in the Vulgate version because it is not found added in Apoc. 3. v. 3. cap. 16. v. 15. I will come to you as a thief; by which Estius asserts that it is added in the Greek text because it is found added in 1. Thess. 5. v. 2. 2. The Greek codices in the N. T. are authentic, from which one must judge the Vulgate version, and not from the streams about the fountains, from the version about the authentic text. Now, however, all Greek codices have this προσδιορισμὸν added. 3. The Greek Fathers, and 4. the Syriac version read it.

2. Almost all Papists gather from this Apostolic passage that the just will be purged by that fire of conflagration by which the world will be consumed. Iosephus Acosta lib. 4. de noviss. temp. cap. 22. p. 639. I think that the wicked will burn by that fire which will precede the face of the judge already descending, raging everywhere, and that the upright and the unjust will indeed be purged, if any stain has settled, as the Apostle insinuates. 1. Cor. 3. but not killed. Salmero in h. l. p. 136. We confess that the bodies of the saints will suffer something from the fire of conflagration, but this will be for them for purgation and for a greater merit of the eternal crown and for a glorious resurrection.

Resp. 1. There is deep silence in the Scriptures concerning the pious and the elect being purged by some material fire. 2. It pronounces rather the contrary, that the pious will be caught up in the air to meet the Lord 1. Thess. 4. v. 17. and therefore will be entirely immune from the flames of that conflagratory fire. 3. Which is also the opinion of Augustine lib. 20. de C. D. cap. 18. Let someone ask etc. at the time of the conflagration of the world, where the saints will be, since it is necessary that they, having bodies, be in some bodily place? We can answer that they will be in the higher parts, where the flame of that fire will not ascend, just as the wave of the flood did not: for such bodies will be in them, that they will be where they wish to be. 4. The pious will rise again in spiritual and glorified bodies, and therefore also incorruptible, in which neither fire, nor water, nor any external force, not even anything of Satan himself, will be able to do anything. Aug. d. l. But neither will they fear the fire of that conflagration, having been made immortal and incorruptible, just as the corruptible and mortal bodies of the three men were able to live unharmed in the burning furnace. 5. This opinion relies on several false hypotheses, namely that with the guilt remitted, the debt of the penalty to be paid still weighs upon the pious; that a certain material fire is given, purging the stain of sin; that the day of judgment, just as the whole universe, is also to purge the bodies of men; that those whom the last day will find alive are to die; that 1. Cor. 3. it is a matter of a certain purgatorial fire, purging sins after this life; that the conflagration of the world by fire is to precede the final judgment. 6. This opinion is not very much approved by Lorinus. For thus he annotates to v. 7 of this chapter: Some just will not need such a purging; but those who will need it, will be able to be purged otherwise, namely in the fire of purgatory etc. Finally, it is against all reason for the just, already resurrected, to feel fire in any way, since they are already either blessed or have deserved no penalty, or have satisfied for it before the resurrection. But if to be tested is not to be tormented, but for the innocence of the pious, who are not tormented, to be known to the tormented impious, in this way it can be conceded what some Fathers sometimes say, that the just are to be tested by fires, even after the resurrection.

3. Estius comments thus on v. 10. The hissing and roaring of the heavens, that is, of the air extended above us, will be previous and precursory to the greater change impending, which will happen through fire.
