Tales in Scripturis vocantur, qui vivunt εὐσεβῶς, σωφρόνως καὶ δικαίως,Tit. 2. v. 12. qui à peccatis contra conscientiam sibi cavent, & quorum vita, utpote labes expers, in nullius iustam reprehensionem incurrunt. 1. Tim. 6. vers. 14. coniunguntur ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀνεπίληπτοι.Iac. 1. v. 27. pura & immaculata religio vocatur, seipsumἄσπιλονab hoc seculo custodire1. Petr. 1. v. 19. Christus vocatur agnusἄσπιλος καὶ ἄμωμος.Eph. 1. v. 4.cap. 5. v. 27. coniunguntur ἅγιοι καὶ ἄμωμοιCol. 1. v. 22.ἄμωμοι καί ἀνέγκλητοι LXX. utuntur voce ἄμωμος pro צדיקiustusProv. 20. v. 7. cumprimis verò pro תם & תמיםinteger, perfectus, innocens, irreprehensibilisExod. 29. v. 2.Lev. 1. v. 3. &c. quem aliàs vocant τέλειον, ὅσιον, ἄκακον, ἄμεμπτον &c. Respicit autem Apostolus hisce epithetis ad vers. 13. cap. praeced. ubi falsos doctores, omni scelerum genere coopertos, vocaverat σπίλους καὶ μώμους, & ad v. 10. ubi mentionem fecerat τῶν μιασμάτων τοῦ κόσμου, ut sit sensus. Nolite aures vacivas praebere ἐμπαίκταις perpetuò ingeminantibus. Ubi est promissio adventûs eius? Sed perpetuâ fidei vigilantiâ Christi ad iudicium adventum ac novos caelos & novam terram singulis momentis expectantes solicitè in id incumbite, ut ab inquinamentis mundi vos immaculatos & innoxios custodiatis, ac irreprehensibiles coram iudice venturo reperiamini.

Pronomen αὐτῷ respectum habet ad Christum iudicem, de cuius adventu egit Apostolus v. 12. ac magna illi inest emphasis. Iudex iste, cuius adventum expectatis est iustus, ergò iustitiae studere debetis; est omniscius, etiam occultissima in lucem producet, ergò in id incumbere debetis, ut immaculati coram ipso inveniamini; retribuet unicuique secundùm opera, ergò id vobis curae esse debet, ut fertiles in bonis operibus inveniamini. Quidam Dativum αὐτῷ reddunt ab eo. Sed concinniùs redditur, coram eo, ut apparet ex loco parallelo Luc. 21. v. 36.Vigilate omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini fugere ista omnia, quae futura sunt, & stare coram Filio hominis, quo modo etiam Lutherus h. l. reddidit, Daß ihr für ihm unbefleckt und unsträflich erfunden werdet. Beda in comm. h. l. Benè, cùm diceret: Satagite immaculati & inviolati inveniri, addidit ei, h. e. Domino, quiae ille solùm perfectè mundus est, unde in laude bonorum coniugum dicitur: Erant iusti ambo ante Deum. Benè ante Deum, quia humana iudicia fallunt. Gloss. interlin. ei, h. e. ab eo vel ad honorem eius venientis & pulsantis.

Ioh. Huss in h. l. Ei sc. iudici Deo non homini tantùm, qui solùm intuetur ea, quae exteriùs apparent.

Ἐν εἰρήνῃ. Quidam hunc προσδιορισμὸν referunt ad participium προσδοκῶντες, ut sit sensus, quòd animo quieto & imperturbato adventum Christi expectare debeant. Quidam ad nomen ἀμώμητοι, ut sit sensus, quòd in pace immaculati & irreprehensibiles inveniri debeant, neque enim omnis pax laudabilis est. Sed rectiùs refertur ad verbum proximum, evi etiam coniungitur, videlicet ad verbum εὑρεθῆναι, ut sit sensus, quòd tempore novissimi adventûs Christi ad iudicium in pace inveniri debeant; quod studere debeant, ut Christus veniens illos inveniat pacificos & pacatos. Sunt, qui ἐν εἰρήνῃ phrasi Hebraicâ positum putant pro μετ' εἰρήνης, sed potest etiam propria significatio praepositionis ἐν retineri.

Καὶ τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε. Vulg. Et Domini nostri longanimitatem salutem arbitremini. In Graeco subintelligendum εἶναι.Longanimitatem Domini nostri reputate salutem vestram esse, i. e. salutem vetram spectare, ad salutem vobis conducere. Posset etiam abstractum pro concreto, substantivum pro adiectivo iuxta usitatum Hebraismum positum accipi. Firmiter statuite, longanimitatem illam Domini vestri, quâ differt suum adventum, nec è vestigio ad iudicium sese sistit, esse hominibus salutarem, quia scil. tempus paenitentiae per hanc dilationem adventûs ipsis conceditur. v. 9. Eâdem phrasi 2. Cor. 7. v. 10.μετάνοια εἰς σωτηρίαν vocatur μετάνοια σωτήριοςpaenitentia salutaris. Syrus h. l. reddidit per [פורקנא] quod redemtionem, liberationem & salutem significat. Circa verbum ἡγεῖσθε notandum, quòd hoc loco significet certam animi persuasionem, quo sensu etiam usurpatur Act. 26. v. 2.2. Cor. 9. v. 5.Phil. 2. v. 25.cap. 3. v. 8.1. Tim. 1. v. 12.

## 3:15
Connection. He confirms the doctrine concerning the final coming of Christ to judgment, and concerning the destruction of the world, by the suffrage of Paul his fellow-Apostle and brother, on which occasion he commends his spiritual wisdom in divine mysteries.

Exposition of the text. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελθός Παῦλος κατὰ τὴν αὐτῷ δοθεῖσαν σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν. Vulg. As also our most dear brother Paul according to the wisdom given to him has written to you. In the Greek it is, beloved brother of ours. He calls him beloved brother, not only by reason of Christianity, Acts 11. verse 1. but also and even most especially by reason of the Apostolic office, in which they were colleagues, and had given to each other the right hands of fellowship, Gal. 2. v. 7. & following. He attributes the praise of wisdom to the Apostle Paul, so that he may the more commend his Epistles, for he says notably, that Paul wrote according to the wisdom given to him (given certainly by GOD), and therefore in his Epistles he demonstrated singular wisdom, that is, an excellent and sublime knowledge of divine mysteries. Chrysostom in the preface to the Epistle to the Romans does not doubt to prefer Paul to all in doctrine and in homily 25 on John to call him the Master of all wisdom.

Latin:

Connexio. Doctrinam de novissimo Christi ad iudicium adventu, ac de mundi interitu suffragio Pauli CoApostoli & fratris sui confirmat, quâ occasione spiritualem ipsius in divinis mysteriis sapientiam commendat.

Textus expositio. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελθός Παῦλος κατὰ τὴν αὐτῷ δοθεῖσαν σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν. Vulg. Sicut & carissimus frater noster Paulus secundùm datam sibi sapientiam scripsit vobis. In Graeco est, dilectus frater noster. Vocat autem illum dilectum fratrem, non solùm ratione Christianismi, Act. 11. vers. 1. sed etiam ac vel maximè ratione Apostolici officii, in quo erant Collegae, sibique invicem dederant dextras fraternitatis, Gal. 2. v. 7. & seqq. Sapientiae laudem Apostolo Paulo tribuit, ut illius Epistolas magis commendet, notanter enim dicit, Paulum secundùm datam sibi (utique à DEO datam) sapientiam scripsisse, ac proinde in Epistolis suis singularem sapientiam h. e. eximiam & sublimem divinorum mysteriorum notitiam demonstrasse. Chrysostomus in prooemio Epist. Rom. non dubitat Paulum in doctrina omnibus praeferre & homil. 25. in Iohann. totius sapientiae Magistrum appellare.

## 3:16
Connection. On the occasion that he had confirmed the doctrine concerning the final coming of Christ to judgment and concerning the destruction of the world by the suffrage of Paul his fellow-Apostle, he complains of the malice of unlearned and unstable men, by which they twist certain difficult passages in the Pauline Epistles into a foreign sense, which scandal he meets in such a way that he warns that the same happens to the remaining Scriptures of the O. and N. T., of whose authority and utility, however, it is permitted to no one to doubt.

Exposition of the text. ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περὶ τούτων. Vulg. As also in all his Epistles, speaking in them of these things. Erasmus ἐξηγήσεως serves the purpose of the little word almost, for thus he rendered it, as also in almost all his Epistles, moved no doubt by the argument that it is not likely that Peter wished to include here absolutely all of Paul's Epistles, since not in all of them are the same matters treated which Peter handles in this place. But even if a certain restriction must be understood, that is not to be immediately inserted into the text. And it is joined with no absurdity to accept Peter's assertion concerning all of Paul's Epistles, since in all of them the subject is faith in Christ and the pursuit of good works, especially in those which are written to entire Churches.

Some think that ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν, should be repeated in this place from the preceding, but it suffices if the word ἐγραψεν is understood without the express repetition of the pronoun, since not all of Paul's Epistles are inscribed to the Hebrews or converted Jews. It can also be understood προσδιορισμὸς, that he wrote in all of them according to the wisdom given to him.

Λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περί τούτων. Vulg. speaking in them of these things. By ταῦτα he understands those things about which he had treated in both Epistles, but especially in this third and last chapter of the latter Epistle, namely, concerning the final coming of Christ to judgment, concerning the consummation of the age, concerning waiting patiently for the return of the Lord, concerning fleeing from those ἐμπαίκταις, who impudently deny the final judgment and the end of the world, and concerning the pursuit of holiness, to which the doctrine concerning the last things ought to excite everyone. Lyranus on this place concerning these things, i.e., concerning the same things about which he wrote to you, namely, concerning the truth of the Catholic faith and concerning preparation for the future judgment, as is evident in the Epistles of Paul in many places.

Ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητα τινα. Vulg. in which are certain things difficult to understand. From this vulgate version it cannot be understood whether that ἐν οἷς should be referred to the preceding ἐν αὐταῖς, or rather to the preceding περὶ τούτων. But from the Greek it is manifest that it is not to be referred to αὐταῖς, from which it differs in gender, but to τούτων. Peter is not disputing whether the Apostle Paul wrote clearly or obscurely, but in those things which look toward the final coming of Christ, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age, which both by himself and by Paul concerning the coming of the Lord and concerning those things which are to be about the coming of the Lord, were written, some he says are δυσνόητα difficult to understand, which cannot be so easily comprehended by just anyone. Some of the Papist interpreters themselves acknowledge this. Salmeron on this passage comments thus: ἐν οἷς is referred to the word περὶ τούτων concerning those things. (He indeed adds, nevertheless you will not err, in which Epistles, because the neuter gender includes in itself the masculine and the feminine. But if Peter were speaking about the Pauline Epistles, he would have said altogether, ἐν αἷς. whence) Lorinus on this passage annotates thus: That, in which, is not referred to the Epistles, but to those things about which it is treated in the Epistles, for the Greek pronoun οἷς is not of the feminine gender, of which the noun is ἐπιστολῶν. Estius is doubtful, for he annotates thus on this passage: In which. Others, for the sake of removing ambiguity, translate, among which. For in Greek it is ἐν οἷς, which cannot be referred to the Epistles, whose gender, as in Latin, so also in Greek, is feminine, but it must be referred to those things which are contained in the Epistles, that is to say, in which things written by him there are some things difficult, for he adds as also the other Scriptures. Some wish, ἐν οἷς placed for ἐν αἷς or certainly that by the carelessness of the scribes ἐν αἷς. has crept in for . For also by Robert three codices are noted, in which it was written Which if it is the true reading, which however I would not easily affirm, the commentary is easier. But what is to be determined concerning these latter words of Estius, we shall see later.

Δυσνόητα The Syriac rendered, [דעסיק לסוכלא] which are hard and difficult to understand.

Ἅ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπάς γραφάς πρός τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν ἀπώλειαν. Vulg. which the unlearned and unstable pervert, as also the other Scriptures, to their own destruction. The Greek ἀμαθεῖς properly signifies indocile, who do not wish to be more rightly instructed and informed, who refuse to give place to the heavenly truth shown from the word of GOD. Luther most rightly Die ungelerige.

Ἀστήρικτοι are those who are destitute of a solid foundation, who are not strengthened and founded in the heavenly truth, who are not yet established in the Christian religion, who are little firm, as Erasmus rendered, from which it follows that they are unstable and inconstant. The Apostle used this word also in the preceding chapter verse 14 δελεάζουτες ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτους. Christ Matthew 13, verse 21Mark 4, verse 17Luke 8, verse 13

he describes them thus, that they do not have a root in themselves. In Greek ἀστήρικτοι they are called by another name ἀνερμάτιστοι. Gloss. interl. unlearned without the light of justice and unstable in mind. Lyranus; unlearned in the holy Scriptures. unstable in faith and morals. Luther rendered Leichtfertigen.

Στρεβλοῦσιν they twist, they deprave, they drag into a foreign and strange sense; they twist, they contort, they distort and they twist back. It is a metaphor drawn from torturers. For just as executioners sometimes so torture an innocent man that he brings forth certain things against his knowledge and conscience: so heretics, like torturers, by applying ropes and racks, strive to drag the Scriptures to their own senses, by so twisting them that they are forced to provide a foreign sense. The LXX use the word στρεβλόω for פתל which signifies to subvert by wrestling, to pervert, with the metaphor taken from wrestlers, who by the entanglement of limbs twist one another now to this side, now to that, until they subvert them. The Syrian in this place rendered it [מעקמין] from the root [עקם] he perverted, he bent, he made crooked. The Syrian uses this word elsewhere for διαστρέφειν which has a certain kinship with the word στρεβλούν. Acts 13. v. 8. it is said of Elymas the Magician, that he attempted διαστρέψαι to pervert, to turn away the Proconsul from the faith, where in the Syriac Paraphrase the same word [עקם] appears in Piel. Acts 20. v. 30. the Apostle says From among yourselves men will arise speaking διαστραμμένα perverse things, Syrian [מעקמתא] to the Hebrews they are עקלקלות tortuous. Tit. 3. v. 10. A heretical man after one and a second admonition avoid, v. 11. knowing, ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος Syr. [מעקם] perverted. Thus therefore heretics pervert 1. the Scriptures. 2. other men. 3. Themselves, deservedly therefore they are judged perverted Luth. rendered in this place Verwirren.

Ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφὰς, understand ἱερὰς, θεοπνέυστούς κανονιστούς, holy, divinely inspired and Canonical Scriptures; for that Peter is dealing with those in this place, appears from the whole context. verse 2. he had made mention of those things which were foretold by the Prophets and Apostles, whose He ordered those to whom he writes to be mindful. Therefore, he understands by the Scriptures in this place the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures.

Πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν αὑτῶν ἀπώλειαν. Vulg. to their own, Greek to their own destruction. He describes the consequences of that heretical depravation and distortion, which is the destruction both of the heretics and of those who allow themselves to be seduced by them. For they distort the Scriptures to cloak their false dogmas, which in the preceding chapter 2. v. 2. are called ἀπωλείαι, because they bring eternal ruin and damnation to all who pertinaciously adhere to them, and do not arrive at the acknowledgment of the truth before the end of life. Luth. Zu ihrem eigen Verdamniß.

It is asked in this place. 1. Why does Peter institute a digression at the mention of Paul? Resp. 1. So that he may commend to those to whom he writes the Epistles of Paul, his fellow Apostle, in which the same doctrine is handed down. 2. Lest, on account of the rebuke Gal. 2. v. 14., he might seem to think less honorably of him, or to harbor secret animosities against him. 3. So that he may fortify his beloved against the depravations and distortions of heretics, by which they were dragging the Pauline Epistles into a foreign sense. 4. Lyranus in h. l. approves of Paul's doctrine, because the Pseudo-Apostles were disparaging him, saying that he was not an Apostle, in that he had not been with Christ, as the others, and therefore they said his doctrine was not to be received as Apostolic. Secondly, they said it contained erroneous things, perverting its meaning. Therefore, the Apostle Peter removes both. First, he shows that Paul is a true Apostle, naming him a most dear brother; secondly, he shows that his doctrine is holy.

Q. 2. Of which Epistle does he speak, when he says, as also our beloved brother Paul wrote to you? Resp. 1. Bede refers this to all of Paul's Epistles. He mentions, he says, that Paul wrote to them; because although Paul wrote specially to certain Churches, he is nevertheless proven to have written generally to all which are throughout the world, and which make one Catholic Church. But the words of Peter do not admit this opinion, in which he speaks distributively, distinguishing the remaining Epistles of Paul from that which he properly insinuates, as, he says, also our beloved brother Paul according to the wisdom given to him wrote to you, as also in all his Epistles. More correctly, therefore, this is understood of a certain Epistle of Paul. 2. Oecumenius thinks that the finger is pointed by these words to the Epistle which Paul wrote to the Romans; which is also the opinion of Lorinus, to the confirmation of which the following arguments serve. First, just as Peter inscribed his Epistles to those converted from Judaism: thus Paul's Epistle to the Romans was written to Jews just as much as to Gentiles who were at Rome and had given their name to Christ. Secondly, in the Epistle to the Romans there occur things which have great agreement with those which Peter proposes here. Peter says in this place, the heavens, which now are, and the earth, are reserved by the word of God unto fire. Paul says Rom. 8. v. 21., that the creature shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption. Peter says in this place, be diligent that ye may be found of him without spot, and blameless. Paul says Rom. 12. v. 1., I beseech you, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. cap. 6. v. 12., Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body. Peter says in this place, account that the longsuffering of our Lord is salvation. Paul says Rom. 2. v. 4., Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness... that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?

3. Peter seems to Salmeron to allude to the Epistle of Paul written to the Galatians, since in it many things are handed down concerning the divinity of Christ, concerning the law and the Gospel, concerning faith and works, which are truly difficult to understand and obscure. Salmeron follows in this part Dionysius the Carthusian, who comments on this place thus. Because the most blessed Peter wrote both his Epistles to the elect strangers of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Asia, etc., it seems that Paul also wrote to the same, who wrote to the Galatians and Asians, as is certain. But this opinion is even less probable than the preceding one. Nor does it contribute anything to establishing this or the preceding opinion, that that which is in the Epistle to the Romans and to the Galatians seems to square most with those things in which there are some things difficult to understand. For Peter does not say this about that Epistle which Paul wrote specifically to those with whom he is speaking, but about the Epistles of Paul in general, about which he had premised, as also in all his Epistles.

4. It is therefore most simply established that Peter is speaking about the Epistle to the Hebrews, so that from this Apostolic place it may be proven that the Epistle to the Hebrews acknowledges Paul as its author and parent. Most Papists rise to this opinion, Baronius vol. 1. Ann. 60. Pererius in the Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans n. 64. Ribera in his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews p. 37. Estius, indeed Salmeron himself on this place, which is proven by the following arguments. First, no other Epistle can be named which Paul wrote to the Jews. Secondly, in the Epistle to the Hebrews Paul from chapter 10 to the end of the Epistle in many ways exhorts the Hebrews to patiently bear tribulations and to persevere in doing good and in the expectation of divine promises, concerning which matter Peter treats in this place. The Greek interpreters furthermore warn that in the Epistle to the Hebrews it is especially treated that the languishing souls of the Hebrews might be excited to the perseverance of faith, and the certain expectation of the goods which have been promised through Christ and are stored up for the future. Theophylact, explaining the argument of the Epistle to the Hebrews, says; Paul indeed proves two things in this Epistle, both that whatever may have happened must be tolerated manfully, and that rewards are to be expected for labors, for the Lord is not going to neglect those whom He destined for holiness from eternity. We have become, he says, partakers of Christ, if yet we hold the beginning of His substance firm unto the end.Hebr. 3. v. 14. We desire every one of you to show the same solicitude to the completion of his hope even to the end.cap. 6. v. 11. Do not lose your confidence, which has a great reward.cap. 10. v. 35. But that Peter speaks of these very things is evident from those which are held in this very chapter 3. We expect, he says, new heavens and a new earth according to His promisev. 13. Wherefore, dearly beloved, expecting these things, be diligent.Hebr. 10. v. 22. says Paul. Let us draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having sprinkled our hearts from an evil conscience, and washed our bodies with clean waterv. 23. let us hold the confession of our hope without wavering, for He is faithful who has promised. To this very thing Peter exhorts when he says v. 14. Expecting these things, be diligent to be found by Him unspotted and blameless in peace, and account the long-suffering of our Lord as salvation. But also that thing from which Peter had begun to discourse concerning the patiently expecting of the coming of the Lord, when he says, some saying, Where is the promise of His coming? clearly agrees with that which is said in the Epist. to Hebr. cap. 10. v. 36. Patience is necessary for you, that doing the will of GOD you may receive the promise. For yet a little and a very little while, He who is to come will come, and will not delay.

It is objected to this opinion, that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not written to the Hebrews dispersed through Asia, to whom Peter wrote, but to the Hebrews who were in Judea, as is clearly known from the Epistle itself. Which argument also disturbs Pererius, and obtains from him that he almost concedes to the first opinion, which is Bede's.

Resp. 1. When Peter says, as also our beloved brother Paul wrote to you, the sense is not, he wrote to you in that dispersion placed, concerning which it is treated in ἐπιγραφῇ of the first Petrine Epistle; but to you, that is, to your nation. For because Paul had written a special Epistle to the Hebrews, and indeed on an argument of such a kind that it would pertain to all faithful Jews, therefore Peter not without reason presupposes that it was communicated by those to whom it had been sent, also to the remaining Hebrews converted to Christ, especially those placed in the dispersion, for their consolation. 2. By the force of this argument, neither can the Epistle to the Romans be understood, since that also was not written to the Hebrews who were at Rome. 3. Estius also advises this. Although the first Epistle of Peter may have been written to the Jews of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, etc., it is not however necessary that this second one be understood as written precisely to the same ones, since that, Behold I write this second Epistle to you, can be referred to the same nation in such a way that it is not therefore referred to the same place, but to the Jews dwelling anywhere. But the circumstances show that the later Epistle of Peter, just as the former, was written to the Jews placed in the dispersion.

Q. 3. Whence did this wisdom, which Peter proclaims in him, happen to Paul? Resp. That more sublime and more exact knowledge of divine mysteries happened to Paul from a certain special heavenly revelation, as he himself testifies, Galat. 1. v. 12. I did not receive the Gospel from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. That, namely, concerning which he treats 2. Cor. 12. v. 2. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago caught up even to the third heaven, v. 4. he was caught up into Paradise, and heard words ἄῤῥητα, which it is not permitted for a man to utter, (where he speaks of himself in the third person for the sake of modesty) 1. Cor. 11. v. 23. I received from the Lord that which I delivered to you.

Q. 4. Where in other Epistles of Paul is it treated of these things, concerning which Peter treats in this place? Resp. Some assign Roman. 8. v. 19. & following, 1. Cor. 15. the entire chapter, 1. Thessal. 4. v. 13. & to the very end of the second chapter. 2. Thess. 2. the entire chapter, etc. But when Peter says in this place that Paul in all his Epistles speaks of these things concerning which he himself had written, he does not speak specifically only of the latest coming of Christ, of the final judgment, of the destruction of the world, of the creation of a new heaven and a new earth, but in general of all things concerning which he had treated in this later and former Epistle, namely of the truth of Christian doctrine, of constancy in faith and the pursuit of good works, the doctrine of which chapters is scattered through all the Epistles of Paul.

Q. 5. What are the causes, on account of which certain πράγματα things in the Scriptures are difficult to understand? Resp. When Peter says, ἐν οἷς δυσνόητα τινα he is not speaking directly of the Pauline Epistles, but of πράγμασι, the things which are treated in them, among which he says there are certain things difficult to understand. Meanwhile, we willingly confess that, from the fact that δυσνόητα those things are treated in the Scriptures, consequently the Scriptures themselves are also in certain places difficult to understand and obscure. The causes of this difficulty and obscurity are both efficient and final. The efficient causes are two. The former is from the things about which it is treated in the Scriptures, which are by their nature difficult to understand, either on account of obscurity, as future things; or on account of their majesty and excellence, as the mystery of the Trinity, of the personal union, of the Eucharist, etc. The latter is from the men who read and unfold the Scripture. The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of GOD, 1. Cor. 2. v. 14. nay, even in the regenerate themselves something still remains of the oldness of the flesh, therefore they perceive only as much of these mysteries as they are renewed. The final causes are. 1. That GOD might commend to us the majesty and greatness of His mysteries. 2. That He might place before our eyes our native ignorance and our ἀδυναμίαν for perceiving divine things. 3. That He might shake off the lethargy from our minds in the investigation of divine things, and excite our diligence in reading, meditating upon, searching into, and comparing the Scriptures. For if all things had been easy, we would have been clearly sluggish and slothful. 4. That He might kindle in us a religious zeal, by piously stopping within the limits of the revealed heavenly truth, for those things which cannot be ignored without fault and can be investigated without danger. 5. That He might remove the loathing of reading and assiduously unfolding the Scripture. For we easily loathe those things which are obvious to anyone for understanding at the very first glance; but on the contrary, He might excite the admiration of Scripture in our minds, lest it should become cheap to us. 6. That He might take away from us the empty and vain persuasion of having already attained perfect knowledge, and might tame our arrogance, because we think too honorably of ourselves, and are accustomed to promise ourselves more than is fitting regarding our cognition. 7. That He might excite us to serious and assiduous prayers, through which we might implore the help of God in understanding the Scriptures and in opening to us the true sense of them, and by this reason He might excite and sharpen in us fervor in praying, diligence in reading, and humility in meditating. 8. That the heavenly truth, inasmuch as it is sought with such great labor and might commend to us more what has been found. For those things which are acquired without labor, we generally despise and hold in little regard; but those things which are found with great labor and study, we hold in greater value. 9. That he might recall our minds, abstracted from the studies of earthly things and the daily occupations of the world, to these more serious matters, and might lead them to the study of divine and heavenly things. 10. That in the Church there might be some Teachers, others Disciples, and that its own honor might be preserved for the holy Scriptures and the divinely instituted Ministry.

Q. 6. What are those δυσνόητα in the Pauline Epistles, which the unlearned and unstable pervert to their own destruction? Resp. 1. Oecumenius in his commentary on this passage thinks that those things which Peter asserts concerning the difficulty of the Epistles of Paul are to be understood especially concerning the Epistle to the Romans. What are those things, he says, which unlearned and unstable men pervert in the Epistles of Paul to their own destruction? For example, Paul said, where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. These men perverted this, saying that Paul teaches this: Let us sin more abundantly, that grace may be given to you more abundantly. They confirm that difficulty of the Epistle to the Romans also from this, that Paul in it, as Irenaeus testifies in book 3, chapter 7, frequently uses hyperbata, and as Origen testifies in his preface to the Epistle to the Romans, uses at times confused and less explicit expressions.

2. Others think that the words of Peter concerning certain things δυσνόητοις in the Pauline Epistles are to be taken especially concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which cap. 6. v. 4. & cap. 10. v. 36. such things δυσνόητα are contained, which heretics twist to the point that they would take away the hope of pardon from those who have fallen even after Baptism, though they are penitent.

3. But the words of Peter manifestly show that the discourse here is not about only one or another of Paul's Epistles, but about all the Pauline Epistles, in which there are said to be such δυσνόητα as are twisted by heretics into a foreign sense. Estius therefore takes this concerning the doctrine of justification and election, about which Paul treats not in one, but in several Epistles. It must be known, he says, as almost all Interpreters note, that Peter by those words, in which are some things difficult, etc., looks back to the doctrine of Paul, by which he taught that a man is not justified by the law, nor by works, but freely through the faith of Christ: for from this they gathered that good works are not necessary for salvation, which was also the heresy of the Simonians, as Epiphanius and Theodoret testify. But that doctrine of Paul is especially delivered in the Epistle to the Romans, although it is also contained in other Epistles of the same Paul, as in that which was written to the Galatians, and

scattered in the Epistles to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, and to the Colossians. But that Peter looks to that place is proved first from this, because in the Pauline Epistles there is scarcely anything else that men who love liberty and the desires of the flesh, such as those Peter described in this and the preceding chapter, could have for the fostering of their own lusts and the defense of their own error. Then, because James in his Epist. ch. 2 manifestly signifies that certain people had been imbued with that perverse opinion, so that they thought faith sufficed for justice and salvation without good works, which he also gravely attacks. But he himself also writes to the same people to whom Peter writes i. e. to the twelve tribes which were in the dispersion. But James indeed was silent about the occasion of the error, which Peter expressed, namely, that it was fabricated from the Pauline Epistles, just as conversely, Peter was silent about the erroneous doctrine itself, which James expressed, whence by mutual comparison, those things which were written by both are illustrated. To this pertains what Augustine teaches book on faith and works ch. 14 and on grace and free will ch. 7 that the Catholic Epistles of the four Apostles were written against the aforementioned error, which certain people willingly drew from the Epistles of Paul wrongly understood. But the doctrine concerning election and reprobation, which Paul delivers similarly and chiefly in the Epistle to the Romans, was added to the occasion of the error. For even by that, works seemed to be excluded from the business of our justification. This is Estius.

4. It is not opposed to us that the Pauline doctrine concerning justification and election is referred to those δυσνόητα twisted by heretics into a foreign sense, provided that it is correctly explained. For neither James nor Peter nor John nor Jude attacks that which Paul teaches in such clear words, that a man is justified by faith in Christ without the works of the law; Item, that election was made out of grace in Christ, and not on account of works. But they attack this, that the words of Paul were being twisted into a foreign sense, and thus by faith they understood nothing else than a naked profession of faith, which, separated and disjoined from works, would nevertheless justify a man. Bede in this place The things difficult to understand in the Epistles of Paul, which he says are depraved by the unlearned and unstable, are especially those in which he speaks about the grace of GOD, which justifies the ungodly, i. e. makes the ungodly just: For he himself says, where sin abounded, grace did superabound; which they not understanding, thought he was saying, let us do evil, that good may come. But far be it that Paul should teach his hearers to do evil to merit good, whose whole intention is to restrain from evils and to good. to summon, as many as he can. But when he says, Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, he commends the gift of grace all the more vehemently through this, which is accustomed to forgive both great and lesser sins to those who are converted. And by how much greater sins one committed before conversion, by so much greater an indulgence of the bestowing grace the converted one received. Therefore, the Apostle speaks here of those sins which we have already committed, lest anyone perish in despair of pardon due to the magnitude of their crimes, but he was not, as the enemies interpreted, persuading to commit more sins so that one might receive better goods through them. Luther, in his commentary on this place, likewise determines that Peter is speaking of the perversion of Pauline doctrine in the article of Justification.

5. Meanwhile, however, because Peter does not determine that some one δυσνόητον was twisted by heretics into a foreign sense, but speaks in the plural, ἐστι δυσνοήτα τινα, therefore this must be accepted in a general sense concerning all things which either heretics or Epicurean men snatched from the Epistles of Paul and twisted into a sinister and perverse sense, such as were the doctrine concerning gratuitous election, concerning justification without works, concerning Christian liberty, concerning the exuberance of grace, concerning the coming of the Antichrist, etc.

6. Furthermore, since the Apostle notably speaks of those things which were predicted both by himself and by Paul concerning the coming of Christ to judgment, and concerning those things which are to be about the coming of the Lord; therefore, these corruptions are to be referred to the class of τῶν δυσνοήτων twisted by heretics into a foreign sense, that the resurrection has already taken place, that for a thousand years Christ is going to administer a corporal and visible kingdom in this world, etc.

Ἐναντιοφάνεια. Peter says at this place that Paul writes about these things in all his Epistles. But at the time when Peter wrote these things, not all of Paul's Epistles were yet in existence. Resp. 1. Peter wrote these things near to death cap. 1. v. 14. Paul, whom most establish to have undergone martyrdom at Rome at the same time as Peter, had undoubtedly already written his final Epistles long ago. 2. And even if they had not yet all been written, Peter's assertion could still be accepted concerning those Epistles of Paul which existed at that time.

Ἔλεγχος. 1. Against the Papists, who keep the laity, as they call them, from the reading of Scripture, we produce such an argument from this Apostolic place. To whom Paul and Peter destined their Epistles, those same people ought also to read the Pauline and Petrine Epistles.

Augustine, book 6 against Faustus, chapter 9: It is impious that we should not read what was written for our sake. But Paul and Peter addressed their Epistles to the laity, for thus Peter speaks in this place: As also our beloved brother Paul wrote to you. Therefore, the laity also ought to read the Pauline and Petrine Epistles. What is published in written books is without doubt proposed to be read by all, says Costerus in Enchiridion, p. 48. Deservedly, therefore, we oppose to the Papists that statement of Athanasius, volume 2, folio 248, Commelin edition: No one would be ignorant of Roman laws without danger. What snares, therefore, are they preparing, who wish to forbid the care and study of the great oracles of the heavenly King? Scripture is the food of the soul. Cease, therefore, O man, to kill the inner man with hunger, and to draw upon yourself a dire famine, not of bread and water, but of hearing the word of the Lord. And afterwards: Revere that eunuch, a lover of the word, set over all the riches of the Queen, who did not neglect reading even on a journey, whose purpose the Lord approving, immediately sent him a teacher, who added knowledge to his reading, and through the Scriptures led him to the Savior. Therefore, He Himself also commanded, Search the Scriptures.

2. Peter says that Paul speaks in his Epistles. It is therefore false and erroneous that the Papists call Scripture a mute letter, and labor to prove from that that it cannot perform the office of a judge. Albert Pighius, controversy 3, p. 89: If you say that this should be referred to the judgment of the Scriptures, common sense proves you ignorant. For the Scriptures are mute judges. Costerus in Enchiridion, controversy 3, concerning the supreme Pontiff, p. 131: If Christ had left us Scripture alone as a judge, it would not have been sufficiently provided and consulted for the Church by this judge, because, as it is a thing without soul and sense, distracted into various and conflicting opinions, it complains of nothing. Basil in Catechism, controversy tract 1, question 8: Scripture is only a mute witness, a law and an edict, which has need of interpretation. Who has ever seen a witness be a judge?

3. From this Apostolic passage it can be gathered that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews is Paul, since no other Epistle can be named in which he wrote to those to whom Peter directed his Epistles. Philastrius in Catalog of heresies, chapter 89, recounts this assertion, that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not Paul's, among the anonymous heresies. There are, he says, some who do not assert that the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews is his, but say that it is either of Barnabas the Apostle, or of Clement, Bishop of the city of Rome. Compare Exegesis, volume 1, article on Scripture, § 275 and following.

Ἐκδίκησις. 1. The Papists strive with their utmost strength to prove the obscurity of Scripture from these words of the Apostle. Salmero on this passage p. 142. Who is there among the ancient Fathers who did not acknowledge many things in Paul to be most difficult, just as Peter also acknowledged? Where are those scoundrels who make all things clear and open in the Scriptures? when nevertheless the Apostles themselves formerly did not grasp most things said plainly and openly. Sixtus Senensis book 6 of the Bibliotheca, annotation 152. One class of Scripture contains hidden and abstruse mysteries of higher wisdom, neither accessible to all, nor necessary for all to know, such as are for the greater part the Epistles of Paul, of which Peter speaking says: In which are some things difficult. Bellarmine book 3 on the Word of God, chapter 1, §. Finally. Peter asserts that in the Epistles of Paul there are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable pervert. Where it is to be noted that the Apostle Peter did not say that there are some things difficult for the unlearned and unstable, as heretics explain, but difficult absolutely. For Blessed Augustine, who certainly was not unlearned and unstable, book on Faith and Works, chapters 15 and 16, confesses that that passage is most difficult for him to understand 1. Cor. 3. If anyone builds upon. and says that this is one of those places which Blessed Peter warned were difficult to understand. Lorinus on this passage. That the Scriptures are difficult to understand, this one testimony of Peter confirms. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage. It is clear from these words against Luther that the Scriptures are not easy and perspicuous to every idiot even. Estius on this passage. This passage is evident against the Sectarians, who teach that holy Scripture is everywhere easy and accessible to all in understanding. For this testimony of Peter is most clear, that in those things which Paul wrote, there are some things difficult to understand. At the same time indicating that it is common to the other Scriptures that unlearned men pervert them also, just as they do the writings of Paul. Although, even if Peter did not say this, the thing itself cries out that they are in most places most difficult to understand, as much concerning the Pauline Epistles as the other Scriptures. Maximilianus Sandaeus in the Secular Theme on abandoning the Protestant Synagogue p. 21, strives to prove the obscurity of Scripture from the same saying.

Resp. 1. The question between us and the Papists does not turn on whether some things in the holy Scriptures are spoken more obscurely and are more difficult to understand—for we grant that not unwillingly—but whether the dogmas of faith, the knowledge of which is necessary for all for salvation, are clearly set forth in it, if not in this, then in another place of Scripture. We say with Chrysostom, homily 3 on the 2nd Epistle to the Thessalonians, col. 1413. πάντα ἀναγκαῖα δῆλα, σαφῆ καὶ εὐθέα. Whatever is necessary, are manifest in the Scriptures. 2. Therefore, the distinction of Sixtus Senensis in book 6 of the Bibliotheca, annotation 152, is not disapproved by us. That, he says, Chrysostom says that the divine Scriptures are so clear that they can be understood by anyone, however unskilled, is to be referred not to the whole, but to the parts. For Chrysostom distinguishes the divine writings into two classes, of which one contains the hidden and abstruse mysteries of higher wisdom, neither accessible to all, nor necessary for all to know. The other section is open and lucid, comprising the first and highest principles of things to be believed and the chief precepts of living well and examples easy to know, such as moral sentences and certain sacred histories useful for forming morals. Similar things occur almost exactly in Salmeron, who comments thus on this Petrine passage, p. 142. If God had given us only expedited and easy oracles, they would not be in value: if only impeded, obscure, and perplexed, there would be no fruit of them: therefore, according to his wisdom, God so tempered the hard with the expedited, the clear with the obscure, the open with the difficult, that we might give attention to both, that through the open (note well) we might arrive at the obscure. 3. These can easily be reduced to a good sense if one adds from Augustine, book 2 de doctrina Christiana, chapter 6: Magnificently and healthfully the Holy Spirit so modified the Scriptures that he might meet hunger with the more open places, but might drive away disgust with the more obscure ones. For almost nothing is drawn from those obscurities which is not found said most clearly elsewhere. Book of the same, chapter 9: In those things which are placed openly in the Scriptures, all things are found which contain faith and the morals of living. 4. The argument which the Papists weave from this Petrine passage for asserting the obscurity of the Scriptures is narrower than the question. For it ought to have been proved, not that there are δυσνόητα, in the Scriptures, but that the whole Scripture is obscure. 5. Peter does not say that the whole and all Pauline Epistles are obscure, even in those places, and indeed in all and singular of them, in which the dogmas of faith necessary for salvation for all are handed down, but τινα he says there are only certain δυσνόητα. in them. 6. He says the same are liable to depravation because of difficulty, not however of all, but only of those who are ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι, who out of malice deprave them, just as they do the other Scriptures. 7. Bellarmine de Baptismo, chapter 22, argues thus: A place cannot be called ambiguous because heretics do not agree in explaining it: for that ambiguity does not arise from the nature of the thing, that is, from the obscurity of the book, but from their pertinacity in defending their errors. And afterwards: If all places in which some do not agree were to be called ambiguous, nothing at all could be proven from the Scriptures, for there are no passages in which one person cannot disagree with another, if he wishes to act obstinately. The same can be answered to ἔγκλημα concerning the obscurity of Scripture. 8. And all these things are said from the hypothesis that one must read ἐν αἷς, in which, namely in the Epistles of Paul, there are some things δυσνόητα.. But if the words are inspected accurately, Peter does not say that the Epistles of Paul are obscure, or that in the Epistles of Paul there are some things that are obscure, but ἐν οἷς in those matters about which the Apostle Paul wrote, he says there are some δυσνόητα,, certainly both on account of the majesty of the things and on account of the infirmity of our mind. But the obscurity or difficulty of things in themselves on account of their majesty must be distinguished from the manner of handing them down. Luther in the diatribe on the enslaved will against Erasmus: Dogmas in themselves are obscure, but insofar as they are proposed in Scripture, they are manifest, if we wish to be content with that knowledge which God has proposed to the Church in the Scriptures ibid. The things of God are obscure, the things of sacred Scripture are perspicuous. 9. Peter says that the things themselves and the doctrines are very arduous and difficult, and that many twist them badly; but he does not condemn the text or the writing of the Pauline Epistles of obscurity. 10. Some of the Papists themselves confirm this exposition. Johannes Gagnaeus annotates thus on this passage: The reading is to be ordered thus: as Paul wrote to you in all the Epistles, speaking in them of these things, namely of the coming of the Lord and his long-suffering, in which are some things difficult to understand. τό in which refers not to the Epistles, because in Greek it is ἐν οἷς, and Epistles is feminine in Greek. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage: The Greek ἐν οἷς is masculine, whence it cannot refer to the Epistles, being of the feminine gender, but to the very sayings and writings, or those things which Paul wrote, in which are many difficult things. 11. Lorinus objects: Peter here understands the difficulty which is in the things, as it is expressed by the words of Paul. But nevertheless it remains certain that the sublimity of things and the difficulty of understanding them is one thing, and the obscurity of words is another.

2. From this same passage the Papists try to evince that the laity are to be forbidden the reading of Scripture as being obscure. Bellarmine, book 2 on the word of God, chapter 15, § Fifth, etc.: If there were any reason why the Scriptures ought to be read in the vulgar tongue in the assembly of the faithful, that would certainly be the most powerful one, that all might understand. But certainly the people would not understand the Prophets and the Psalms, and other things which are read in the churches, even if they were read in the mother tongue. For we who know Latin do not therefore immediately understand the Scriptures, unless we read or hear expositors. How therefore would unskilled men understand? especially since the Scriptures are the more obscure, the more they are translated into foreign languages.

Resp. 1. Peter inscribed this Epistle of his to the whole Church, not only to Presbyters, but also to the Laity; and not only to the learned, but also to the more unrefined. 2. He wrote it with that end, that it might be read by all. 3. He also commends the Pauline Epistles to the same, with the very same end, namely that they might be read by all. 4. Therefore the corpse of the consequence is this. In the Scriptures there are certain δυσνόητα, which ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι twist, therefore the Laity are to be kept away from the reading of Scripture. 5. Nay, we invert the argument. In the Scriptures there are certain δυσνόητα. Therefore the Scriptures are to be unfolded and searched with greater zeal, so that from clear and easier passages we may penetrate to the knowledge of those more difficult ones. Men ἀμαθεῖς & ἀστήρικτοι twist the Scriptures. Therefore the Scriptures are to be unfolded with greater zeal, so that we may learn the truth of heavenly doctrine from them, and be more solidified in it, and thus be fortified against the corruptions of doctrine and Scripture. 6. Thence the Apostle, after he had said that there are in them, of which Paul wrote, certain δυσνόητα, which ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι they pervert, adds v. 17. You therefore, beloved, knowing beforehand, keep yourselves, lest being led away by the error of the unwise you fall from your own steadfastness. v. 18. But grow in the knowledge of our Lord J. C. And yet the fortification against apostasy and the means of progressing in the knowledge of Christ is the holy Scripture, just as on the contrary the cause of error and apostasy is ignorance of Scripture. Matt. 22. v. 29.Marc. 12. v. 14.Do you not therefore err, because you do not know the Scriptures? 7. The Apostle does not say, abstain from those difficult and obscure Pauline Epistles, be content with the implicit faith of mother Church, choose only certain chapters, expect new revelations, but he sends them back to the Prophetic Word, and commands them to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place 2. Epist. 1. v. 19. But what he says about the prophetic word, that is to be accepted far more about the Apostolic word, and thus also about the Pauline Epistles.

3. Estius on v. 16. annotates thus ἀμαθεῖς are unwilling to learn. Such are all heretics, for they are unwilling to hear the Church, which alone is the pillar and foundation of the truth,1. Tim. 3. v. 15.whence also they are unstable, that is, without a foundation. Hieronymus Baptista de la Nuza tract. Evang. 8. §. 48. Peter calls the unlearned heretics because they are not taught by anyone but deceived by their own Spirit; unstable, because since they cling to no firm foundation, and recede from the Church, which is the pillar and foundation of truth, they have no firmness in you.

Resp. 1. The proper and adequate rule of heavenly truth is the word of God, which is the foundation of both faith and the Church; those who do not wish to hear this word, which is recorded in the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, are ἀμαθεῖς; who do not build their faith upon this foundation, they are ἀστήρικτοι. Isa. 8. v. 20.John 5. v. 39.chap. 17. v. 17.Eph. 2. v. 19.2. Pet. 1. v. 19. 2. Thence Paul in the same place expressly premises. These things I have written, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of GOD. Therefore he does not refer Timothy absolutely to the Church, as if truth depended solely and uniquely upon it, but to the word of God, which is the unique rule of truth and the foundation of the Church itself. Irenaeus lib. 3. cap. 1. The Apostles first preached the Gospel, afterwards by the will of God they handed it down to us in the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. lib. of the same cap. 1. The pillar and firmament of the Church is the Gospel and the Spirit of life. 3. The Church is called στύλος pillar of truth, either in a political sense; insofar as the tablets of the divine law and the Gospel are hung and affixed to it as to a public pillar; or in an architectural sense, but rightly understood. This formula of speaking seems to be taken from the Jerusalem temple, which was called the house of God. That was not only adorned with peristyles, but also furnished with columns, which τό ὑπερῶον supported and kept it safe from collapse, so that the Priests could perform their duties and carry out sacred rites, and thus the heavenly truth and the worship of God could be preserved and propagated. The Church, as the spiritual house of God, still today sustains the same parts regarding the doctrine of heavenly truth revealed by Christ, and its confession, profession, and publication, so that the faithful like columns Rev. 3. v. 12. may remain stable, built upon the rockMatt. 7. v. 24. or the unique foundation, which is Christ1. Cor. 3. v. 11. But as those columns did not supply the foundation for the temple, but they themselves also rested upon the foundation: so neither does the Church supply the foundation for heavenly truth, but it itself also leans upon the foundation, namely Christ and the sacred Scripture testifying of Christ. 4. The Church is also called the ἑδραίωμα. of truth. That, however, does not primarily denote foundation or stabiliment, but properly seat, stool, repository from ἑδραίω I place, I cause to sit together, whence is ἕδρα seat, ἑδραῖως sessile, so that it may be signified that the Church is as it were a sacred seat and repository, in which the heavenly truth may be deposited. 5. We concede, therefore, that the Church, as the pillar and repository of heavenly truth, is to be heard, but only that Church which does not falsely boast of this name, but is the true Church of GOD, which is built upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles Eph. 2. v. 20. Cyprian, book 2, Epistle 3. He is not joined to the Church who is separated from the Gospel. Epiphanius, book 2, against heresies, volume 1, heresy 48, against Marcion. He who is found to be at variance with the divine Scriptures is an alien to the holy Catholic Church.

4. The same Estius comments on the same verse thus. In the Pauline Epistles there is hardly anything that men who love liberty and the desires of the flesh, such as Peter described in this and the preceding chapter, can draw to the fostering of their own desires and the defense of their own error, than what Paul teaches; that a man is not justified by the law, nor by works, but freely through faith in Jesus Christ; which the Lutherans also did in this century. Resp. 1. The true use of the doctrine of gratuitous justification by faith in Christ alone consists in this, that all the glory of justification may be left intact to the merit of Christ alone and to divine mercy; that consciences terrified by the threats of the law may have firm consolation; that the distinction between the law and the Gospel may be kept unshaken, etc. 2. The abuse of this doctrine is most wicked if men who love liberty and the desires of the flesh draw it to the fostering of their own desires and the defense of their own error, while they either understand by the name of saving faith an empty boasting of faith, destitute of the testimony of good works, or persuade themselves that faith can exist without good works, or think that the same faith can consist with sins against conscience, or think that it is permitted for them to do whatever they please at will. 3. We, however, oppose all those corruptions and abuses of this doctrine with all the zeal we can, teaching that faith alone is indeed that medium by which we apply to ourselves the benefits of Christ offered in the word of the Gospel, meanwhile that faith is not separated and disjoined from good works; and likewise that true and saving faith does not consist with sins against conscience, but is lost and driven out by them.

5. Salmero comments on this place thus, p. 141. It was fitting that the supreme Pastor of the Church should approve Paul's Epistles and teach that they are consonant with the Holy Spirit. Lorinus on this place. This canonical approval of Paul's writings can be seen to have proceeded from Him whose right it is to give it. Cornelius à Lapide on this place. From this eulogy of Peter, great authority was added to Paul and his Epistles.

It is the task of St. Peter and the supreme Pontiffs his successors to separate, approve, and define the Canonical Scriptures from the non-Canonical.

Resp. 1. That suffrage and encomium which Peter bestows upon the Pauline Epistles does not confirm his Monarchical authority, for otherwise John the Evangelist would have to be acknowledged as the Monarch of the Church, since Eusebius, Hist. Ecclesiast. book 3, ch. 21, records of him that when the writings of the three Evangelists had reached him, he approved them and gave testimony of their truth, yet he desired in these writings only a narrative of those things which were done by Christ at the beginning of his preaching; for the sake of a Monarch, Judas the Apostle would also have to be acknowledged, who in his Epistle v. 17 & 18 approves Peter's Epistles and teaches that they are consonant with the Holy Spirit. Be mindful, he says, of the words which have been spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who told you that in the last time there will come mockers walking according to their own desires. 2. Nor does the rebuke which Peter received from Paul with an equal mind Gal. 2. v. 14, the mutual agreement that Peter should evangelize primarily to the Jews and Paul to the Gentiles v. 7 & 8, and the offering of the right hand of fellowship v. 9, etc., admit a suspicion of a Monarchical primacy of Peter over the universal Church and Paul himself. 3. But this alone is elicited from that illustrious encomium of the Pauline Epistles, that both the Epistles of Paul and of Peter are θεόπνευστοι,, having proceeded from one and the same Spirit, handing down one and the same doctrine, and directed to one and the same goal.

6. The same Salmero in the said place freely loosens the reins of a slanderous tongue and pours out all the poison of bitterness upon us when, among other things, he writes thus: They are not only unlearned, even though these scoundrels sell themselves as Pauline Theologians, but also unstable, who sing and recant, and change squares into rounds. Elegant is the saying of Frederick, Duke of Saxony, who, when asked by Catholics what his Lutherans believed, replied: What they believe now, I know well; but what they are going to believe in the following year, I am entirely ignorant. Therefore they distort the Scriptures and deprave them, partly by saying according to their own will that these books are Canonical and those are not, partly by carping and tearing at the Interpreters with bitter words who translated from the Hebrew or Greek, asserting that they have erred most shamefully and have been hallucinating. Furthermore, in investigating the sense, they have provoked the ancient Fathers with injuries and insults, because they did not attain the true sense, even if by the decrees of the Church or the definitions of Councils, or the authority of the Pontiffs, or of the ancients Let them be consonant with the opinions of the Fathers. To prove which, he brings forward certain passages from Luther in the book, On the Bondage of the Will, and from Bugenhagen in his commentary on Jonah, in which they seem to speak contemptuously of the Fathers.

Resp. 1. The Confession of our Churches exists in the Symbolic books, which we embrace with unanimous suffrage, and we constantly defend the doctrine proposed in them. 2. That Luther in the progress of time condemned certain things in the Papacy which he had previously approved can no more be turned into a fault for him than it can for Augustine, because he wrote the books of Retractations. 3. But what witness does Salmero bring forward for that false witticism used by Frederick the Wise, Duke of Saxony, concerning the Lutherans? Rosinus in his Oration on the life of this Frederick records that when the Papal flatterers were always repeating and had in their mouths the Roman Church, Frederick once replied, that he did not see, nor did he find in the Creed of the faith any mention of the Roman Church, but of the holy Catholic Church. Luther recites the same in his Table Talk, chapter 45. This is certain, that although not only the Roman Pontiffs Adrian 6. and Clement 7. but also Emperor Charles 5., Henry 8. of England, and Louis, Kings of Hungary and Bohemia, George Duke of Saxony, Henry Duke of Brunswick, warned this Frederick through letters and messengers, that he should beware of Luther and his depraved dogmas, and should not provide any patronage to him: yet he was so far from obeying their warnings and casting Luther out of his borders, or handing him over as a captive to the Pontiff, that he rather cherished the same, and urged the messengers of the Pontiff to convince him of errors by divine Scripture, and bring him back to the way. 4. In assigning the distinction of the Canonical and Apocryphal books we do not follow the guidance of our own will, but the testimony of the Israelite and Christian Church near to the times of the Apostles, and especially the inherent κριτήρια proper to the Canonical books. That only the Hebrew text and the Greek in the N. Test. is authentic, and that all versions whatsoever must be judged from it, can be confirmed by invincible arguments, some of which are taken from the Canon Law itself. What of the fact that Salmero himself sometimes, having left the streams of the versions, appeals to the fountains, Disp. 4. on the Epist. to the Ephesians §. To the fourth. Disp. 16. on 1. Tim. §. After this. Disp. 6. on the Epist. of James §. Eighthly. In the commentary of this very 2. Epist. of Peter, Disp. 2. §. To the tenth etc. where he writes thus: We have not followed unlearned fables, the Latin version has. More probable it is a Greek reading, which reads σεσοφισμένους, that is, fables composed with learning and art and eloquence. 6. We do not provoke the Fathers, as they are called, that is, the most ancient Doctors of the Church, with any injuries or insults, but following the counsel of Augustine, book 2 against Cresconius, chapter 32, which is related in the Canon law itself, we do not hold their writings as Canonical, but we consider them from the Canonical, and what in them agrees with the authority of the divine scriptures, we receive with their praise; but what does not agree, we reject with their peace. 7. Nor was the opinion of Blessed Luther or D. Bugenhagius any other. The labors of the Fathers, writes Luther on chapter 2 of Genesis, p. 27, it is fitting to venerate, they were great men, but nevertheless men, who have fallen, and could have fallen, let us not exalt them, like the Monks, who thus adore all their things, as if they could not have sinned. To me, rather, great consolation seems to be placed in this, that they are found to have erred, and sometimes to have sinned. For thus I think, if God forgave them their errors and sins, why should I despair of pardon? On the contrary, it induces despair if you believe that they did not suffer the same things that you suffer. But it is certain that there is a great difference between the calling of the Apostles and the Fathers. Why therefore should we esteem the writings of the Fathers equal to the writings of the Apostles? 8. The Papists themselves do not attribute authentic authority to the Fathers, but submit their writings to the judgment of the Roman Pontiff.

Observations. 1. Peter, by this eulogy of his, testifies that the Pauline Epistles are divine and Canonical writings, while he not only asserts that Paul according to the wisdom given to him (certainly spiritual and heavenly) wrote, but also places the Pauline Epistles with the remaining Scriptures (namely, sacred, divine, and Canonical) into one class.

2. Peter, although he was the first of the Apostles, did not disdain to read the Epistles of Paul, and indeed to commend the same to the Church. He had heard Christ αὐτοφώνως, he had seen the same αὐτοπροσώπως, he had been illuminated by the gift of the Holy Spirit poured out upon him on the day of Pentecost ἐξοχικῶς, nevertheless, he deemed it not at all unworthy of the height of his Apostolic office to read the Epistles of Paul, his fellow Apostle. What shall we judge must be done by us?

3. Just as there was a most beautiful consensus in doctrine between Peter and Paul: so the faithful Ministers of the Church ought studiously to foster and preserve a pious concord among themselves. The right hand does not need the ministry of the left hand as much as the concord of the Doctors of the Church is necessary.

4. Gregory, Homily 18 on Ezekiel: Behold, Paul wrote in his Epistles that Peter was blameworthy ( Gal. 2. v. 14.), & behold, Peter in his Epistles asserts that Paul is to be admired in those things which he had written. For certainly, unless Peter had read the Epistles of Paul, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found that he himself is called blameworthy therein. Therefore, a friend of the truth praised even that for which he was blamed, and it pleased him for this very reason, because he had not been pleased in those things which he felt otherwise than he ought, and he gave himself to consent even to a lesser brother, and in the same matter he became a follower of his inferior, even so that he might lead in this, insofar as he who was first in the summit of the Apostolate, was first also in humility. Consider on what summit of mind he stood, who praised those Epistles in which he found himself written as blameworthy. Bede on this passage: Paul blames Peter in his Epistles, and yet Peter himself, reading over the same Epistles, judges them worthy of praise, because, of course, this very thing, that he found himself deservedly blamed in them, he accepted not as an injury to be spurned, but as a duty of devotion to be welcomed. Such things mortals do not know how to be toward one another, but only those who have learned from the Lord to be meek and humble of heart, who know how to anticipate one another with honor.

5. It is also gathered from this passage that, already at that time when Paul was still living, his Epistles were of great authority among all. 2. Cor. 10. v. 10. The false Apostles themselves confess concerning them that they are βαρεῖαι καὶ ἰσχυραὶ. In a certain Epistle from the number of those which are circulated under the name of Seneca to Paul, the author of it testifies, that from the Epistles of Paul collected into the form of a little book, which were circulated in the city, he had offered and read two, namely to the Galatians and to the Achaeans, to the Prince Nero, not yet infamous for tyranny, who had greatly admired such wisdom and doctrine.

6. It is to be noted that in this passage Peter praises the wisdom of Paul, but Paul himself says of himself, 1. Cor. 1. v. 9. I am the least of the Apostles, I am not worthy to be called an Apostle. Bede on this passage: Behold, Paul, mindful of his former infidelity, humbles himself and prefers the innocence of other Apostles. Behold, the first of the Apostles, as if forgetful of his own primacy and the keys of the kingdom given to him, admires the wisdom given to Paul, because, of course, it is the custom of the elect that they admire the virtues of others more than their own, through which they excite themselves to progress. Dionysius the Carthusian on this passage: Holy men do not seek or love their own praises, but the proclamations of the truth, They consider the sublime things of the virtues, the zeal for justice, the honor of GOD, the salvation of souls, and also their own reproof to be a benefit.

7. What Peter says about Paul, him according to the wisdom given to him, that must also be accepted concerning the remaining Apostles and Evangelists. Therefore, the doctrine contained in the writings of Paul and the other Apostles and Evangelists was not devised by human means, but divinely revealed through the Holy Spirit. 1. Cor. 2. v. 10. & 12.

8. It is a matter of candor and of the reverence owed to GOD to recognize the gifts of GOD in others, and to esteem highly their labors undertaken for the benefit of the Church, and to commend them to others. He who honors the gifts of GOD in others, honors GOD Himself; he who disparages the gifts of GOD in others, brings ignominy upon GOD Himself, the author of those gifts.

9. Yet we ought to honor and praise other men worthy of praise in such a way that we refer everything that is praiseworthy in them to GOD, the fountain of all gifts and goods, Gal. 1. v. 24. they were glorifying GOD in me, giving thanks to GOD, who made a defender out of a persecutor, as Ambrosiaster notes on that passage.

10. Heretics are injurious to the Holy Scriptures in many ways. First, by tearing away and truncating truly Canonical books, or certain parts of them, from the body of the Scriptures, which it is established from Tertullian was familiar to Marcion. Second, by sewing Apocryphal books onto the Canonical ones like a tattered rag onto a beautiful garment. Third, by twisting the Scriptures into a foreign and strange sense, and thus doing violence to them, and forcing their own preconceived sense upon them; concerning which matter the pious ancients complain thus. Clement of Alexandria, book 7, Stromata, p. 156, they do not use all the Scriptures, then not the perfect ones, nor as the body and context of the prophecy dictates, but choosing those things which are said ambiguously, they translate them to their own opinions, plucking a few words here and there, not considering that which is signified by them, but using the bare diction itself. Tertullian, on the resurrection of the flesh, chapter 40, Heresies could not exist if they could not also be understood wrongly, although they are refutable by the same letters. The same author teaches in the book on prescription, chapter 17, either certain Scriptures are not received by heretics, or they are inverted by additions and subtractions, or they are not received whole, or they are converted by inventing diverse expositions. Bede on this passage, Heretics deprave all the Scriptures, for there is no book of either the O. or N. Test. in which they have not only understood many things perversely, but have also often perverted the Scriptures themselves from their own state either by taking away, or by adding, or by changing, whatever their perfidy had dictated: just as it is established that the Arians erased from the Gospel what the Savior says, that GOD is Spirit, because they did not want to believe that the Holy Spirit was almighty GOD.

11. The German name Ketzer is derived either from the ancient heretics Cathari, or from קוץ which signifies a thorn, since they are compared to thorns Matth. 7. v. 16. or from קצר he tore, he rent, because they mutilate, deprave, and tear apart Scripture.

12. Cornelius à Lapide on this passage rightly annotates thus: Let preachers note this, who too licentiously twist Holy Scripture to their own concepts, willing or unwilling, that by doing so they deprave it. For those who twist it into foreign meanings, these deprave it, for the force and mind of Scripture consists not in the words, but in the sense. Furthermore, St. Gregory, book 6, Epistle 7, reproves those who at the ordination of Bishop Cyriacus had shouted for joy: This is the day which the Lord has made, because these words were spoken properly of Christ Psal. 118. But for the praise of a creature, he says, that voice ought not to have been given, which belongs to the Creator alone.

13. Just as Peter in this place, because of the corruptions of Scripture, compares heretics to torturers: so Paul compares them to gamblers Eph. 4. v. 14. Let us not be carried about by every wind of doctrine ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Κυβεία notes the craftinesses and frauds of gamblers, for it is derived from the game of dice, in which he who is able, circumvents the other.

14. Indeed, such depravation and twisting of the Scriptures is a huge sin, whence Peter says that heretics deprave the Scriptures to their own perdition, on which passage Oecumenius comments thus: Equal is the perdition of those who killed the Prophets and Apostles, and of those who corrupted their writings and discourses, and both are subject to the same judgment of GOD and condemnation and vengeance. For those killed the Prophets and Apostles, so that others might not follow their saving doctrine: but these deprave their discourses and writings, so that others, grasping their right and sincere understanding, might not be saved. The same thing can also be declared by this similitude. If a forger of a testament disposing of an earthly and vile inheritance is not undeservedly judged to sin gravely: how much more gravely do they sin, who nefariously corrupt and deprave the Testament of the eternally living God, in which the disposition concerning the inheritance of eternal salvation is contained.

15. The Apostle rightly calls heretics unlearned and unstable, because they have neither the light of knowledge, nor the stability of mind by which they might remain among the learned until they are instructed. For the only remedy for the unlearned is to offer a hearing to the words of the learned with humble stability: which grace of stability because heretics do not have, like light chaff they are carried away from the Church by the wind of pride. Bede in this place.

16. Therefore, let us take heed with the greatest zeal, lest we twist those things which are difficult to understand in the Scriptures into a foreign sense, or offer our ears to those who are twisting them, and lest we stubbornly refuse to give place to the truth shown from the word: or be unstable and inconstant in the faith.

Latin:

Connexio. Occasione eâ, quòd doctrinam de novissimo Christi ad iudicium adventu & de mundi interitu Pauli CoApostoli suffragio confirmaverat, conqueritur de indoctorum & instabilium hominum malitia, quâ difficilia quaedam loca in Epistolis Paulinis in alienum sensum detorqueant, cui scandalo eo modo occurrit, ut moneat, idem accidere reliquis V. & N. T. Scripturis, de quarum tamen autoritate atque utilitate dubitare nemini liceat.

Textus expositio. ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περὶ τούτων. Vulg. Sicut & in omnibus Epistolis loquens in eis de his. Erasmus ἐξηγήσεως causâ inservit voculam ferè, sic enim reddidit, sicut & in omnibus ferè Epistolis, argumento procul dubio motus eo, quòd non sit verisimile, Petrum omnes omninò Pauli Epistolas hic comprehendere voluisse, cùm non in omnibus de iisdem rebus, quas Petrus hoc loco tractat, agatur. Sed si vel maximè restrictio quaedam subintelligenda, illa tamen non statim textui inserenda. Ac nulla cum absurditate coniunctum, de omnibus Pauli Epistolis Petri assertionem accipere, cùm in omnibus de fide in Christum & studio bonorum operum agatur, maximè in illis, quae sunt ad integras Ecclesias scriptae.

Quidam ex praecedentibus hoc loco repetendum censent ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν, sed sufficit, si verbum ἐγραψεν sine expressa repetitione pronominis subintelligatur, cùm non omnes Pauli Epistolae Hebraeis sive conversis Iudaeis sint inscriptae. Potest etiam subintelligi προσδιορισμὸς, quòd in omnibus secundùm datam sibi sapientiam scripserit.

Λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περί τούτων. Vulg. loquens in eis de his. Per ταῦτα intelligit ea, de quibus in utraque Epistola, cumprimis verò in hoc tertio & ultimo posterioris Epistolae capite egerat, videlicet de novissimo Christi ad iudicium adventu, de consummatione seculi, de reditu Domini patienter expectando, de fugiendis ἐμπαίκταις, extremum iudicium & mundi finem protervè negantibus, de studio sanctitatis, ad quod doctrina de novissimis quemvis excitare debet. Lyranus ad h. l. de his h. e. de eisdem, de quibus scripsivobis, scil. de veritate fidei Catholicae & de praeparatione ad futurum iudicium, sicut patet in Epistolis Pauli in pluribus locis.

Ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητα τινα. Vulg. in quibus sunt quaedam difficilia intellectu. Ex hac vulgata versione intelligi nequit, an illud ἐν οἷς referendum sit ad praecedens ἐν αὐταῖς, an verò ad praecedens περὶ τούτων. Sed ex Graeco manifestum est, non ad αὐταῖς, à quo differt genere, sed ad τούτων referendum esse. Non disputat Petrus, an Apostolus Paulus perspicuè, an obscurè scripserit, sed in istis, quae ad novissimum Christi adventum, extremum iudicium & consummationem seculi spectant, quae tùm à se, tùm à Paulo de adventu Domini & de iis, quae circa adventum Domini futura sunt, scripta erant, quaedam dicit esse δυσνόηταintellectu difficilia, quae non ita facilè à quibusvis possint comprehendi. Agnoscunt hoc quidam ex ipsis Pontificiis Interpretibus. Salmeron. ad h. l. sic commentatur. ἐν οἷςrefertur ad verbumπερὶ τούτωνde iis. (Subiungit quidem, non tamen aberrabis, quibus Epistolis, quta genus neutrum complectitur in se masculinum & femininum. Sed si de Epistolis Paulinis Petrus loqueretur, omninò dixisset, ἐν αἷς. unde) Lorinus ad hunc l. sic annotat. Non refertur illud, in quibus, ad Epistolas, sed ad ea, de quibus tractatur in Epistolis, nam Graecum pronomenοἷςnon est feminini generis, cuius est nomenἐπιστολῶν. Estius dubius est, sic enim ad h. l. annotat. In quibus. Alii tollendae ambiguitatis causâ vertunt, inter quae. Nam Graecè estἐν οἷς,quod non potest ad Epistolas referri, quarum ut Latinis, ita & Graecis genus est femininum, sed referendum ad ea, quae Epistolis continentur, q. d. in quibus ab eo scriptis sunt quaedam difficilia, subiungit enim sicut & caeteras Scripturas. Quidam volunt,ἐν οἷςpositum proἐν αἷςaut certè Scribarum incuriâ irrepsisse opro a. Nam & à Roberto tres Codices annotantur, in quibus scriptum fueritἐν αἷς.Quae si vera est lectio, quod tamen non facilè affirmaverim, facilior est commentarius. Sed quid de his posterioribus Estii verbis statuendum sit, postea videbimus.

Δυσνόητα Syrus reddidit, [דעסיק לסוכלא]quae sunt dura & difficilia ad intelligendum.

Ἅ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπάς γραφάς πρός τὴν ἰδίαν αὐτῶν ἀπώλειαν. Vulg. quae indocti & instabiles depravant, sicut & caeteras Scripturas, ad suam ipsorum perditionem.
